#6412. Democrats flip the Senate with stunning victories in deep-red terrain

South Carolina Democratic Senate nominee Annie Andrews delivers her victory speech at her election night party in Charleston on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

Democrats won control of the Senate on Tuesday, sending shock waves through Washington on a historic night that saw them flip seats in deep-red states such as Texas, South Carolina and Kansas.

Hours after The Associated Press called the Senate for Democrats, the party was projected to flip the House as well. As of 1:50 a.m. Wednesday, Senate Democrats had wrested seven seats from Republicans — a stunning result that gives the party new powers to confront President Donald Trump in his final two years in office.

Winning the Senate was considered an unlikely prospect for Democrats at the beginning of the year, given the number of red states they needed to compete in. But strong candidate recruitment and a favorable political environment put the chamber within Democrats' grasp.

With their majority, Democrats are expected to serve as a significant check on Trump, who could now have a more difficult time advancing his nominees through the chamber.

“Against all odds, we Democrats have won the Senate, and we have five words for the American people: Relief is on the way,” Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer said Thursday night in Washington.

“The American people reduced the red brick wall to a pile of bricks,” the New York Democrat added. “As a result, there is now a generational remake of the Senate map that is going to change America now and on into the future.”

The Democratic path to the majority ran through several deep-red states that have proved hostile to the party in recent years and that Trump carried by double digits in 2024.

In Texas, state Rep. James Talarico defeated scandal-plagued Republican state Attorney General Ken Paxton, becoming the first Democrat to win a Senate election in the Lone Star State since 1988. Paxton had defeated Republican incumbent John Cornyn in a primary runoff earlier this year.

In perhaps the biggest shocker of the night, South Carolina Democrat Annie Andrews defeated appointed Sen. Darline Graham, a shocking flip in a state that last elected a Democratic senator in 1998. Graham was appointed to the Senate in July after the death of her brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, and ran for the full term with Trump’s strong endorsement.

And the longest Senate drought in the country ended Tuesday when Democrat Adam Hamilton, pastor of the nation’s largest United Methodist church, unseated Republican Sen. Roger Marshall in Kansas, a state that had not elected a Democrat to the Senate in 94 years.

Other flips came in onetime battleground states that had turned decidedly red in recent cycles. In Ohio, Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown defeated Sen. Jon Husted, who was appointed to the Senate to complete the unfinished term of Vice President JD Vance. And in Iowa, Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek defeated Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson to succeed retiring GOP Sen. Joni Ernst.

In blue-leaning Maine, a 30-year Senate career came to a close with Republican Sen. Susan Collins losing her bid for a sixth term to Democratic former state Senate President Troy Jackson.

The night began strongly for the party, with key holds in Georgia, where Sen. Jon Ossoff easily dispatched GOP Rep. Mike Collins, and New Hampshire, where Rep. Chris Pappas defeated a comeback bid by former Sen. John E. Sununu.

Former North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper also gave Democrats their first flip of the night, defeating Republican Michael Whatley, the former Republican National Committee chairman.

Democrats also held the open seat in Minnesota, with Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan prevailing over former NFL sideline reporter Michele Tafoya.

A Democratic majority in the Senate could run into a president who has said he would become “Mr. Veto” against any legislation coming out of chambers controlled by the opposition party.

With Trump in that position, Democrats will likely push “for legislation that may set the agenda for the future in case a Democrat’s elected in 2028,” according to Christian Grose, a professor of political science and public policy at the University of Southern California.

But in a Tuesday night interview with CBS News, Trump also said, “My message is, congratulations to the Democrats, and I look forward to working with you for the good of our country.”

With control of the Senate, Democrats are also poised to block Trump’s nominees, escalating the opposition they mounted while in the minority during his first two years back in office.

“Very few of them are going to get through,” Schumer told Semafor in October. “It’s the quality of the candidate that matters. Thus far, Trump has a record of notoriously bad candidates.”

Those nominees would likely extend from the Cabinet to the judicial branch, potentially even hindering confirmation of a Supreme Court pick in case of a vacancy.

Schumer told reporters ahead of the October recess: “The bottom line is, one of the reasons we want to do everything we can to take back the Senate is not let Trump put such horrible justices — MAGA justices — on the Supreme Court and the lower courts.”

Other Democrats have agreed with that sentiment and pointed to 2016, when Mitch McConnell led the Senate and blocked the confirmation of President Barack Obama’s Supreme Court nominee Merrick Garland. That left the seat open for more than a year, with Trump eventually filling the spot with Neil Gorsuch.

As Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., told reporters recently: “We’ve got to do exactly what McConnell did to us.”

Senate Democrats will also gain subpoena power, bolstering their ability to investigate Trump and his administration. Those investigations could include his handling of the conflict in Iran, his family’s business ties and wealth gains while in office, or his ties to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

“We have a real duty to investigate all of this just absolutely blatant corruption that’s so dangerous to our national security,” Senate Judiciary member Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut said in September, shortly after reporting emerged about wedding after-party celebrations for Trump’s eldest son, which were financed by a Russian businessman with ties to the Kremlin.

While Democrats in Congress could in theory pursue a third impeachment against the president, the appetite to seal the deal in the Senate would likely fall short, given they would need 67 votes to convict.

John T. Bennett contributed to this report.

#6411. The 7 Best Noise-Canceling Headphones Clear Out the World So You Can Listen to What You Love

These cans and earbuds knock out background noise so you can focus or relax.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Noise-canceling headphones were once a niche category, dominated by high-priced over-ear cans. Throughout most of the 2010s, those seeking to drown out ambient noise distractions at work or during travel had to spend upward of $300 to get a pair up to the task. These days, that's no longer the case. The market is jam-packed with quality noise-canceling headphones, including reliable models that start below $100. Having so many options to choose from can rightfully be overwhelming even for tech-savvy shoppers. To help you find the best noise-canceling headphones worth investing in, I spent months testing highly rated options from leading brands and created this buying guide to share my recommendations.

Read more related reviews in our best wireless headphones and best wireless earbuds buying guides.

I’ve been testing consumer tech products, including audio gear, since 2011. Before I began testing, I spent a day sifting through product specs and features to handpick up-to-date products from reputable makers across the price spectrum—from budget to premium.

My testing routine included spending at least a week with each headset on this list. I used it at work, during my daily commutes, and, of course, while traveling domestically and internationally. These scenarios allowed me to properly evaluate the products’ design and ergonomics.

To evaluate the audio performance of the headphones, I streamed a carefully curated Apple Music playlist with tracks in various genres, including live albums. The eclectic music selection helped me experience the ability of the headphones to produce bass, treble, and midrange. I also used the cans to stream podcasts, watch video content, and play video games.

Traveling by plane and working in a large open office gave me perfect scenarios to test the noise-canceling capabilities of all headphones. I paid close attention to how each set performed in this critical area, keeping in mind its form factor and price tag.

Ambient mode for being aware of your surroundings is just as essential and a key component of my testing routine. I also made sure that the headphones performed well during telephone, FaceTime, Microsoft Teams, and Zoom calls.

Regarding battery life, I meticulously observed how frequently I had to charge each headset. Spending days without battery anxiety was a benchmark for excellence in this department.

Lastly, where available, I tinkered with the companion app of every pair of headphones. I looked for tools to customize sound and additional features that help enhance the overall experience.

With all of the above tips in mind, enjoy a more peaceful daily and travel routine by switching to one of the products I vouch for below.

Bose QuietComfort headphones (and earbuds) have been synonymous with best-in-class noise cancellation for years. It stands to reason, then, that the Ultra cans top this product category.

The Bose QuietComfort Ultra 2 headphones, which launched in late 2025, offer up to 30 hours of battery life and superior wired playback. The headphones’ ability to tune out ambient noise distractions by generating almost complete silence is commendable and alone worth splurging on. What’s more, their companion app lets you customize its intensity and save the setting for easy access in a specific scenario. Such a level of modularity sets the product apart from its rivals, just as the core feature’s performance does.

On the audio front, the Bose QuietComfort Ultra headphones deliver a balanced sound that’s customizable via an app. Dubbed Bose Immersive Audio, the cans’ ability to deliver multidimensional spatial sound with optional head tracking is superb and, crucially, easy to access. I like that the feature works with any audio content rather than requiring Dolby Atmos-enhanced audio. I successfully used it to make live music albums and videos more lifelike during my testing.

The 24-hour battery life of the QuietComfort Ultra headphones leaves a little to be desired, as competitors, including those in lower price tiers, can last longer between charges.

With an under-$100 sticker before additional and frequent discounts, the SonoFlow Pro HQ51 noise-canceling headphones by 1More are a legit impulse buy for such a product without skimping on design, ergonomics, performance, and battery life. The cans are surprisingly sleek and comfy, capable of delivering a high-quality audio experience across the board, as well as long battery life.

The sound quality of the headphones thoroughly exceeded my expectations when I put them through their paces. Tuned by a master audio engineer, the cans treated me to a balanced sound that made me feel like I was using a much pricier set. The tools for customizing the sound via their companion app are just as impressive.

When it comes to noise cancellation, the SonoFlow Pro HQ51 is among the best for the money. The headphones did a solid job in tuning out distractions, but couldn’t match the serenity of costlier cans. That’s totally fine considering their agreeable price.

With up to a staggering 65 hours of battery life with noise cancellation, the SonoFlow Pro HQ51 leaves rivals that cost several times more in the dust. I could easily spend a week using them without battery anxiety. And believe it or not, you can get up to 100 hours of wireless playback from the 1More headphones by disabling the core functionality.

The Beats Studio Pro headphones are a must-have for owners of multiple Apple devices. Just like AirPods (and other Beats products), the cans will instantly connect to Apple devices that are linked to the same iCloud account. Once I paired them with my iPhone, I could instantly use the cans with an iPad, a MacBook, and a Mac mini, as well as keep tabs on their whereabouts in the Apple Find My app.

In addition to the seamless hardware compatibility mentioned above, the Beats Studio Pro headphones deserve the attention of Apple users for their ability to deliver a superb spatial audio experience. Accessing the functionality on an iPhone or an iPad is as easy as long-pressing the volume control button in the command center.

The Studio Pro headphones’ audio quality and noise cancellation are among the best in their price category. Their sound is balanced, melodic, and versatile, making it suitable for a wide range of music styles. There is no option to customize it via an app, but I didn’t feel like I had to make any changes while using the cans.

Unlike many competitors, the Beats Studio Pro headphones can deliver lossless audio over a direct USB-C link to phone, tablet, or computer. Listening in higher fidelity doesn’t include noise cancellation. Thankfully, I could access the latter via the standard audio jack when I needed to use the entertainment system during a flight.

The Beats headphones integrate well with Android and Chrome OS hardware, too, but I prefer the Apple experience for its superior spatial audio and because I don't need to install a companion app. Consider the recently released AirPods Max 2 over the Beats Studio Pro if you have a bigger budget for Apple-ready headphones. Their audio performance, craftsmanship, and controls are on a much higher level. However, you’ll have to settle for a heavier headset with shorter battery life and spend extra on a suitable protective case and a cable with a standard audio connector.

On-ear headphones have largely taken a back seat to larger over-ear ANC headphones, which offer more passive noise cancellation, and earbuds for their pocketable form factor. Marshall’s Milton ANC headphones offer a now-rare premium on-ear design that gives you the best version of a middle ground between the two, with a lightweight design, great sound quality, and a less ostentatious on-ear fit. With a foldable design and scratch-resistant ear cup covers, the Milton wears really well over the course of a long day on the go.

On the audio front, the Marshall Milton ANC impressed me with crisp, energetic sound that's customizable via a companion app. Its noise cancellation is also stellar, though does not generate the same auditory void as my top over-ear picks.

The headphones’ knob and customizable button controls are a benchmark for excellence and miles ahead of their competitors. The same goes for its 50-hour battery life. (Or 80 hours if you turn the ANC off.)

On-ear headphones are especially niche if ANC is your top priority, but it’s a great everyday carry headphone if your earbuds just aren’t cutting it. If you dig Marshall’s look, but would prefer an over-ear solution, the Monitor III ANC has a similar design and controls, but with a heavier, more deeply isolating form factor.

Reviewed: Marshall Milton ANC Wireless Headphones

The Bowers & Wilkins PX8 S2 wireless headphones are, hands down, my favorite wireless ANC headphones for discerning audiophiles looking for something more detailed than the standard options from Sony, Bose, and Apple.

Like the legendary British audio maker’s (very) expensive floor speakers, these over-ear cans produce pristine, infinitely customizable stereo sound that faithfully generates every detail of whatever you’re listening to.

At a time when wireless headphones generally try to earn attention with digital enhancements like spatial audio, the PX8 S2 impressed me with Their old-school approach to audio fidelity. (Note: B&W has added spatial audio since my review via a firmware update.) Experiencing the headphones’ sound with noise cancellation enabled is like listening to Bowers & Wilkins speakers in your own private space.

For $800, you know every aspect of these headphones has to work incredibly well, and they do. Its craftsmanship and tactility, headlined by genuine leather and metal accents in several colors, are a marvel for folks with extremely discerning taste... And plenty of disposable income.

The Skullcandy Crusher ANC 2 headphones are all about delivering incredibly powerful bass that’s available and adjustable via a dedicated button on the left cup. The sensory experience is truly remarkable and unlike anything rivals can offer, even though it predictably impacts the overall audio fidelity. The headphones’ noise cancellation is solid, if not on par with pricier sets from leading makers.

I didn’t reach for the Crusher ANC 2 when I felt like streaming classical jazz, but I grinned every time I played my favorite downtempo tracks on the product. Using the cans for playing action-packed games with the bass cranked up was also a ton of fun.

Disabling the thunderous low-end brought me a more “grown-up” sound, customizable via an app. That’s not what I’d recommend the product for, however. This Skullcandy Crusher ANC 2 is all about celebrating bass.

The Crusher ANC 2 is also comfy to wear and equipped with convenient button controls. I also like the headphones’ integrated Tile tracker, as well as their sleek design with a contrasting, brightly colored button for activating the Crusher experience. There are tons of color options.

Skullcandy’s Icon ANC wireless headphones are handily the best for exercising on this list. The surprisingly affordable cans have a compact on-ear design, a secure fit, and an IPX4 rating for sweat- and water resistance. These qualities, together with convenient button controls, make the Icon ANC equally suitable for indoor and outdoor workouts.

The default sound of the headphones has an enhanced bass, which helped me stay motivated during my workouts. The Skullcandy app has several presets for customizing the sound, as well as a graphic equalizer to create your own. The noise cancellation worked, but it didn’t stop me in my tracks with its efficiency. That’s hardly a surprise considering the product’s price category.

I found the Skullcandy Icon ANC’s multidirectional control knob to be incredibly convenient during my testing. Their 50-hour battery life with noise cancellation exceeded my expectations, too. I didn’t expect this longevity from a compact pair of wireless headphones.

Skullcandy offers the Icon ANC in several colors. Every set comes bundled with a soft carrying pouch.

Noise cancellation relies on built-in microphones that continuously monitor your surroundings. A dedicated chip processes the sound captured by the microphones before sending its exact aural opposite to your ears via the headphones' audio drivers. This sophisticated technology naturally contributes to the cost of noise-canceling headphones. Translation? The more you spend, the better you'll isolate yourself from your surroundings. Prepare to drop north of $300 if you are looking to achieve (almost) complete silence from your purchase.

High-quality sound is also a must for a great pair of noise-canceling headphones. Support for immersive spatial audio is particularly important for top-shelf headphones. It makes live albums and video content more immersive and the listening experience more lifelike, especially if dynamic head tracking is available. Spatial audio is available on most top-shelf noise-canceling headphones. High-end sets without this functionality make up for it by producing pristine stereo sound, which makes them worth investing in. Speaking of stereo sound, today's best headphones in this space, including budget-friendly models, support lossless audio over wireless and wired connections. If you are using a streaming service that offers lossless audio, keep an eye out for this feature. It will serve you well.

Your next set of headphones should get you at least 20 to 30 hours of wireless playback between power-ups with noise cancellation. That’s the bare minimum for these products, with class-leading sets by Apple, Bose, and Sony delivering battery endurance in this ballpark. That’s enough to get you through a long flight or hectic workday in silence.Remarkably, cheaper cans now have much longer battery life. Some will give you double the endurance of the class-leading options with noise cancellation and a three-digit number of hours without it. Those numbers are remarkable, but trust me, stronger noise cancellation and higher-quality sound are worth the more frequent charging sessions.

A companion app for customizing the sound and the noise cancellation, among other things, is essential for any set of wireless headphones or earbuds today, so look for it while shopping. Apple AirPods and Beats products don’t have an iPhone app. Their settings are easily accessible directly in iOS, iPadOS, and macOS.

Stefan is an award-winning consumer technology editor with over a decade of experience in reviewing gadgets, particularly smartphones, tablets, smartwatches, desktop and laptop computers across multiple form factors and platforms, as well as accessories for them. He also covers televisions and audio equipment, including headphones, earbuds, wireless speakers, and soundbars. Since joining Hearst in 2015, Stefan has contributed to BestProducts, Popular Mechanics, and numerous other publications. Prior to his current role, he served as the US Editor for GSMArena.com.

Scientists on China's Tiangong space station used a laser trap to cool a clump of atoms to just above absolute zero, setting a new record.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Scientists have cooled atoms to the coldest temperature ever recorded, using a laser trap aboard China's Tiangong space station.

Tiangong included an experiment in which atoms were cooled to 10 picokelvins, which is barely above absolute zero, the coldest theoretical temperature possible in physics. Absolute zero is minus 459.67 degrees Fahrenheit (minus 273.15 degrees Celsius) and the threshold at which all particles in an object are believed to stop moving.

Scientists hit the mark using "optical tweezers," known more formally as an optical-dipole trap (ODT), which hold atoms in a laser beam," the scientists reported Nov. 5 in the journal Science.

The team placed 20,000 rubidium atoms in the trap in order to restrict their motion. This reduced motion, along with the weightlessness induced by the low-gravity environment aboard the space station, caused the cloud of atoms to cool to much lower temperatures than are possible on Earth.

The experiment's results could help improve future space-based research, the team said.

"This record-low temperature could stimulate a new generation of ODT-based experiments in quantum simulation and precision measurements in space," the researchers wrote in the paper.

Despite this achievement, it's doubtful that scientists could ever hit absolute zero. One interpretation of the third law of thermodynamics, which looks at how systems behave when they approach absolute zero, is that the particles would always have a bit of entropy (disorder) associated with them, making absolute zero unachievable.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"One version of the third law states that it would require an infinite number of steps to reach absolute zero, which means you will never get there," Saibal Mitra, a professor of physics at Missouri State University, told Live Science in a 2024 interview.

The second law of thermodynamics, which states that entropy always increases, would also be violated if scientists could reach absolute zero, he added. "If you had a heat sink at absolute zero, then you could build a machine that was 100% efficient," Mitra said.

That said, space makes it easier to get close to absolute zero because microgravity allows atoms to "float" and become more efficient at cooling, Science News reported. The researchers took their weightless collection of atoms and created a quantum state of matter known as a Bose-Einstein condensate, in which very cold atoms clump and create a "fifth state" of matter as they behave akin to a single atom.

Tiangong's very cold clump follows similar experiments on the International Space Station that reached 52 picokelvins and from a weightless fall induced by a drop from a tall tower, in which atoms hit 38 picokelvins, Science News added.

Xiong, W., Li, T., Jin, S., Huang, Q., Wang, B., Li, L., He, Y., Li, X., Chen, D., Song, T., Ji, J., Zhou, C., Lai, C., Zhang, Z., Tian, J., Guo, Y., Yao, H., Hou, X., Liu, L., . . . Chen, X. (2026). Quantum gases below 10 picokelvin in space. Science, eaea5324. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aea5324

#6407. Trump made midterms about himself, and voters rejected him

President Donald Trump dances to "YMCA" after speaking to a Republican midterms convention at the American Airlines Center in Dallas on Sept. 9. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

President Donald Trump consistently told voters this midterm campaign to pretend he was on the ballot.

Voters responded by making election night a disaster for the Republican Party the president has spent a decade remaking in his own image. Trump spent his first two years back in the White House focused almost exclusively on his “Make America Great Again” base.

One GOP strategist, granted anonymity to be candid, called the election results for Trump a “2006-style massacre,” referring to President George W. Bush’s second midterms when Democrats picked up a combined 37 House and Senate seats amid frustrations with the Iraq war, the economy and other issues at home.

“This is much bigger than a couple of candidates here and there. … The issues were Americans prefer cheap gas and not the Iran conflict, and [Trump’s] tariffs were … an issue given grocery prices,” the GOP strategist said in a text message as midnight approached Tuesday in Washington, D.C. “What’s going on in Texas … could be the shot heard around the world.”

That was a reference to Texas going blue on Trump’s watch, his handpicked GOP Senate nominee, state Attorney General Ken Paxton, losing his race to Democratic state Rep. James Talarico, and Trump-backed GOP Gov. Greg Abbott losing to Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa. Trump blamed Abbott, whom he had long praised, in a late-night post, calling the three-term governor a “RINO,” or Republican in name only.

For 21 months, multiple public opinion polls charted the independent voters who pushed him to a second nonconsecutive term in 2024 steadily leaving his coalition. Many of the same polls showed an electorate fed up with the high prices of groceries, health care, travel and other everyday items.

Even as voters already were casting votes Tuesday, Trump continued to dismiss the country’s “affordability” crisis, which he for months dismissed as a Democratic-manufactured lie. The president who long sold himself as the one true messenger of the forgotten American man and woman dismissed voter concerns as a “hoax.”

Down went Senate candidates he rallied for in the homestretch of the campaign, including Sen. Darline Graham in South Carolina, Kansas Sen. Roger Marshall, GOP nominees Ashley Hinson in Iowa and Michael Whatley in North Carolina, and Paxton in Texas.

Several media outlets called Democrats winning control of the House before or just after 10 p.m. Eastern time. In South Carolina, Trump backed Graham over veteran GOP Rep. Ralph Norman, and in Texas, he put his grudge against longtime Sen. John Cornyn — who didn’t endorse him to be the GOP presidential nominee in 2024 — over Paxton’s baggage.

Former GOP Rep. Charlie Dent said “the president's support among Republicans has been slightly diminished leading up to this point, and I suspect it will become more diminished after the election.”

“Over the next two years, many Republicans will be looking forward, not backward, and I think that the president will be less of a factor in the party. He’ll still be a factor, don’t get me wrong, but I think less of one,” Dent said in a telephone interview. “The [2028] presidential nominee, whoever that is, will be the one who will be trying to determine the future of the party.”

An ever-defiant Trump took to social media Tuesday night as the results rolled in and blamed GOP candidates, writing: “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE! Thank you for your attention to this matter.” Except, he had pleaded with voters for a month to “pretend” he was on the ballot.

One White House official tried to deflect blame away from the boss, writing in an email that “candidate quality matters, and President Trump did a better job promoting many of the candidates on the ballot than the candidates did themselves.”

But Marc Short, who worked in the Trump 1.0 White House, on Tuesday night said the blame fell squarely on 1600 Pennsylvania Ave. “It’s hard to think of a WH that’s sabotaged House and Senate candidates more than this one,” he wrote on X.

Leading up to election night, however, Trump was dug in on defending his second term’s record.

“The inflation is solved. … I mean, everything’s going good,” Trump said Tuesday morning on “Fox & Friends” on Fox News Channel, calling his unpopular tariffs “tremendous.”

“I mean, we have a thing going that nobody has ever seen before, and that includes China and other countries, and they will let you know,” he said.

Trump’s campaign-trail economic message was further complicated by his decision to join Israel in striking Iran. The conflict, which started Feb. 28, defied his pledge of no new prolonged military conflicts, which had been a hallmark of his foreign policy for a decade.

Even as polls showed majorities of Americans placing high gas and diesel prices atop their lists of most-concerning issues, Trump for months shrugged them off, predicting oil prices would plummet, eventually.

“The onus and the blame is going to be right on the president of the United States, which of course he is going to resist,” Dent said. “At his rallies, there were these never-ending comments on things that were just really not connected to what most voters care about, which was inflation and the cost of everything and how challenging their lives are, from a financial standpoint. And the president just didn’t focus on those issues and talked about all these other things that, frankly, were irrelevant.”

Trump would not allow his party’s candidates to put distance between their campaigns and his unpopular second term.

As some House and Senate GOP candidates attempted to run on messages that downplayed Trump, he announced the first-ever Republican midterms convention in Dallas. The primetime spectacle spanned two nights, with Trump as the headlining act on Sept. 9 and Sept. 10 at the American Airlines Center.

During his lengthy appearance on the opening night, Trump got pushback from even some Republican lawmakers when he pledged he would send every U.S. citizen $5,000 — but only if his party retained control of the House and Senate.

On night two, Trump’s loyalists in the large arena — home to the NBA’s Dallas Mavericks — agreed to his demand that they raise their right hands and declare allegiance to him.

The convention made clear Trump would not ease his grip on the GOP.

Then came his October campaign rally blitz, with the president continuing to dismiss voters' economic worries and issue cryptic threats about the accuracy of American elections and what he called Democrats' collective intention to “cheat.”

By the end of his midterm rally sprint, Trump increasingly went for laugh lines, a striking contrast to his fire-and-brimstone events in 2016. Audiences of his supporters from Gastonia, N.C., to Corpus Christi, Texas, to Dalton, Ga., to Salina, Kan., to Wasilla, Alaska, chuckled along at times.

His closing-argument event Monday at the Reflecting Pool that sits between the Lincoln Memorial and the World War II memorial on the National Mall offered another example of Trump’s predilection for talking about matters relatively unimportant to voters. He talked about pool liners, his White House ballroom and other non-election issues.

By late Tuesday night, Trump appeared to have moved on, telling The New York Times he would accept the outcomes of the election results.

In other media interviews, the GOP president said he was ready to meet congressional Democrats at the negotiating table but that he had his veto pen ready.

“We’re going to work with the Democrats to make sure things go well for our country,” he said on a Politico livestream Tuesday. “They've already called and they want to work with me.”

Niels Lesniewski contributed to this report.

Over 300 Live Science readers responded to a recent poll about whether they'd train themselves to lucid dream if they could.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Lucid dreaming describes when you realize you're in a dream as it's unfolding. Sometimes, people can control the content of their dreams from this state of awareness.

Recently, researchers claimed that they found a way to "train" people to lucid dream by having them meditate and complete virtual-reality-augmented exercises while they were awake. Following the release of that study, Live Science asked its readers whether they would learn to lucid dream if they could.

Over 300 readers weighed in, with 77% saying "Yes, I'd want to try to control my dreams." Additionally, 17% of respondents said "No, I already lucid dream enough without training," 3% said "No, I don't see the point," and the final 3% said they weren't sure.

In the comments, one reader shared that they'd once experimented with hypnagogic napping, a technique famously used by Thomas Edison and Salvador Dalí in which the famous luminaries would wake themselves up just as they were drifting to sleep. Edison claimed that this helped him access a creative sweet spot at the edge of sleep and wakefulness.

"When I was experimenting with the hypnagogic state (using the Edison method) I started having spontaneous lucid dreams," the reader wrote. "I can confidently say, that there were some of the most profound experiences of my life, so the answer is definitely yes."

Another reader reported having lucid dreams "about once or twice a year," adding that they typically wake up shortly after realizing it's a dream. "My most recent one was of my recently deceased wife. I became very sad when I realized she wasn't supposed to be there," the reader wrote. "I hugged her and told her I don't want to be without her. She replied that I could live a long life if I took care of myself (This was a very typical response from her...lol). I feel very blessed to have had that dream."

Other readers chimed in on Facebook. "Already have it [lucid dreaming], but if I didn't I would certainly practice to do so," one wrote. "Hell yes," another said, in response to the idea of training themselves to lucid dream.

Other readers noted that they already lucid dream quite often or that they can consistently control their dreams, with one even saying that all of their dreams are lucid. Another said, "Some nights I interrupt it [my dream] like Monty Python — 'Too silly!' and start over."

But while one person compared lucid dreaming to "writing and directing your own movie," another noted that "lucid dreams can be boring, repetitive, annoying." So while many people would practice lucid dreaming if they could, not everyone sees the appeal.

Nicoletta Lanese is the health channel editor at Live Science and was previously a news editor and staff writer at the site. She is a recipient of the 2026 AHCJ International Health Study Fellowship, with a project focused on antibiotic stewardship practices in Japan and the U.S. They hold a graduate certificate in science communication from UC Santa Cruz and degrees in neuroscience and dance from the University of Florida. Beyond Live Science, Lanese's work has appeared in The Scientist, Science News, the Mercury News, Mongabay and Stanford Medicine Magazine, among other outlets. Based in NYC, she also remains involved in dance and performs in local choreographers' work.

#6403. Can DC’s new delegate get Congress to care about statehood?

Robert White greets supporters during a Monday news conference. He resigned from his D.C. Council seat ahead of Tuesday’s delegate election. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

When Robert White gets sworn into Congress on Jan. 3, he’ll have one thing on his mind: convincing the rest of his party that D.C. statehood belongs on the priority list.

As Democrats look forward to life in the majority, they’ve got big plans as they try to deliver on their affordability campaign promises and conduct oversight of the Trump administration. White, a 44-year-old former councilmember who was born and raised in the District, has his pitch ready.

“The agenda gets done if you have the votes — and D.C. statehood gives you more votes,” he said.

His election marks a new chapter for the District’s nonvoting delegate. As Eleanor Holmes Norton retires after more than three decades, he’ll be just the third person to hold the seat in modern times. It also comes as President Donald Trump has tried to exert more control over local affairs in the nation’s capital.

White has the delicate task of paying homage to the legacy of his former boss (he once worked as her legislative counsel) while also putting some distance between them. Norton was known as a fierce advocate for the District but lately appeared to struggle through prepared remarks as her influence diminished. Earlier in her time in Congress, she pushed through both concrete and symbolic incremental wins, such as securing delegates the right to vote in what’s known as the committee of the whole.

He said Norton “built powerfully” on the work of Walter Fauntroy, who served as delegate from 1971 to 1991. “And my job is to build on top of what Norton built.”

At a Monday event, White’s father, Robert White Sr., wore a shirt with a slogan to that effect: “FAUNTROY & NORTON & WHITE.”

A crowd was assembled outside the John A. Wilson Building that night to mark White’s departure from the D.C. Council, after a last-minute uproar over a provision in the 1970 law establishing D.C.’s delegate position. Although he had hoped to serve on the council until January, the law states a delegate must hold “no other paid public office” on the date of his election, and White ultimately decided to resign before Election Day. As he stepped up to the podium, someone shouted a rallying cry that has only grown louder after Trump deployed National Guard troops to patrol the streets last year: “Free D.C.”

White won’t be the only freshman member next Congress who can’t cast a vote on the House floor — Alicia Limtiaco is another newcomer, after beating incumbent Del. James Moylan in Guam.

One way White thinks he can further his cause is by boosting his own name recognition.

“I need to make sure I’m developing a national profile for this seat,” he said. “I’ve got to hire the right comms director with the experience to help me get it done. I’m going to use the proximity of my seat here in D.C., making sure that all the national outlets know that when other members go back to their district, I’m still here and available to do interviews. Everything that we can do, including building relationships in other media markets, including through my leadership PAC, we’re going to be doing.”

He plans to start making his case before the new Congress even begins.

“I’m already starting to put together materials for all incoming members, and talking to leadership to see if I can carve out a piece of new member orientation to talk about D.C. both being a resource to members while they’re here, but also D.C. statehood,” he said.

He knows that even in his own party, standing up for D.C. can be a tough sell. A number of moderate Democrats have voted with Republicans on bills seeking to undermine D.C.’s autonomy and roll back local criminal justice laws over the last few years.

“We have seen D.C. used as a bargaining chip by the party,” he said. “The Democratic Party has not consistently been a firewall for D.C.”

Party consensus on D.C. statehood has evolved over time, but it hasn’t always been a unifying issue. In 1993, 105 House Democrats joined 172 Republicans in voting against a bill from Norton that would have paved the way for statehood and for the addition of two senators and a representative in Congress. When the House voted on statehood bills again in 2020 and 2021, it passed with near-unanimous Democratic support but stalled in the Senate.

Asked how he would respond to Democratic peers in Congress who might say they support D.C. statehood but need to focus first on issues like affordability that more directly affect their constituents, White countered with a question of his own.

“How’s that been going without the two senators from the District of Columbia?” he said.

He sees parallels with Republicans using redistricting to gain seats in Congress.

“People need to say to their constituents, ‘Look, not only are we doing what is right under democracy, but we are helping get the votes for our agenda.’ That is what the Republicans tried to do with redistricting. So, if you think you’re going to keep playing around the margins and start winning when that hasn’t worked, we’re fooling ourselves,” he said.

The way White sees it, appeals to the principles of democracy still ring true when arguing for full representation for the District’s some 700,000 residents. But pragmatic arguments matter, too.

“When they see D.C. statehood as their ticket to securing reproductive rights, their ticket to being able to afford health health care, then they start to see D.C statehood in a different light — and that is the light that I want to make sure I’m putting on this issue now,” he said.

A new AI model, called Brain-IT, can transform brain scans into images and reverse the process, turning images into what they'd look like as brain activity.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

An artificial intelligence (AI) tool can use brain scans to recreate the images people looked at with eerie accuracy.

The system, called Brain-IT, uses data from functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to measure activity in the visual cortex, the part of the brain that processes visual input. A computer model then predicts both the broad layout of an image and high-level information about its content. It then passes those predictions to an AI image generator, researchers explained in a study uploaded to the preprint database arXiv. The research was presented at the ICLR 2026 conference, held April 23-25, and publicized by its authors in September.

Brain-IT builds on an approach called the Universal Brain Encoder. That model begins with an image and then predicts the fMRI response that would be expected in individual "voxels" ‪—‬ small 3D units ‪—‬ in a brain scan.

"The key idea is that every voxel, a tiny cube of brain tissue, gets its own learned vector that captures what it cares about in images," said study first author Roman Beliy, a doctoral candidate in the Department of Computer Science and Applied Mathematics at the Weizmann Institute of Science in Israel.

Some voxels may be tuned to relatively simple elements of an image, such as edges, textures or locations. Others might be responding to higher-level abstract categories, like faces, bodies or scenes.

Traditional image-to-fMRI systems have generally been custom trained for each participant and dataset. The Universal Brain Encoder is more flexible. It learns from data from multiple people and can transfer information across participants, datasets or different MRI systems with varying magnetic-field strengths, according to the study.

A voxel can determine which parts of an image are relevant to it based on its learned profile, essentially saying, "I recognize edges. Which parts of this image are edges?"

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The Universal Brain Encoder starts with an image and predicts brain activity; Brain-IT starts with measured brain activity and reconstructs the image the person saw. In other words,it asks "based on this brain activity, what was the subject looking at?". It sorts thousands of tiny brain-scan measurements from the visual cortex into 128 groups based on the kinds of visual information they tend to carry.

The system then lets those groups share clues with one another, allowing it to combine, for example, information about a scene's shape, color and possible objects, to build a more complete picture of the image, Beliy explained.

The decoder produces two types of visual predictions. One captures semantic information ‪—‬ the features associated with what is likely in a scene; for an image of a dog standing in grass, for instance, this would include things like the features of a dog and an outdoor, grassy setting. The other captures structural information, like the broad visual layout or how forms are arranged.

In the above example, this would be aspects like the outline of the dog or where it was positioned in the frame. The structural prediction gives the generator a starting point for the image, rather than beginning from pure noise, while the semantic info guides an image generator that removes the remaining static until the image emerges.

Although the new tool can recreate what people see, it can't reproduce memories or imagined scenes.

"We're not reading people's thoughts," study co-author Michal Irani, a computer scientist at the Weizmann Institute of Science, told Live Science. "The images we do manage to recover from fMRI require people's cooperation and full intended collaboration."

The original image of a baseball game (left) and the reconstruction (right) generated by the Brain-IT AI model based on the brain activity of a person viewing the image.

Brain-IT's synthetic images were compared with the images that participants saw. Brain-IT surpassed prior leading methods on standard objective reconstruction metrics and produced more faithful results, the study authors wrote. The system shined when limited fMRI data from a new participant was available, with just one hour of data from a new participant producing results as accurately as earlier approaches that had been trained on 40 hours of recordings.

A high-scoring or realistic-looking output should not be mistaken for a perfect copy of what someone saw, however.

In the final stage of processing, the system uses an off-the-shelf diffusion generator trained on massive numbers of images. Models like this generate plausible images and can smooth textures, sharpen facial features or fill in missing details.

Beliy said this "beautification" can make reconstructions more polished and convincing and introduce details that don't necessarily come from the brain data itself. In other words, the scan constrains the generated picture, but the AI model supplies some of its realism from learned patterns in photographs.

While the new system produces impressive results for seen images, it can't be used to reconstruct an imagined or remembered image.

"Brain-IT relies on how the brain processes a seen image," Irani said. "Information flows from the eyes to the primary visual cortex and onward through a series of visual areas that recognize objects and scenes."

In a controlled experiment, researchers also know precisely which image was shown, giving the model a target during training and evaluation. In contrast, memories and imagined images do not offer the same clean reference. They can be vague and shaped by brain networks involved in memory and thought, with only partial and weaker reactivation of visual regions, Irani said. One limitation that would prevent this technology from being widely deployed is that the only way to get reliable results is from fMRI scanning, which is cumbersome and expensive. The team is currently experimenting with using easier-to-collect electroencephalogram (EEG) data, which is obtained via electrodes on the head, but that work is in the very preliminary stages, according to Irani.

The new system could help brain researchers better understand which visual information is represented in different brain regions, how those regions interact and how individuals’ patterns differ. Such tools could eventually reveal differences in visual processing that could help clinicians spot neurological, neurodevelopmental and psychiatric conditions.

"There are numerous useful medical applications which we are currently striving toward," Irani said. "These include using our brain encoder/decoder to detect and analyze brain disorders such as MS, PTSD, autism and psychiatric disorders."

Beliy, R., Zalcher, A., Kogman, J., Wasserman, N., & Irani, M. (2025, October 29). Brain-IT: Image Reconstruction from fMRI via Brain-Interaction Transformer. arXiv.org. https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.25976

#6400. This may be the best evidence yet that dinosaur blood can fossilize

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Minerals may have preserved remnants of ancient blood in a dinosaur bone, but some are skeptical

Using a technique called scanning electron microscopy to peer inside an 115 million-year-old dinosaur limb bone, researchers captured images of tiny ellipsoid structures, about 20 micrometers in diameter, that may be fossilized red blood cells. Molecular analyses found preserved heme — the oxygen-carrying component of hemoglobin — in the bone.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

The life and times of a dinosaur may be written in its blood — if blood can be preserved in bone.

Tiny microstructures found in the limb bones of a fossilized 115-million-year-old specimen are the remnants of red blood cells, researchers report November 2 in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. The team says these are both the oldest red blood cell structures yet identified and the first to be chemically proven. But not everyone is as sanguine about that conclusion.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The ability to identify such structures could offer a powerful molecular window into the physiology of long-extinct animals, including their metabolism and even activity levels, says paleontologist Kliti Grice of Curtin University in Bentley, Australia.

The bone, from a fossil-rich site in northeastern Brazil called Mina Pedra Branca, belonged to the dinosaur Aratasaurus museunacionali. Grice and her colleagues used a variety of chemical and imaging analyses to study the Cretaceous Period specimen.

Maurilio Oliveira/Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 4.0)

The team prepared thin cross-sectional slices of bone and imaged details of the limb bone’s internal structure with focused electron beams. That revealed ellipse-shaped microstructures within the limb’s fossilized network of blood vessels.

A map of the ellipsoids’ chemical element composition revealed that they were full of iron, carbon and nitrogen, all components of a biomolecule called heme. Heme is an iron-bearing, ring-shaped molecule found in hemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen throughout the body.

Then, the researchers used a technique that identifies molecules by how they scatter laser light. Those analyses suggested the presence of porphyrins, ringlike organic compounds found in blood — and the precursors of heme. Finally, they ruled out contamination from other porphyrins, such as the pigment chlorophyll, by separating and identifying the molecular contents of a bone extract. That experiment also suggested heme.

Taken together, these findings point unequivocally to the preservation of molecular traces of ancient blood, the team says. They also offer a clue to a novel pathway that might preserve those traces for so many millions of years.

Blood cells decompose within days of the death of an organism. Only unusual and fast-acting environmental and biochemical conditions could have stopped decay and held those tissues in place as the organism fossilizes.

In this fossil, the secret ingredient was a manganese oxide mineral called hausmannite, the researchers say. The team’s analyses had found the mineral within the ellipsoid structures. That mineral, they propose, may have acted as a time capsule, preserving the cellular structures and protecting the molecules within, including collagen amino acids.

Distinguishing fossilized blood cells from nonorganic minerals that formed within a fossil after the organism’s death is a tricky task. During fossilization, mineral-rich fluids seep in and around the bones, and the minerals that form within the fossil can bear a strong resemblance to bodily structures.

In a 1997 study, two paleontologists analyzed tiny spheres found inside the limb of a fossil, possibly a pterosaur. The spheres were once thought to be the fossilized remnants of ancient blood cells, but the duo determined that the spheres were instead pyrite, an iron mineral that had been deposited in the bones after death.

Those paleontologists suggested that, going forward, several criteria should be met before proposing a blood cell origin for fossilized structures, including comparing the shape of the structures with that of living related organisms and identifying certain biomarkers in the structures. One of those biomarkers is heme compounds.

Grice and her colleagues say that their study meets these criteria. Unlike the pyrite, hausmannite was crucial to preservation, “rather than simply a mineral that replaced biological material after it had disappeared,” she says. The close spatial relationship between the hausmannite, the blood cell-like structures and the chemical signatures of heme “raises the possibility that mineralization helped stabilize, entomb and protect components of the original biological material during fossilization.”

But Mary Schweitzer, a paleontologist at North Carolina State University in Raleigh who was not involved in the new study, says she doesn’t think these findings do fully meet those criteria.

The heme biomarkers, for example, don’t appear to be localized to the round structures alone, as would be expected in fossilized blood cells, but come from analysis of the entire bone. The proposed red blood cells also differ in size and shape compared with red blood cells from living birds and reptiles, she says.

Schweitzer is no stranger to skepticism over the discovery of ephemeral tissues in fossils. In 2005, she and her colleagues reported the first recovery of flexible, soft-tissue blood vessels from the 68-million-year-old fossilized leg bone of a Tyrannosaurus rex. It was a landmark study that sparked debate, including over how it would even be possible to preserve such tissues through deep time, as well as the most surefire way to detect them in the present.

“I am not convinced” that the research team has definitively identified heme compounds, Schweitzer says. “I do applaud them for bringing a plethora of methods to the study. Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence, and that does require state-of-the-art technology.”

No one really knows what a dinosaur’s red blood cell shape would be, let alone how the process of fossilization might distort the original shape of the structures, or allow heme-related molecules to escape their cellular confines over time, Grice says.

And, she says, her team’s interpretation of the evidence doesn’t just rely on the observations of those structures. “[It] rests on the convergence of anatomy, morphology, mineralogy, elemental analysis and molecular chemistry,” she says. “That combination is critical.”

As for whether other fossils might have molecular traces that have been preserved by hausmannite, “we simply don’t know yet,” Grice says. “But this type of preservation may not be quite as rare as we currently think.”

Questions or comments on this article? E-mail us at feedback@sciencenews.org | Reprints FAQ

K. Grice et al. Heme signatures in mineralized red blood cells within vascular canals of a 115-million-year-old dinosaur bone. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. 2026. doi: 10.1073/pnas.2614248123

D.M. Martill and D.M. Unwin. Small spheres in fossil bones: Blood corpuscles or diagenetic products? Palaeontology. 1997.

#6399. I’m a Neurosurgeon. My Near-Death Experience Showed Me ‘Universal Consciousness’ for the First Time.

By comparison, it makes our material world feel “murky.”

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:

When I earned my medical degree at Duke University, I was taught that consciousness is created out of chemical reactions occurring within the brain, a foundational assumption of scientific materialism, or physicalism—the notion that only the physical exists. After eleven years of rigorous training, I practiced as a neurosurgeon for more than two decades, including 15 years teaching and operating at Harvard Medical School.

I performed surgical procedures that took patients from extreme discomfort to full relief by releasing a nerve blockage or removing a tumor. I could stimulate the brain in conscious patients and affect their mental experience, which initially seemed to support my physicalist worldview. At the same time, patients deeply comatose from brain maladies would sometimes become fully alert right before dying. I couldn’t explain these phenomena, and so I dismissed them. That is, until November 2008, when a severe case of bacterial meningitis caused me to spend seven days in deep coma—and later reshaped my view of the universe.

Over three hours, I went from back pain and headache to epileptic fits and coma, as E. coli bacteria devoured my neocortex, or the outer surface of the brain, the part that is most responsible for human mentation. Healthcare professionals use the Glasgow Coma Scale to measure decreases in consciousness, with scores less than 9 indicating deep coma. A corpse would score a 3, the lowest grade on the scale, and my scores were 6 to 7 during most of that week—the doctor was out! Lumbar puncture revealed my cerebrospinal fluid to be filled with pus under pressure, and the glucose level in that fluid was only 1 mg/dl (normally 80-90, with severe bacterial meningitis occasionally as low as 20). CT and MRI scans revealed my entire neocortex was involved, meaning there was no physical functioning brain left to produce a dream or hallucination.

By the tenets of modern neuroscience, my awareness should have been zero. Without a functioning neocortex, my brain was incapable of producing a simple thought or image—and yet, I lived through a vivid, richly-detailed, hyper-real event, by comparison making this material world appear murky and dreamlike. I was unbound by space and time, immersed in universal consciousness, and wrapped in unconditional love. I had visions revealing structure to the non-physical realm that fully relates to and intertwines with our lives here on earth.

Back in the hospital, my prospects for survival were down to 2 percent when, on day seven, I startled everyone as I began to awaken. My doctors were even more surprised when I fully recovered over about two months. As my medical knowledge returned, I reviewed my records and scans, and discussed them with my doctors, trying to make sense of it all. I searched for a physicalist explanation, yet the case was unyielding—no conventional explanation could suffice. I was forced to acknowledge that an expansive model of reality was required to explain my experience.

In 2018, when my case records were peer-reviewed before publication in the Journal of Nervous and Mental Disease, the editors asked the authors to explain my unprecedented recovery. They replied that my miraculous recovery occurred because of my spiritual journey, knowing of similar extraordinary recoveries in the near-death literature. Due to techniques of cardiac resuscitation developed in the 1960s, millions of others have escaped the shackles of the physical brain and body, and reported similar near-death experiences (NDEs) of connection with a non-physical realm. Those descriptions have been categorized and evaluated using Greyson’s NDE Scale (developed by UVA psychiatrist Bruce Greyson), which quantifies the cognitive, affective, paranormal, and transcendental aspects of the experiences.

The vast evidence from these unusual experiences has convinced many former physicalists that their model is outdated. A more sufficient explanation is that the brain serves as a transceiver or antenna for tuning in to a larger, collective consciousness. Renowned Harvard psychologist William James, French philosopher Henri Bergson, and English writer Aldous Huxley, all postulated this “reducing valve” role for the brain in the early 20th century, noting that a shift in the primary physicalist assumption was required to explain these phenomena.

With a growing abundance of data, it is clearer that consciousness is fundamental and influences physical matter from the top down, rather than the bottom-up model of physicalism, where consciousness arises from the brain. Spontaneous remissions and the placebo effect confirm the power of the mind over matter and validate the observer effect seen in quantum mechanics experiments.

The “hard problem of consciousness” remains unsolved because its underlying premise is false.

I believe merging first-person subjective inquiry with rigorous empirical science will take us farther in knowing the true nature of our consensus reality.

To that point, humanity will thrive when science finally acknowledges that we are interconnected through love and part of one larger consciousness, with free will to become the best version of ourselves, both as individuals and collectively. The golden rule is woven directly into the fabric of the universe, providing a moral compass that shows that, ultimately, what matters most is how we treat each other.

#6398. Democrats flip House as Republicans confront ‘blue tsunami’

From left, House Minority Whip Katherine M. Clark, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, DCCC Chair Suzan DelBene, Democratic Caucus Vice Chair Ted Lieu and New York Rep. Gregory W. Meeks celebrate onstage at an election night watch party in Washington. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Democrats seized control of the House on Tuesday by safeguarding vulnerable incumbents and flipping districts in both battleground and deep-red terrain, delivering a sweeping repudiation of Donald Trump and Republicans that threatens to stall the president’s remaining agenda.

The Associated Press call came at 1:26 a.m. Eastern time Wednesday, hours after Democrats were projected to win a majority in the Senate, with a string of victories in deeply conservative states.

“The American people have spoken and made clear they've had enough of the extremism, enough of the corruption,’’ House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is poised to become the first Black speaker, told cheering supporters in Washington. “They want a Congress that's going to deliver for the American people, and that is exactly what House Democrats will do.”

Recent polls had forecast a strong Democratic showing amid rising discontent with the president's policies and economic anxiety driven by rising prices and the Iran war. But the magnitude of the Democratic majority surprised even the most optimistic Democratic partisans.

The “blue tsunami” marked an extraordinary turnaround for a party that suffered withering losses in 2024, when Trump returned to the White House and Republicans won a governing trifecta in Washington.

Republicans had hoped that a mid-decade redistricting push driven by Trump would help them keep their majority by flipping House seats in Texas, North Carolina, Florida and Ohio, among other states. Instead, many of those districts remained in Democrats’ hands.

Trump put himself front and center of the midterm campaign, imploring voters to “pretend that I’m on the ballot.” On Tuesday, he posted on social media that he “wasn’t on the ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!”

But in a later interview with CBS News, Trump congratulated Democrats on their rout. “My message is, congratulations to the Democrats, and I look forward to working with you for the good of our country," he said.

Among the night’s Democratic pickups were seats in rural and Republican-leaning districts. Farmer Jamie Ager defeated Republican state Rep. Jennifer Balkcom to flip a Western North Carolina seat that was left open after Republican Chuck Edwards announced his retirement after facing allegations of sexual harassment.

In Kentucky’s 6th District, Democrat Zach Dembo, a Navy veteran and former federal prosecutor, defeated former state Sen. Ralph Alvarado for an open seat anchored in Lexington.

Democrats also swept perennial battleground districts, flipping seats in states such as New Jersey, Colorado and Wisconsin. And in Pennsylvania, Democrats were projected to flip all four seats they were targeting, including the Philadelphia-area district of GOP Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick.

Anger over Trump’s tariff policy drove discontent in farm country, with Democrats ousting Republican Reps. Zach Nunn and Mariannette Miller-Meeks in Iowa and flipping the seat of Senate hopeful Ashley Hinson, who lost her bid to succeed retiring Sen. Joni Ernst.

Meanwhile, Latino voters, who were credited with helping propel Trump back into the White House in 2024, bolstered Democratic successes in Texas, scuttling GOP hopes of making good on the party’s mid-decade redistricting gambit.

Texas Republicans believed Latino voters would stick with the party this year when they redrew the state's congressional map to create up to five pickup opportunities. But anger over the president’s immigration policies, coupled with economic anxiety, has driven Trump’s approval numbers among Latinos to historic lows.

In South Texas, a pair of Democratic incumbents — Reps. Vicente Gonzalez and Henry Cuellar — easily held on to their redrawn seats, while former Bexar County sheriff's deputy Johnny Garcia prevailed over Air Force veteran Carlos De La Cruz in a district newly redrawn to elect a Republican. Democratic attorney and educator Katy Padilla Stout flipped the open 23rd District, which stretches across the state’s border with Mexico, and Tejano singer Bobby Pulido routed GOP Rep. Monica De La Cruz in another South Texas race.

The strength of the Democrats’ performance was evident in several under-the-radar races the party won in traditionally red districts, including Missouri’s 2nd District, where Republican Rep. Ann Wagner was ousted, and Indiana’s 5th, where Rep. Victoria Spartz lost reelection.

Speaker Mike Johnson, who crisscrossed the country to boost Republican candidates in the final weeks of the campaign, noted Tuesday night that history wasn’t on the GOP side: The president’s party almost always loses seats in a midterm election.

"From the first day of this election, we knew that to keep the House and sustain our majority we would have to defy more than a century of midterm history," Johnson said in Shreveport, La. "It looks like history will be kept tonight."

The new Democratic majority is expected to dedicate resources to investigating the activities of the Trump administration as well as the president.

The likely new Democratic chairman of the House Judiciary Committee is Maryland’s Jamie Raskin, while the Oversight and Government Reform panel is likely to be led by California Rep. Robert Garcia. Raskin and Garcia have already been busy making oversight requests of the administration.

For instance, the two lawmakers joined on a letter last week calling for the retention of conversations between the president and AI chatbots on matters of policy.

"The President and his advisors’ use of AI exposes the country to malign influence from unknown and unaccountable third parties. We already have ample evidence that AI chatbots can be manipulated to suit the commercial, political, or personal agendas of their designers​," Raskin and Garcia wrote.

Beyond the oversight, Jeffries outlined last month some of his legislative priorities for the next Congress.

"I think we need to put money in the pockets of everyday Americans by doing things like expanding the Child Tax Credit, as well as the Earned Income Tax Credit​," Jeffries told News12. "And, of course, we also need to end this war because the war has dramatically increased gas prices, fertilizer prices and diesel costs.​"

That was a reference to the military campaign against Iran, which appears likely to ratchet back up after the midterms.

I​n a pre-election interview with CNN, Jeffries said priorities that unite the Democratic Caucus include action on stopping the president's sweeping application of tariffs, as well as on reversing cuts to Medicaid and extending Affordable Care Act tax credits.

Mary Ellen McIntire contributed to this report.

A tiny asteroid entered Earth's orbit in April and is expected to leave in January. Meet the minimoon 2026 QQ8.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Earth and its moon will have company this holiday season. In April, our planet picked up a passing "minimoon," pulling the space rock into a temporary orbit, astronomers have confirmed.

The object, dubbed 2026 QQ8, was first observed by Hungarian researcher Krisztián Sárneczky in August. It was officially reported by the International Astronomical Union's (IAU) Minor Planet Center — the body that logs and confirms new solar system objects — on Oct. 29. This extraterrestrial traveler is expected to stick around until January 2027, extending its stay through the holidays before breaking free of our planet's influence.

2026 QQ8 is tiny — only about 6 feet (2 meters) across, according to the IAU. If it got too close to Earth, it would likely burn up in our planet's atmosphere. However, researchers don't think there is much chance of that happening, since 2026 QQ8 is currently orbiting at around 1.5 times the average distance of the moon.

2026 QQ8 takes 359 days — almost a full Earth year — to orbit the sun. It comes close to our planet every 10 years or so. This minimoon is classified as an Aten asteroid; this population of space rocks occasionally cross into Earth's orbit and have semimajor axes smaller than Earth's, meaning they typically orbit closer to the sun than our planet does. Large Aten asteroids are considered the most dangerous type of asteroid, as they can easily get lost in the sun's glare before speeding toward Earth — but, again, our new mini companion is far too small to pose a threat.

2026 QQ8 is not the first minimoon discovered circling Earth. That distinction belongs to 1991 VG, which was around 30 feet (10 meters) in diameter when it was detected in November 1991. Astronomers now think Earth grabs minimoons pretty frequently; we are likely to have at least one at any given time. Most of the space rocks stay around for less than a year, although a handful may remain in Earth's gravitational pull for decades.

New telescopes ‪are expected to help researchers spot more minimoons as they enter and leave Earth's orbit. These include the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile, which began operation earlier this year. The Rubin observatory, which takes a full scan of the entire Southern Hemisphere sky every few days, has already spotted what may be a new dwarf planet lurking in the outer solar system, as well as a new satellite galaxy of the Milky Way. Over its planned 10-year mission, the observatory is expected to detect millions of previously unknown moving objects in space.

#6396. Humans Have Used the Same Comb Design Since the Stone Age. This One Might Finally Beat Baldness.

Named after Disney’s Tangled, this comb zaps hair-growth molecules straight into shrinking follicles.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

The oldest-known comb, fashioned from animal bone, dates back nearly 8,000 years to mesolithic Syria. But in those intervening 10,000 years, the comb hasn’t seen much innovation. Sure, plastics have long since replaced bone as the material of choice for this particular piece of grooming gear (though animal bone combs are still a thing). But the comb’s overall shape and function—individual tines and all—has remained remarkably unchanged.

“The basic design evolved from the fingers of the human hand,” the Pitt Rivers Museum at the University of Oxford writes on its website. “From Bronze-Age man to Cleopatra, to Napoleon's wife, Josephine, all would recognize these items as such.”

But just because something’s remained largely unchanged for millennia doesn’t mean there isn’t room for innovation. Take, for instance, the “Detangle,” an experimental comb developed by Beihang University in China as a tool for tackling androgenetic alopecia (AGA), or just simply baldness. At first glance, the comb looks much like any other hand-inspired comb—there’s a long handle and the recognizable tines. However, that’s where the similarities end, because this comb has teeth packed with embedded electrodes as well as small compartments for delivering molecules designed to stimulate hair growth. Researchers published a study detailing the efficacy of this experimental comb in the journal Nature Communications.

“Androgenetic alopecia affects over 1.5 billion individuals, causing progressive hair loss with psychological and quality-of-life burdens,” the authors write. “This system features electronic teeth embedded with height-differentiated electrodes and integrated drug-loading modules, which generate an enhanced electric field penetrating up to ~9 times deeper into hair follicle regions than conventional external application.”

This “Detangle” device, whose name the authors admit was inspired by the Disney animated film Tangled, isn’t a new hair-loss treatment so much as a revolutionary way to deliver one. One of its most high-tech features is a control circuit that creates pulsed electric fields across two types of electronic teeth. These teeth have different heights that generate a stronger electric field than if the teeth were aligned. That generates a positive environment for the transmembrane delivery of a therapeutic molecule into the impacted follicular cells, increasing uptake by more than three times, the authors report.

The authors tested the comb on mouse models and found hair growth recovered near 100 percent within a month, a steep increase from the approximate 70 percent recovery rate of typical minoxidil treatments—one of the go-to FDA-approved treatments for hair loss. To achieve this impressive recovery rate, the authors relied on the SRD5A2 siRNA molecule and a VEGFA plasmid. The first molecule inhibits dihydrotestosterone (DHT), a hormone that causes hair follicles to shrink, while the latter boosts blood vessel growth around the impacted follicles.

“By co‑delivering VEGFA plasmid and SRD5A2 siRNA, the Detangle system promotes hair follicle regeneration via a dual mechanism that synergizes electrostimulation with molecular regulation,” the authors write. “Given the multifaceted signaling abnormalities in AGA, the Detangle system presents a versatile platform for co‑delivering therapeutic agents beyond metabolic modulation.”

After 10,000 years, the comb finally gets a serious glow up.

#6395. A high-fiber diet may clear away plastic in the gut

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Mice that ate lots of fiber had far less particles accumulate in the body

A diet that includes high-fiber foods, like these vegetables, might come with a surprise benefit. Fiber could help carry nanoplastics out of the body, suggests a new study in mice.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Here’s a new reason to eat your beans and greens.

A high-fiber diet may help sweep plastic particles from the gut, researchers report October 15 in Nature Communications. In mice that ingested plastic, eating loads of fiber daily kept the particles from piling up in the intestines. The finding hints at fiber’s power to protect the body from environmental garbage, says Eddy Y. Zeng, an environmental scientist at South China University of Technology in Guangzhou.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Researchers have long known that fiber can improve our health, in part by lowering cholesterol, keeping blood sugar levels in check and easing food through the gut. But now, Zeng says, his team’s results suggest an additional benefit.

We live in a world littered with plastic, much of it too small to see. These micro and nanoplastics, shed by disposable water bottles, fast food containers and other worldly junk, can make their way into our bodies. It’s not completely clear what such shards do to our health, but we have some hints. Scientists have linked plastic particles in people’s arteries to increased risk of heart attack and stroke. And mice that ingest tiny bits of plastic can show signs of organ injury.

Zeng’s team thought dietary fiber might provide some defense. Fiber forms a complex network of polymers that could trap ingested plastics like flies in a spider web, he says.

The researchers put mice on low-, medium-, or high-fiber diets, then fed them plastic particles. Over the next 24 hours, the medium- and high-fiber groups of mice cleared more particles from their bodies than their low-fiber counterparts, the team discovered. That’s important, Zeng says, because these particles can do damage. After a week of daily plastic feedings, his team saw gut tissue damage — but only in the low-fiber group. Experiments in test tubes suggest that fiber physically wraps around and sticks to plastic particles.

It’s too soon to say if dietary fiber does the same in humans. Zeng’s study was performed in mice and not tethered to realistic fiber numbers. Though mice in the high-fiber group ate far more fiber than what what’s recommended for people, he thinks the findings are worth pursuing in follow-up studies.

And even if fiber doesn’t end up purging plastic from people’s guts, Zeng says, it probably wouldn’t hurt for us to add a little more to our diets.
