#6379. City crows let people get closer, but country crows can be bolder in their own way

City crows tolerate people better than rural crows, but unfamiliar objects near food can make them more cautious.

City crows let people get closer than rural crows do. But when researchers put a lamp base in a pile of peanuts, city crows were less likely than rural crows to take a peanut.

The study of American crows around Ithaca, New York, suggests that a crow’s fears are shaped by its past experience.

Two experiments were run by Dave Colucci and Anne Clark, biologists at Binghamton University. In the first experiment, objects were left next to food on crow territories.

In the second, Colucci walked toward crows and measured how close he got before they flew.

The evidence for greater wariness in city crows comes from a single object.

It also comes from only one of the three measures used by the team. In addition, the city sites were closer to suburbs than to a downtown.

In crows, Colucci said, fear of anything new exists side by side with a great deal of curiosity. The fear does not always prevail, he added, so a new opportunity is sometimes seized.

Ten crow families were chosen from parking lots, parks, and dead-end streets near Ithaca.

Another 10 families lived on farmland and natural areas in the nearby town of Dryden.

American crows live in family groups that share a territory.

On most days of the week, Colucci scattered two cups of unsalted peanuts in the shell on each territory.

The same spot was used each time. He continued until the family had fed there three times in a row.

A single object was then set in the middle of the peanuts on four separate mornings. The crows were filmed by a hidden camcorder. Colucci watched from at least 164 feet (50 meters) away.

The trials were run in July and August of 2019 and 2020. Four objects were used: a rock, an ear of corn in its husk, a takeout box, and a lamp base.

The box was paperboard, and the lamp base was made to look like wood.

Every crow was expected to find the lamp base new. Bright colors, shiny surfaces and sharp angles are typical of human-made things.

These features are probably better known to crows living in cities. None of them was present on the lamp base.

When only peanuts were offered, nearly every crow that came within about 10 feet (3 meters) took one.

The team estimated the probability of eating at 99% for such city crows and 97% for rural crows.

With the lamp base in place, the estimated probability dropped to 76% among rural crows and 53% among city crows.

Wariness of new things is called neophobia by biologists. By this measure, the city crows had more of it.

The other two measures concerned only the first crow of each family to arrive and to eat. Their timing was compared with that on days when no object was present.

With the lamp base in place, the first crow to arrive and the first to eat were about as quick in city families as in rural ones.

To Colucci and Clark, that result suggests both places have some bold crows.

Results from earlier experiments on city and country birds have not agreed with one another. Lower wariness in cities has been reported in some of them, higher wariness or no difference in others.

Colucci and Clark wrote that some of those experiments used human-made objects, which city animals may know better.

A second idea was tested with the corn and the takeout box. An ear of corn should be ordinary to a crow that lives beside farm fields.

That ear of corn should seem strange to a crow whose home is beside a parking lot. For a takeout box, the reverse should be true.

More rural crows were put off by the takeout box, and more city crows were put off by the corn.

The team could be confident of that pattern only in the share of crows that ate. In how quickly the first crow arrived or ate, the pattern was too weak to be sure of.

A one-mile (1.6 km) stretch of road was also walked in each setting once a week for three weeks. Every human-made object was recorded.

A total of 341 objects was counted, with 169 along the city road and 172 along the rural road. A typical object nevertheless remained in place for a shorter time along the city road.

Objects turned over faster along the city road, but city crows were still more reluctant to eat beside the lamp base.

City crows are thus exposed to a constant turnover of objects, yet their wariness of new things hasn’t been reduced.

The authors suggested that most litter may be treated by city crows as one category.

In the second experiment, crows were approached on foot by Colucci 145 times over three summers. These approaches took place across upstate New York and Quebec.

During some approaches his gaze was fixed directly on the crow. During others his whole face was tilted toward the ground. A camera on his chest streamed video to a phone in his hand so that his direction could be maintained.

The average crow took flight while he was still about 150 feet (45 meters) away. A distance of 33 feet (10 meters) or less was reached in only eight approaches.

Closer approaches were tolerated by city crows than by rural crows, as is usual for city animals. Rural crows fled from far away regardless of the direction of his gaze.

In the most built-up areas, crows let him get about 82 feet (25 meters) closer when his face was down. The authors wrote that the true effect of his gaze could be either small or large.

A similar but smaller effect was found in a 2013 study of crows in Seattle. To the authors’ knowledge, a difference between two populations in the use of human gaze had not been shown before.

Hunting is one possible explanation for the behavior of the rural crows.

Within city limits in New York, crows may not be hunted. Hunting them in rural areas is legal from September 1 to March 31.

The rural response was described by Clark, an associate professor emerita of biological sciences, as a blunt defense against predators. “Don’t take any chances, don’t stop to assess; let’s just be safe,” she said.

Clark added that such a habit would not work for city crows. People pass by too often in a city for a crow to take flight every time.

The peanut experiment also provided evidence of greater caution among rural crows. With no object present, the first city crow reached the peanuts at about four times the rural rate.

The number of people living within about half a mile (800 meters) gave the best prediction of a crow’s reaction. When smaller or larger circles were used, the predictions were poorer.

A circle of that size is larger than the territory held by a crow family.

It was suggested by the authors that crows average their experience of people over a wide area. They then adjust to the person approaching them.

Individual people who have threatened them are also remembered by crows.

The study leaves open whether city crows gain any advantage from being more cautious around an unfamiliar object. Two possible explanations have been put forward by the authors.

One is that cities contain dangers which cannot be predicted even by a crow that knows its neighborhood well.

The other concerns the crows that first settled in towns about 70 years ago. Those birds may have had little fear of new things, with caution proving useful only later.

It is also uncertain whether the lamp base was equally new to both groups. Its shape is perfectly symmetrical, and such symmetry is rare in natural objects.

City crows might therefore have found it more familiar than the team had intended.

Were that the case, the authors wrote, the difference between city and rural crows could be underestimated.

Future research could test whether wariness slows crows down when new problems have to be solved. It could also test whether cities hold more unfamiliar threats.

For comparisons of urban wildlife with rural animals, a first step was recommended by Colucci and Clark. They wrote that the objects present in each environment ought to be identified first.

The full study was published in the journal Behavioral Ecology.

#6378. Toxic secrets are hiding in Arctic ice

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

A century-old pollution trail leads scientists back to Montana mining

At the turn of the twentieth century, the Anaconda Smelter in Montana spewed arsenic into the air — those heavy metal particles that are now trapped in Arctic ice cores.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Ice cores record Earth’s secrets, even the dirty ones.

Some of the cylindrical sections of ice extracted from the Arctic contain elevated levels of arsenic, lead and other heavy metals that circulated in our planet’s atmosphere in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Those pollutants, which have been tied to declines in IQ and higher rates of certain cancers, were probably emitted by a mining and smelting company in Montana whose grounds are now designated as multiple Superfund sites, the researchers report November 3 in Nature Sustainability.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The ice cores contain tiny particles that were once airborne — including pollutants, volcanic ash and salt from ocean spray — and fell to our planet’s surface within a few days or weeks. In polar regions, that fallout combines with snow and is preserved as ice.

Joseph McConnell, an environmental scientist at the Desert Research Institute, and his collaborators recently analyzed 10 ice cores collected across Canada, Greenland and Russia. The cores contained material that had fallen to Earth as early as 210 BCE, but the interval spanning the Industrial Revolution in the United States — from roughly 1870 to 1914 — was what caught the team’s collective eye.

In the ice layers from that period, arsenic concentrations in some of the ice cores were up to 15 times higher than pre-Industrial Revolution levels. Because the heavy metal exposure has been tied to upticks in the rates of certain cancers, McConnell and his team set out to determine the most likely source of all that pollution.

The largest increases in arsenic existed in the ice cores from Greenland. That finding was a big hint, McConnell says, because atmospheric circulation patterns tend to move material from west to east. “The only way you can explain that pattern of deposition is if the emissions are coming from North America,” McConnell says. “Had it been from Europe, we would have seen much larger increases in the Russian Arctic.”

The most likely source, the team concluded, was a massive copper mining and smelting operation in southwestern Montana operated by the Anaconda Copper Mining Company. It was one of the largest in North America during the Industrial Revolution and, unlike other copper mining operations in the area, it worked with copper ore that contained heavy metals like arsenic and lead. It was no secret that those toxic metals were entering the atmosphere, says Fred Quivik, a historian and the author of Smoke and Tailings, a book about the environmental history of copper smelting in Montana. “Ranchers and farmers started seeing their livestock die from arsenic poisoning.”

Based on the concentrations of arsenic in the ice cores and models of how material disperses in the atmosphere, McConnell and his colleagues estimated that the Anaconda Copper Mining Company was emitting roughly 30 tons of arsenic per day into the atmosphere in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. By comparison, Chile, currently the world’s largest producer of copper and home to more than 20 mining operations, collectively emits roughly one quarter as much arsenic today.

Beginning in 1919, the Anaconda Copper Mining Company installed devices near its smokestacks and other facilities to capture arsenic and prevent its release into the atmosphere. Arsenic emissions dropped by about 60 percent as a result, the ice core data showed, but by then hundreds of thousands of nearby residents had already been exposed for decades. That exposure could have been lessened, McConnell says, if the Anaconda Copper Mining Company hadn’t waited so long to install the pollution-abatement technology. “They delayed installation for about a decade.”

These new findings should be combined with census records to trace the effects of this pollution on human health in the 19th and 20th centuries, McConnell and his team suggest. “We hope that epidemiologists will take this information and really investigate potential impacts on human populations.”

#6377. Peregrine falcons are much smarter than we thought, using fake attacks to tire out their prey

A new study reveals that peregrine falcons deliberately use false attacks against their prey, making them much easier to catch later on.

When a peregrine falcon dives at a flock of birds and comes away with nothing, it looks like a failed hunt.

At one bay in British Columbia, some of those failed hunts may never have been meant to succeed. A study of peregrines and small shorebirds called Pacific dunlins suggests that early attacks send the flock into the air too soon.

A few hours later, the dunlins are often back on the ground, and that’s when the falcons make the most kills. If the researchers are right, the early attacks make the dunlins easier to catch later.

Ron Ydenberg and two colleagues at Simon Fraser University’s Centre for Wildlife Ecology published the analysis in October 2023. Their case rests on the timing of flights and kills at a single bay.

Predators are “imagined as clever in novels and movies, like the velociraptors in Jurassic Park,” Ydenberg said. But biologists who work from evidence, he added, tend to doubt such ideas.

Between 20,000 and 40,000 dunlins spend the winter at Boundary Bay, feeding on mudflats that the tide covers twice a day.

As the tide rises, the dunlins have to feed closer to the shoreline, where a falcon can ambush them from cover.

Like other shorebirds, dunlins used to rest on shore at high tide. During the 1990s, as more peregrines wintered at the bay, the dunlins largely stopped.

Now they often spend daytime high tides circling in a loose flock high over the bay. Almost every dunlin the falcons were seen to kill was outside that flock.

But circling takes energy. On days when the dunlins made these flights, they averaged 3.1 hours in the air.

By the team’s estimate, the three most dangerous hours for a dunlin on the ground run from one hour before high tide to two hours after.

On those days, the dunlins spent 89% of the hour before high tide in the air and 95% of the hour after.

But in the second hour after high tide, the dunlins were in the air only 44% of the time. The falcons did best in that hour, making 43 of the 139 kills recorded in 905 hours of watching.

The dunlins had done a lot of their flying earlier, more than an hour before high tide, when the danger was low. Compared with the safest schedule, their flights started early and ended early.

To explain the early flights, the researchers used a 2007 model inspired by killer whales hunting sea lions.

In that model, a predator can gain by making attacks that have little chance of success. The prey still has to flee, then make up the lost feeding time by taking more risks later.

At Boundary Bay, that would mean falcons attacking before high tide to send the dunlins up early.

The team couldn’t test the idea, because even experienced observers can’t easily tell a serious attack from a half-hearted one.

In data the team hasn’t published, peregrine hunts at the bay peak two to four hours before high tide, hours before the kills do.

The records come from Dick Dekker’s winter visits to Boundary Bay between 1994 and 2012.

Falcon attacks were recorded on 151 days. The dunlin flocks were timed from dawn to dusk on 34 days, and they made their high-tide flights on 23 of them.

The authors wrote that Dekker became “the world’s foremost watcher of wild falcons.”

The authors offered two other explanations.

Less skilled falcons might be the ones attacking early, while skilled falcons hunt just after high tide. Or the dunlins might land early because feeding is especially good on a falling tide.

To test those explanations, researchers would have to track individual falcons closely, Ydenberg said. That doesn’t look practical at Boundary Bay, where the falcons weren’t marked.

He added that the idea could be tested in other predators and their prey, where the same logic should apply.

The full study was published in the journal Frontiers in Ethology.

#6375. 15 lessons from the midterms as Democrats rebound with historic wave

Democratic staffers cheer Tuesday as results roll in during an election night watch party in Washington with House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

ANALYSIS — It wasn’t exactly a surprise that Democrats did well on Tuesday, but the breadth and depth of their victory was stunning. Votes are still being counted, but it’s looking like a massive blue wave with very few Republican survivors.

Just two years ago, Donald Trump delivered one of the biggest Republican victories in recent history. The GOP won back the White House, finished ahead in the national popular vote, recaptured the Senate majority and held on to the House. But what Republicans thought was a permanent realignment of the party coalitions crumbled under the weight of an unpopular war in the Middle East and voter frustrations over the economy and president’s economic policies.

The complete analysis will come in the weeks and months ahead, but here are a few initial thoughts.

Trump is a political mortal. Despite the pervasive narrative that normal political rules don’t apply to the president, election night showed that is simply not true. Sure, he was a surprise victor in 2016, but as an unpopular sitting president in 2018, his party lost a net of 40 House seats. When he ran for reelection in 2020, again as an unpopular president, he lost. When he got to run against an unpopular Democratic administration in 2024, he won again. And when his job approval rating sank to historic lows, his party was routed in the midterms.

Polls pointed in the right direction. Despite a decade of ridicule and abuse, the polling industry had a good cycle. Of course, there were a few outliers, but much of the public and private data (at least on the Democratic side) pointed to a good midterm for Democrats. Surprise outcomes on Tuesday were likely more due to a lack of data than poor data. And, if anything, some surveys underestimated the support for Democratic candidates. Pollsters still have methodological challenges, particularly with low response rates, but it’s time to ditch the narrative that polls always underestimate Republicans.

Democrats captured the Senate. Democrats are going to gain at least seven Senate seats: Iowa, Kansas, Maine, North Carolina, Ohio, South Carolina and Texas. They might gain up to nine with wins in Alaska and Mississippi. (Both races haven’t been called as yet by The Associated Press). They needed to gain four seats for a majority. Our projection of a Democratic gain of four to six seats was directionally accurate but will fall at least slightly below the final tally.

It could have been worse for Republicans. While it’s almost hard to believe, the night could have been a bigger catastrophe for the Senate GOP. Louisiana Rep. Julia Letlow won the open seat by 2 points; appointed Florida Sen. Ashley Moody won by 3 points; and Nebraska Sen. Pete Ricketts was leading by 7 points as of Wednesday morning. If Sens. Cindy Hyde-Smith of Mississippi or Dan Sullivan of Alaska survive, they’d do so by narrow margins. Meanwhile, Democrats didn’t really have any close calls, as they held Michigan (6 points as of Wednesday morning), Minnesota (10 points), New Hampshire (14 points) and Georgia (18 points).

Democrats captured the House. While dozens of races remain uncalled by the AP, Democrats will gain the House majority as expected. But the size of the wave is going to be bigger than expected. Democrats will likely clear our projection of a net gain of 20 to 30 seats and could approach their 40-seat gain during Trump’s first midterm.

Redistricting flopped for Republicans. Republicans are struggling to gain any of the seats they intentionally redrew to elect new members of their own party. Florida, North Carolina, Ohio and Texas ended up as debacles for the GOP with near total domination by Democrats up and down the ballot, all in states Trump won just two years ago. North Carolina Republican Tim Moore is on track to lose a district that he helped draw for himself.

It didn’t have to be this way. Even though Republicans are placing the early blame on history and inevitability, Tuesday’s results were not a foregone conclusion. Things could have been very different had Trump not started the conflict with Iran, which resulted in domestic economic hardship, or waged a tariff war with friendly countries. Or if he had limited his immigration policy to closing the border and deporting violent criminals in the country illegally. Republicans would have held the Senate, and it would have been an extremely close fight for the House. No matter who or what Republicans choose to blame, the party is here because of Trump.

Sometimes history repeats itself. Twenty years ago, there was an unpopular Republican president in the White House with a war in the Middle East that was driving up fuel prices. Democrats won majorities in both chambers of Congress as Republicans lost 30 House seats and six Senate seats — a remarkably similar outcome to this cycle.

Midterms portend the future, except when they don’t. Democrats had a great night this week but that’s no guarantee the success will continue. In their best-case scenario, 2026 could be the first part of a two-cycle wave, similar to 2006 and 2008, when Democrats expanded their House majority and won the White House. But 2028 could also look like 2012 in reverse, with Republicans bouncing back from a disastrous midterm as Democrats did after the 2010 tea party wave.

Candidate quality is only a fraction of the story. Republicans can try to blame their candidates or campaigns, whether it’s Hyde-Smith, Ken Paxton in Texas or Sen. Roger Marshall in Kansas, but all of them would have won in a political environment in which the president was even modestly popular. Without Trump’s self-inflicted policy wounds, candidate quality would not have mattered as much for Republicans, and they could have exploited Democrats with vulnerabilities, including Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan. Gina Hinojosa’s victory over GOP Greg Abbott in Texas, where Democrats also appear on track to sweep every other statewide race, is proof that Republican problems in the Lone Star State extended beyond Paxton’s baggage.

The Trump coalition collapsed. The coalition that brought Republicans to the mountaintop didn’t stick around very long as the party lost ground among a host of key demographic groups that were supposed to be a permanent part of its voter bloc. Trump finished behind Kamala Harris by just 11 points among voters aged 18-29. Republican candidates lost those voters by 47 points on Tuesday, according to the exit polls. Trump finished 5 points behind Harris among Latino voters, but Republicans lost them by 27 points this year. Trump lagged Harris by just 3 points among independent voters but Republicans lost them by 17 points this week. Trump bested Harris among male voters by 12 points in 2024, but Republicans ran even with Democrats with this group on Tuesday. Republicans even lost ground among voters without a college degree. Trump was +13 against Harris in 2024, but Republicans were just +4 in the midterms.

Personal brands matter until they don’t. Sen. Susan Collins of Maine and Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania’s 1st District came into the cycle with stellar reputations about bucking partisan trends, but both Republicans went down to defeat. Rep. Mike Lawler of New York’s 17th could join them. It’s just evidence that voters have a limited tolerance for voting against their own partisan tendencies.

Pay attention to special elections. For two years, Democratic candidates significantly overperformed in special elections and regularly scheduled off-year elections. Republicans dismissed the results as “special,” finding excuses to explain them away. But that was a mistake. Their turnout problem was right in front of everyone for more than a year.

Elections are humbling. Losing twice to Trump was a humbling experience for Democrats. Seeing most of those gains wiped out in a single night should be humbling for Republicans. But we’ll see what lessons each party chooses to take from these results.

White evangelicals couldn’t save Republicans. White evangelical voters continue to be one of the most reliable pieces of the GOP coalition. After supporting Trump with 76 percent in 2020 and 82 percent in 2024, and Republican candidates with 83 percent in 2022, white evangelicals supported GOP candidates once again, with 82 percent. But turnout did not keep pace. According to the exit polls, white evangelicals made up 17 percent of the midterm electorate after consistently comprising around a quarter of voters for more than a decade.

The Pan American Health Organization has determined that the U.S. has lost its measles elimination status, meaning domestic spread of the virus is now significant and sustained.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Editor's note: The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) officially announced its decision to revoke the United States' measles elimination status on Nov. 17, 2026. The week prior, the Wall Street Journal reported that the PAHO had reached that decision.

Measles is officially back in the United States after the disease had been eliminated from the country for more than 25 years.

The U.S. officially eliminated measles in 2000, meaning that at that time, the country had gone over a year without continuous domestic spread of the disease. Travelers would occasionally bring measles into the country, sometimes sparking significant local outbreaks, but these didn't tip enough dominoes to lead to ongoing domestic transmission.

That status has now changed, the Wall Street Journal reported Friday (Nov. 13). The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), which is the regional office of the World Health Organization for the Americas, has reevaluated the United States' measles elimination status and determined that it should be revoked. With this decision, the U.S. joins several other nations that have seen a local return of measles, including the U.K. and Canada.

The decision follows a series of major measles outbreaks that kicked off in January 2025. Nearly 2,300 cases were reported nationwide in 2025, and so far in 2026, almost 5,412 confirmed cases have been confirmed, although both tallies are likely undercounts.

"When January 2025 picked up, I felt like this might be the point of no return," Maimuna Majumder, a distinguished scholar in the Computational Health Informatics Program at Boston Children's Hospital, previously told Live Science. "I do want to just stress that measles elimination has always been a tenuous prospect, and it is, by design, tenuous," she added.

It takes work to keep an eliminated disease from resurging. The effort rests largely on keeping vaccination rates above a critical threshold — because the measles virus spreads so easily, at least 95% of the population needs immunity via either vaccination or past infection to prevent large outbreaks from occurring and fueling uncontrolled spread. National measles vaccination rates have been falling in recent years, with just 10 states reporting rates above the immunity threshold among kindergarteners for 2025-2026.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Experts point to several factors to explain the trend, including declining funds and staff for public health efforts and wavering public trust in vaccines and scientific expertise. The appointment of vaccine skeptic Robert F. Kennedy Jr. as health secretary and the loss of long-standing federal health leadership further fueled the trend, they say, as vaccine guidance has been changed in ways that likely sow confusion and the federal rhetoric around vaccines now frames their safety and effectiveness as open questions when they are actually well-established.

Measles infections can have serious consequences, including long-term disability and death.

The nation's first measles-related deaths this year were reported in Pennsylvania in August, and five more have followed, according to state health officials. (Some of these deaths have not been confirmed by the federal government.) A death reported in Wisconsin and another in New York have brought the current total to eight, per states' counts.

In the U.S., about 1 to 3 out of every 1,000 measles cases results in death. Pennsylvania has recorded just over 1,500 cases, so its number of reported deaths is higher than expected, hinting that the state's true case rate has not been fully captured in the data.

In survivors, measles can cause long-term health problems, including brain damage and immune amnesia, in which the immune cells tasked with remembering past infections have their "memories" wiped.

The PAHO's meeting to reevaluate the United States' status was originally scheduled for April but was pushed to November.

To regain its measles elimination status, the U.S. must go 12 months without continuous spread of the virus.

#6373. New species of flying frog discovered in a mountain pond called Coca-Cola Lake

Scientists identified a new flying frog species in Indonesia's mountains. DNA, body features, and calls helped confirm the discovery.

A seasonal pond sits high in the mountains of Sulawesi in Indonesia. Climbers know it as Coca-Cola Lake.

A new species of flying frog has been collected there and it has been named Rhacophorus kurniatiae.

Body measurements barely separate this frog from its closest relative. The difference shows up when the animals breed. The relative builds a nest of foam.

The new species leaves its eggs in a loose mass of jelly instead.

No other flying frog on Sulawesi has been documented laying its eggs in a loose, irregular mass of jelly.

The frogs were collected on November 18, 2011, by Wahyu Trilaksono. Trilaksono is a herpetologist with Indonesia’s National Research and Innovation Agency.

Four colleagues from Indonesia and the United States joined Trilaksono in describing the new species.

Thirty-one adults were collected in total. Every one of them came from that single pond.

Males measure 1.7 to 1.8 inches (43 to 47 millimeters) from snout to rump. Females are larger at 1.9 to 2.2 inches (49 to 57 millimeters). That is roughly the length of an AA battery.

The pond is found 6,155 feet (1,876 meters) up in the Mekongga Mountains. This range lies on the southeastern arm of Sulawesi.

The pond is not natural. It was created by a logging company as a place to store logs.

Rain and seepage fill the pond for part of the year. No stream runs into it or out of it. During the dry season, it shrinks to a few pools and exposed moss.

Loggers worked these mountains before they became a protected forest in 1994.

The 2011 trip belonged to a series of expeditions run for the ICBG Indonesia Project.

The project was a biological inventory of the mountains. Its Indonesian and American partners included the Museum of Wildlife and Fish Biology at the University of California, Davis.

The field team was led by Alan Hitch, who is a research affiliate at that museum. Hitch recalled reaching the pond on the way up the mountain. Green frogs were all over it.

“You don’t really see frogs in big congregations like that,” Hitch said.

Biologists describe an event like this as explosive breeding. Adults gather suddenly along the edge of the water for a brief burst of mating. Heavy rain appears to trigger it at Coca-Cola Lake.

Asian flying frogs are tree frogs. Their name comes from gliding, which is done on large webbed feet. A foam nest is where the typical flying frog lays its eggs.

Rhacophorus boeadii is the closest relative of the new frog, and it breeds that way. Scientists named it last year from mountains in central Sulawesi.

Coca-Cola Lake is shared with a third flying frog. Its eggs are packed into compact balls of gel.

R. kurniatiae does neither of these things. Its eggs are laid straight into an irregular mass of jelly that contains no foam. The mass hangs above the water or is loosely attached to whatever is nearby.

The frogs showed no preference for any plant species or leaf shape. The embryos stay inside the jelly until they become tadpoles.

The authors wrote that the habit may reflect an adaptation to water that comes and goes.

The team needed to check whether the pond frogs were a species of their own. Twenty-eight body measurements were taken on preserved specimens for that purpose.

The 81 specimens came from six flying frog species found on Sulawesi and nearby islands.

Eighteen of them were the new frog. Its females were compared with R. boeadii females. None of the 28 measurements differed reliably between them.

Three measurements did differ among males. These were eye width, the length of the first toe and the width of the pad on the fourth toe.

The DNA was close as well. One stretch of mitochondrial DNA differed by 2.19% to 2.43% between the two species. The gap between the new frog and the other four species was about 4% to 5.7%.

Andrew Engilis Jr. is the curator of the UC Davis museum and a co-author of the study.

Species can sometimes “look the same, but their behavior is different and their genetics are different,” Engilis said.

Animals like these are known to biologists as cryptic species.

A few features do set the new frog apart on close inspection. A small flap of skin is present on each heel. A fold of skin runs along its limbs and its third finger carries more webbing.

The call of one male was recorded on a digital camera at 6:40 p.m. It lasted about 1.4 seconds.

Four notes made up the call. A single short pulse opened it. Three notes of three to five pulses each came next. The call of R. boeadii is a single note.

The team also wanted to compare the call with that of the third flying frog at the lake.

Call measurements published in 2015 by Hellen Kurniati were used for this. She was a long-serving herpetologist at Indonesia’s Museum Zoologicum Bogoriense.

The new species has been named in honor of Kurniati. She died before it was described.

Only one recording from one male was good enough to be analyzed. The authors wrote that the opening note may be that male’s own variation. It may not be a trait of the whole species.

R. boeadii is known from two mountain regions in central Sulawesi. R. kurniatiae has been found only on the southeastern arm.

Two major faults run close to the line between those ranges. Faults are long breaks in Earth’s crust where blocks of land slide past each other.

The authors suggested that the faults may have acted as barriers, splitting an ancestral frog population in two.

A similar pattern is seen in the flying lizards and macaques of Sulawesi.

Closely related species live on different arms of the island. The idea has not been tested for the frogs. More genetic analysis will be needed for that, the authors wrote.

So far, researchers have found the frog only at Coca-Cola Lake.

This raises potential conservation concerns, the authors wrote. They pointed to pressure from farming, deforestation and climate variability across Sulawesi.

The amphibians of Sulawesi have been studied less than those of Java, Sumatra and Borneo.

Thirty-three amphibian species are known from the region and six of them are flying frogs. The researchers expect the true number to be higher.

Several species have been added by recent fieldwork. One of them is a fanged frog that nests on land.

Engilis said the region is a candidate for national park status. Continued species discovery could help speed that process, Engilis added.

The authors called for targeted surveys of the island’s mountain habitats.

Other high ponds in the Mekongga Mountains could be surveyed in the future. Such work could show whether Coca-Cola Lake is the frog’s only home.

The full study was published in the journal Zootaxa.

A Michigan woman uses a brain implant to speak with her neurosurgeon. Efforts to restore speech highlight what’s at stake when we lose opportunities to talk.

Scientists are racing to restore people’s ability to communicate. Powerful AI-based methods to decode speech signals and predict words, along with advances in technology, promise success.

This episode of The Deep End: Talk to Me takes listeners through the breadth of scientific efforts to restore words, emotions and even gestures to people who can’t move or talk.

We’ll hear from Casey Harrell, a man with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis who can no longer talk. A user of today’s technology, Harrell has a unique perspective on what he’d like to see improved for the technology of tomorrow.

And as season two wraps up, listeners will be left with a reminder of the power of a voice: a piece of comedy from Jules Rodriguez, performed with his voice clone in front of a live crowd.

“Being backstage and then seeing him come out, like, roll out his wheelchair, and everybody goes nuts because they’re like, ‘What is going on here? This doesn’t make sense,’” says Jules’ wife, Maria Aleandra Fernandez. “And every time I was like, ‘This is life. This is love. This is passion. What else is there?’ I don’t know that there’s anything else more powerful than what this guy is doing here.”

Laura Sanders: OK, I want to ask who your favorite comedians are and why. Who makes you all laugh?

Sanders: Paradromics has developed its own brain-computer interface for communication. The device is about the size of a dime, and it sits on the motor cortex. That’s the part of the brain that creates speech signals. The chip then detects these signals as a person thinks about saying a word.

Matthew Willsey: So the cortical module has 421 tiny little sensors.

Sanders: That’s neurosurgeon and biomedical engineer Matthew Willsey, of the University of Michigan Health. He’s describing the device from Paradromics here.

Willsey: They’re about one and a half millimeters long. And you know, it’s smaller than your thumbnail, like kind of all the way around. It’s like a cylinder. And at the bottom of the cylinder are the electrodes, is what we call them. And we get them really close to the brain. And then when we deploy it, what it does is it pushes those electrodes down into the brain.

Sanders: Those tiny sensors are listening to the nearby neurons that control the muscles required for speech.

Willsey: The principle is to try and get these things as small as possible to disrupt the least amount of tissue as possible, and then to get them really, really close to the individual cells, the neurons themselves that have the information we’re trying to record.

Sanders: The goal here is to restore a person’s ability to talk.

Willsey: So in the ideal situation, the electrodes would sit, you know, right next to those neurons. This type of technology that’s very intuitive, that can record activity from the brain in kind of a high-throughput way, can put the words up at a good speed and a good accuracy, allows them to kind of regain the ability to communicate with others close to how they maybe were before they had the illness. So that truly is very powerful.

Sanders: You might remember that Casey’s implant, called the BrainGate 2 system, requires ports on his head that are connected to external wires.

Casey: What is annoying about this device is really easy to answer. It is not portable, and it is not implanted only inside my head.

Sanders: Unlike Casey’s implant, the Paradromics device is fully implantable. That means it’s wireless. This summer, Willsey implanted Paradromic’s device in a volunteer’s brain. The brain belonged to a 68-year-old woman who lives in Michigan. She has primary lateral sclerosis, a disease that has taken away most of her ability to talk. So far, the Paradromics system is up and running, and the volunteer is testing her abilities out.

Here she is talking with Willsey and other researchers in a video provided by Paradromics. You’ll hear her natural voice, which is hard to understand, and then a digital voice speaking the words her brain implant decoded.

[Audio] I love the change of seasons in Michigan. And my favorite one is the fall. I love the change of seasons in Michigan. And my favorite one is the fall. Yeah, it’s good.

Sanders: This volunteer has used the device to talk to her grandkids on the phone. But this is just the very beginning for this research project. There’s so much more to test.Casey is still working on his system, too — particularly, streamlining the process. When Casey uses his brain-computer interface, it decodes speech signals from his brain, then puts words on a screen. Casey then selects a button, using his eye movements or his brain-computer interface, to say these words out loud with a digital voice. Here’s Casey.

Casey: It is not fast enough to provide enough instant conversation with other people that need to slow down to talk to me.

Sanders: But scientists want to skip this middle part — the words written on a screen. They want instead to go straight to speech, and perhaps make conversations faster. Casey says this goal to go directly from brain signals to a speaking digital voice would be his top priority.

Casey: That one is the holy grail of what this will become in terms of speech. It will allow you to have a seamless conversation. I am talking about, yes, I will intend to talk, and then it will just translate that automatically into speech, like we do, and you are doing right now.

Sanders: In an earlier episode, we talked about attempts to do just this with Casey’s system, to push it to do what they call brain-to-voice. Early attempts were hard to decipher. But it has already improved, by a lot. In the latest tests, this brain-to-voice process produces words that are understandable – reaching about 95 percent accuracy for listeners. Here’s Casey speaking test sentences. It comes from a preprint manuscript posted on the website bioRxiv.

[Audio] The day is not over yet. Please come in with me.

Sanders: Scientists have another thing on their to-do list. And this one goes beyond the words themselves. Here’s Gilja, from Paradromics.

Gilja: Let’s say I identify whether a sentence is a statement or a question. Well, now you can pass that information on to speech synthesis, so that you get these two different versions.

Sanders: The same words could be a statement or a question. You see what he means. You see what he means? And that information can be pulled out from a person’s brain activity.

Gilja: If I’m decoding prosodic information, if I’m decoding speed, when a word is meant to appear, that can also be passed on to modern speech synthesis systems, so that you’re more accurately capturing the prosody that somebody intends. Same thing with loudness, right? So you can see how as that information becomes available from the neural channels, it can be provided to the AI speech synthesis to get closer to the intended voice in the moment that the individual wants to generate.

Sanders: All of these signals can be collected and used to build a more accurate voice — one that says things exactly how a person intends to say them, like a Minnesotan’s ooftah or a slow southern hey y’all. Now, today’s voice clones can add these emotional layers onto words already. Here’s what Jules told me when I asked him about whether his voice clone can do it.

Jules: Oh, there are plenty of things it does that are all the above. But one thing in particular is how it inserts tone and inflections on words. Sometimes my wife will get mad because my response can come off with some sass.

Sanders: So there’s loudness, emphasis, pitch — all of these things contribute to what words means. But imagine if a brain implant can pick up these cues directly — no typing required. Here’s Hochberg.

Hochberg: There’s a lot that can be conveyed through the emphasis, through the tone, through even the humor that can sometimes be conveyed by the way that somebody who’s able-bodied may speak a particular sentence. All of those, I think, really can be captured by these implantable brain-computer interfaces by harnessing the rich neural activity that’s available from the brain. We should be able to restore a lot of that.

Sanders: Sergey Stavisky is one of the UC Davis researchers working with Casey and Hochberg. He and his colleagues are working on some of these ideas.

Stavisky: And even now we’re continuing to improve that and actually adding additional layers. So we have one forward-looking project where we can maybe decode the kind of emotional valence of how he’s trying to say it. Is he trying to say something in an angry way or in a surprised way or in a happy-sounding way, to kind of further make it more expressive.

Sanders: They’re even trying  to decode singing. Well, OK, it’s really more of a hum at this point, he says. But those sorts of tone shifts could, in theory, be deciphered.

Stavisky: We definitely have our work cut out for us on the singing and melody side of things.

Sanders: All sorts of voice signals could be pulled from brain activity.

Stavisky: Ultimately, we want people to be in full control of what they’re communicating. This should come from their intent. So, yeah, we are trying to decode all of the aspects of his voice, whether it’s the pitch, the timbre, the loudness, the intonation, which word he’s stressing. All of that, ideally, we would decode from brain activity, including kind of all of that emotional nuance.

Sanders: Voice clones can speak with various emotions. You heard my voice clone do just that in earlier episodes. But the difference here is that a person wouldn’t have to type in the instructions. They would come straight from their brain, seamlessly. Other nonverbal signals can be pulled from the brain, too.

Samantha Brosler: In the past five years or so, there have been a lot of advancements in the field of BCIs for restoring individual functions to people with paralysis.

Sanders: That’s Samantha Brosler, a bioengineer at the University of California, San Francisco. Some brain-computer interfaces can pick up movements. We haven’t talked much about them, but these implants have their own very successful research history. They’ve allowed people to control a robotic arm, for instance.

Brosler: Most of these devices so far have been designed to restore one function at a time, whereas in reality, frequently people who are paralyzed are missing both the ability to speak and perform body movements. And so in this study, we asked whether a single brain implant could be used to decode both speech and movement at the same time.

Sanders: It turns out, it could. She and her colleagues were able to decode gestures for communication — things like thumbs up, or a head nodding yes — and words. This combo approach is a more natural way of getting a point across.

Brosler: We naturally use gestures alongside our speech. So for example, some gestures can substitute for speech entirely, like nodding yes, shaking your head no, waving, shrugging, giving a thumbs up. But they can also add or change the meaning of what we’re saying. So for example, if you say maybe combined with nod head yes, that has a very different, you know, meaning than if you say maybe and shrug or shake your head no.

Sanders: My kids know that a slow maybe with a skeptical eyebrow raise is much closer to a no than my fast upbeat maybe with a little head nod. There is so much subtext in our body language.

Brosler: So I think of, you know, gestures and body movements as an additional communication channel that can work together with speech to add expressivity to what we’re trying to say.

Sanders: In the study, the output was a digital avatar who looked like the person. Success looked like the avatar moving and getting the word right.

Brosler: And the idea is that we enable the participants to use speech and gestures alone or together. So in theory, someone could say hello while waving.

Sanders: The researchers started simple, with just a few phrases — hello, bye, good idea, how’s it going, let’s go — and just a few gestures, like a shrug or a point, a fist pump, thumbs up.

Brosler: Of course, ultimately, we’re hoping to expand this to even larger vocabulary and more range of body movements across the whole body to help allow people more expression in their communication.

Sanders: The sheer number of different approaches to restoring communication is a sign that this neurotechnology is coming fast. Here’s Willsey.

Willsey: I think it’s good. There’s a lot of players that are entering into the field that have a variety of different ideas where they can run the clinical trials and see how these different devices stack up.

Sanders: There are lots of reasons to be optimistic about the future here, and it’s a future that isn’t even that far off. Here’s David Brandman, one of the researchers at UC Davis who works with Casey. He’s also the neurosurgeon who implanted Casey’s device.

Brandman: I think I’m about five years away from being able to meet a patient with ALS and having the following conversation, and saying, you know, Ms. Smith, I’m sorry you’ve been diagnosed with ALS. I don’t have a cure for you, but I do have a device that I can implant that can help you communicate despite facing a future of paralysis. It’s a device that would be implanted. It’s fully wirelessly. It’s cosmetically invisible, and you’d be able to use it to communicate your needs and have a meaningful conversation with friends and family. So I think that kind of conversation is about five to 10 years away.

Sanders: It’s a beautiful vision. When you’ve been a reporter as long as I have, you’re skeptical when scientists say something big is just five to 10 years away. But in this case, I see it.

It’s easy to get drawn into the technical details here. Different types of implants, the decoding processes, AI-powered voice clones and what they can do and can’t do — what they should do and shouldn’t do. But if you step back and really look, you’ll see that this research is all propelled by a very simple and powerful fact: The human voice is too important to lose.

Casey: What does my voice mean to me? It means so much. I think it is the most important thing that I have lost in this whole disease.

Sanders: So now we are here, in this moment, as Jules would say, right here, right now. And right now, the human voice is shifting and changing, expanding in ways that were completely unthinkable even just a few years ago. The future of the human voice and its many replicas is anybody’s guess.

Sanders: In one of Jules’ comedy sets, the one he did in November of 2024, he wheels out onto the stage as the song “Walking on Sunshine” plays.

As the crowd settles and finishes their clapping and woo-ing, Jules pauses. You can’t see this, but he wiggles his eyebrows — a lot. The crowd goes crazy every time. He hasn’t said a single word yet. After another pause, he deadpans with his voice clone: “That is all the time I have. My Make-A-Wish covered only a few minutes. Goodnight, everybody.”

And with that, Jules takes control and he’s off on a tear, ripping through stories of a weatherman who seems too happy about standing out in hurricanes, the exquisite guilt trips lovingly crafted by his Cuban parents, and the indignities of having body parts shaved with his sister right there in the room. Jules has the audience laughing so hard. It’s magnificent.

MA: And being backstage and then seeing him come out, like roll out in his wheelchair and everybody go nuts because they’re like, what is going on here? Like, this doesn’t make sense. And every time I was like, this is like life. This is love. This is passion. This is like, what else is there? Like, I don’t know that there’s anything else more powerful than what this guy is doing here and what I can help him do.

Sanders: I get what MA meant when she said that comedy is something that heals. When his set actually does come to a close, he tells the audience. [Audio] Now you have to watch me slowly get off this stage. Goodnight, everybody.

Sanders: It’s hilarious. It’s happy. It’s sad. It’s perfect.

This is The Deep End, Talk to Me. I’m Laura Sanders. If you like this podcast, tell your friends and leave us a review. It helps the show a lot. Send us your questions and your comments at podcasts@sciencenews.org.

The Deep End is a production of Science News. It’s based on original reporting by me, Laura Sanders. This episode was produced and mixed by Ella Rowen. Our project manager is Ashley Yeager. Nancy Shute is our editor in chief. Our music is by Blue Dot Sessions. The podcast is made possible in part by the Burroughs Wellcome Fund, with support from PRX.

#6370. Your favorite foods may soon contain less sodium

Most of the sodium Americans eat comes from packaged and prepared foods. A new FDA rule could help cut sodium at the source.

Starting in December, a new FDA rule will let food makers replace some or all of the added salt in products such as bread, cheese, and canned vegetables.

That could make a difference because Americans get more than 70% of their sodium from packaged and prepared foods.

One option is a salt blend that replaces some sodium chloride with potassium chloride. Few Americans use salt substitutes at home.

Daniel W. Jones, a professor emeritus at the University of Mississippi School of Medicine, chaired the committee that wrote the 2025 U.S. blood pressure guideline, which recommends potassium-enriched salt substitutes.

In the journal JAMA, Jones said the FDA rule could help reduce sodium intake.

Table salt is sodium chloride. In a potassium-enriched salt substitute, some of that sodium chloride is replaced with potassium chloride.

Potassium chloride is a salt made with potassium in place of sodium.

According to Jones, a blend of 25% to 30% potassium chloride is recommended. A higher proportion is not accepted by American tastes, which is part of the reason.

Stores sell a wider range, from blends of equal parts to pure potassium chloride. The equal-part products are usually labeled “light” salt.

Wanpen Vongpatanasin of UT Southwestern Medical Center directs the center’s section on hypertension.

Vongpatanasin noted that blood vessels are affected by sodium and potassium in opposite ways. Sodium makes arteries stiffer, while potassium generally relaxes the blood vessels.

“You get a twofer with a potassium-enriched salt substitute,” Jones said.

A person who switches consumes less sodium and more potassium, he added. Both changes are considered healthy.

Blood pressure is measured in millimeters of mercury, the units used in a reading such as 120 over 80. Jones noted that a blend with 25% potassium chloride lowers blood pressure by 5 to 7 points on average.

The top number is lowered by 8 to 10 points with most blood pressure drugs, he added.

Jones also explained the significance of such a drop for people with high blood pressure. Their risk of heart attack, heart failure, stroke, and kidney disease is reduced with every 10 points lost.

The reduction was estimated by Jones at about 15% to 20%.

The substitute was tested in a trial that was published in 2021 and conducted in 600 villages in rural China. The 20,995 participants had either survived a stroke or were at least 60 years old with high blood pressure.

The villages that received the potassium blend were selected at random and the remaining villages continued to use regular salt. One quarter of the blend consisted of potassium chloride.

The participants were followed for almost five years. About 29 strokes a year were recorded among every 1,000 people who cooked with the blend.

Roughly 34 strokes a year were recorded among every 1,000 people who used regular salt.

Deaths from any cause were also less frequent in the villages that used the blend. Blood pressure differed less than Jones’s average. The top number was about 3 points lower in villages using the blend.

Vongpatanasin and her colleagues examined how many people use these products. A national health survey of about 37,000 U.S. adults was analyzed for that purpose.

In the survey years 2013 and 2014, 5.4% of adults said they used a salt substitute. No other survey round recorded a higher share. By 2017 to 2020, that figure was 2.5%.

Use was low throughout and later fell by more than half. A substitute was rarely used by patients being treated for high blood pressure, either. Fewer than 1 in 10 of them reported it.

Taste is one reason. Vongpatanasin noted that potassium chloride can taste bitter or briny. The effect is stronger in larger amounts and for people who prefer heavily salted food.

She advised cooking with the substitute, along with other seasonings, instead of sprinkling it on cooked food. People become accustomed to the taste in about two weeks, Jones said.

Cost was also identified as a barrier in the 2025 guideline in which the World Health Organization suggested the switch. The guideline noted that the blends can cost more than regular salt and that public awareness is low.

A small consulting arrangement with the drugmaker AstraZeneca has been disclosed by Vongpatanasin.

She is also named as a co-inventor on a University of Texas patent for potassium magnesium citrate. No revenue has been generated by that patent to date.

Only a small part of dietary sodium is changed when a household switches completely to a substitute.

Roughly 11% of the sodium eaten by Americans is added during cooking or at the table. That estimate was reported by the FDA.

Average intake in the United States has been put at about 3,400 milligrams a day by the same agency. About 2,300 milligrams of sodium are contained in one teaspoon of table salt.

Federal dietary advice sets that amount as the daily limit, and the 2025 heart guideline aims for less than 1,500.

The recommendation of the WHO applies only to salt that people add themselves.

This limit was explained by Rain Yamamoto, a scientist in the nutrition and food safety department of the agency.

The advice is most relevant in countries where most salt is consumed through home cooking, Yamamoto said. The United States does not belong to that group of countries.

“Standards of identity” are maintained by the FDA for foods such as bread, sour cream, and mayonnaise.

The ingredients that a product needs before it can carry such a name are listed in each standard. Salt was allowed or required under 139 of those standards while a substitute was not permitted.

In October, the agency issued a final rule that lifted the restriction on substitutes in all 139 standards. Some or all of the salt in those foods may be replaced when the rule takes effect in December.

The affected foods include mayonnaise, salad dressing, many cheeses, canned vegetables, canned fish, bread, and pasta.

Potassium-enriched salt is not suitable for every patient. People with chronic kidney disease, especially end-stage disease, should not use potassium-based substitutes.

Other types of substitute such as herb blends can still be used by those patients.

Blood potassium can also be raised by several kinds of medicine. Some diuretics are included in that group and are commonly known as water pills.

Two common families of blood pressure drugs are included as well. These are the ACE inhibitors such as enalapril and the angiotensin receptor blockers such as losartan.

A doctor should be consulted first by patients on those drugs so that blood potassium can be monitored.

The WHO’s recommendation excludes pregnant women and children because evidence in these groups is limited.

Serious events linked to high blood potassium occurred at similar rates in both groups.

However, the trial had excluded people with serious kidney disease and people who were taking potassium supplements. Blood potassium was also not tested routinely during the trial.

No new labeling requirements were added by the FDA rule, which makes those exclusions relevant to packaged food.

A required warning about high potassium on those foods was declined by the agency. Potassium chloride will still be listed by name among the ingredients.

Use of a substitute is allowed by the FDA rule but no manufacturer is obliged to change a recipe.

No minimum level of replacement was set and no penalties were listed for companies that keep regular salt.

The rule leaves the choice of substitute to manufacturers.

Potassium chloride is mentioned in the rule as one example beside yeast extracts, MSG, and amino acids. Sodium in bread or cheese could therefore be lowered by a manufacturer with no potassium added.

A related question was left open by the 2021 trial in China. The blend was used for home cooking in that trial and people who ate most meals elsewhere had been excluded.

Packaged food that already contains the blend was not examined in that trial.

Concern about the rest of the diet was expressed by Sotiria Everett, who is a dietitian at Stony Brook University. Little effect is expected from cooking with a substitute if deli meats, cheese, and bacon are still eaten, she said.

A fruit or vegetable at every meal was recommended by Everett because potassium intake is then increased naturally.

The rule was published on October 13 and takes effect 60 days later in December. A report on progress toward the voluntary sodium targets of the FDA is also expected later in 2026.

The decision to use potassium salt in pursuit of those targets will be made by each manufacturer.

The full report was published in the journal JAMA.

In this excerpt from "The Secrets of our DNA," geneticist Turi King examines how DNA was used to reveal the ultimate fate of the last members of the House of Romanov.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In 1917, the Russian Revolution was in full swing. Tsar Nicholas II had abdicated, and he and his family were exiled to a remote Siberian town. There were plans to get the family to the U.K., but King George V (Nicholas' first cousin) and the British government withdrew their offer of asylum over concerns of the ramifications.

After the Russian Provisional Government was overthrown by the more extreme Bolsheviks in October 1917, Nicholas, his wife, their children and several members of the family's staff were moved to Ipatiev House in Yekaterinburg, where, in July 1918, they were executed. Their bodies were hidden and remained lost to time ‪for nearly a century —‬ until modern technology, with some help from the British royal family, unraveled the fascinating story of their disappearance.

In this excerpt from "The Secrets of Our DNA: How Genetics Has Changed the World" (Pegasus Books, 2026), author Turi King, director of the Center for Evolution at the University of Bath, looks back at the incredible story of how DNA was used to solve a major mystery of modern history: What happened to the last members of the House of Romanov?

I was sitting in a lecture theatre at Cambridge University in 1994 when one of my lecturers, Erika Hagelberg, spoke about a new study she had just been involved in. It was the first major case to combine both mitochondrial DNA and DNA fingerprinting to identify human remains: those of the Russian imperial family.

But first I need to take you back to Russia in 1917 and the abdication of the tsar following the Russian Revolution.

The Russian royal family, the Romanovs, had been the reigning imperial dynasty since 1617, and three centuries later, Tsar Nicholas II was on the throne. Nicholas was the cousin of George V, king of the United Kingdom, their mothers being sisters, and had married George's cousin Princess Alix (Alexandra) of Hesse, who was apparently Queen Victoria's favourite grandchild. Nicholas and Alix had five children, four daughters (Olga, Tatiana, Maria and Anastasia) and a son, Alexei.

The tsar and his wife were not well liked by the Russian population and political unrest culminated in the revolution of 1917, when Nicholas was forced to abdicate. The family were kept under house arrest and in 1918 they were moved to Ipatiev House in Yekaterinburg with the royal physician, Dr Botkin, and three of their staff. On the night of 16 July, the family, their doctor and staff were herded into the cellar together and executed. Their bodies were then taken to a secret location and placed in a hastily dug communal grave, doused in sulphuric acid in an attempt to disfigure them and hinder identification, and then covered over, the location of the grave being lost for more than 70 years.

The Ipatiev House in Yekaterinburg, 1919.

Ironically, the new Russian government had wanted to get the Romanovs out of Russia due to the risk of their becoming a rallying point, but a plan to grant asylum to the Romanovs in the U.K. because of their links with the British royal family fell through, owing to a reluctance on the part of George V to grant it. Yet those links with the British royal family would eventually prove crucial in their identification.

Fast-forward to 1991, when several skeletons were found in a shallow grave some 20 miles from Yekaterinburg. Many of the bones were badly damaged but it was possible to determine, based on examination of the skeletal remains, that there were nine individuals — two short of the 11 killed that night. The faces of the skulls were badly damaged in all of the skeletons, all of them showing evidence of violence either in the form of bullet holes or bayonet wounds or both. Before the genetic study, Russian forensic scientists had used numerous techniques alongside historical data to tentatively identify the remains as some of the members of the Russian royal family, their doctor and servants.

These included examining the bones, to determine approximate age and sex, and some of the teeth, the expensive dental work, incorporating gold, platinum and porcelain, indicating that certain remains must belong to members of an aristocratic family. The team worked out that the two missing individuals would have been two of the children, one of the daughters (while it was hard to determine which one it would be, given how close in age they were, it was thought that it was either Maria or Anastasia) and the son, Prince Alexei.

The Russian chief forensic medical examiner then contacted a team in the U.K., which included Erika, to see if genetic evidence could be used to confirm the identification. The U.K. team used the amelogenin genetic sex test, now part of standard forensic DNA testing, which confirmed the sex of the skeletons (four male and five female bodies), while an early form of DNA profiling showed that there was a family group here — two parents and three children — and four unrelated individuals. So far, so good.

Next, they needed to prove that this was the Russian royal family, and they did this using mitochondrial DNA analysis. As you'll remember, mitochondrial DNA is passed down by a mother to all her children, male and female, but only daughters can pass it on — so if female-line family members of Tsar Nicholas and Tsarina Alexandra could be found and would agree to give a DNA test, their mitochondrial DNA should match that of their royal ancestors. It just so happened that the late Prince Philip, husband of the late Queen Elizabeth, was related to the tsarina through the female line: she was his great-aunt, his maternal grandmother being the sister of the tsarina. He kindly gave a DNA sample.

The testing that they did was standard for the time in that they looked at two regions known as hypervariable regions 1 and 2 (HVR1 and HVR2). You'll remember that mitochondrial DNA has 37 rather crucial genes on it where any "typo" that occurs as the DNA is being copied could have serious consequences if the mutation is deleterious. By contrast, in those parts of the mitochondrial genome that don't code for anything, such as these two hypervariable regions, mutations can occur more freely without necessarily causing issues, meaning that these regions contain much more genetic variation. These are the sections of mitochondrial DNA that scientists began analysing for identification purposes. While it's not as precise as DNA profiling because many thousands of people will all have the same mitochondrial DNA type, it can be very helpful in a case such as this.

Prince Philip's DNA was eventually used to confirm the identities of the lost Romanov family.

When the team sequenced these two regions, Prince Philip's mitochondrial DNA was found to match that of the putative remains of the tsarina and her daughters. Next they found two living female-line relatives of the tsar, descended from his maternal grandmother: a great-great-niece, Princess Xenia Cheremeteff Sfiris, and a first cousin twice removed, James Carnegie, 3rd Duke of Fife. The mitochondrial DNA from these two matched each other perfectly, and they, in turn, matched that of the tsar, except at one base where there was both a match and a mismatch.

This is because the tsar had what's known as a heteroplasmy at this position: some of the mitochondrial DNA sequences showed a T and others showed a C, his maternal relatives showing a T. Heteroplasmy is known to take place primarily through mutations occurring when the DNA is copied to make new cells in a person's lifetime, but it can be inherited from a maternal ancestor with heteroplasmy. Extremely rarely, it can come from paternal mitochondrial DNA making it into the cell. So the fact that heteroplasmy existed in the DNA sample didn't negate the match, and the probability that these were the Romanovs was still between 70 to 1 through to 840,000 to 1 in favour. But, it did sow some seeds of doubt. Incidentally, we now know that heteroplasmy is fairly common, with potentially over half of the human population having at least one heteroplasmy, albeit at a low percentage in terms of their mitochondrial DNA carrying it.

So, to be doubly sure, in 1996 the remains of the tsar's brother, Georgij, who had died in 1899, were exhumed and he was found to have exactly the same mitochondrial heteroplasmy. Given the very low chance of two people having this particular heteroplasmy if they weren't related, this pointed to the mitochondrial DNA data the researchers obtained being 130,000,000 times more likely if these were the Romanovs than if they were an unrelated family.

The case was solved in terms of identifying the tsar, tsarina and three of their daughters, but the mystery still remained as to what had happened to the two other children. In the scientific paper reporting the results, the authors conjectured that possibly the two children had been buried separately, or that they could have survived the massacre. Incidentally, there was a woman living in the U.S. who claimed to be Anastasia, saying she had managed to escape being executed, and so the fact that two of the children were missing from the Romanov family group only fuelled the idea that maybe she truly was the missing princess.

Then, in 2007, a group of amateur archaeologists, digging a mere 70 metres away from the previously discovered mass grave, came across more human remains. Skeletal evidence showed that they were the remains of two bodies, a young woman aged 15-19 and a probable male aged 12-15. DNA analysis was brought to bear and again showed that the two individuals were siblings and related to the Romanovs already identified. As an extra DNA test, Y-chromosome testing was carried out, the Y chromosome being passed from father to son, to confirm that the Y chromosome of the newly found male skeleton was indeed male and that it matched the Y chromosome of the tsar. This also then matched male-line relatives — a second cousin once removed of the tsar (third cousin of Alexei) through Tsar Nicholas I. The missing Romanov children had been found.

Fascinating, compassionate, and entirely captivating, The Secrets of Our DNA is the essential book that explains how genetics has changed and transformed the world around us.

#6367. America’s biggest data centers use nearly as much electricity as an entire state

A study estimates that 403 major U.S. data centers used 82 terawatt-hours of electricity in a year, with natural gas and coal supplying more than half.

Every backed-up photo, every chatbot answer and every streamed show lives somewhere called the cloud, which sounds like nowhere at all. It is a set of windowless warehouses.

At the high end of the estimate, 403 of the largest U.S. data centers together used nearly as much electricity in a year as Indiana uses statewide.

More than half of that electricity came from burning gas and coal.

A team led by the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health and the Harvard Data Science Initiative mapped 403 of these buildings, known as hyperscale data centers.

The researchers then estimated what each one drew from the grid between May 2024 and April 2025.

The totals are estimates built from each building’s electrical capacity, not meter readings.

“Data centers are growing incredibly fast, driven largely by AI, and decisions about where to build them and how to power them are being made right now,” said lead author Gianluca Guidi, a postdoctoral fellow in the Department of Biostatistics.

“But there’s very little facility-level information about their environmental footprint.”

“Our study helps fill that gap,” Guidi added.

Hyperscale data centers are the largest class of data center, the kind that runs cloud services and trains big AI models. The buildings in the sample had an average electrical capacity of about 40 megawatts.

The team started with 675 candidate sites from a commercial database and kept the 403 it could confirm. Each address was matched to a rooftop and its footprint checked against OpenStreetMap.

Then the researchers looked at satellite and aerial images for the signs of a data center: big uniform roofs, cooling equipment and a substation next door.

Virginia had 142 of the 403, more than any other state. Oregon had 56 and Ohio 38.

No data center runs at its full rated capacity every hour, and the companies don’t publish their real loads. So the team multiplied each facility’s capacity by the hours in a year and by a load factor.

The researchers ran four versions of that factor, from a light load to one meant to bracket heavy AI training.

Across the four versions, the 403 facilities used an estimated 68 to 99 terawatt-hours of electricity over the year. The central estimate is about 82 terawatt-hours, or roughly 1.8% of all the electricity the country used.

Indiana, Michigan and Tennessee each use about 100 terawatt-hours a year. So at the high end these warehouses matched a whole state, and even the central estimate covers most of one state’s use.

The central figure is about 3.6 times a 2021 estimate of what hyperscale centers used in 2018. Projections of AI’s appetite for electricity look ahead; this study counts the buildings that exist now.

To work out where the electricity came from, and the power emissions behind it, the team assigned each data center to its regional grid operator.

The team then allocated the data centers’ electricity demand across power plants in each region based on how much electricity each plant generated.

The plant-by-plant generation and emissions figures came from the Environmental Protection Agency.

On that basis, 53.9% of the electricity came from fossil fuels: 38.2% from natural gas and 15.2% from coal.

Nuclear plants supplied 20.9%, and hydro, wind, solar, biomass and geothermal together supplied 25.3%. Nuclear and renewables together fell short of half.

The result was about 25.7 million metric tons (28.3 million U.S. tons) of carbon dioxide under the central version, and 21 to 31 million metric tons across all four.

A 2021 study estimated that U.S. hyperscale data centers were responsible for greenhouse gas emissions equivalent to about 10.5 million metric tons of carbon dioxide in 2018.

Virginia alone accounted for about 21 terawatt-hours, roughly a quarter of the total. Oregon followed with about 11, Ohio with about 9 and Iowa with about 7.

Virginia, Oregon, Ohio and Iowa together made up more than half of the electricity use, so the industry is heavily concentrated.

Oregon’s data centers drew more electricity than Ohio’s. Yet Oregon’s were tied to about 1.3 million metric tons of carbon dioxide and Ohio’s to 2.9 million, because Oregon’s grid runs far cleaner.

The fuel mix behind each state’s grid decides the carbon.

Virginia’s data centers were tied to about 7 million metric tons, the most of any state.

PJM, the grid operator serving Virginia, oversaw the region with the highest data center electricity demand. Its territory spans parts of 13 states and the District of Columbia.

There, about 60% of the attributed electricity came from fossil fuels and 33% from nuclear plants.

The method gives each data center the average fuel mix of its regional power grid. It doesn’t trace which plant physically fed which building.

It also doesn’t count the renewable power contracts some operators sign, unless that power shows up in the regional mix. The authors wrote that the numbers describe the grid, not any company’s performance.

Measured that way, the data centers’ electricity was slightly cleaner than the national average: about 314 grams of carbon dioxide per kilowatt-hour against 348 for the country.

About 23% of the demand, though, sat in regions dirtier than that average.

The data also can’t separate AI work from ordinary cloud computing inside a building. And the 272 candidate sites the team couldn’t verify were left out, so the totals likely run low for the industry as a whole.

Guidi said the picture has already moved on.

“The data center boom hasn’t slowed down since our study period ended in April 2025. New facilities have been built, existing campuses have expanded, and demand for AI computing continues to grow,” he said.

The researchers estimated electricity use and carbon dioxide emissions.

The team plans to examine the health effects next, according to study co-author Francesca Dominici, director of the Harvard Data Science Initiative.

“The fossil fuel power plants in the regional electricity systems associated with this demand also release other pollutants, such as fine particulate matter, nitrogen oxides, and sulfur dioxide, that are directly linked to heart and lung disease and premature death,” Dominici said.

The people who breathe those pollutants live near the power plants, which may be far from any data center.

Earth.com has covered the industry’s other local footprints, from heat zones around server farms to the one in four data centers in water-stressed regions.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Sustainability.
