#6366. House GOP races to lock down new leadership after blue wave

Rep. Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, left, is seen in a House Republican Conference speaker election meeting on Oct. 13, 2023. Now he has his eyes on the minority leader post for the next Congress. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

A sweeping tide of Democratic wins Tuesday left Republicans preparing for a new face atop the House GOP leadership ranks as the party gears up to defend President Donald Trump from a list of investigations.

It’s shaping up to be a battle between sitting Majority Leader Steve Scalise of Louisiana and Judiciary Chairman Jim Jordan of Ohio, pitting two lawmakers Trump has publicly praised against one another.

Speaker Mike Johnson of Louisiana had been trying to stay the course before Republicans dropped a stunning amount of seats, including ones considered deep-red. The cascade of losses, which will give Democrats a sizable majority in the 435-member chamber, forced Johnson to stand down. He told his staff on a Wednesday morning call he would not seek the minority leader job for the next Congress when the GOP conference votes behind closed doors next week.

In a possible sign of what’s to come when the often-raucous conference meets to hear from candidates and vote, some GOP insiders were split Wednesday on which lawmaker should take over as leader.

“It might be Jordan’s for the taking. I think the real fight will be at whip and conference chair,” said one GOP source with ties to each member’s office, granted anonymity to be candid.

In a letter to colleagues Jordan circulated Wednesday, he pitched himself as “battle-tested on the oversight front,” which could help as Democrats go full-tilt on probing the Trump administration. “For too long, we have operated without a clear plan to survive the hour or the day in front of us. That will not cut it against an emboldened and energetic Democrat majority,” Jordan’s letter reads.

But another person familiar with Scalise’s thinking said “his No. 1 goal will be to lead the conference back into the majority,” describing Scalise as a “proven and tested leader who is ready on day one.”

“The conference knows him, how he fights, and that he’s a trusted leader,” the person said.

Spokespersons for Scalise and Johnson did not immediately respond to emails seeking comment on their plans.

Heading into the midterms, it appeared Rep. Tom Emmer of Minnesota, the sitting majority whip, had been working behind the scenes to shore up his standing with House GOP members in a bid to become the No. 2 Republican in January.

Republican Study Committee Chair August Pfluger of Texas has also pitched himself for minority whip, writing in a Wednesday letter to colleagues that he believed his conference needed “fresh ideas” and had “missed many opportunities.”

The scope of Tuesday’s losses had some calling for a completely clean slate, with Rep. Greg Steube, R-Fla., posting a message on social media to House and Senate brass: “Please do us all a favor and step aside so new leadership can take a truly conservative direction.”

“Having Jordan and Emmer in as leadership won’t be much of a change at the top,” the first GOP source said. “But President Trump should want a warrior like Jordan with impeachment experience in charge, given the Democrats will inevitably be pursuing impeachment by August recess despite their disciplined statements to the media pre-election.”

To that end, Maryland Democratic Rep. Jamie Raskin, likely the incoming House Judiciary Committee chairman, said in a brief interview before the chamber adjourned in September to campaign that “there’s a long list of potentially impeachable offenses” to look at from the president, his family members and inner circle.

An aggressive investigatory push by Democrats could make Jordan, in Trump’s eyes, an attractive candidate to lead the conference. Jordan fought hard against Trump’s two first-term impeachments, including with fiery cable news hits that were praised by the TV-focused chief executive.

Whatever happens, it will cap off a rocky ride for Johnson, who claimed the gavel in the tumultuous weeks after Kevin McCarthy was ousted as speaker in October 2023.

In a statement released early Wednesday morning, Johnson did not reveal his next move.

“While the outcome of this midterm is not what we’d hoped and fought for, a new battle is just beginning. This Democrat House majority will be led by the most radical and extreme leftists in American history,” Johnson said. “However, Republicans will never stop fighting to defend the Constitution and protect the foundations that have made America the greatest nation in the history of the world.”

Notably, during a phone interview with Politico late Tuesday night, Trump was asked about Johnson — but did not endorse him for minority leader.

“I think he’s done a very good job,” the president said, his voice hoarse from an October-long rally blitz that did not pay off for his party. “I mean, they’re going to have to make that decision. He’s going to have to make that decision. But he’s a good person and a good man.”

On Wednesday Trump told reporters at the White House he intended to stay out of the coming House GOP leadership race.

While Republicans are eager to avoid repeating the bitter public battles of the past, the fight for minority leader is in some ways a rerun. Both Scalise and Jordan tried for the speaker’s gavel back in 2023 after McCarthy’s sacking but neither landed the job.

A former high school and college wrestler who later coached grappling, Jordan was once considered too much of a firebrand to lead the entire caucus.

“Early on he wasn’t really given the opportunity to show what he’s capable of because of his steadfast conservative positions,” Ray Yonkura, who was Jordan’s chief of staff for a decade and has done political work for him, told CQ Roll Call in October 2023. “He was oftentimes pushed to the side, or different Republican leaders tried to keep him down.”

“Once he was given an opportunity to show what he’s capable of, I think a lot of people realized that this is somebody whose skill set can actually be good in a leadership role,” Yonkura said then.

Jordan has faced questions over the years about what he knew about sexual abuse by a doctor at The Ohio State University when he worked there as an assistant wrestling coach starting in the 1980s. He has repeatedly denied knowing of the abuse, and multiple Republicans told CQ Roll Call in 2023 that it hadn’t factored into their support for Jordan.

As for Scalise, he went through a public ordeal in 2017 when he was shot by a gunman at a GOP baseball practice, sustaining serious injuries. He later was diagnosed with multiple myeloma, a type of blood cancer, and in 2024 said he was in remission.

Beyond the House leadership shuffle ahead of the start of the 120th Congress, G. William Hoagland, a former Senate GOP leadership aide, said there would be a broader battle among Republicans as they analyze their losses and look ahead to 2028.

“I take Steve Bannon’s comment recently seriously that the Republican Party will be engulfed in a civil war over the future of the party,” he said, referring to recent comments from Trump’s former chief 2016 campaign and White House strategist. “Expect that civil war to play out over the next couple of weeks in the midst of all the other legislative issues they have to deal with in the lame-duck session.”

Niels Lesniewski, Savannah Behrmann, Paul Krawczak and Michael Macagnone contributed to this report.

#6365. Unusual warmth has reached the seafloor off Canada’s Pacific coast – and scientists may know why

A seafloor sensor off Vancouver Island logged its highest temperature since monitoring began in 2009, and researchers say El Niño may be behind the spike.

El Niño is usually described as a warming of the surface waters in the tropical Pacific.

This fall, sensors off Canada’s west coast recorded unusually warm water hundreds of feet below the surface.

One seafloor sensor logged its highest temperature since monitoring began there in 2009. The scientists who operate the sensor said the warm pulse is consistent with a strong El Niño.

The sensors are operated by Ocean Networks Canada, an ocean-monitoring initiative of the University of Victoria.

The readings were announced by the organization itself this week. They have not yet been published as a study.

The record was set at a site called Barkley Canyon Upper Slope, off Vancouver Island. A sensor rests on the seafloor there, about 1,300 feet (400 meters) down. That depth is roughly a quarter of a mile.

On November 8, the water at this site reached 46.8°F (8.21°C).

Jay Cullen is the interim president and chief executive of Ocean Networks Canada.

“We’re seeing significant warming not just at the surface, but hundreds of meters below it,” Cullen said.

The November 8 reading was 4.5°F (2.49°C) above the long-term average for the site. It was also 1.6°F (0.89°C) warmer than the previous record, which was set in 2019.

The water has cooled since then, but normal temperatures have not returned. In mid-November, it was still about 2.9°F (1.6°C) warmer than average.

Warm water has been found at other sites too. The Barkley Canyon sensor is one part of a much larger network. Roughly 530 miles (850 kilometers) of seafloor cable connect its five main research sites.

One of those sites is Clayoquot Slope, which lies more than 3,900 feet (1,200 meters) down. Temperatures well above average are being recorded there as well.

Since late summer, sites between 1,300 and 4,100 feet (400 and 1,250 meters) deep have logged record seasonal temperatures.

The deepest site is the exception. At Cascadia Basin, about 8,700 feet (2,650 meters) down, temperatures remain within their usual range.

El Niño was declared by the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration in June.

On November 12, the agency’s Climate Prediction Center said El Niño was still strengthening.

A strong or very strong event was judged likely to continue into early 2027. The chance of that was put at more than 79%.

How can El Niño affect waters off Canada’s Pacific coast?

Steve Mihaly is a senior scientist at Ocean Networks Canada. According to Mihaly, the energy of a strong El Niño travels north from the equatorial Pacific.

It moves as waves that follow the coastline, and oceanographers call them coastal trapped waves.

Sea level has also been above normal since the warm water arrived. The rise was recorded by tide gauges at Bamfield and Tofino, two communities on Vancouver Island.

Pressure recorders on the seafloor picked it up as well. By mid-November, sea level was about 10 inches (25 centimeters) above normal. Local wind and atmospheric effects were accounted for first.

The scientists then attributed about 6 inches (15 centimeters) of the rise to the waves.

At Barkley Canyon Upper Slope, the water temperature began climbing sharply in late October and reached a record on November 8.

Mihaly said northwest winds persisted into the fall, pushing warmer surface water offshore and drawing colder water upward.

This process, known as upwelling, helped mask the warming at depth.

A second network, called VENUS, is run by Ocean Networks Canada in the Salish Sea.

These sheltered waters are shared by British Columbia and Washington State. The VENUS sensors reach depths of about 980 feet (300 meters).

Temperatures in the Strait of Georgia, which is part of that sea, have been above average throughout 2026.

Jordan Watson is the science director of Ocean Networks Canada.

“Since the start of 2026, the VENUS observatory has shown temperatures consistently higher than we’ve previously observed,” Watson said. “And this was before any El Niño effects started to appear.”

Watson described the area as known for migrating salmon, spawning herring, and marine mammals.

Warming from El Niño could add to the already high temperatures there. That would put more stress on marine ecosystems, the organization said.

So far, only temperatures and sea levels have been reported by the scientists. No effects on marine life have been reported yet.

The record is also a short one. Monitoring at Barkley Canyon began in 2009, so it covers less than two decades.

The scientists were not certain about the cause either. They said the warming likely marks the arrival of El Niño’s effects on Canada’s Pacific coast.

Cullen noted that conditions will be monitored closely over the coming months.

A new tool is also being planned by Ocean Networks Canada and CIOOS Pacific, a regional ocean-data group. It will track ocean conditions across the region.

The seafloor data will be combined with measurements from other groups around the Salish Sea.

Fisheries and Oceans Canada and the University of Washington are among them. More details will be shared later this year, the partners said.

Live and long-term readings can be viewed on Ocean Networks Canada’s data dashboard.

#6364. Lucid Dreaming Was Once a Rare Gift. Now Scientists Say They Can Help You Learn It.

Researchers built dreamlike virtual worlds to teach people how to realize they’re dreaming—and it worked.

Some people don’t just dream. They often realize they’re dreaming and can even control the dreamworld, from giving themselves powers that defy the laws of physics to escaping a nightmare by waking themselves up. Lucid dreamers can go on adventures most of us can only dream about (pun intended). But is it possible to train yourself to do the same?

Dreams can happen during any stage of sleep, but they usually occur during REM sleep. When dreamers suddenly become aware that they’re dreaming, they’re in a lucid state. However, people who frequently have lucid dreams are rare. Researchers from the University of Trento in Rovereto, Italy, wanted to find out whether standard exercises, meditation, and virtual reality could teach people to have lucid dreams. Participants in the experimental group practiced open monitoring meditation, which is meant to sharpen sensory awareness and perception through nonjudgmental observation. They then did VR training that took them into virtual worlds full of bizarre, dreamlike scenarios. For comparison, a control group used VR that had nothing to do with dreaming, while a third group did only the standard training, without VR.

All participants started with the same baseline training, which they did while awake to practice dream recall and reality checks. They were told to keep a dream diary, noting each morning whether they remembered any dreams and, if so, what the dreams were about. Participants were also told to do reality checks, such as pinching themselves, to test whether they were awake or dreaming. They did these checks whenever they ran into something strange or simply thought of something strange. On top of that, phone alarms went off every hour for 12 hours each day to prompt more checks. The idea was that the habit would eventually carry over into their dreams. On top of this training, the experimental group did open monitoring meditation sessions in the lab to prepare for their VR training. During these sessions, participants observed their breathing, bodily sensations, thoughts, and emotions without reacting to them. Each session also included a guided exploration of an environment designed to look like a scene from a dream.

“Through repetition, [reality checks] are intended to become habitual and to transfer into dreams via ‘dream residue,’ where they may be triggered by dream signs that are unusual, surprising, or incongruent events, and thereby precipitate insight into the dream state,” the researchers wrote in their study, recently published in Frontiers in Psychology.

To build these scenes, the researchers created LucidDreamingVR, a program inspired by Tibetan dream yoga. Unlike the VR control group, whose content had nothing to do with dreaming, the experimental group completed eight sessions that grew steadily more elaborate, taking participants from recognizing a dream to controlling one. The early tasks taught them to spot dream signs: the virtual surroundings would suddenly shift, cueing a reality check, much as an odd detail might inside a dream. Later sessions drew on dream yoga techniques to let participants rehearse what they might do once they became lucid. With a single spoken command, they could fly, leap to incredible heights or, like Alice after tumbling down the rabbit hole, grow and shrink at will.

The researchers counted both lucid and semi-lucid dreams as “lucid-like” dreams. By the end of the experiment, 11 of the 13 participants who had trained with LucidDreamingVR had reported at least one lucid-like dream. By contrast, eight of 13 people in the control group without VR and only four of 12 in the VR control group reported one. Nearly 12% of the dreams the experimental group remembered were lucid-like, compared with about 3% for the control group without VR and about 1% for the VR control group. Surprisingly, the LucidDreamingVR group remembered the fewest dreams overall, so they also reported the fewest ordinary, non-lucid dreams. These results suggest that combining open monitoring meditation with dream-themed VR may increase lucid dreaming. However, because neither control group meditated, the study can’t show which part of the training mattered more.

“[Our] findings support the use of immersive environments as…cognitive-enhancement tools,” the researchers said. “Future work should combine VR-based rehearsal with objective sleep verification, factorial designs, and waking cognitive measures to clarify mechanism, specificity, and transfer.”

She lurks right outside New York City with her parrot, Lestat. When not writing, she can be found drawing, playing the piano or shapeshifting.

#6363. This magic mushroom can kill

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Hallucinogens and poisons have never been found in the same mushroom — until now

Meet the dark magic mushroom, Galerina indica. The tiny fungus makes both a hallucinogen and a deadly toxin.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

People who eat this tiny magic mushroom may hit a lethal low instead of getting high.

The fungus makes hallucinogenic psilocybin and deadly amatoxin, researchers report November 11 in Current Biology. Dubbed “dark magic mushrooms,” it is the first species of fungus discovered to make both types of compounds.

Chemist and fungal biologist Andrew Kunik found the dark magic mushroom in 2025 growing on a decaying moss-covered palm trunk in a central Florida wetland. Kunik, who was then doing post-baccalaureate research in the lab of fungal biologist Matthew Smith at the University of Florida in Gainesville, identified the mini mushroom as Galerina indica.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

That species had not been reported in Florida before, Kunik says. “It’s quite rare and unusual.” He also found two other new related species, tagged with the placeholder names Galerina species 1 and Galerina species 2.

Other researchers had previously described G. indica’s appearance and found DNA signatures that distinguish the fungus from related species. But no one had cataloged the mushroom’s complete chemical or genetic makeup.

Related Galerina species make amatoxins, deadly chemicals that can kill in even tiny amounts and are found in death cap mushrooms and other species. Kunik and colleagues looked for those toxins in G. indica and the two other new Galerina species. G. indica makes a previously undiscovered form of amatoxin the team is calling alpha-proamanitin, the chemical analysis revealed.

The small mushroom also had blue bruises, a clue that it might make psilocybin, a psychedelic chemical being tested as a treatment for mental health disorders. Fungi usually make either amatoxin or psilocybin. Not both. Galerina species 1 also makes psilocybin but doesn’t make amatoxin, and species 2 makes neither.

“This finding shows that there’s a lot more diversity in [fungal] chemistry and the ways that they’re combined than we had really thought about,” says Anne Pringle, a mycologist at the University of Wisconsin–Madison who was not involved in the work.

Discovering these dual compounds in one mushroom was both exciting and required further analysis to confirm, Kunik says. “Surprising discoveries require great depth of evidence,” he says.

A complete workup of the mushroom’s DNA revealed genes for producing both types of chemicals. Ancestors of these dark magic mushrooms probably picked up those genes by swapping DNA with other species. Such DNA swapping, called horizontal gene transfer, is one way that organisms can quickly evolve new traits, like when bacteria exchange antibiotic resistance genes with unrelated species.

Ancestors of G. indica and its relatives probably acquired amatoxin genes early on. Those toxins are made by many of G. indica’s cousins, which indicates that amatoxins are probably heirlooms passed down from common ancestors. Ancestors of species 1 and species 2 seem to have dropped the amatoxin genes at some point since they no longer make the compounds.

The two psilocybin-producing species may have independently obtained the psychedelic genes in separate DNA swap meets, or a common ancestor may have picked up the genes and then passed them down to G. indica and species 1. There’s not enough known about the fungi’s family tree to sort out which scenario is correct.

And there’s another unsolved evolutionary mystery, Pringle says. “We still don’t know why mushrooms are poisonous.” Many scientists think it is for defending against predators, but hard evidence is lacking, she says.

“Can I eat it?” is often the first question people ask when finding a new mushroom, Pringle says. “I’m always so uncomfortable with that question and that conversation. And this paper confirms that, in fact, you should be uncomfortable.” After all, eating these dark magic mushrooms could send people tripping into the grave.

#6362. Howler monkey droppings hold clues about the fragmented forests they live in

In southern Mexico, the mix of gut bacteria in howler monkeys varied with forest patch size, the trees growing there, and how well the patches were connected.

Howler monkeys can survive in small patches of forest.

A study in southern Mexico found that the mix of bacteria in their guts varied with the size of those patches, the trees growing there, and how well the patches were connected.

Researchers found these patterns in droppings from adult male mantled howler monkeys.

Repeating that sampling could help conservationists track changes over time without capturing the animals.

The study was led by Tabor Whitney while she was a doctoral student at Northwestern University. She worked with primate researchers at Universidad Veracruzana in Mexico.

The work was carried out in the Los Tuxtlas Biosphere Reserve in the state of Veracruz. About 60% of the original forest cover in the reserve has been lost. The remaining forest is broken into patches among pastures, farm fields, and towns.

The 10 study patches ranged from about 5 acres to nearly 500 acres (2 to 199 hectares). Farmland or pasture bordered every one of them.

Whitney and field assistants followed adult male howlers in October and November, during the 2022 rainy season. When a male defecated, the fresh droppings were collected from the ground with sterile sticks.

The team tested the droppings for three things. The first was the bacteria in them. The second was the fatty acids that those bacteria produce. The third was the breakdown products of stress hormones.

The trees in every patch were also measured. Across patches, average trunk width ranged from about 10 to 16 inches (25 to 42 centimeters).

Biologists call the community of microbes in an animal’s gut its microbiome.

“An awesome takeaway of the study is the knowledge the gut microbiome is the most sensitive to ecological change,” Whitney said.

Gut bacteria were analyzed in 41 samples from 32 males. Monkeys from different patches carried different mixes of bacteria.

These differences were linked to all four measures of a patch’s size and layout. Its area and its distance from other forest were among those measures. All seven measures of the trees growing in the patch were linked to the differences too.

Plant fiber is digested by some of the bacteria involved. One such group is Prevotella, and monkeys in larger patches carried more of it.

A different group of bacteria was most common where trees were small. The same was true where few rows of trees linked a patch to other forest.

Only one forest measure predicted the diversity of bacteria carried by a monkey. That measure was trunk thickness. Less variety was found in monkeys from patches with thicker-trunked trees.

The authors suggested that monkeys in mature forest may eat a narrower diet. Fewer kinds of microbes may be taken in as a result.

The team also tested distances to the nearest houses and roads. Neither distance predicted any of the three health measures in the main analysis.

Stress hormone levels were measured in 36 males. They didn’t differ clearly from patch to patch. One pattern, however, was the reverse of what the team had predicted.

Males in larger patches tended to have higher hormone levels, not lower ones.

Higher levels were also found in patches with more fig trees. Figs are a central part of the howler diet.

The authors explained the result in social terms. Several howler groups are supported by larger patches. More than one group may be attracted to the same place by fig trees.

Hormone levels could be raised by competition during encounters with rival groups, not by food shortage. Ordinary demands such as reproduction and fighting infection are also known to raise these hormones.

A monkey with a high level is therefore not necessarily in trouble.

Plant fiber is fermented by gut bacteria, and small fatty acids are released in the process.

Those acids are used by the animal for energy. These acids also help maintain the gut lining and the immune system.

No difference between patches was found in the amounts of these acids. Instead, the team’s attention was drawn to the balance between propionate and butyrate, two of the acids.

A surplus of propionate over butyrate has been proposed as a sign of an unbalanced gut. That pattern has been documented both in people and in wild primates that are short of food.

More propionate than butyrate was present in the droppings from all 10 patches.

In four of the 10 forest patches, the ratio of propionate to butyrate was about 2.6 or higher.

Human studies have linked that threshold to gut disorders. Whether it signals a health problem in howler monkeys remains unknown.

The authors wrote that a reduction in butyrate-producing bacteria may be indicated by the pattern. The reduction may extend across the whole landscape.

The researchers also raised the possibility of long-term effects on the monkeys’ gut lining and immune function.

Howlers in southern Mexico suffered a mass die-off in 2024. Up to 31% of some local populations died from the combined effects of extreme heat, drought, and habitat degradation.

Baseline health records are needed if early warning signs of decline are to be detected, the authors wrote.

Two conservation priorities were recommended by the authors. Patches of mature, varied forest should be protected and enlarged. Rows of trees and wooded strips along rivers should keep those patches connected.

The researchers also suggested that a wider variety of trees be planted, including fruiting species. Howlers would then be able to move through the canopy in search of food and mates.

Permission from local landowners was needed before the team could reach the monkeys.

“Landowners we’ve spoken with are really open to these conversations,” Whitney said.

“They’ve said they love seeing the monkeys, and if they can help them travel on the trees, they’re very interested in it.”

She said the same sampling could be repeated every five or 10 years. Changes could then be compared over time, and the effect of conservation work could be checked.

Every sample came from an adult male. All of the samples were collected in a single rainy season.

Female and young howlers have different energy and hormone demands. The results therefore can’t be assumed to apply to them.

The gut bacteria samples were also limited and unevenly distributed across patches. Some patches supplied one sample, while others supplied as many as 12.

The team identified which bacteria were present. What those bacteria were doing inside the monkeys was not measured.

The study found links between forest features and gut bacteria.

Further research could test whether changes to the forest lead to changes in the monkeys’ gut bacteria.

The authors also noted that forests across Los Tuxtlas may be too uniformly degraded.

That could explain why the fatty acids varied so little. Comparisons with other landscapes are needed, they wrote.

Future research could pair repeated sampling with long-term records of the monkeys’ behavior. Such work could test whether these signals change as the forest does.

The team is now preparing a study comparing the gut bacteria of male and female howlers.

The full study was published in the journal Animal Conservation.

Think that cows are the king of flatulence? There's another animal that likely blows the competition away.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Flatology, the study of flatulence, sounds more like a joke than a serious scientific discipline. But studying farts actually helps biologists understand an animal's diet and digestion.

We know that a host of creatures ‪—​​ from whales, to snakes, to sloths ‪— pass gas. But do we know which animal is the top tooter? Experts told Live Science the answer is blowing in the wind.

"Getting quantitative measurements for farts per animal is pretty difficult," Nick Caruso, a data scientist and co-author of '"Does It Fart?: The Definitive Field Guide to Animal Flatulence'' (Quercus Publishing, 2017), told Live Science in an email.

What we can do is hypothesize using the data we do have. Expelled gas is made partially of methane, so comparing methane emissions produced by different species may provide a clue. However, this method does have limitations, experts pointed out.

Researchers measure the methane animals produce by placing them inside respiration chambers, then inserting a capsule into the stomach that releases a tracer gas while strapping them with a harness that samples their breath. Alternatively, they capture their breath at stations where they feed or are milked.

Research points to livestock, especially cows, as major methane emitters. A recent report puts their total methane emissions at 117 teragrams per year. (One teragram is equal to 1 billion kilograms, or 2.2 billion pounds.) A buildup of cow-generated methane gas even caused a dairy shed in Germany to explode. However, contrary to what many people believe, the "overwhelming majority" of methane emissions from livestock is released through burping, not flatulence, Ermias Kebreab, a professor of animal science at the University of California, Davis, told Live Science in an email.

The reason comes down to where in the gut the gas is made. Herbivores can't break down plant material on their own; they rely on microbes in their guts to ferment it, and that fermentation releases gases such as methane and carbon dioxide, Dr. Marcus Clauss, head of research and co-director of the Clinic for Zoo Animals, Exotic Pets and Wildlife at the University of Zurich, told Live Science in an email. Some of this gas is absorbed into the bloodstream and exhaled. The rest tends to leave by the nearest exit ‪—‬ animals that ferment their food toward the front of the digestive tract mostly burp it out, while those that ferment it toward the back mostly pass it as wind, Clauss explained.

Feed your curiosity with an exclusive mystery every week, solved with science and delivered direct to your inbox before it's seen anywhere else.

Cows and other ruminants ‪(such as buffalo, sheep, goats and camels)‬ ferment their food in a chamber called the rumen, located near the front of the digestive system, so most of the methane they produce is through belching, Matthew Hayek, an associate professor of environmental studies at New York University, told Live Science in an email.

So if it's not cows, which animal is the top farter based on their methane emissions? The best candidates are hindgut fermenters ‪—‬ herbivores that digest plant matter in the large intestine (the hindgut). Meat eaters, by contrast, typically produce far less methane than herbivores do, Clauss said.

Are cows really the top contender for animal farts?

One possible contender are termites, which break down wood and grass in their hindguts. Their global population is estimated to be around 27 quadrillion (that's 15 zeros) individuals, and they collectively emit 10 teragrams of methane per year.

But, per individual, the title might go to horses. According to a 2019 report from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, horses have the highest methane emissions among hindgut fermenters — around 40 pounds (18 kg) of methane per horse each year.

However, Clauss is skeptical. "The ranking of horse as highest is only because it has been measured," he told Live Science in an email. "But there are so many hindgut fermenters not measured, like rhino ... Who knows?"

If we consider methane emissions per unit of bodyweight, the nutria (Myocastor coypus) ‪—‬ an herbivorous, semiaquatic rodent ‪—‬ would have higher methane emissions than the horse, Clauss said.

Clauss also questioned the accuracy of using methane emissions data as an indicator of flatulence. "There is some methane in flatulence, but most likely the majority of methane produced by an animal is exhaled, i.e. it goes via blood to the lungs," he said.

So until scientists figure out how to measure animal farts, any ranking remains speculative. For now, scientists have developed ways to track intestinal gas in people, including swallowable electronic capsules that measure gases inside the gut and clip-on underwear sensors that detect hydrogen in farts.

Methane is a particularly potent greenhouse gas when released into the atmosphere, and the quantities that large herds of cows and other ruminants emit through burping are enough to contribute to climate change. Indeed, scientists are experimenting with ways to reduce methane emissions from cattle — for example, by adding seaweed to their diet.

But animal flatulence is not a major contributor to global methane increases, Hayek said.

Even methane emissions from termite flatulence, while large, do not have an impact, Stefan Arndt, a professor of physiological and ecosystem ecology at the University of Melbourne in Australia, told Live Science in an email. "A large proportion of that methane is then consumed by methanotrophic bacteria in the soil," he said. These bacteria use methane as an energy source, thereby reducing the net methane emissions from termites substantially.

"Their emissions are part of the natural cycle of methane that has always been there for millennia," Arndt added. "The increasing methane concentrations in the atmosphere that are leading to climate change are caused by humans."

Clarissa Brincat is a freelance writer specializing in health and medical research. After completing an MSc in chemistry, she realized she would rather write about science than do it. She learned how to edit scientific papers in a stint as a chemistry copyeditor, before moving on to a medical writer role at a healthcare company. Writing for doctors and experts has its rewards, but Clarissa wanted to communicate with a wider audience, which naturally led her to freelance health and science writing. #6360. Wildfire smoke is making two kinds of air pollution spike together

As wildfire smoke travels across the U.S., fine particle pollution and ground-level ozone are more often spiking on the same day.

Two air pollutants are reaching unusually high levels on the same days more often across the contiguous United States. A new study links that rise to wildfire smoke.

The research comes from a team at the Penn State College of Earth and Mineral Sciences. Researchers in the Department of Geography looked at public data from 48 states.

They studied the co-occurrence of fine particulate matter (PM2.5) and ground-level ozone.

PM2.5 includes microscopic soot, ash, and other inhalable particles.

Ground-level ozone forms when nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds react in sunlight.

Intensified by wildfires, vehicle emissions, and other sources, the pollutants are often evaluated separately.

Exposure to both pollutants at once may increase risks to the heart and lungs.

Starting in 2011, wildfire smoke was more often present on days when both pollutants spiked across large parts of the country.

During many of these widespread pollution episodes, both PM2.5 and ground-level ozone exceeded U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) thresholds.

The study did not evaluate individual health impacts. But researchers assessed high-level regional and national pollutant patterns known to affect health.

Increases in the combined pollutant levels appeared alongside steady growth in summertime wildfire smoke. They were most dramatic in the eastern half of the country.

The analysis incorporated observations from 2004 to 2023.

The researchers merged EPA monitoring data, satellite smoke mapping from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, and a blend of weather information.

“We’ve been experiencing many summertime instances when wildfire smoke from the western U.S. or Canada has traveled into large parts of the eastern U.S., especially the Northeast,” said lead author Manzhu Yu from Penn State.

Researchers found growing odds of combined pollution hazards across the continental U.S.

In the West, the likelihood of both pollutants spiking on the same day during summer wildfire smoke events roughly doubled over the study period.

Those risks may move progressively eastward.

The paper’s overall findings may help public health researchers and clinicians study, evaluate, and prevent emerging health risks through a regional lens.

Yu said she is especially interested in the eastern U.S. Its smoke comes from several sources, not only the large wildfires in the West.

Regional smoke sources include prescribed burns, such as those to clear acreage for agriculture or general land management. Local wildfires are another source.

The distinct smoke types occasionally overlap, deepening health concerns.

Different smoke carries distinct components. These range from inorganic and organic carbon to heavy metals and influence PM2.5 co-occurrence with ozone.

“We are particularly curious about the links among smoke composition and cardiorespiratory ailments, which involve the heart, blood vessels, and lungs,” Yu said.

A larger goal at Penn State is to understand future wildfire risks and impacts in the eastern U.S.

“I can’t say we’re excited about the work – it’s not good news,” said co-author Erica Smithwick from Penn State.

“People have underestimated the effect of wildfire smoke in this region. But we are pleased to see progress in mapping out and estimating risk factors because of the impact on human health.”

The analysis should help local and regional decisionmakers plan for hazardous smoke conditions. That includes risk-reducing steps at public schools, in older buildings, and for people with medical vulnerabilities.

“In ongoing research elsewhere, we’re learning more about longer-term exposures to air pollution,”  Smithwick said.

“It may affect everything from acute stressors such as sore throats and eye irritation to longer-term effects like mental health and dementia.”

“We’re hoping that evidence-based information about the increase in compound pollutant exposures will help prioritize decision-making around mitigation and resilience to those stressors.”

Air pollution from wildfires historically centered in the western U.S. But longer-range distribution of western and Canadian smoke from bigger fires is posing sharply higher co-occurrence risks.

That now includes the Midwest and Ohio Valley, in addition to the Northeast.

During the study period, researchers found 2012, 2018, 2021, and 2023 were peak years for co-occurrence of the pollutants nationally.

They also determined that widespread co-occurrence days became more frequent, persistent, and intense.

A widespread day is when both pollutants exceed local 90th percentiles over more than 10% of the country.

For each pollutant, the local 90th percentile is the concentration that about 90% of daily values in that area fall below.

Light to moderate smoke raises co-occurrence risks. It introduces particulate organic compounds and nitrogen oxides that promote ozone production.

At the same time, more dense smoke can limit ozone production by blocking sunlight.

To predict the likelihood of combined pollution extremes, the researchers created a machine-learning model. They call it the Spatiotemporal Bayesian Neural Field.

Their model combines the effects of smoke, ground-level pollution, and weather patterns to establish risk.

Parts of the West have fire seasons more than a month longer than they were 35 years ago.

Estimated carbon emissions from forest fires grew 60% globally from 2001 to 2023, according to NASA.

Researchers attributed the changing fire conditions largely to global warming and a drier climate.

“We need to think about community awareness and community perception around smoke and have people be aware of the ecosystems they’re living in,” Smithwick said.

“There should be a general awareness of when not to burn a debris pile in your backyard, or when to be more careful with a campfire because of heightened risks.”

“We want to work with municipalities and communities to think about the educational backbone of this work.”

The study is published in the journal Environmental Science & Technology.

#6359. ‘I’ll be reelected as majority leader,’ Schumer says

Senate Minority Leader Charles Schumer speaks outside the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee in Washington on Wednesday about his party’s big night. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

As Democrats look ahead to their new Senate majority for the next Congress, their current leader Charles E. Schumer made a prediction on Wednesday: “I’ll be reelected as majority leader.”

Schumer, a Democrat from New York, would be helming a larger caucus than most anticipated, ranging from 54 to 56 seats after the dust settles from Tuesday’s wins.

Not all the new incoming members say they will support the 75-year-old, and some have called for new blood. But so far, no formidable opponent has emerged.

“The issue is not me,” Schumer told reporters outside the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee headquarters on Wednesday morning when asked about working with those new senators. “The issue is focusing on the American people and what they want.”

The leadership election for Senate Democrats will likely take place in early December and include the senators-elect in a secret ballot race.

Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, who won a Senate election against Republican Michele Tafoya, told NBC’s Meet the Press NOW in August, “I think it is time for new leadership,” when asked if she’d support Schumer.

She reupped that sentiment on a Wednesday press call, saying, “Many of us were elected who refused corporate PAC money, who are beholden only to the people who elected us, and are ready to fight for bold change. And so I think it’s time for new leadership.”

Schumer has served in both the minority and majority as Democratic leader after landing the job in 2017 when then-leader Harry Reid retired. He faces reelection in 2028.

Former state Senate President Troy Jackson of Maine, the Democrat who defeated Republican Sen. Susan Collins in her bid for a sixth term, told reporters on Monday, “I’ve already said that I told Sen. Schumer that I’m gonna support somebody else. It’s no different now.”

He said he would push Schumer to deliver on health care changes like “Medicare for All.”

Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas of New Hampshire, who bested John Sununu in his bid to return to the Senate, said in an interview last week that “it’s very clear voters are hungry for new voices at the table and for a new generation of leadership in the Senate.”

“I’ve heard that throughout this campaign. I think above all, people want folks who understand the challenges out there and are going to fight with the urgency that these challenges deserve,” he said. “Too often, we’ve seen leadership flat-footed.”

His campaign did not immediately respond to questions Wednesday about whether that was indicative of his support for Schumer.

Democrat Adam Hamilton, the pastor of the nation’s largest United Methodist church who unseated Republican Sen. Roger Marshall in Kansas, told CNN in September: “I’m not supporting Schumer for leader.”

“I mean no disrespect for Chuck Schumer, but we need new leadership. We need new, younger leadership, young blood. I don’t mean just age, but people who are bringing fresh ideas and fresh leadership,” he said. “We’ve got to have leaders that can unite us, bring us together. Not just Democrats, but bring together Democrats and Republicans to solve real problems.”

“I think people are frustrated with the gridlock and the sense that people are not working together,” he added, pointing to Democrats blocking the farm bill in the Senate Agriculture Committee earlier this year.

Abdul El-Sayed, who defeated Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers in Michigan, told MS NOW earlier this fall he would want to support Maryland Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen as leader.

“I would definitely support Sen. Chris Van Hollen and I would love to see him as Senate majority leader,” he said.

Van Hollen is seen as a presidential contender, and has been “kicking the tires” on 2028 instead of Senate leadership when he’s been asked.

El-Sayed told NBC’s Today Show on Wednesday, just hours after his race was called, “We need action. We need leadership toward that action. I’m interested to see, working with our caucus, to see what options we’ve got,” saying he hopes there is “two or more options” but not mentioning Van Hollen.

“I’m going to vote for the option that gives me the best chance at getting money out of politics, money in pockets, and Medicare for All,” he said.

Illinois Lt. Gov. Juliana Stratton made it part of her Senate primary pitch earlier this year that she was the only Democrat in the race who didn’t support Schumer. “I’ve made it clear that I would not support Chuck Schumer as leader of the Democratic caucus because I think right now what I’m hearing from voters all across the state of Illinois is that they are fed up. They’re fed up with what’s happening in Washington,” she told political YouTube commentator Jack Cocchiarella in March.

A spokesperson for Stratton’s campaign reiterated Wednesday her position hasn’t changed. The campaigns of El-Sayed, Hamilton and Jackson did not immediately respond to questions Wednesday about their stances.

Even if some candidates were eager to distance themselves from establishment Democrats on the campaign trail before facing voters, it’s hard to deny that Schumer helped bring home a resounding victory for Democrats on Tuesday night.

So far, among Democratic incumbents, it’s not clear anyone would have the appetite to challenge Schumer, who flexed his political prowess and recruited several of the key flips last night, like former and incoming Sen. Sherrod Brown, who beat Sen. Jon Husted in Ohio to recapture the state for Democrats.

Having prevailed in a special election, Brown is expected to be seated before the end of the year.

A Democratic staffer familiar with the current mood of the caucus predicted: “Nope. Schumer will be the leader,” when asked if there was any serious challenger.

Former Senate Democratic leader Tom Daschle of South Dakota had a similar prediction. “Given the big night Senate Democrats had, I doubt anyone will challenge him. But some new members may withhold their vote, in keeping with their campaign comments,” Daschle said.

Schumer on Wednesday said Democrats will be united in addressing costs for the American people with what he described as “an amazing crop of new senators” and a “generational remake of the Senate map that is going to change America not only now, but on into the future.”

“These voters did not give us the majority so we can do whatever we want. They entrusted us with the majority to do what they, the American people, want,” he said. “Republicans received that opportunity two years ago and completely squandered it. The GOP misread Americans’ demand for change as a mandate to do Trump’s self-serving bidding, and Trump spent half his time talking about things that were irrelevant to their lives.”

#6357. What happened when scientists kept birds and bats away from cocoa trees?

An experiment on cocoa farms in the Peruvian Amazon reveals how nearby trees, birds, and bats can help protect the harvest.

In the Peruvian Amazon, the trees beyond a cocoa farm can help determine how much cocoa it produces.

Farms surrounded by forests, orchards, and other tree crops had some of the highest yields in a new study, and an experiment pointed to an unlikely pair of allies: birds and bats.

To find out how much those animals mattered, researchers put nets around some cocoa trees and left others open.

Where forests covered 30–35% of the surrounding landscape, the cocoa trees that birds and bats could reach produced nearly twice as much as the netted trees.

An international team led by the University of Vienna mapped the connections between shade trees, wildlife, and cocoa productivity across 28 organic agroforests in the northern Peruvian Amazon.

The researchers estimated that cocoa trees accessible to birds and bats would yield about 265 kilograms per hectare per year where trees covered roughly 20% of the surrounding landscape.

Where surrounding tree cover reached 70–80%, the estimated yield was nearly four times as high, at about 1,000 kilograms per hectare per year.

At 2023 cocoa prices, the researchers valued the extra cocoa associated with bird and bat activity at about US$1,640 per hectare per year.

For smallholder farmers in a region where average incomes are modest, that’s not a rounding error. It’s the difference between scraping by and building something.

“Birds and bats can be powerful allies for cacao farmers, but only if the surrounding landscape provides enough habitat. If these landscapes become large monocultures, much of this natural pest-control benefit is lost,” said senior author Bea Maas from the University of Vienna.

The intuitive assumption – more shade trees, more biodiversity, better farm – doesn’t hold up cleanly.

Shade-tree cover benefitted wildlife, improved soils, and buffered temperature extremes. But very dense shade starved the cocoa of light and substantially cut yields.

On farms in tree-rich landscapes, a mix of tall and short shade trees helped support biodiversity.

Dense shade, meanwhile, reduced cocoa yields by limiting sunlight.

“Our data show that cacao farms do not need uniform shade to support biodiversity. A mosaic of tall and short trees, tree clusters and open patches can create habitat for wildlife while maintaining production,” said lead author Aycart-Lazo from the University of Vienna.

The researchers surveyed birds, bats, and arthropods. They measured cocoa yield, natural pest control, pollination rates, pest and disease incidence, soil fertility, and microclimate.

Then they used drone imagery and remote-sensing data to connect what was happening inside each farm to what the surrounding landscape looked like.

The finding that probably matters most for policy is this: what’s outside the farm fence may be more important than what’s inside it.

A farmer can do everything right on their own plot and still lose most of the pest-control benefit if the surrounding land has been stripped bare.

This is an uncomfortable truth for programs that focus exclusively on farm-level certification.

A certified organic plot in a deforested landscape doesn’t get the same ecosystem services as one embedded in a matrix of forests and orchards.

“Our results show that these benefits depend strongly on how trees are managed both within farms and across the surrounding landscape,” Aycart-Lazo said.

The team proposes a landscape-level formula for the region: roughly 30–35% forest cover, another 40–45% in tree-based habitats like agroforests or orchards, and 20–30% in open areas for annual crops.

That mix, they argue, could create multifunctional landscapes that sustain both high biodiversity and strong cocoa production.

This is a recommendation though, not a decree. Different regions have different land pressures, different communities, and different histories.

“This is not a one-size-fits-all blueprint. Landscape strategies need to be adapted to local land availability and developed together with local communities,” Ocampo-Ariza said.

The study was conducted in one of the world’s most biodiverse regions. The specifics belong to the northern Peruvian Amazon.

But the underlying logic is portable. Wherever crops depend on natural pest control, the surrounding habitat either supports or undermines it.

The study cuts against a stubborn narrative in tropical agriculture – that farmers must choose between productivity and conservation. The data from these 28 Peruvian farms suggest the opposite.

Biodiversity didn’t just coexist with cocoa production. It actively drove it.

The ecosystem services provided by wildlife – pest control above all – were the mechanism converting habitat into yield.

That doesn’t mean conservation is free. Managing a structurally varied canopy takes skill.

Maintaining landscape-level forest cover requires coordination across farms, communities, and governments. But the economic argument is now harder to wave away.

For cocoa growers, keeping forests nearby can help protect the harvest.

The study is published in the journal Communications Earth & Environment.

After nine days in space, the Artemis II crewmembers faced their final and riskiest challenge: splashdown. In this excerpt from the book "Earthrise: Inside Artemis II, the Groundbreaking Human Mission into Deep Space," astronaut Jeremy Hansen describes the moment from his chair.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

After nine days in space, the four crewmembers of NASA's Artemis II mission looked out their capsule window on April 10, 2026, and saw the bright-blue Earth below them. The crew had traveled more than 250,000 miles (400,000 kilometers) from our planet — farther from Earth than any humans had ever gone — and now, home was just a few hundred miles straight down.

Only one milestone remained: splashdown, a fast and fiery plunge into the Pacific Ocean that would mark the end of humanity's first crewed mission to the moon in more than 50 years.Mission specialist Jeremy Hansen, the lone Canadian Space Agency astronaut on the crew, had every reason to be confident that the team's Orion crew capsule would hold up just fine. But this was Hansen's first time in space, and his first time dropping through the sky like a fireball at 24,600 mph (39,600 kmh).

It wasn't that he was afraid for himself, Hansen explains in "Earthrise: Inside Artemis II, the Groundbreaking Human Mission into Deep Space" (Hanover Square Press, 2026), which he co-wrote with John Larsen). Rather, he knew that his wife Catherine and three children would be among the millions of Earthlings watching the most dangerous moment of his mission from below.

In this excerpt from the book, Hansen describes the thrilling intensity of splashdown and the euphoria of knowing that he and his crewmates were going to make it back safely — and make history.

CSA astronaut Jeremy Hansen smiles inside the Orion crew capsule during the Artemis II lunar flyby.

Immediately after jettisoning the European Service Module, and exactly half an hour before we were due to splashdown, Mission Control initiated the crew module raise burn. This nineteen-second burn was the first and only burn using the small thrusters built into our Orion capsule. It slightly shallowed our entry trajectory to put us right in the sweet spot while also providing some added distance from the service module, as we'd be hitting the atmosphere in near succession. It, too, went flawlessly. I tightened my straps; it was time for the fireworks.

A re-entry into the Earth's atmosphere is absolutely on the short list of the most incredible experiences of my life. We slammed into it at 7:53 p.m., thundering down at over 10 kilometres [6.2 miles] per second. Per second.

The thrusters fired almost constantly to stabilize the capsule: loud thuds, as if Thor himself were hammering on our spacecraft, as the G-forces quickly began to build, aggressively scrubbing off the velocity we had added to our rocket nine days earlier. Within seconds, we saw plasma forming outside our windows, and the heat at the base of our capsule grew so intense that flames soon engulfed us. It started red and transformed into a bright, bluish-green, pulsating light. It was breathtaking, the bright colors igniting our senses.

It was insane to think about what we were doing. We all knew how this worked; we all knew the science. But deep inside, I also recognized that astronauts must have a screw loose to do this. Nobody in their right mind would strap themselves inside a metal canister that itself was sitting inside a giant fireball. But there was no other way down, and I had accepted the realities of this journey long in advance.

Although I was at peace, I felt guilty for the stress I was putting on my family. I had talked to them openly about the mission's risks, and this was the highest-risk moment. I tried to send my love telepathically, telling them it was going great.

The Orion capsule drops toward the Pacific Ocean with all parachutes successfully deployed.

As we continued our freefall, it looked like a thousand camera flashes were exploding inside Integrity. I lowered the sun visor on my helmet. There were only centimeters of heatshield and aluminum separating me from the more than 2500°C heat outside. Almost instantly, the heat inside our cramped home also began to rise, an increase that engineers refer to as "thermally benign." All I know is that I couldn't feel it, blissfully wrapped in my thermally controlled garments.

As we continued to fall, the G-forces built up to nearly four times the pressure we feel on Earth. I wasn't too worried, having endured more than five minutes of the same G-force, or more, in the NASA centrifuge trainer. I had half-expected the freefall back to Earth to seem short, but it was a long six minutes before the flames finally ceased and we re-established communications with Mission Control.

It had already been a wild ride, but I also knew another crazy part — parachute deployment and the actual splashdown — lay ahead. My adrenalin kept pumping.

Within seconds, we saw plasma forming outside our windows, and the heat at the base of our capsule grew so intense that flames soon engulfed us.

"Integrity, Houston. Comms check, post-blackout," we heard from Mission Control. It was music to our ears. It was exactly 8:00 p.m.

"Houston, Integrity," Reid [Wiseman, mission commander], replied. "We have you loud and clear."

This is when people the world over clapped, hugged, and, in some cases, cried. For the folks at NASA, it was clear that all had gone well during the descent — a small fleet of NASA and Air Force planes had captured it on high-resolution cameras. But, for me, it wasn't over yet. I wouldn't truly feel safe until our three main parachutes successfully deployed. If they didn't, we'd be a chunk of metal slamming into the ocean at incredibly high speed, and the chances of surviving that would be somewhere between minimal and non-existent.

I've watched many of my close friends return from space, and I find the minutes after surviving the re-entry heat until the parachutes deploy to be the hardest part to watch. When I see a capsule plunge through the clouds with no chutes, I always worry they might not appear at all. That's completely terrifying.

Jeremy Hansen arrives on the deck of the USS John P. Murtha after being recovered from the Orion capsule. All four crewmembers were in perfect health after splashdown.

I thought of Catherine and the kids, sending them a "don't worry, gang" message in my mind. Catherine later told me that she had a very bad feeling about the heatshield, so when we emerged from blackout, she began crying and didn't even focus on the parachutes.

Three minutes later, at an altitude of 7,100 metres, timed explosions released small chutes that pulled off the cover for two larger chutes, called drogues because they are intended to slow our acceleration to a speed that would allow our main parachutes to open without ripping. They did their job perfectly, but it was wild inside the capsule, jerking us back and forth like a ride at the fair.

This is when people the world over clapped, hugged, and, in some cases, cried.

One minute later, at only 1,500 metres above the ocean, the drogue chutes cut loose, and, for a few moments, we felt like we were falling backward. Then, in succession, the three main parachutes began deploying, blossoming slowly so they wouldn't tear apart. The rate of our fall slowed as the red-and-white nylon canopies, each 35 metres in diameter, filled with air. The thrusters kept firing, aiming the capsule's base directly toward the point of impact.

"Integrity, we see three good-looking parachutes," we heard from our CAPCOM. Within seconds, our splashdown speed had reduced to 27 kilometres per hour.

That's it, I said to myself. I'm pretty sure we can survive whatever else could be thrown at us now.

Christina [Koch, mission specialist] seemed to agree. We grabbed one another's hands in a moment of celebration.

Excerpted from "Earthrise: Inside Artemis II, The Groundbreaking Human Mission Into Deep Space" by John Larsen with Jeremy Hansen. © 2026 by John Larsen, used with permission by HarperCollins/Hanover Square Press.

#6355. One November storm changed how California’s Sierra Nevada looked from orbit

An early storm brought nearly a foot of snow to Donner Pass, offering a first look at the snowpack that helps supply California with water.

Fresh snow stretches across California’s Sierra Nevada in a satellite image taken on the morning of November 14.

Around Lake Tahoe and farther south, white covers much of the high country.

Along part of the range’s western side, green slopes still show through, making it easy to see where the storm left its mark.

A Pacific storm swept through the previous day, bringing heavy rain to the Sacramento area and close to a foot of snow to some mountain locations.

A break between weather systems gave NASA’s Terra satellite a clear look at the mountains after one of the season’s first major snowfalls.

The instrument that captured the view, the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer, or MODIS, takes in long stretches of the mountain range at once.

From that vantage point, the snow that fell on individual peaks and mountain passes comes into view as a broad band of white.

NASA Earth Observatory paired the November 14 view with an image from two days earlier, when snow was largely confined to the highest ridges southeast of Lake Tahoe.

The earlier view gives a sense of how much changed in the time it took for one storm to cross California.

A separate regional analysis from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) estimated that snow covered about 43 percent of its Sierra Nevada analysis area on November 14.

A month earlier, the estimate was less than 1 percent. The comparison shows how quickly snow can spread across terrain that was largely bare in mid-October.

At Donner Pass, northwest of Lake Tahoe, the Central Sierra Snow Laboratory recorded nearly 12 inches of snow on November 13.

Officials closed Interstate 80 in both directions over Donner Summit that evening.

Farther south, Mammoth Mountain reported 9 to 13 inches of fresh snow. In Yosemite National Park, officials closed several roads ahead of the storm.

The reports from Donner Pass and Mammoth give a sense of how much snow fell at specific locations across the long stretch of mountains visible from above.

The storm also brought heavy rain to the Sacramento area, west of the Sierra Nevada.

Elevation helped determine what reached the ground. Where the air was warm enough, precipitation fell as rain.

Higher in the mountains, colder conditions allowed snow to accumulate.

The green slopes along the western side of the range are a reminder that a storm can bring very different weather to places only a short distance apart.

The broad cover visible on November 14 raises a question that matters well beyond the mountains.

How much water is in all that snow? Hydrologists answer it by measuring snow water equivalent, the depth of water that would remain if the snow at a given spot melted.

A foot of light, powdery snow can hold less water than a shallower layer of dense, wet snow.

California’s Department of Water Resources uses that measurement to help forecast how much water could flow out of the mountains as the snow melts.

Some of that runoff reaches major reservoirs in spring and early summer, helping supply water during the state’s dry months.

Timing matters because California receives much of its precipitation during the cooler part of the year.

Rain can reach streams and reservoirs soon after a storm.

Snow can stay in the mountains for months before melting, releasing some of that water later, when storms are less frequent.

The November storm arrived about six weeks into the water year, the 12-month period hydrologists use to track precipitation and runoff beginning October 1.

The Sierra Nevada snowpack generally peaks around April 1, leaving several months for new storms to add to it or for warm spells to melt some of what has already accumulated.

More snow was already in the forecast when NASA released the image on November 18.

The National Weather Service had issued a winter storm warning for parts of the Sierra Nevada through November 20, with around four feet of snow possible at some locations above 8,000 feet.

The November 14 image captures the mountains at the start of that longer process.

In a single day, snow spread across enough of the Sierra Nevada to change how the range looked from orbit.

Over the coming months, the same slopes will collect or lose snow with each shift in the weather.

By spring, what remains will help determine how much meltwater reaches California’s reservoirs as the state heads into its dry season.

Image Credit: NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison, using MODIS data from NASA EOSDIS LANCE and GIBS/Worldview

#6353. Stone Age children left fingerprints on ancient art projects

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Clay figurines hint at hands-on learning in the Levant

Stone Age hunter-gatherer children from the Levant may have helped make small clay sculptures of birds, gazelle, humans and more (some shown).

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Children have been making art with help from grown-ups for millennia.

Fragmented clay figurines dating as far back as 15,000 years ago, discovered in what is now Israel, preserve the fingerprints of both adults and young children. The finding suggests the grown-ups taught the kids how to shape and decorate clay, researchers report November 11 in PLOS One.

Children’s contributions to prehistoric art and culture aren’t well understood. Concrete evidence of their involvement has been hard to find, says archaeologist Laurent Davin of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

In recent decades, researchers have found a handful of objects made by children — including 200,000-year-old rock art bearing child-sized handprints in Tibet and 30,000-year-old clay sculptures pockmarked with child-sized fingerprints in Czech Republic.

Davin and colleagues hadn’t set out to find Stone Age children’s artwork. They were investigating whether the Natufian culture — a group of hunter-gatherers who formed some of the first permanent settlements in the Levant about 14,000 years ago — made clay art before the advent of agriculture in the region.

The archaeologists came across the first set of fingerprints while sorting through 40 kilograms of clay collected at three Natufian sites, which range in age from 15,000 to 11,600 years old. Among tens of thousands of clay lumps, the team found some 150 fragments of sculptures, including 15 recognizable bird, gazelle and human figures. Around 60 of these pieces preserved fingerprints from where people had pinched or prodded the clay.

The distances between the fingerprints’ ridges, which are influenced by age and sex, suggest that most of the figurines were made by women and children — some younger than 10. Only a few sets of fingerprints belonged to men. And the torso of one tiny human statue had both adult and child fingerprints, hinting that an elder and child had passed it back and forth. Davin suspects that the adult actively taught a child how to work the clay.

This evidence of intergenerational learning so far back in time is fascinating, says archaeologist Steven Dorland of Grand Valley State University in Allendale, Mich. It demonstrates how much researchers can learn from broadening their focus beyond adult males, he says. Dorland has used pottery to understand social learning in Indigenous societies of the Great Lakes region. He has even studied children’s fingerprints on some of those artifacts.

The purpose of the Natufian figurines is unclear. Most of the statues are less than 2 centimeters long and don’t display signs of intense use, the team found, suggesting they weren’t treated as precious heirlooms.

Davin suspects the figurines may have represented stories, like how kids draw Disney characters today, he says. “Maybe the idea is that the role of children here is not necessarily to learn to make figurines, but more to learn the story behind them.”

Questions or comments on this article? E-mail us at feedback@sciencenews.org | Reprints FAQ

L. Davin et al. Modeling symbols among the first-sedentary communities: Emergence of clay figurines in Epipaleolithic Southwest Asia. PLOS One. 2026. doi: 10.1371/journal.pone.0360388

Freda Kreier was a fall 2021 intern at Science News. She holds a bachelor’s degree in molecular biology from Colorado College and a master’s in science communication from the University of California, Santa Cruz.
