#6325. In National Geographic’s “Expedition: Saving Our Seas,” it’s all hands on deck

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Narrated by Auli’i Cravalho, the documentary dives into how oceanographers are racing to understand the world’s changing waters

Aerial imagery of research vessel Star Keys safe harboring in Abel Tasman, New Zealand.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

As documentaries about Earth’s accelerating climate crisis go, Expedition: Saving Our Seas is surprisingly buoyant.

The ocean covers more than two-thirds of Earth’s surface. And “as the climate heats up, our seas are under pressure like never before,” narrator Auli’i Cravalho, the voice of the title character in Disney’s Moana, says at the opening of The National Geographic Society’s new documentary. The film documents how oceanographers are racing to document and mitigate climate change’s impacts on ocean and coastal habitats.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Expedition: Saving Our Seas premieres November 13 on the National Geographic Channel at 9pm EST and streams the next day on Disney+ and Hulu.

Despite that solemn mission, Expedition: Saving Our Seas is full of hope — and stunning visuals. The documentary offers a window into the scientists’ wonder and joy in their work as they discover new life forms in the depths of the Southern Ocean, or successfully nurture young corals threatened by warming in the Pacific Ocean.

The film opens with a twist on the usual world map: At the center is one great ocean, surrounded by land. Trivia buffs know Earth has five oceans: the Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern and Arctic. But geographic names aside, these five oceans are just one, linked by a global system of currents known as the Great Ocean Conveyor Belt.

“It’s this giant connected ocean that ignores all of the political boundaries, ignores all of the names we call them,” says Andrew Thurber, a biological oceanographer at the University of California, Santa Barbara, whose research is among those featured in the film.

The documentary loosely follows the current’s path as it zips around the world from project to project.

The first project in the documentary is Thurber’s. He’s on board a research vessel in the frigid Southern Ocean, which rings Antarctica. Using a remotely-operated vehicle dubbed SuBastian, Thurber and his colleagues are scanning the seafloor, hunting for the world’s southernmost hydrothermal vent.

Hydrothermal vents spew superhot, chemically-enriched seawater. In the generally nutrient-poor Southern Ocean, that makes these vents a potential food oasis to support deep sea life.

Throughout the night, as the ROV scans the seafloor, Thurber and his colleagues stay glued to the video it sends back, oohing and aahing as never-before-seen life-forms come into view. “It was a marathon of excitement,” he says now.

Then they see it: A large black smoker, the southernmost hydrothermal vent ever found. And all around it: swarms of pregnant female krill.

“That blew all of our minds,” Thurber says. Krill are the keystone species of the entire Southern Ocean food web, a crucial food source for baleen whales, seals, penguins and fish. But krill are threatened by both industrial fishing and climate change. This discovery, Thurber says, helps make the case for a marine protected area, a region where fishing and other human activities should be restricted.

From the Southern Ocean, the Great Ocean Conveyor Belt flows thousands of kilometers to the north, where marine ecologist Maiyai Taal Hocheimy is tracking how the rising waters of the Atlantic Ocean are encroaching on Banjul, the capital of The Gambia in West Africa. Her hope is that salt-tolerant mangrove trees along the coast, with their dense network of soil-retaining roots, might help hold back the sea in the coming decades — provided that the community can be enlisted to help maintain the mangroves.

I found Hocheimy’s work especially inspiring because she is working to shape the future of oceanography. In 2017, she founded the GREAT (Gaining Research Experience in Africa for Tomorrow) Institute, the first aquatic and coastal science research institute in The Gambia. The mangrove project recruited young local scientists to help conduct the research.

“The goal is to train the next generation of environmental stewards,” Hocheimy says. “We have to show that mangroves have value, so they’ll understand and want to protect them. It is their future at stake.”

That sentiment is echoed many times in the film — the importance not only of enlisting young scientists but also centering local scientists who pose new questions that oceanographers who parachute in from other places may not think to ask, says marine biogeochemist Kristina Brown.

In the documentary, Brown, of the University of Manitoba in Canada, co-leads an expedition to explore the waters of Sherman Basin, a large bay north of the Arctic Circle in Nunavut, Canada. This region has been hunted and fished by Inuit people for centuries.

But it might change beyond all recognition in the next few decades, Brown says. So, the local Inuit community invited her to help create the first catalog of what species are present in the waters and on the seafloor. “[It’s] the first project I’ve been involved in where the local community both defined the research questions and have brought their own unique expertise to the research project.”

Watching how communities around the world are increasingly taking ownership of studies in their own waters was, for me, the most exciting takeaway of this documentary.

“We want to democratize access to the deep sea, to enable people who haven’t had access to these kinds of tools to ask more and new questions,” says Katy Croff Bell, the founder and president of the Ocean Discovery League, a nonprofit ocean exploration group based in Saunderstown, Rhode Island.

As a result of inaccessibility, little of Earth’s vast ocean has been mapped, particularly the deep sea. Bell’s organization is developing inexpensive technologies such as a hardy little camera and sensor system dubbed DORIS, for Deep Ocean Research and Imaging System. It can descend to 6,000 meters and costs less than $10,000.

Expedition: Saving Our Seas offers just a few scant minutes to each project before moving on around the globe to the next, so there’s no time to learn about each project in depth. But the overall takeaway of watching these vignettes, back to back, is that there is a young, energetic community of scientists taking on the challenge.

Mitigating climate change’s impacts on the oceans is, after all, a race against time. So it’s nice to think we might have all hands on deck.

This story was updated on November 13, 2026, to correct the spelling of Katy Croff Bell's name, and to correct the location of the corals mentioned in the story from the Indian to the Pacific Ocean.

Carolyn Gramling is the earth & climate writer. She has bachelor’s degrees in geology and European history and a Ph.D. in marine geochemistry from MIT and the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution.

#6324. The 4 Best Laser Printers For Your Home and Small Office

If you print a lot of professional-grade documents, a laser printer is a worthy investment.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Laser printers, known for printing crisp, professional-looking documents quickly, are generally considered big, expensive machines designed for large offices. While some larger models live up to that reputation, plenty of compact options fit into your home office if you print files often.

While more expensive than an inkjet printer, most laser printers are a better long-term investment, with lower operating costs and designs built for heavy-duty printing. That said, choosing the right one at a glance can be tricky, and may vary based on your needs.

Printers aren’t the most exciting tech products, and many folks see them as frustrating, unreliable machines that require constant repair or replacement and are increasingly unnecessary for the average person in the digital age. While that may be true for some, they remain essential for workers who need to print contracts or create physical records, and students who need hard copies of their homework. With a little research, you can find a good laser printer that makes life easier and lasts a long time.

The recommended printers are based on my personal experience and knowledge of printers, as well as research from reputable publications, including PCMag and The Wirecutter. I looked for printers with performance and features that suit both home and small office users, with price and value in mind. I also spent months testing the best overall pick and using it as my everyday printer to ensure it’s a worthy recommendation.

I have been reviewing tech products for 25 years, including computing peripherals such as inkjet and laser printers. As an editor at Computer Shopper magazine, I helped develop the printer testing methodology used in the reviews. I then brought that expertise to publications such as Digital Trends and Business Insider, applying real-world usage that resonates with shoppers in the evaluation.

There’s no perfect laser printer, but if you’re looking for a reliable, easy-to-use unit that produces high-quality prints, the HP LaserJet Pro MFP 3101sdw fits the bill. I’ve been using this printer for several months and found that it’s an ideal fit for my home office. It also has plenty of advanced features that would make it a good fit for a small business.

With a 35ppm print speed, the 3101sdw is fast for its intended audience. When connected to a typical home Wi-Fi network, it takes about 5 seconds from pressing print to outputting the first page. Printed text looks good even at lower-quality settings, with small fonts staying sharp and legible. I found the scan quality more than adequate for everyday use, but 300 dpi is too low for designers, photographers, and other creative users. It also runs quiet, which is always a nice bonus.

Anybody who needs to make copies will find the ADF-equipped scanner handy, while the 2.7-inch touchscreen makes setup easy. It took me less than 10 minutes to get it up and running. Whether you connect via USB, Ethernet, or Wi-Fi, the printer responds quickly. It also has a USB port for quick prints or saving scans to a flash drive.

While the 3101sdw is small enough to fit on a large desk, it’s more practical to put it on its own stand. I wouldn’t call it “lightweight,” but I could carry it down five floors without much effort. It won’t win any design awards, either, which is too bad because HP generally knows how to make great-looking products.

The paper tray has an average 250-page capacity, but a notable drawback is that it has no manual feed tray. I didn’t find this an issue, but if you need to, say, print on envelopes, it could be problematic because you'd have to switch out the paper in the main tray. Another expert reviewer dinged the 3101sdw for lacking a fax function, but my workaround is to use the HP Smart companion app to scan and send (but not receive) faxes.

The 3101sdw offers stronger print quality, a better build, and ease of use. It’s hard to say how long mechanical devices like this will last, but HP’s printers are known for their reliability—I have a LaserJet from the 1990s that’s still going strong.

In my experience, Brother makes affordable laser printers that consistently deliver solid performance and text quality. At 36ppm and under $200, the HL-L2460DW is a strong basic option for a home or small office. Despite its barebones design, it has useful features like double-sided printing, Ethernet connectivity, wireless printing, a generous 250-page paper capacity, and a mobile app. Plus, it’s lightweight and doesn’t take up too much space.

The HL-L2460DW supports a 1,200-page standard-yield toner cartridge or 3,000-page high-yield toner cartridge, but comes with a starter cartridge that only yields 700 pages out of the box. (This is typical of printer manufacturers.) If you plan to print a lot, I’d recommend buying a high-yield cartridge right when you buy the printer.

This is a “budget” option, though, so this printer comes with a few caveats. I don’t love the small LCD display, which has a basic interface that doesn’t display much info and doesn’t feel as well-made. The basic operation means there’s no scanning, copying, faxing, ADF, or other multi-function capabilities. Plus, black-and-white graphics and images don’t look as good as text. User reviews have also complained about its reliability. Still, given its balance of price, speed, and print quality, the HL-L2460DW is a good value regardless of budget.

If it’s for personal use and you only plan to use it every so often, I’d steer you toward a different model, the HL-L2420DW, which has a 30ppm speed and every aforementioned feature except Ethernet. It’s perfect for casual printing, and it costs $50 less.

Most offices shy away from color laser printers because they are expensive to buy and maintain, and employees often use them to make wasteful prints. Likewise, at home, you’re probably better off going with a color inkjet printer. That said, if you truly need color prints, I love the HP Color LaserJet Pro MFP 3301fdw, which delivers excellent print quality and attractive features like glossy paper support. It’s a strong, if pricey, complement to any office.

Despite its compact footprint, the 3301fdw has a 50-page duplexing ADF and a 250-page paper tray. It’s not the fastest color laser printer, but its 26ppm speed is more than adequate for home or small business use.

Print quality is where HP’s laser printers excel. You can expect documents with crisp text and well-saturated, natural-looking color graphics and photos. Unlike most laser printers, the 3301fdw is compatible with select HP glossy paper, so you can make photo prints. They don’t really compare to inkjet photo printers, but it’s fine in most cases.

Like our overall pick, the 3301fdw is a breeze to set up via its 4.3-inch color touchscreen. For connectivity, it supports USB, Ethernet, and Wi-Fi, which covers most home and office networks.

You may have guessed the printer’s big con is that it’s pricey to operate. Whether you’re using the standard or high-yield toner options, the cost per page is high. If you’re looking to spend a little less, I’d look at the Brother MFC-L3380CDW, which has a comparable feature set to the 3301fdw and a lower operating cost. You’re compromising a bit on print quality and performance, though, which is why the HP leads the pack.

A true small-business laser printer needs to be a workhorse. It should offer a robust, office-centric range of features, print fast, support multiple users, hold enough paper, and have a high duty cycle. Experts agree that Brother makes some of the best laser printers for offices, and the monochrome MFC-L2900DW multi-function model is a particularly good option.

Imagine the L2900DW as an enhanced version of the HL-L2460DW. It shares a similar design, small footprint, and print engine, but features a high-capacity 50-page ADF for copying or scanning multi-page documents. The L2900DW also has a single-page duplexing scanner for two-sided pages. There’s even a fax function.

A large 3.5-inch touchscreen makes setup and on-device operation easy without a computer, while USB, Wi-Fi, and Ethernet give you options for connecting. Combined with a fast 36ppm speed, sharp text print quality, low operating cost, and the option to use high-yield cartridges, you’ve got a very capable all-in-one laser printer.

Graphics don’t look as sharp as text, but that shouldn’t matter if your office prints mainly documents. While its 250-page paper tray is adequate for a small business, expect to reload often if multiple users print often. This model offers no option for a larger or expandable paper tray.

The ADF has a scanner resolution of just 600 dpi, but that is plenty for text documents; the flatbed scanner has 1,200 dpi, which is fine for color images. The output tray’s 100-page capacity is low for heavy usage. One missing feature is a front USB port, which is handy for printing or faxing documents from a flash drive or saving scans to one.

If you need to support a large number of workers, consider stepping up to Brother’s MFC-L5915DW. It has a 70-page ADF and a 5-inch LCD, and you can expand its paper capacity beyond the standard 250 pages. With a faster 50ppm speed, support for 18,000-page high-yield cartridges, and a higher duty cycle, it’s an ideal choice for busy offices. It’s a big jump in price, which is why I went with the L2900DW, but it may cost less to operate in the long run.

Whether for the office or your home, a laser printer is a good option if you often print many multi-page documents. If you need a home printer for occasional printing, a more affordable inkjet printer may make more sense. Again, a laser printer costs more up front but pays dividends in the long run as a professional tool or a home tech staple. If you’re on the fence about what to buy, here are the things I look at when I evaluate laser printers:

Most prints from a laser printer are black-and-white text documents, and most models deliver decent print quality. If you need to print impactful pages with photos and charts, a color laser printer can print higher-quality graphics. Even the best monochrome printers we’ve tested and researched can’t match the detail and clarity of color ink toner. For example, if you have a multi-colored pie chart, a monochrome reproduction can only do so much to separate the different color shading.

Keep in mind, though, that even the cheapest color laser printer will be expensive, and its print quality may not rival that of higher-end models. They also do not support specialty media like glossy photo paper.

A basic laser printer’s sole function is to print documents, and that’s enough for most people. It’s generally compact and fits on a desk. But if you run a small business or work remotely in a home office, you may want a multi-function, “all-in-one” printer that scans and copies, too, among other tasks. Multi-function printers are far more useful, but they’re larger and cost more due to the extra hardware inside.

“Yield” refers to the estimated number of pages you can get out of a single toner cartridge. Most laser printers should get around 1,500 pages from a toner cartridge, while high-yield cartridges should last 3,000 pages or more.

Toner cartridges are expensive, especially for color printers, but they offer a better cost per page than ink. My rule of thumb is that high-yield toners will save you money in the long run.

Similarly, a laser printer’s “duty cycle” rating refers to the maximum number of prints per month that the manufacturer recommends to keep it in proper working order. Basic laser printers have a duty cycle of around 5,000 pages or less, while heavy-duty models have ratings of 10,000 or higher. Printing beyond the rated duty cycle can lead to breakdowns, more maintenance, or a shorter lifespan.

For personal use or small businesses that print occasionally, 25 to 30 pages per minute (ppm) should be fine. Small offices with a few employees that print often may want a faster printer with a speed of 35 to 40 ppm. In a larger office, I’d look for at least 40 ppm, if not more. Keep in mind that manufacturers measure speeds under ideal conditions, and real-world results may not always match. Expect a small discrepancy of a few pages.

Most printers rely primarily on a USB cable to connect to your computer, but a hard-wired connection alone isn’t practical in today’s world of wireless laptops, phones, and tablets. I recommend choosing a printer with a wireless connection compatible with your most-used devices, such as Wi-Fi or Apple AirPrint. Some laser printers also support Ethernet for a high-speed hard-wired connection. Office-focused machines may include a front USB port so you can plug in a flash drive with the files you need to print.

Most laser printers have a paper tray that holds 250 pages, which is enough for personal and small business use. Some compact printers may have a smaller capacity–around 150 pages. If you expect to print a lot, consider a model with a higher-capacity tray or support for multiple trays, and look for an output tray large enough to hold everything you print out. All printers also have a multi-purpose tray for manually feeding non-standard paper like envelopes.

In addition to the essentials, there are some features that I look for which are nice to have, but won’t make or break a printer:

Depending on the model, it can be basic or advanced. Depending on your use case, you may consider some or all of these essential. That said, they aren't universal, and some printers work well without them.

Laser printers use toner, a powder heated onto paper, while inkjet printers spray ink droplets. Laser printers are considered superior for their speed and print quality, but they are expensive to purchase and maintain. Inkjet printers offer color printing and affordability, but prints need time to dry, and the cost per page can be higher with heavy use.

However, the best modern inkjet printers today are fast and deliver great-looking prints, especially photos. They also support different paper types and sizes. Laser printers can also print in color, but they're pricey. Beyond speed, their advantages include consistent print quality and long-term reliability.

Which technology is better ultimately depends on your needs. Most people will find an inkjet printer sufficient and more versatile, but those who print often may find a laser printer more economical in the long run. In an ideal setup, consider an affordable laser printer for frequent print jobs and a good inkjet printer for color documents and photos.

Color laser printers can print photos and graphics on standard paper, but if you want to print on photo paper, an inkjet is the better choice, especially one that supports multi-color ink tanks. Laser printers aren’t designed for photo-quality reproduction, and generally don’t work with specialty paper. (As we discussed, some HP models are compatible with select glossy paper.)

Depending on usage and maintenance, a laser printer can last for many years. It’s a mechanical device, though, so there’s no guarantee that it won’t break down and require service. Here are a few tips to keep your printer running as efficiently as possible and maximize its lifespan:

An unusual pair of seated figurines was discovered in a Stone Age grave in Romania in the 1950s.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Two Stone Age figurines ‪—‬ the Thinker and the Seated Woman ‪—‬ were discovered in a prehistoric cemetery in Romania.

In 1956, archaeologists unearthed two unique figurines from one grave while excavating a Stone Age cemetery in southeast Romania. The unusual figurines — known as the Thinkers of Cernavodă or the Thinker and the Seated Woman — were made by people from the Hamangia culture and may be linked to ancient astronomical beliefs.

The Thinkers of Cernavodă are in the collection of the National Museum of Romanian History and are a key part of the country's cultural heritage. They were crafted from fired clay and measure about 4.5 inches (11.5 centimeters) tall. The two figurines may represent a man (the Thinker) and a woman (the Seated Woman), according to the museum.

The Thinker sits on a low, four-legged stool. He bends forward slightly, rounding his back and neck, and his arms are bent. He rests his elbows on his knees and his head in his hands. This pose gives him a meditative quality, according to the museum, which is why he has been named after Auguste Rodin's famous 1904 bronze sculpture. The Seated Woman also has a long, bent neck and a small face. She has prominent hips, thighs and breasts. Her right leg is bent, and her hands rest on her knee.

The figurines are about 7,000 years old and were made by the Hamangia people, a Late Neolithic culture that stretched from the Danube River to the Black Sea. According to archaeologist Dumitru Berciu, who excavated the Cernavodă cemetery, the Hamangia culture lasted from about 5200 to 4500 B.C. The people focused primarily on sheep and goat herding, and they built defensive hilltop settlements. They also crafted spiral-decorated pottery and human-shaped figurines. But while Berciu found dozens of male and female figurines in the Cernavodă cemetery, he noted that both Thinkers were unusual for being depicted seated rather than standing.

The specific meaning of the Thinkers is unclear. Berciu suggested that the figurines were somewhat stylized, rather than realistic, because they served a magical or religious purpose. Since solar worship was common among later Bronze Age groups in Europe — as evidenced by artifacts like the Nebra sky disc from Germany and an ornate sun chariot from Denmark — Berciu interpreted the figurines as possibly connected to sun worship.

But the National Museum of Romanian History has suggested that the two figurines may have been made specifically as a pair, representing the complementary principles of masculine and feminine natures or a Neolithic family unit. Another interpretation is that the sculptures depict a pair of mourners who were buried with the deceased.

While the original meaning of the 7,000-year-old sculptures remains a mystery, people continue to be drawn to the contemplative pair, and the male Thinker figures prominently today in the logo of the National Museum of Romanian History.

#6322. These former members are returning to Congress next year

Former Ohio Sen. Sherrod Brown, here at a Oct. 20 campaign event near Ohio University in Athens, won his comeback bid Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Even in an election cycle marked by surprises and upsets, Capitol Hill observers will spot some familiar faces (identical twins notwithstanding) among this year’s midterm winners.

At least seven former members won comeback bids Tuesday.

The winners included alumni who dusted themselves off after election losses just two years ago. But other winners haven’t been in office in nearly two decades, their service predating the addition of a women’s restroom in the House (more recent than you may guess).

Here’s how these former members did on election night:

Carl lost a primary to fellow Republican Rep. Barry Moore in 2024 after a new map placed them in the same district. But with Moore running for the Senate in 2026, Carl had an easier path back to his old seat, which was redrawn again this year. He defeated his Democratic opponent Tuesday by 18 points.

It has been nearly two decades since Solis last served in Congress. She left in 2009 to serve as President Barack Obama’s first Labor secretary. Solis was in her sixth term as a Los Angeles county supervisor when she announced a bid for Congress after California voters approved a map that created five Democratic pickup opportunities.

Solis faced limited resistance on her path to victory in the 38th District, especially after Democratic Rep. Linda T. Sánchez opted to run for the redrawn 41st District.

Bean is making her way back to the House after losing her suburban Chicagoland seat in the conservative tea party wave of 2010.

A decade-and-a-half later, she won an eight-way primary for the 8th District seat Democrat Raja Krishnamoorthi vacated for an unsuccessful Senate bid. Winning the nomination all but guaranteed Bean a November victory in the deep-blue seat.

One of the cycle’s biggest comeback stories was in the Buckeye State, where Sherrod Brown was mounting a bid two years after Republican Bernie Moreno had unseated him. Positioning himself as an opponent of data centers, Brown defeated appointed GOP Sen. Jon Husted in a special election for the remainder of now Vice President JD Vance’s term. He could take office as early as December but would have to run again in 2028 if he wants another full term.

First elected in 2018, Allred left Congress two years ago after an unsuccessful Senate campaign against Republican incumbent Ted Cruz. After briefly launching a second Senate bid, Allred switched to a redrawn open House seat and won his primary over Rep. Julie Elizabeth Johnson, his successor in the chamber. Allred had no trouble winning his general election Tuesday for a fourth House term.

McAdams served one term in Congress representing a battleground Utah seat, before being unseated by Republican Burgess Owens in 2020. But after a state judge approved a new congressional map that created a heavily Democratic seat anchored in Salt Lake City, McAdams jumped into the race. He comfortably won his primary over more progressive opponents and stomped his way to a second term on Tuesday.

Once a high-ranking member of the House Armed Services Committee, Luria lost her Hampton Roads seat in 2022 to Republican Jen Kiggans.

But a week after Virginia Democrats posted strong showings in the commonwealth’s 2025 off-year elections, Luria launched her House comeback bid and went on to oust Kiggans on Tuesday.

Former House Intelligence Chairman Mike Rogers left the House after the 2014 elections and made his first Senate bid 10 years later. He lost to Democrat Elissa Slotkin but sought the seat of retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters the following year.

Rogers tried to take advantage of Democratic divisions between primary winner Abdul El-Sayed and Rep. Haley Stevens, even winning a late endorsement from the congresswoman. But it was not enough to stop El-Sayed on Tuesday.

Republican John E. Sununu served three terms in the House and one in the Senate before losing to Democrat Jeanne Shaheen in 2008. With Shaheen retiring, Sununu attempted a comeback but ended up losing decisively to Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas.

Perriello won an upset victory in a Charlottesville-anchored district in 2008 before losing reelection in the tea party wave two years later. He launched a comeback bid this cycle for the current version of the seat, but the Republican incumbent, John McGuire, narrowly prevailed.

Two years after losing her at-large House seat to Republican Nick Begich, Peltola chose to challenge Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan. The race was rocked by late revelations by The New York Times that top aides to Peltola’s campaign were closely involved in recruiting a second candidate named Dan Sullivan into the race to peel votes from the incumbent. As of Wednesday afternoon, Peltola was clinging to a narrow lead as votes were counted.

#6321. The Sky Today on Tuesday, November 17: Spotlight on the Pleiades

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

Early this evening brighter targets are best, as the Moon doesn’t set until late. Ready for viewing as the winter constellations start to dominate earlier each day is the Pleiades, an open cluster cataloged as M45.

Known since antiquity and readily visible to the naked eye, the Pleiades contains several bright stars arranged in a tiny dipperlike shape. Located in northwestern Taurus, the cluster is sometimes mistaken for the Little Dipper, although that asterism is much larger and lies in the northern sky, anchored at the end of its handle by Polaris, the North Star. The Pleiades shines with a collective magnitude of 1.6 and spans roughly 110’ — a huge swath of sky. It lies above the sideways V-shape of Taurus’ face as the Bull rises in the east this evening, and is already 30° high by 7:30 P.M. local time. How many stars can you make out with the naked eye? Most observers see six or seven.

Once you’ve taken in the cluster without any optical aid, zoom in with binoculars or a finder scope. (Any higher magnification and you won’t see most of the cluster at once, but instead be limited to a smaller portion.) Many more stars will now pop into your field of view. If you do opt for high magnification, look for a faint grayish haze around the stars — this is nearby dust reflecting the stars’ light, and requires clear, dark conditions to make out.

The Leonid meteor shower peaks tonight, with the best meteor viewing overnight into the early-morning hours of November 18, as the Moon sets around midnight and the radiant rises higher. Keep reading for more detail below on how to observe the shower.

Sunrise: 6:47 A.M.Sunset: 4:42 P.M.Moonrise: 12:56 P.M.Moonset: —Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (57%)*Times for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location.

The peak of the Leonid meteor shower, caused by the dusty debris of Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, is best seen early on the morning of the 18th, after the Moon has set and the shower’s radiant rises high in the hours before dawn.

Two hours before sunrise, Leo is high in the southeast, with bright Jupiter and Mars joining the curved shape of the Sickle asterism. The Leonids’ radiant is located just inside the cuved blade’s inner edge, near 3rd-magnitude Zeta (ζ) Leonis to the upper left (north) of Mars and Jupiter. The two planets appear roughly side by side in the sky around this time, with ruddy Mars at left and more golden-yellow Jupiter at right. Regulus sits just to their lower left.

To catch the most meteors, you’ll actually want to look a little ways away from Leo, about 40° to 60° to the left or right of the constellation. This is where meteors with the longest trains will also occur. Although this shower isn’t particularly strong, you can expect to see roughly a half-dozen or more Leonid meteors per hour. The Leonid shower produces some of the fastest-moving meteors we experience all year, streaking through the sky at some 44 miles (70 kilometers) per second.

#6320. Most transgender youth satisfied after choosing hormone therapy

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Taking gender-affirming hormone therapy was the right decision for 97 percent surveyed

Demonstrators rally at the U.S. Supreme Court in 2025 in support of gender-affirming health care for transgender youth. The vast majority of transgender and gender diverse young people are satisfied with their decision to take hormone therapy, according the largest survey on the topic.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

An overwhelming percentage of transgender and gender diverse young people in the United States express satisfaction with gender-affirming hormone therapy.

Almost 400 transgender and gender diverse young people reflected on their decision to take hormone therapy in the largest such survey to date. Nearly 97 percent affirmed it was the right decision, researchers report November 9 in JAMA Pediatrics. Only about 3 percent, or 10 individuals, said they regretted the step, and of those, seven felt the experience was harmful.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

With concerns around youth well-being fueling limits on gender-affirming hormone therapy, the researchers write, “the results provide further support for the existing standards of care [and] do not support efforts to categorically restrict or ban access.”

Gender-affirming hormone therapy — with the masculinizing hormone testosterone or the feminizing hormone estrogen — allows a person’s body to better match their gender identity. Around 3 percent of 13- to 17-year-olds in the United States identify as transgender.

Among the study’s 376 young people, who were former patients of a clinic for transgender and gender diverse youth, nearly 92 percent began hormones at 17 or younger. Thirty percent took estrogen and 70 percent took testosterone, with the amount of time since starting the hormones averaging five years.

As per clinical guidelines for transgender health care, young people interested in medical treatment, joined by parents or guardians, began with an assessment visit with a mental health professional. For the study, participants took a yearly survey, filled out anytime from one month prior to six months following the anniversary of this initial visit. The research team analyzed surveys submitted from 2023 to 2025.

The new research adds to growing evidence on the benefits of gender-affirming hormone therapy for transgender young people. Gender-affirming hormones improve the alignment these young people experience between their appearance and their gender, increase their satisfaction with life and reduce depression and anxiety.

But state bans have curtailed young people’s access to gender-affirming care, which can include hormone therapy and puberty blockers. As of November 2026 in the United States, 28 states have laws or policies that limit this care, according to the health policy organization KFF. More than half of transgender young people age 13 to 17 reside in states that restrict gender-affirming care. The American Academy of Pediatrics and the Endocrine Society support gender-affirming health care for young people and provide evidence-backed guidelines for treatment.

#6319. The 6 Best Floor Scrubbers for a Deeper Clean on Any Surface

There's no need to get down and dirty when you have one of these powerful machines.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

There's no reason to get down on your hands and knees to clean your floors. If you want to get the job done with minimal effort, invest in a floor scrubber to do the dirty work for you. Floor scrubbers lift out set-in grime, stains, and surface mildew quickly and efficiently on practically any hard surface—without the back-breaking labor.

While a few non-powered floor scrubbers are worth considering (we recommend one), most have powerful electric motors. The full-size machines on our list are corded, and we’ve also included a battery-powered spin scrubber for tighter spaces like bathrooms. These machines use floor-safe abrasive pads, bristle brushes, and microfiber rollers to deliver a level of deep clean that's virtually impossible to get with a mop or hand tools alone. Some add steam to clean and sanitize or suction like a vacuum, and some even tackle carpet.

We used our cleaning and home care expertise to find models worth your attention and investment. These are the best floor scrubbers we recommend.

To find the best floor scrubbers for this story, we relied heavily on our deep knowledge of cleaning products and our coverage on related topics. We looked to trustworthy cleaning brands such as Oreck, Shark, and Bissell to recommend models that’ll last. We also vetted specs including power source, materials, and compatibility with a range of hard surfaces while comparing models. Our final list covers the best floor scrubbers across categories and price points to match different preferences and budgets.

One of the best-value floor scrubbers on the market, this commercial-grade Orbiter from Oreck can scrub out even the toughest stains. Unlike many other options on our list, it's compatible with virtually any surface type, including carpet. By swapping out its spinning head attachment, the floor scrubber can buff, polish, sand, wax, and refinish. Another plus is the extra-long 50-foot cord.

While it’s designed for commercial use, this floor scrubber is small enough to fit in a closet or laundry room. Its price is a bit higher than some other options on this list, but as an all-in-one floor care machine, it's well worth the investment.

Forget the batteries and cords; this floor scrubber gets things done the old-fashioned way. The scrub brush may require a bit more elbow grease, but it should more than make up for it with its affordable price tag and powerful, stiff bristles.

While basic, this scrubber includes a few nifty features, including a built-in squeegee on the top of the brush to wipe away water or cleaning solution after you’ve scrubbed.

It also has an extendable handle and can be fully disassembled for storage or maintenance. The handle is also angled at 45 degrees, so you don’t have to bend your back to position the head correctly.

Take your cleaning to the next level with a floor scrubber that vacuums and washes at once. The CrossWave Edge has separate clean and dirty water tanks, and its spinning brush roll works water and your cleaning solution into the floor while suction pulls the dirty water right back up. There's no follow-up mopping and no long wait for floors to dry.

One side of the brush roll sits flush with the edge of the cleaning head, so it gets closer to baseboards and cabinets than most machines. The 0.75-liter clean water tank lasts about 20 minutes of continuous cleaning. You can also run it with the tank empty as a quick vacuum for dry debris. When you're done, place it on the included stand to run a self-cleaning cycle.

With a spinning head and up to 90 minutes of runtime per charge, this battery-operated floor scrubber is built to break down the toughest grime.

The Labigo spin scrubber comes with four different brush heads designed to tackle different areas, from bathtubs to shower corners. Combined with the extendable, angled handle, the machine reaches every crevice that needs cleaning. This maneuverability is also one of the key reasons many of the head attachments are smaller and shaped with fine points.

We recommend this scrubber for tackling messes in your bathroom, whether on tile, in the shower, on bathtubs, or in and around toilets. While it comes with a flat-head attachment that can cover more ground, this option performs best in tight spaces rather than larger areas like your living room.

This is another commercial-grade choice that works on almost any surface, including carpet. The dual scrubbing rotators have stiff bristles that break down heavy stains and set-in grime.

You can then attach the buffing or polishing pads to finish your tile or hardwood, leaving it shining smoothly. The commercial-strength design requires corded power, but the long plug means you don't need to buy an extension cord.

This option is a bit more expensive than others on the list, but it's from a reputable brand and one of the most versatile models.

Instead of relying only on cleaning detergents, the Shark floor scrubber includes a powerful steamer. The two rotating pads, at over 150 scrubs per minute, work with a steady flow of hot steam to break up grime, wipe it away, and sanitize your floors at the same time. Three steam modes let you go light for quick cleanups or deep for stuck-on messes.

One benefit of using steam is that it avoids chemical-based cleaners that might be unsafe for kids and pets. Another plus is that this floor scrubber has LED headlights that illuminate dirt and dust on the floor—for better or worse.

This scrubber may be less effective on stains that require extra elbow grease, but it is perhaps the easiest machine on our list.

The floor scrubbers we cover work on just about any hard surface. This includes hardwood, laminate, tile, stone, concrete, and brick, though note that some scrubbing bristles may be too coarse for certain types of vinyl or unfinished wood. Also, if your hardwood floorboards have lots of space between them, it may be best to go with a model that cleans without water.

Some of the models we cover—including our Best Overall pick—are safe for carpet. While floor scrubbers may be great for deep cleaning some carpets and rugs, our recommendations below are tailored to hard surfaces. To deep clean your carpet, check out our story on the best carpet steam cleaners.

Non-powered floor scrubbers are essentially heavy-duty push brooms with features that make cleaning easier, like telescoping poles and squeegees on the side opposite the bristles. They're far more affordable and compact than electric floor scrubbers, so if you’re short on space or don’t want to spend $100 or more on a new product, opt for the manual model we recommend.

If you go electric, corded and cordless models use a spinning or suction mechanism for fast, deep cleaning. When paired with water or a cleaning solution, they remove grime and scum much faster than a non-powered floor scrubber. Some models add in steam to break up baked-in dirt and sanitize.

Many floor scrubbers include features that enhance cleaning, including multiple scrubber heads to tackle different spaces, like tight corners or bathroom floors. Some models, like our Best Overall pick, are all-in-one cleaning machines that clean, sand, and finish floors with buffing pads or polishing heads.

In recent animal tests, tiny robots released into the bloodstream showed promise for treating blood clots.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Microrobots controlled by magnets can sweep drugs towards hard-to-reach blood clots in the body, boosting the efficacy of these life-saving treatments, early tests in animals suggest.

In tests with pigs, the microbots helped to dissolve clots around 10 times faster than medication alone. The research team is now working on further safety testing to ready the technology for eventual human trials.

"The whole construct is inspired by nature," said lead researcher Simone Schürle, professor of medical microsystems at ETH Zürich. "There are these tiny bacteria that have little magnetic backbones which they use to navigate with the Earth's magnetic field, and we were really struck by the physics and the properties of them when exposed to rotating magnetic fields," Schürle told Live Science.

ETH Zürich announced the research in a statement on Nov. 9. It has not been described in a peer-reviewed study yet.

Left untreated, blood clots can cause life-threatening damage. These blockages can restrict the flow of blood to the body's key tissues, triggering serious cardiovascular events, such as heart attacks or strokes, which starve cells of oxygen.

Doctors can either remove clots manually with tools or deliver clot-dissolving drugs, called thrombolytics, close to the site of the blockage. However, getting these medications through the final few millimeters of their journey is often the hardest part.

"When a pipe becomes blocked in a branched pipe system, the fluid encounters greater resistance and instead flows through alternative routes where it can pass more easily," Schürle explained. "So when you then try to bring in drugs to dissolve the clot, they won't flow into this area because it's occluded [blocked off]."

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

This is where microbots can help. The bots are tiny particles whose movements can be controlled by external magnets, which send them rotating and tumbling through blood vessels. These bots can redirect the interrupted blood flow and thus carry essential drugs straight to their target, Schürle and her team say.

Each bullet-shaped microbot contains a magnetic backbone of iron oxide nanoparticles, which is surrounded by a protective sheath of hydrogel polymer. When exposed to a rotating magnetic field, the microbots essentially start to somersault through the blood vessel, creating little vortices that help carry the drugs along with them.

Crucially, the bots' rigid backbone ensures that they spin predictably, while the gel body prevents the particles from sticking together and forming a clump.

The researchers introduce the tiny robots into blood vessels where clots are present.

The robots' motion helps to direct blood-clot-dissolving drugs toward the clots in question.

The team first tested the microbots in a silicon model of a blood vessel that contained clots of pigs' blood. Aided by the rotating microparticles, a thrombolytic drug dissolved the blockages around 10 times faster than medication alone did. That's a potentially life-saving difference, the researchers said.

They then repeated the experiment in live pigs, placing clots in vessels in each of the animals' kidneys. "When we introduced our micro-robots with a conventional, state-of-the-art drug, we could reperfuse [restore blood flow to] a much larger area than if only the drug was there," Schürle said. "The next step is doing safety studies over a longer time and in larger animals."

Earlier safety studies in mice showed that both the iron oxide and the gel sheath polymer safely break down in the body within a few weeks. However, the team will now need to demonstrate that the device is safe in larger mammals before it can be trialed in human patients; their latest test in pigs did not look at how the device broke down or how the pigs fared after the clots were dissolved.

Ultimately, the researchers hope that the bots could be injected into the body alongside the thrombolytic medicine. Once inside, they'd be controlled by targeted electromagnets, making the technique easy to integrate into existing clinical procedures for treating clots.

The team's research is still undergoing peer review, but Schürle has applied for a patent for the microbots' production, which uses a droplet-based microfluidics technique to form each individual particle.

"It's a very cheap, high throughput method to produce the micro-robots," she said. "It's about improving the [clot-dissolving] procedure where it is lacking and helping the drugs travel the last millimeters to be really effective."

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

Currently based in York (UK), she formerly worked as a science content developer at the University of Oxford, and later as a member of the Chemistry World editorial team. Since becoming a freelancer, Victoria has expanded her focus to explore topics from across the sciences and has also worked with Chemistry Review, Neon Squid Publishing and the Open University, amongst others. She has a DPhil in organic chemistry from the University of Oxford.

#6316. Meet the history-makers of the 120th Congress

Democrat Annie Andrews, here addressing supporters at her election night party in Charleston, S.C., on Tuesday, is the first woman elected to the Senate from South Carolina. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

The incoming freshman class of the 120th Congress includes several people who scored historic wins in their states and the nation at large.

Among them were women breaking glass ceilings in the Senate and trailblazers for Native American representation. Beyond Washington, a handful of nominees pulled off milestone victories in gubernatorial elections, including four Black candidates. Congress is also poised to witness history next year with New York Democrat Hakeem Jeffries expected to become the first Black speaker.

Here are some of the candidates who made history on election night, both in Congress and in the governor's mansions:

Alfonso, the son-in-law of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, is the first Gen Z Republican elected to Congress with his victory in Wisconsin’s open 7th District, a seat his father-in-law once held.

Andrews, a pediatrician, becomes the first woman elected to the Senate from South Carolina after defeating appointed Republican incumbent Darline Graham, the first female senator from the Palmetto State.

With her victory in New York’s 13th District, Avila Chevalier becomes the first Muslim person elected to Congress from the Empire State. She succeeds Democratic Rep. Adriano Espaillat, whom she defeated in the primary.

Benitez-Thompson, a former majority leader of the Nevada State Assembly, is the first Democrat elected to represent the state’s 2nd District since its creation after the 1980 census.

With his victory over Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, Colom, a district attorney, will be Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction. He will also be the Magnolia State’s first Black senator elected directly by voters.

Conely, a Navy veteran, unseats Republican Rep. Mike Lawler to become the first openly gay woman elected to Congress from New York.

Dandiya, the daughter of Indian immigrants, becomes the first South Asian American elected to Congress from Florida with her victory in the redrawn 22nd District. She is also one of the first adherents of Jainism to be elected to Congress, along with Arizona's Amish Shah (see below).

With his victory over Republican Mike Rogers, El-Sayed, the son of Egyptian immigrants, becomes the first Muslim person elected to the Senate.

A member of the White Earth Band of Ojibwe, Flanagan becomes the first Native American woman elected to the Senate with her victory over Republican Michele Tafoya. The outgoing Minnesota lieutenant governor is also the first Native American to represent the state in Congress.

Ford, a state senator, unseated Republican Rep. Victoria Spartz to become the first openly gay person elected to Congress from Indiana.

Hamawy, a former Army surgeon who emigrated from Egypt to the U.S. as an infant, is the first Muslim person elected to Congress from New Jersey, with his victory in the state’s 12th District.

Killin, an Army veteran and onetime chief of staff to former second gentleman Doug Emhoff, is the first Democrat elected to represent Colorado’s 5th District since its creation after the 1970 census.

Kiros, who upset Rep. Diana DeGette in the Democratic primary for Colorado’s 1st District, easily won the general election to become the first Black woman elected to Congress from the Centennial State. Kiros, who was born in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, and emigrated to the U.S. as an infant, is also the first Gen Z woman elected to Congress.

Koh, the son of a Korean American father and a Lebanese American mother, is the first Asian American elected to Congress from Massachusetts. The former Biden administration alumnus will succeed Democrat Seth Moulton in the state’s 6th District.

Letlow, the first Republican woman elected to the House from Louisiana, earns the same distinction in the Senate with her victory over Democrat Jamie Davis in the open-seat race to succeed GOP Sen. Bill Cassidy.

Limtiaco will be the first Chamorro woman to represent Guam in Congress after she unseated Republican Del. James C. Moylan. She previously was the first woman to serve as U.S. attorney for the Districts of Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands.

McCann, a state senator, defeated Republican Rep. Bill Huizenga to become the first Native American elected to Congress from Michigan. McCann is a member of the Citizen Potawatomi Nation.

Moss, the president pro tempore of the Michigan Senate, keeps Rep. Haley Stevens’ 11th District in Democratic hands, becoming the first openly gay person elected to Congress from Michigan.

The grandson of a Mexican immigrant, Ojeda, who defeated National Republican Congressional Committee Chairman Richard Hudson, is the first Latino elected to Congress from North Carolina.

By defeating former Sen. John E. Sununu, Pappas, a fourth-term congressman, becomes the first openly gay man elected to the Senate.

The daughter of immigrants from Chile and Cuba, Powell is the first Latino person elected to Congress from Nebraska after flipping the state’s 2nd District. She is also the first Democratic woman elected to Congress from Nebraska.

Unofficial returns show Sarauw winning the open-seat race to succeed outgoing Del. Stacey Plaskett, making her the first openly gay person elected to Congress from the U.S. Virgin Islands.

The son of Indian immigrants, Shah is the first South Asian American elected to Congress from Arizona. The former state legislator is also one of the first adherents of Jainism to be elected to Congress, along with Florida’s Pia Dandiya.

A citizen of the Ysleta del Sur Pueblo Nation, Valdez is the first Native American elected to Congress from New York. The New York State assemblywoman will succeed retiring Democratic Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez.

Wiener, a state senator who succeeds former Speaker Nancy Pelosi in California’s 11th District, is the first openly gay person elected to represent San Francisco in Congress.

With her victory over Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, Acton becomes the first woman elected governor of Ohio. Republican Nancy Hollister briefly served as the state’s top executive in the late 1990s but was never elected governor.

The son of Mexican immigrants, Becerra, a former congressman and Health and Human Services secretary, is the first Latino to be elected governor of California. He is the state’s second Latino governor after Romualdo Pacheco, who was never elected to the role but briefly succeeded an incumbent in 1875.

Blackburn, Tennessee’s first female senator, will soon become the Volunteer State’s first female governor after her victory over Democrat Jerri Green.

Crowley, the Milwaukee County executive, will be the first Black person elected governor of Wisconsin after he defeated Republican Rep. Tom Tiffany.

Republican Rep. Byron Donalds will become Florida's first Black governor after he defeated Democrat David Jolly, a former GOP congressman.

Ford, the current Nevada attorney general, will become his state’s first Black governor after defeating Republican incumbent Joe Lombardo.

Haaland, a member of the Pueblo of Laguna, will become the first Native American woman to be elected governor in the U.S. after defeating Republican Gregg Hull. The former Interior secretary was also one of the first Native American women elected to Congress, along with Kansas Rep. Sharice Davids, in 2018.

Hinojosa, a state representative, will become the first Hispanic person elected Texas governor since statehood after she unseated three-term Republican incumbent Greg Abbott.

Klobuchar, the first woman to be elected senator from Minnesota, makes history again with her election as her state’s first female governor.

With her victory over Republican businessman Rick Jackson, Lance Bottoms becomes the first woman to be elected governor of Georgia. The former Atlanta mayor is also the state’s first Black governor and the first Black woman to be elected governor anywhere in the country, along with Del. Stacey Plaskett in the U.S. Virgin Islands.

Unofficial returns show Plaskett, the nonvoting delegate from the U.S. Virgin Islands, becoming the first woman to be elected governor of the island territory. She is also one of the first Black women to be elected governor in the country, along with Lance Bottoms in Georgia.

#6315. Nov. 17, 1966: A phenomenal Leonid meteor storm

On Nov. 17, 1966, the Leonids put on one of the greatest meteor shows in recorded history, during which eyewitnesses reported a sky that seemed to “rain shooting stars.” Observers in North America witnessed a peak of thousands of meteors per minute; Kitt Peak National Observatory reported 40 meteors per second. This peak occurred around 12:00 Universal Time, and lasted for about 15 to 20 minutes. As the requisite rate of 1,000 meteors per hour was not just met but superseded dozens of times over, the event was firmly classified as a true meteor storm.

Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.

#6314. We know how to stop computer worms. But what if AI helps them persist?

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

AI worms could spread like octopuses or slime molds, exploiting smart devices

Common forms of cyberattack include viruses and worms. Researchers recently added new styles of attack to the twisted menagerie: worms that act more like octopuses or slime molds.

VICTOR HABBICK VISIONS/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY/Getty Images

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

AI is already powering new, more adaptable forms of cyberattack, but hackers typically wield the technology from afar. What if they set the AI models themselves loose to self-replicate and spread in a malicious manner?

Recent experiments have demonstrated two different ways this could happen. Two independent teams showed how a cyberattacker could turn an AI model into a “worm,” a type of malware that, unlike a computer virus, spreads on its own. And AI unlocked a new worm power: adapting attacks to different devices.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The results hint at a new way AI could be used to ramp up cybersecurity threats — not just to computer systems but to smart devices such as security cameras or refrigerators. The good news is that the world still has time to build up defenses as several obstacles remain before this type of malware would work in the real world, says AI researcher Jonas Guan.

AI could indeed make a worm “much harder to stop,” he says, but “there are a lot of kinks to iron out before something like this really works at scale.”

Here is how a worm cyberattack works. A malware worm squirms through the internet, copying itself onto whatever systems it can hijack. Hackers can then mine hijacked systems directly for their data or link them together into a botnet and use its computing power, often to send spam email or overwhelm websites with traffic, knocking them offline.

Historically, computer worms have been small, simple programs preprogrammed to take advantage of specific security weaknesses. So they could only get into devices that had that weakness. When defenders patched a worm’s target, it could no longer spread. With an AI model directing its actions, however, a worm can adapt and learn on the fly, choosing its line of attack depending on the device, says Guan, of the University of Toronto.

That adaptability enables the worm to burrow into many different types of devices, both experiments showed. When hackers unleash AI from afar, they orchestrate what the model does. An AI worm that copies itself widely could hypothetically escape anyone’s control.

Still, there’s a caveat to the experiments’ results, says Michael Alexander Riegler, a cybersecurity researcher at Simula Metropolitan Center for Digital Engineering in Oslo, Norway. Both teams’ test environments made it easier for the AI worm to spread than it would be in the real world, says Riegler, who was not involved in either study.

And there’s another practical obstacle to the unleashing of AI worms. They use more computing power and take up more space than a conventional worm. The Mirai worm, which took down a slew of websites including Reddit and Spotify in 2016, was a few kilobytes in size, while the medium-sized AI models in the experiments were tens of gigabytes. That’s still way smaller than the massive, top-of-the-line models behind the “rogue AI” incidents that made headlines earlier in 2026. (And those weren’t worms, because they didn’t copy themselves and spread.)

Most devices — including typical laptop computers — don’t have enough space or the right kind of chips to run worm-capable AI models, Guan says. But new versions of devices, such as security cameras, are coming out with advanced hardware for running AI, researchers at the AI company Anthropic write. And at the same time, even smaller AI models are becoming more capable of sophisticated cyberattacks. These developments could expand the pool of devices an AI worm could exploit.

“The ingredients are converging” to make AI worms more realistic, Riegler says. How quickly they will converge is up for debate. Anthropic puts the timeline at months into the future, but both Riegler and Guan say it will probably take longer.

The Mirai worm spread itself through smart devices including home routers, security cameras and even baby monitors. It broke into these devices by trying a small set of common default usernames and passwords. “Just using this very simple technique, this Mirai botnet was able to infect hundreds of thousands of devices,” says cybersecurity expert Zane Ma of Oregon State University in Corvallis, who presented an analysis of the attack at a 2017 security symposium. High-profile downed sites such as Reddit were actually collateral damage: A small group of young hackers had created the worm to mess with gaming servers.

Rebooting an infected device cleared Mirai. Changing its default login credentials prevented reinfection through the same route. But an AI-powered worm might make cleaning up this type of cybersecurity breach much more difficult. Why? Because the AI worm acts more like an octopus, Guan says.

Guan and colleagues tested this octopus-worm in a virtual network. Anchored by several powerful computers that each had a chip called a graphics processing unit, or GPU, the faux networks also contained simulations of smart devices, including office printers and security cameras.

The octopus’s AI model head started on a single machine with a GPU. From there it sent out tentacles to take control of smaller devices. Upon encountering a new device, the head would use AI to plan how its tentacle could hack in. Often, a hack wouldn’t work, but the octopus wouldn’t give up. It would use info about how it failed to come up with a new hack to try. That ability is “a new, hypercharged way of attacking systems,” Riegler says. Whenever it found a computer with a large enough GPU, it would copy its head onto that new machine.

An attacker would probably launch an octopus-style AI worm from the cloud. Click through this slideshow to see how it might spread autonomously. First, it takes over and copies itself onto a device with the right kind of hardware (chip icon) to house an AI model (first image). From there, it sends out tentacles (red arrows) to hack into any connected devices, like 3-D printers and security cameras (second image). Devices that don’t have enough space for the AI model become jumping-off points for the octopus-worm to discover new places to copy itself (third image).

J. Hirshfeld; adapted from J. Guan et al/arXiv.org, 2026

J. Hirshfeld; adapted from J. Guan et al/arXiv.org, 2026

J. Hirshfeld; adapted from J. Guan et al/arXiv.org, 2026

The head could also search a simulated internet for information about newly discovered vulnerabilities. (The team didn’t connect it to the real internet for obvious reasons — protection against an AI octopus invasion — and spent considerable effort making sure their creation couldn’t escape the lab, Guan says.)

The octopus-worm even came up with a way to survive a reboot, something Guan says they hadn’t asked it to do. The team posted a preprint of their findings at arXiv.org on June 2, and the paper is now going through peer review.

Meanwhile, at Anthropic, researchers showed another way an AI worm might work by building on Guan and his colleagues’ research. If an octopus-worm wasn’t weird enough, Anthropic dubbed its creation a “digital slime mold”, a name that captures the model’s slow, oozing behavior. Anthropic declined to comment for this story, but Guan says the company’s work shows that “unlike human reasoning, AI reasoning can be distributed.” That means an AI worm wouldn’t necessarily need to hijack a powerful computer to copy and run itself — it could spread its “thinking” out among smaller devices.

And that’s exactly what the slime mold version of an AI worm does. It breaks itself up and runs pieces of the model on multiple smaller devices. In their report posted online October 12, the Anthropic researchers used 15 Android smart TVs that they had networked together.

Anthropic’s chopped-up model processes data thousands of times more slowly than what’s possible with GPUs similar to the ones Guan and colleagues relied on. That’s because the model’s data has to travel over internet connections that could take it all around the world during processing, rather than remaining in one place, within chips optimized for AI processing. That pace was too slow to demonstrate an ability to spread like a computer worm, Guan notes. So the Anthropic team ran a separate experiment with an AI worm running on GPUs that showed it could spread and adapt its attacks to different kinds of devices.

Whether AI worms are coming in months or whether we have longer to prepare, defenders should get ready now, Guan says. And AI worms do have weaknesses.

For one thing, the large size of an AI worm could be its downfall. Even if smaller AI models become more capable, these are still big programs that guzzle computing power. You might not notice if your fridge or microwave suddenly started sending lots of traffic onto the network, but your internet service provider would. They’d realize “there’s something weird going on on these devices,” Ma says. From there, they could quarantine affected devices, disconnecting them from the internet to prevent further spread.

Ma also points out that most smart devices in a person’s home aren’t directly connected to the public internet. Most home networks use a router as a central hub, and that provides a layer of protection against a worm attack.

Strong passwords, regular updates and other normal security measures would also protect against the attacks demonstrated in both experiments, Riegler says.

Guan and some colleagues are now testing specific defenses to stop AI worms, including devising an AI-driven defender. Trying to anticipate emerging threats and protect systems ahead of time is “what I’m passionate about,” Guan says. “We are working on the problem day and night.”

Up to 15 shooting stars per hour may be visible as the Leonids peak under dark skies tonight (Nov. 16 - 17), with the moon setting before the best viewing hours.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

One of November's best meteor showers peaks tonight (Nov. 16-17) and is expected to bring up to 15 "shooting stars" per hour to a near-moonless night sky.

Although the annual Leonid meteor shower, which is famous for occasionally producing spectacular meteor storms, is active from Nov. 6 to Nov. 30, the peak on Monday into Tuesday is the best time to look, according to the American Meteor Society.

Although the Leonids typically produce around 15 meteors per hour under ideal conditions, they're among the year's fastest shooting stars, reaching 43 miles per second (70 kilometers per second), and often produce bright meteors that leave glowing trails.

The best time to see them is between midnight and dawn Tuesday (Nov. 17), when the constellation Leo, from which the meteors appear to radiate, climbs higher in the eastern sky. However, shooting stars can appear anywhere in the sky.

A 45%-lit waxing crescent moon will set just before midnight, leaving dark skies for meteor watching. For the best views, find a spot away from artificial lights, lie back with a wide view of the sky, and allow about 20 minutes for your eyes to become adapted to the dark. Don't use binoculars or a telescope during a meteor shower; they will only restrict your view. However, you can try your hand at photographing the shower with your smartphone or a good astrophotography camera.

The Leonids are produced by tiny particles of dust and debris left behind in the inner solar system by Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, which takes about 33 years to orbit the sun and is about 2.2 miles (3.6 km) in diameter. Tempel-Tuttle last visited the inner solar system in 1998 and is due to return again in 2031.

Although no rapid-fire "meteor storms" are expected this year, the Leonids are famous for occasionally producing outbursts of 1,000 shooting stars per hour. Such storms occurred in 1833, 1866, 1966, 1999, 2001 and 2002, according to the American Meteor Society. The next storm is expected to hit in 2099.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

After the Leonids, the next major meteor shower will be the Geminids, which peak overnight on Dec. 13-14. The Geminid meteor shower, which is caused by an asteroid rather than a comet, can produce up to 120 meteors per hour. This year, the Geminids will peak in dark skies, thanks to a slim crescent moon setting shortly after dark on Dec. 13.

Jamie Carter is a Cardiff, U.K.-based freelance science journalist and a regular contributor to Live Science. He is the author of A Stargazing Program For Beginners and co-author of The Eclipse Effect, and leads international stargazing and eclipse-chasing tours. His work appears regularly in Space.com, Forbes, New Scientist, BBC Sky at Night, Sky & Telescope, and other major science and astronomy publications. He is also the editor of WhenIsTheNextEclipse.com.
