#6297. I Tested SwitchBot’s Tiny Robot Vacuum, and It Reaches Under Couches Where Bigger Bots Can’t

It stands just 3.6 inches tall, picks up pet hair and cat litter, and docks in a station that’s nice enough to leave out.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

I’ve had a SwitchBot robot vac running laps around my home’s lower level for more than a year, so I figured the K11+ Pro wouldn’t hold many surprises. The robot itself is the same compact cleaner I already know from the SwitchBot K10+ Pro Combo, minus the handheld attachments that come with the Combo. Then I unpacked the docking station.

It takes up less floor space than a sheet of printer paper, has a creamy finish with a faux wood top, and looks more like home decor than a cleaning appliance. It’s the perfect way to upgrade the form and function of our guest suite—adding a cute cleaning tool without taking up too much space or making the room feel like a utility closet.

SwitchBot calls the K11+ Pro the world’s smallest robot vacuum, and that diminutive size is the whole appeal. Most robot vacuums stop at the edge of the couch or bed. This one disappears underneath furniture and comes back out with the pet hair, lint, and stray cat litter that I can rarely reach with an upright vacuum or cordless stick vac.

After weeks of frequent cleaning, I’ve come to appreciate this little robot for exactly what it is. It’s not a do-everything flagship, and it doesn’t try to be one. It’s one of the easiest robot vacuums to live with—and its price makes it even easier to like.

I ran the K11+ Pro on hardwood, laminate, tile, and low-pile carpeting, and I sent it under every sofa, bed, and dresser it could fit under. My house supplies plenty of test material, including pet hair, tracked cat litter, crumbs, and lint.

I tested the mapping, no-go zones, mopping pads, and voice prompts, and I watched how it maneuvered around pet toys, shoes, blankets, cords, and my weird little cat who likes to get in the way of every robot vacuum. Since I’ve used the K10+ Pro for more than a year, I also had a long-term reference point for how this robot holds up day to day.

At 3.6 inches tall and just under 10 inches wide, the K11+ Pro fits under furniture that blocks most other cleaning robots. It slides beneath my couch and beds without getting wedged, and it cleans hidden zones just as well as the open floor.

Corners usually give round robots trouble, but SwitchBot’s Anti-Tangle Twin Side Brush helps solve this problem. The brush extends to sweep debris out of corners and along walls, so the K11+ Pro gets closer to full edge-to-edge coverage than I expected from a robot this size.

The smaller footprint pays off in another way, too. The robot weighs about 5 pounds, so I can carry it to another room, set it down, and let it work. That makes it handy for a single room, a home office, or a spot that needs a quick cleanup.

With up to 150 minutes of runtime, it can handle my home’s entire lower level before heading back to the dock. When I set it to do just our guest suite, it’s back on the charger long before it runs low on battery.

I didn’t expect a whole lot of cleaning power from a robot this compact, but 12,000 Pa of suction gives the K11+ Pro more pull than its size suggests. I watched it collect pet hair, lint, cat litter, and crumbs from hard floors and the surface of low-pile carpet without leaving trails behind. It’s a solid fit for pet-friendly homes that mostly have hard floors and area rugs.

The rubber roller brush resists tangles. I never had to cut hair off the roller itself, though hair can build up at the ends of the brush. SwitchBot includes a combination cleaning and hair-cutting tool, which handles that in a few seconds.

Thicker carpet is a different story. Like every robot vacuum I’ve tested, the K11+ Pro lifts debris from the top of the carpet but doesn’t reach down to the pad. For deep carpet cleaning, I still rely on a full-size machine like the Dyson Ball Animal 3, since upright and canister vacuums reach deeper into thicker piles.

The K11+ Pro’s docking station is where this model separates itself from the K10+ Pro. It takes up even less room, and the extra-large 4-liter dust bag fills the whole upper cabinet.

SwitchBot says a bag can last up to 90 days, and based on how slowly mine has filled, I believe it. Lifting off the top to check the bag takes a second, and the dock comes with a bag preloaded, so I had it running within minutes of unboxing.

The one catch here is noise. The robot runs at a comfortable volume while it cleans, but the self-emptying cycle gets loud for such a small machine. It lasts only a few seconds, though, and I just schedule runs for times when I don’t need a quiet house.

The K11+ Pro uses LDS LiDAR to map rooms and plan efficient cleaning routes, and side sensors help it steer around chair and table legs. Drop sensors keep it away from stairs, and it climbs thresholds up to 1.7 cm, which includes every transition strip in my house.

I named rooms on the map and set no-go zones in a few minutes. It steered around pet toys, blankets, and shoes, and kept cleaning even while one of my cats stalked it from room to room. It will swallow cords, though, so check under and behind furniture before a run.

It also lacks the headlight many costlier robots use to spot obstacles and stay visible in dark rooms. LiDAR units don't need light to map or run, so I didn’t notice any trouble with navigation, but it’s worth knowing if having a lighted vacuum matters to you.

The K11+ Pro comes with premoistened mopping pads you attach to the bottom of the unit by hand, and they work for light cleanup on hard floors. But think of it as making passes with a Swiffer rather than a powerful scrub. The pads pick up dust and light spills, and the no-go zones come in handy for keeping the damp pad off rugs and carpet.

If you need deep mopping, you’ll want a different tool for the job. A wet-dry vacuum like the Dreame H15 Pro Heat or G10 Pro tackles sticky spills and dried-on messes, and a robot with a self-cleaning roller mop, such as the Eufy Omni E35, handles hands-off scrubbing.

Setup was a breeze. I just followed the quick-start guide: turn on the switch under the top cover, open the app, and connect it to WiFi. I already had the SwitchBot app loaded on my phone, and it connected right away.

I’ve always found the SwitchBot app easy to use. Starting a full cleaning run, picking a single room to tackle, or drawing a no-go zone takes a couple of taps. The robot also talks, announcing what it’s doing and when it needs something, which saves me from checking the app.

If you already run a smart home, it’ll fit right in. The K11+ Pro works with Alexa, Google Home, Apple Home, and Home Assistant without an extra hub.

I love the K11+ Pro, and that comes down to expectations. It’s not a full-size robot vacuum and mop with every bell and whistle. If you want a robot that scrubs floors and washes its own mop, a model like the Eureka J15 Pro Ultra fits that role. The K11+ Pro does something different. It squeezes into tight spaces, cleans under and around furniture, and keeps hard floors and low-pile rugs tidy with very little help from me.

While it’s not the top choice as the main vacuum in a larger home, it’s perfect for apartments, smaller homes, individual rooms, and anyone who wants a dependable robot vacuum for pet hair on hard floors. Pair it with a lightweight stick like the Levoit Aero or another cordless stick vacuum for quick spot cleanups, and you’ve got most of your floors covered.

#6296. At the Races: After the deluge

Tuesday’s rout by Democrats has led one group dedicated to electing more Republican women to Congress to warn of a “crisis-level decline” of female GOP members on Capitol Hill.

Danielle Barrow, the president of Women for Women Action Fund, drew parallels between this week’s results and the 2018 blue wave.

“After 2018, when Republicans lost 40 seats and elected only one new Republican woman, the party made a real commitment to recruiting and investing in women – and it worked,” Barrow said in a statement Wednesday, adding that women accounted for 11 of the 15 House seats the GOP picked up in the 2020 election. But she cautioned that the party needs to sustain that focus across election cycles.

“Republicans cannot only make this investment after a wipeout election and abandon it when things improve,” she said. “It is time for party leaders to treat this as a permanent strategy, not a crisis response.”

The ranks of House Republican women won’t plummet to as low as after the 2018 elections, when the caucus had just 13 female members. At least 18 Republican women have won House races so far, according to The Associated Press, and two others are leading as of Thursday afternoon. The conference is likely to see two new female members: Florida’s Sydney Gruters, the wife of RNC Chairman Joe Gruters, and Washington state’s Amanda McKinney, who holds a comfortable lead as votes continue to be counted.

Still, those figures are worlds apart from House Democrats, whose caucus will have more than 100 women next year.

“We have always known that when women run, women win,” Florida Rep. Lois Frankel, chair of the member-led Elect Democratic Women PAC, said in a statement Wednesday.

Those incoming new members span the ideological range of the party, including progressives from New York and California who scored big primary wins this summer, to more moderate Democrats who flipped seats in Virginia and Pennsylvania.

House Democrats had set a public goal this cycle to push their female membership past 100. Former Speaker Nancy Pelosi, who is retiring at the end of the year, said electing Democratic women had been her “passion” since she joined the House in 1987.

“We made a decision to make more room for women at the tables of power – and generations of candidates, organizers and supporters have carried that work forward,” she said.

Blue breakthrough: Democrats flipped the House and Senate this week, giving the party one of its biggest nights in decades. On the Senate side, they wrested seats from Republicans in Texas, South Carolina, Kansas, Iowa, North Carolina and Ohio, while finally flipping Maine. Meanwhile, on the House side, Democrats were on track to not just win every race rated a Toss-up by Inside Elections but also pick up seats in deep-red territory that weren’t considered competitive until late in the cycle. Mary Ellen and Daniela summed up their initial election night takeaways, including how Democratic moderates and progressives both cheered the results and why many of Trump’s picks flopped at the ballot box.

Not going anywhere: The top Senate Democrat, Charles E. Schumer of New York, is confident he will be elected majority leader by his caucus, especially after the party’s resounding midterm wins. Several of his incoming members have promised to support others, our colleague Savannah Behrmann reports, but the reality is there’s no real plausible alternative. Schumer’s own seat is up in 2028.

Redistricting rout: Republicans’ redistricting gambit hasn’t paid off as they’d hoped, the latest election results show, with the GOP appearing poised to flip only a handful of redrawn seats. Democratic incumbents who sought reelection from their reconfigured seats appeared poised to all win, although the race for Rep. Darren Soto’s Central Florida seat remained uncalled as of Thursday afternoon.

Taking the chair: Among the bruising defeats that North Carolina Republicans suffered this week was National Republican Congressional Committee Chairman Richard Hudson’s loss to Democrat Richard Ojeda, a former West Virginia state senator. Hudson is now the second party campaign chief to lose reelection this decade after New York’s Sean Patrick Maloney , who lost in 2022 while serving as the DCCC chair.

New senators: The incoming Senate Democratic class includes a returning senator, a former governor, two lieutenant governors and a congressman, a notable amount of governing experience. Meanwhile, five Republican House members are moving across the Rotunda after winning open Senate seats.

Member-to-governor pipeline grows: Five newly elected governors will be departing Capitol Hill to become the top executive of their state or territory, Savannah reports. Additionally, two former members who also served in the Biden administration were elected governor, though a trio of House Republicans fell short in their gubernatorial bids.

Comeback season: Roll Call’s Nick Eskow reports on the former members who are poised to return to the House or Senate next year, with at least seven winning comeback bids Tuesday.

The firsts: Several candidates made history this week with their elections to Congress or the governorships of their state. Roll Call’s Andrew Menezes rounds up the milestone wins.

D.C. in the House: Robert White, D.C.’s newly elected nonvoting delegate, told our colleague Nina Heller that he plans to lobby fellow Democrats next year to support D.C. statehood. A potential selling point: The party could tackle affordability concerns better with two Democratic senators from the deep-blue District, he said.

Keeping count: As of 4:30 p.m. Thursday, Democrats had flipped 42 seats in the House and seven in the Senate, according to the AP. Republicans have so far picked up two House seats, both through redistricting. Twenty-eight House contests and two Senate races (Alaska and Mississippi) remain uncalled as of publication time. Check out Roll Call’s results tracker for updates as the races are called.

Indie losses: Independent Senate hopefuls running in deep-red states did not find success on Tuesday, even in races without a Democrat on the ballot. In Nebraska, former union leader Dan Osborn came up short in his second Senate bid. In Idaho, former state legislator Todd Achilles failed to dislodge Sen. Jim Risch, while Navy veteran Brian Bengs couldn’t topple South Dakota Sen. Mike Rounds. In Montana, where the Democratic nominee did not drop out, former university president Seth Bodnar lost to Republican Kurt Alme. On the House side, Alaska GOP Rep. Nick Begich comfortably leads commercial fisherman Bill Hill, though below the 50 percent threshold needed to avoid a ranked-choice runoff. With votes still being counted, the AP had yet to call the race at publication time.

Not just Congress: The blue wave that broke Republican majorities on Capitol Hill also washed over state legislatures. Democrats are poised to hold new majorities in 12 legislative chambers, including the North Carolina House and Texas House, according to the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee, although some results aren’t official yet. The party also won governing trifectas in Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin. Meanwhile, in blue states, Democrats tightened their grip on government: In Rhode Island, Republicans are on track to hold just 10 seats in the entire 113-member legislature, while next door in Connecticut, the 36-seat Senate could have as few as three GOP members.

Blame game: As Republicans take stock of what went wrong for them in the midterms, Vice President JD Vance was quick to point to the Iran conflict as an insurmountable albatross. “The reason we lost is the war,” Vance said in a lengthy X post. “If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. … But everyone knows why we lost.”

But the tariffs: A pair of Republican former senators, Arizona’s Jeff Flake and Pennsylvania’s Patrick J. Toomey, both also urged their party to focus on the impact of Trump’s tariff policies. “Arbitrary and capricious tariffs directly raised costs for all American consumers,” Toomey wrote Wednesday on X. “Many voted for Democrats yesterday.”

Staying put: Pennsylvania Rep. Brendan F. Boyle says he will remain in the House, where he’s poised to become the next Budget Committee chair, rather than launch a Democratic primary challenge to Sen. John Fetterman next cycle.

Bayh Bayh Bayh: A third generation of Indiana’s famed Bayh family won political office this week, with Beau Bayh’s election as secretary of state. Bayh, a Marine Corps veteran, follows in the footsteps of his father, Evan Bayh, who won the same post 40 years ago before going on to serve as governor and senator, and his late grandfather, Birch Bayh, who won three terms in the Senate. Indiana Democrats had a breakthrough election this week, defeating GOP Rep. Victoria Spartz, winning a second statewide office, unseating the speaker and breaking the GOP supermajority in the state House.

A win and a loss: Nebraska Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts won reelection, but his wife, Democrat Susanne Shore, lost a special election for a seat on University of Nebraska Board of Regents, which governs the university system. Shore, who lost to a fellow Democrat in the officially nonpartisan race, was making her first bid for elective office.

Bans on the ballot: Voters in Arizona, Nebraska and Washington state have approved new measures barring transgender athletes from participating in girls sports. A similar proposal in Colorado also appears likely to pass, although the AP had yet to call it as of publication time.

Roll Call elections analyst Nathan L. Gonzales of Inside Elections shares 15 initial lessons from the midterm elections, from the president’s “political mortality” to candidate quality and the power of personal brands. And, Nathan writes, as bad a night as it was for Republicans, it could have been even worse.

As Maine goes: The New York Times caught up with with Republican Sen. Susan Collins, who lost her bid for a sixth term in Maine. Collins, who had survived tough cycles before, spoke of getting “caught up in the Trump tsunami” and how she finally had her “Margaret Chase Smith moment.”

“These are extinction-level numbers”: Texas Monthly sat down for an interview with former state House Speaker Dade Phelan, who anticipated a down-ballot GOP rout but not the full extent of it. “MAGA needs to be dead,’’ said the Republican, who led the push to impeach state Attorney General Ken Paxton in 2023 and then was targeted for defeat by Trump. He opted against reelection this year.

Corruption a top issue: The Associated Press reported that its 2026 voter poll found corruption at the top of the list of concerns for voters who helped sweep Democrats into power on Capitol Hill.

Tar Heeled: Among the states where Republicans suffered their biggest defeats Tuesday, perhaps none was more stunning than North Carolina, where they've so far lost five U.S. House seats and are trailing in one another and lost control of the state House. The (Raleigh) News & Observer looks at how maps “designed to deliver strong Republican majorities [failed] so spectacularly at that goal.”

Support and discord: Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed’s sharply critical views toward Israel roiled the Jewish community in Michigan. But exit polling suggests most Jewish voters backed him, albeit in smaller numbers than they might have had a different Democrat run, Religion News Service reports.

That's how many House districts won by Trump in 2024 have been called for Democratic candidates by the AP as of 4:30 p.m. Eastern time on Thursday.

Twenty-eight additional Trump-won districts remain uncalled at publication time, and Democrats are currently leading in eight of those races.

The figures stand in sharp contrast to the start of the cycle, when there were just 13 House Democrats in districts that backed Trump in 2024.

Since then, several Republican-led states redrew their congressional maps in an effort to increase the number of Trump-won districts and improve their party’s chances of holding the House.

In large part, this effort appears to have backfired in 2026, with the Democratic wave cresting high enough to wash over dozens of Trump-won districts. Twenty-one of the 52 Democratic wins so far have come in states that redrew their congressional lines: Texas (six Trump-won seats), North Carolina (six), Ohio (five), Florida (three) and Alabama (one).

Congressional Republicans are holding leadership elections next week as they transition from the majority to the minority party. Speaker Mike Johnson is not seeking his conference’s top post, setting up a clash to be the next House minority leader. On the Senate side, South Dakota’s John Thune hopes to continue leading his party in the chamber.

#6295. Nov. 18, 1989: The Cosmic Background Explorer launches

A glow undetectable to the human eye permeates the universe. This light is the remnant signature of the cosmic beginning — a dense, hot fireball that burst forth and created all mass, energy, and time. The primordial cosmic microwave background (CMB) radiation has since traveled some 13.8 billion years through the expanding cosmos to our telescopes on Earth and above it.

Extracting clues from the CMB has taken multiple generations of telescopes on the ground, lofted into the atmosphere, and launched into space. Specifically, three satellites — COBE, WMAP, and Planck — revealed that our current cosmos, which is complex and filled with clusters of galaxies, stars, planets, and black holes, evolved from a surprisingly simple early universe.

The Cosmic Background Explorer (COBE) launched on Nov. 18, 1989. One of its instruments measured the intensity of the microwave glow at wavelengths ranging from 0.1 to 10 millimeters across the entire sky. The COBE science team’s first announcement, in 1990, was the result of that measurement. The radiation’s intensity plotted by wavelength makes it obvious that the CMB has a very specific intensity curve, where the strongest signal is at 2 mm. That wavelength corresponds to a temperature of 2.725 K. (The wavelength of light, and thus how much energy that light carries, is directly related to its temperature; redder light has less energy and a lower temperature than bluer light.)

COBE’s other instrument broke apart the seemingly uniform 2.725 K glow into more detail, looking for spots where the temperature is warmer or colder than average. It turned out there is a difference of only a tiny fraction of a degree, about 0.00001 K, between hotter and colder spots.

This nearly identical cosmic glow with exactly the right temperature was concrete evidence that the entire sky — the entire observable universe — began in a Big Bang. With such tiny temperature differences across vast regions of sky, those spots must have been in contact at early times. COBE leaders John Mather and George Smoot won the 2006 Nobel Prize in Physics for their work.

Liz Kruesi is science writer with a background in physics who specializes in astronomy and space-related news.

Physicists at the Large Hadron Collider have detected a rare, 1-in-10-billion particle interaction that opens a view into the 'zeptoverse,' the smallest distance scale ever measured.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Using the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), the world's largest particle accelerator, scientists have gotten the first glimpse of the "zeptoverse" — the universe as it behaves within less than a hundred-trillionth of a wavelength of visible light, the smallest scale that researchers have explored to date.

The new findings may one day help to answer long-standing cosmic mysteries, such as why there is far more matter than antimatter seen in the universe, and what makes up the dark matter that constitutes about 85% of all matter in the universe, the researchers announced Nov. 3 at a seminar at CERN (the European Organization for Nuclear Research), the organization that operates the LHC. The study, available as a preprint, has not yet been peer reviewed.

At the LHC, located near Geneva at the border of France and Switzerland, researchers were investigating elusive particles called beauty quarks. These subatomic particles are cousins of the standard "up" and "down" quarks that make up the cores of all atoms in the universe.

When beauty quarks are created — in this case, when the LHC smashes atoms together at incredibly high speeds — they live for just one and a half trillionths of a second before they decay. There are a number of ways beauty quarks can break down; researchers hope that analyzing rare forms of these decays might reveal that they might not unfold as expected.

Such outcomes could then shed light on new kinds of physics found only at very tiny scales of zeptometers, or trillionths of a nanometer. (For comparison, a wavelength of visible light ranges from about 380 to 750 nanometers.)

An artist's visualization of a beauty particle decaying into two muons.

By exploring this zeptoverse, scientists hope to discover new particles that have escaped detection until now.

"We're confident there must be new particles to discover, and these could help explain mysteries like dark matter and the existence of matter in the universe," study co-author Harry Cliff, a particle physicist at the University of Cambridge, told Live Science.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"Why haven't we seen these particles yet? One answer, and perhaps the most likely answer, is these new particles only become manifest at very, very short-distance scales. So by probing into the zepto scale, we give ourselves the best chance possible of finding these new particles that could explain these mysteries."

We're now recording in a single year what took 10 years to record in the past.

Now, after hunting for more than four decades, physicists have found the first evidence of the rarest kind of beauty-quark decay seen yet. "Only one in 10 billion beauty particles decay this way," Cliff said.

In this form of decay, technically known as the B0 to mu+ mu− decay, a beauty quark collides with an oppositely charged beauty antiquark. They annihilate each other, generating a pair of smaller particles ‪—‬ a muon and an antimuon. Previous research suggested that this requires a complicated set of interactions, making this kind of decay extraordinarily rare.

An experiment at the LHC called LHCb was specifically designed to study beauty quarks. In 2024, a major upgrade to LHCb made it possible to distinguish different types of particles. Using machine learning techniques, the researchers suppressed huge amounts of background noise, which helped them detect the first evidence of the B0 to mu+ mu− decay.

"We're now recording in a single year what took 10 years to record in the past," Cliff said. "And so we have this massive sample of beauty decays, and that is ultimately what allowed us to see this decay for the first time."

The new results suggest that the way this rare decay happens matches the predictions of the Standard Model of particle physics, the current best description of how the basic building blocks of the universe behave. As such, the researchers have not yet discovered signs of new particles or new physics beyond the Standard Model.

"For me, I think the most exciting thing about this result is the fact that we are probing these unimaginably short distance scales," Cliff said. "Seeing the evidence for this decay begins a new area of research where we can start to make precision measurements that will give us the best chance of finding new physics in the future."

The researchers would now like to upgrade LHCb to fully exploit the improvements to the LHC's luminosity that are currently planned for the 2030s.

"However, there is some doubt over that now because the U.K. recently withdrew funding from the project," Cliff said. "So we are really trying to figure out if we'll be able to continue this type of research."

In an ideal world, "we'll collect many hundreds of these decays in the future, make precise measurements and probe deep into the zeptoverse," Cliff said.

#6293. The 8 Best Lawn Sweepers Make Clearing Leaves a Breeze

Whether you attach one to your lawn mower or buy a dedicated push-behind model, using a lawn sweeper makes it easy to keep your lawn pristine.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

For many of us, the pretty early days of colorful autumn trees have passed, and now we’re dealing with a deluge of leaves covering the ground. During my years in grounds maintenance, much of it landscaping, fall cleanup meant long days with a rake and a blower, then bagging everything we'd piled up. A lawn sweeper thankfully takes most of the bending out of that job and is much more efficient.

With this rake on wheels, it’s the device doing all the work. As it rolls, a gear in each wheel spins a shaft of brushes several times faster than the wheels turn, and the brushes flick leaves, grass clippings, and pine needles back into a fabric hopper—the collection bag stretched over a frame. There's no engine and no cord.

The range of lawn sweepers varies from 26-inch push sweepers you use like a lawn mower, suitable for a small lawn or a patio, to tow-behinds, some of them 54 inches wide, that are pulled with lawn tractors or zero-turn mowers. To find the right one for you, look at how fast a lawn sweeper’s brushes spin at a safe ground speed (the pace you drive or walk), how far the brushes adjust into the grass, and whether the hitch holds the machine level.

Here are our top recommendations spanning various categories and use cases.

With decades of experience testing and researching lawn care equipment, our Popular Mechanics test team compiled the following recommendations based on brands we know and trust. Lawn sweepers are typically suited for large properties, with the majority of our selections in this guide being the type of models you tow behind a lawn tractor.

The recommendations here are capable of clearing large amounts of grass clippings and leaves from lawns that span a half-acre or more. For quarter-acre yards, we generally recommend a leaf blower to clear leaves and a mower with a bagging attachment to collect grass clippings. That said, we still include two lawn sweeping options for smaller yards.

Adding expertise to this article is freelance writer James Fitzgerald, who started as a ranch hand, then apprenticed as a carpenter, and spent several years in residential construction. Fitzgerald followed that with time as a production tree climber and aerial lift operator, then transitioned into facilities and grounds maintenance across multiple residential and commercial properties. All of these efforts involved a great deal of landscaping. His byline has appeared in Family Handyman, Bob Vila, The Spruce, This Old House, and Forbes Home.

For this most recent update, Fitzgerald reviewed manufacturers' specifications, owners' manuals and parts lists, and consumer reviews. For tow-behinds, he gave preference to a published brush-to-wheel ratio (written like 5:1, for five turns of the brushes to each turn of the wheels) and speed limit. Those with a hitch that adjusts to the height of a tractor's hitch plate (the flat bar at the back of the tractor with a hole for the pin) were also given preference. For push sweepers, capacity, weight, and price mattered more.

If you’ve got a lawn tractor and more yard than you want to rake, this is the sweeper that is best. It's one of the pricier picks, but what more money buys you is time. Its brackets assemble for hitch plates (the flat bar at the back of the tractor with a hole for the pin) 7 to 9, 9 to 11, or 11 to 13 inches off the ground, so it rides level whether your hitch sits low or high. The hitch can be offset so that it runs to one side of the tractor, enabling you to pick up the clippings right out of your discharge chute. Picking up already-mowed leaves theoretically lets the collection hopper fit more debris, saving you further time as you don’t have to empty as often.

Its 5.6:1 gearing spins the brushes about 470 times a minute at a 3 mph cruise, fast enough to throw debris to the back of the 28-cubic-foot hopper.

It dumps with a handle you work from the seat, which is better than a rope for the leverage on a full load of wet grass. Empty it more often when the grass is wet, since a heavy load can bend the hopper's support tubes.

At 72.7 pounds, the Yard Commander's 42-inch sweeper is the lightest of the tow-behind options in this guide. Its universal hitch attaches quickly to most lawn tractors and ATVs but not to zero-turn mowers.

Four 10-inch nylon brushes sweep into a 17.79-cubic-foot hopper, which holds a little over three lawn bags' worth and empties with the pull of a string. The corrosion-resistant steel construction delivers stability and ensures use season after season. Yard Commander doesn't publish a gear ratio or a top speed.

This mid-size lawn sweeper behind a tractor is worth a look. Its 42-inch path makes it manageable to steer easily around beds and trees, and the 22-cubic-foot hopper, about four lawn bags' worth, empties with a rope from the seat. Five hitch positions let you choose the one that leaves the hitch tubes (the bars running from the hitch to the sweeper) roughly level with the ground.

Its four spiral brushes twist along the shaft, so part of each always touches the grass and it doesn't bounce and chatter over uneven ground the way straight brushes can. Sealed bearings (ones that come greased and closed) keep dirt and grass dust out of the brush shaft, so it keeps turning freely.

I like fiberglass-reinforced nylon wheels on a machine that lives outdoors, since the glass fiber stiffens them against knocks and a solid wheel can't go flat.

Ohio Steel doesn't publish a wheel size, but a retailer lists 11-inch wheels, and smaller wheels turn more often. At a 3-mph cruise, that puts its 4.5:1 gearing at about 410 brush turns a minute, so its lower ratio costs it less than the number suggests.

Width saves laps on a big lawn, and Brinly's 54-inch sweeper has both the widest path and the largest hopper in this guide, at 54 inches and 30 cubic feet. Brinly says its six Double-Helix brushes (brush strips that twist in a spiral around the shaft) pick up continuously, even through turns. Brinly lists no brush speed, but its 12-inch wheels and 5:1 gearing put it at about 420 turns a minute at a 3 mph cruise, or 560 at the 4-mph cap. A 10-position lock arm sets brush height from about 1/4 inch to 3-1/4 inches, high for deep leaves and low for clippings.

Its clevis (the U-shaped fitting at the front of the hitch that pins to your tractor) mounts two ways, for hitch plates 7 to 10 inches off the ground or 11 to 14, so it rides level on a low hitch or a high one. At nearly 62 inches across, it needs a wide gate and shed door.

Set aside a few hours for assembly. The vinyl hopper is a tight fit, so work it onto the frame a section at a time. With acres to clear and a tractor that fits its hitch, this is the one I'd want. It's the most expensive sweeper in this guide, but the width and the hopper are what the extra money will buy you.

For a lawn that doesn't justify a tractor, Agri-Fab's 26-inch push sweeper is the one I suggest. Its hopper holds 6.2 cubic feet, a little more than one lawn bag, and that’s a lot for a machine this size. Its four brushes are geared at 5:1.

Small wheels help here. Its 9.8-inch wheels turn more often than a tow-behind's, so at a brisk 3-mph walk the brushes spin about 515 times a minute, and they slow down when you do. Brush height adjusts by sliding a tube and locking it with a knob.

At 26 pounds, it's light enough to hang on a garage wall, and the hopper frame comes off if you'd rather store it flat. Upkeep is a few drops of light oil on the brush-shaft bearings twice a year, plus cleaning and lightly greasing the wheel gears every two years.

While it's simple to put together, the plastic body flexes, so be prepared that it pushes hard with the brushes low and needs a flat lawn to pick up well. On a small, level lawn, it's the push sweeper to get.

Scotts' 26-inch push sweeper is the lightest machine recommended here, and it's sized for small jobs like a townhouse lawn, patio, or a driveway after a windy night. Its hopper holds 3.6 bushels, about 4.5 cubic feet, or a little less than one lawn bag, which is the smallest hopper in this guide. The whole sweeper weighs under 22 pounds. The hopper unhooks from the frame so you can carry it to the compost pile and tip it out.

American Lawn Mower Co. makes it under the Scotts name, touting its adjustable height control for moving between grass and hard surfaces. For my own setup, it's the one that I'd likely choose. I move around the country a lot and keep my gear modular, and a sweeper this light and small is the easiest to toss into storage.

Keep in mind that it’s best suited for a light fall of leaves. Plan on more than one pass, and if light debris sails past the hopper, slow your walk until it lands inside. Leave heavy, damp leaf piles to a bigger machine.

Brinly's 42-inch sweeper is built for a thick layer of leaves. Two things lift a deep layer—how many sweeps the brushes make and how high they reach, and it ties for the most in this guide on both.

The brush roll is highly adjustable with 10 labeled height settings. This lets you tailor the sweeper to your desired height based on the density of your leaves and yard and grass type.

While not the lightest tow-behind option in this roundup, the Brinly is on the lighter end of the spectrum, which makes it easier to hitch up to your tractor and also puts less strain on it when full of wet, heavy leaves.

Continuous-contact Double-Helix brushes, geared at 5:1, according to the company, last 2.5 times longer than other brushes. Its clevis fits hitch plates 7 to 10 or 11 to 14 inches off the ground, so it rides level on a low or a high hitch.

Ohio Steel's 50-inch model is sturdy, and its heavy steel build runs across a 50-inch path, which suits a big, open lot with pine needles, cones, and sticks to clear. Against a 42-inch sweeper, the narrowest tow-behind size here, its extra 8 inches cut about one pass in six, so an hour's sweeping takes about 50 minutes.

Its brush shaft runs on sealed ball bearings, so you never have to oil them, while some sweepers' brush shafts need oil every season. The chute (the opening debris flies through into the hopper) is 9 inches across, room for a pine cone or a fist-sized clump of wet clippings. Anything bigger catches on the lip and dams everything behind it.

Its 26-cubic-foot hopper holds about five lawn bags' worth, one of the larger hoppers in this guide, so on a big lot you stop to empty it less often. Behind a 50-inch path, I'd want that capacity, since a wider sweep fills a hopper sooner.

What can be an issue is a hopper bottom that wears through where it meets the ground, so set the hitch height that keeps the hitch tubes level and the bag off the ground. Among sweepers under $400 in this guide, it's the widest.

There are a number of important considerations to make before you purchase a lawn sweeper. Below this section, we’ll cover the following topics in further detail.

Before you shop for a lawn sweeper, walk your property. Note how big your lawn is, whether you have a riding mower or lawn tractor to tow with, how steep the slopes get, how wide your gates are, and what type of debris you’ll be picking up, from leaves and pine needles to cones and sticks.

Consider how you'll use a sweeper, towed or pushed, and if you’re using a riding mower, measure the height of the hitch plate from the ground. Then weigh sweeping width (how wide a strip it clears in one pass) against hopper capacity (how much it holds before you empty it, measured in cubic feet). A wider sweeper will obviously cover more area per pass, and if you have lots of thick, dense leaf cover, you want to make sure you aren’t having to stop and empty the hopper every five seconds.

Look hardest at ground speed and the brush-to-wheel ratio, because together they set how fast the brushes sweep. This in turn affects how much debris is pulled into the hopper in relation to the speed you are moving at. The brushes and how far they adjust come next. You want to make sure you aren’t scalping your lawn with the brushes, but also make sure you can adjust them to a height sufficient to pick up debris. The wheels and weight come last, since they mostly decide grip and the load on your tractor.

A push sweeper suits a small lawn, a patio, or a strip of driveway. A tow-behind needs a tractor of some kind, either a lawn tractor or a zero-turn mower with a rear hitch. If you don't have a riding mower or lawn tractor, check out our buying guides to the best riding lawn mowers and the best zero-turn mowers.

Keep in mind the working capacity of your riding mower. A tow-behind sweeper full of wet, heavy leaves can double its dry weight and put strain on your mower’s transmission. Before you buy, find the towing capacity in your tractor's manual and compare it with the sweeper's loaded weight. One final aspect of weight to factor in is the operator’s weight, which can affect the operating capacity of the mower.

Keep a tow-behind off steep slopes. Each sweeper's operator’s manual details slopes its own way, and there is no universal numbering system. One maker's published figure is 10 degrees, which is a rise of about 2 inches per foot, so read the slope warning for the model you're considering if your lawn has a grade. Your tractor's manual sets a slope limit too, sometimes a lower one for towing, and the lower of the two is the one to follow.

To measure a grade, lay a 2-foot level on the slope pointing downhill, lift the downhill end until the bubble centers, and measure the gap under that end in inches. Half that gap is the rise per foot.

"Fits all tractors" usually means the hitch pin (the steel pin that drops through the sweeper's hitch and the hole in your tractor's hitch plate to join them) fits. What varies is height. Hitch plates sit at different heights on different tractors, and the sweeper has to ride level at whatever height yours sits. A sweeper that tips forward or back changes the height its brushes run at, so they either dig in or skim. Tipped forward, it can also drag the front of its hopper on the ground.

The level check is one you can see. Hitched up on level ground, the hitch tubes should sit roughly level with the ground.

You don't need the sweeper in hand to check fit. Before you order one, park your tractor on level ground, measure from the ground to the bottom of the hitch plate, and compare that with the hitch heights the sweeper's maker lists, checking its manual for where it measures from and how it rounds. If your measurement falls outside every height a maker lists, look for a model whose range covers your dimensions.

Height range is varied with hitch brackets that assemble differently for different heights, a clevis with more than one set of mounting holes, or a hitch with several height positions. Some add an offset hitch, so you can mow and sweep in one pass.

Push sweepers usually cover a path of about 2 feet, and tow-behinds run wider, some to 54 inches. A 54-inch path covers more than a quarter more ground per pass than a 42-inch one, which saves more than one pass in five. On a lawn that takes 20 passes with a 42-inch sweeper, a 54-inch one finishes in about 16, which means less time on the seat and fewer turns at the ends.

Wider is harder to steer around beds and trees, and a tow-behind's frame can be close to a foot wider than its path. Makers list the assembled width in their specifications, so check it, and the height, against your gate and your shed door.

Hopper capacity is measured in cubic feet, and a 39-gallon lawn bag holds a bit over 5 cubic feet. Hoppers run from a few cubic feet on a small push sweeper to 30 on some large tow-behinds, and a bigger one means fewer trips to empty it. Treat the numbers as approximate, since retailer listings don't always match the maker's figure.

Tow-behinds usually empty from the seat, with a rope or a handle that tips the hopper. Push sweepers empty by lifting the hopper off the frame or tipping the whole machine forward. Given the choice, I prefer a dump handle. A rigid handle gives you leverage on a heavy, wet load, and there's no rope to tangle in the brushes. If you get a rope dump, fasten the rope or its pull handle to the tractor and cut off any loose tail, so nothing trails into the brushes or wheels. On a push sweeper, I like a hopper that lifts off, so I can carry it straight to the compost pile.

Because the wheels drive the brushes, your ground speed sets your sweeping power. Drive too slowly, and debris won't carry all the way to the back of the hopper. Drive too fast, and you risk damaging the wheels and gears.

Manufacturers generally cap ground speed between 4 and 6 mph. What I have found to be a smart rule of thumb is to start at a 3 mph cruising pace (covering about 44 feet in 10 seconds), and then gradually speed up, staying under the maker's limit, until the material is reliably hitting the back of the hopper. A 4-mph cap works out to about 59 feet in 10 seconds, and 6 mph to 88 feet. Stop now and then and look at the load. If it heaps up at the front of the hopper, the brushes need more speed, and if light debris sails over the top, slow down.

With your top speed limited, the real sweeping power comes down to the sweeper's gearing and wheel diameter. Manufacturers express this as a ratio, such as 4.5:1.

If you tow a sweeper with 12-inch wheels at 3 mph, the wheels turn at roughly 84 revolutions per minute (rpm). With a 4.5:1 ratio, those brushes are spinning at about 380 rpm. Bump that gearing up to 5.6:1 on the exact same wheels, and your brushes will spin at about 470 rpm.

Sweepers carry anywhere from two to six brushes on the shaft, and more brushes mean more sweeps for every turn. Some makers twist their brushes into a spiral or a double helix along the shaft, so part of each brush is always touching the grass and the sweeper runs smoother over bumps.

Brushes wear out, though, and can be costly to replace, which is why some warranties exclude them. Along with checking whether the warranty covers brush replacement, check that replacements are sold for the model you buy.

Brush height is a buying question, too. Some sweepers publish their range, about 1/4 inch to just over 3 inches, with a chart matching settings to conditions. Others give only a target of about 1/2 inch into the grass and no top height. For a deep layer of leaves, look for a range that reaches past 2 inches, which generally covers heavy leaves.

A sweeper's wheels turn its brushes, so a wheel that slides instead of rolling slows the sweep, and grip on the grass is part of pickup. Most sweeper wheels are semi-pneumatic tires (rubber tires that aren't inflated) or hard nylon or plastic, often reinforced with glass fiber, and none of these can go flat.

Diameter also matters. At the same ground speed, a smaller wheel turns more often, so it spins the brushes faster at the same gearing. At 3 mph, a 12-inch wheel geared at 5:1 turns its brushes about 420 times a minute, and a 10-inch wheel with the same gearing about 500.

On a push sweeper, weight is what you shove and lift. On a tow-behind, empty weight is only the starting point, and the loaded weight is what has to stay under your tractor's rated towing capacity.

Check the brush height first. Brushes set too low drag in the grass, and the wheels skip and slip instead of turning them. Stop the mower safely and go check the sweeper. Then raise the brushes one setting and try again. If the wheels still skid, stop again and look for something wrapped around the brush shaft or jammed in a wheel. If you have to pull a wheel to clear it, follow the owner's manual and take off one side at a time, since the left and right wheel gears often aren't interchangeable.

Some, but it isn't the best job for one. Wet leaves mat down and weigh far more than dry ones, which adds to what your tractor has to pull and stop, and dropping the brushes to dig into a wet mat only makes the wheels skid. Pushing into a wet mat of leaves loads the machine the same way, and a sweeper that already needs a flat lawn or several passes on dry leaves will struggle more with wet ones. Skip the job entirely on a muddy lawn. Sweep after the surface dries if you can, and empty the hopper right away. Damp material left in the hopper damages the bag, and a stored load of damp clippings can heat up enough to catch fire.

Keep the brushes as high as they'll still sweep, which cuts drag and wear on the brushes and wheels. Agri-Fab's 44-inch manual, for example, calls for oiling the wheel bearings once a season, lubricating the brush shaft at the start and end of the season, and greasing the wheel gears every two years. Some manuals call for white lithium grease on the wheel bearings and gears, and others call for light oil, so check the owner's manual before using anything.

Store the sweeper empty and clean with the brushes off the ground. When the brushes leave debris behind at a setting that previously worked fine, it's time to replace them.

She has written about, tested, and reviewed everything from turkey fryers to high-definition TVs. Her byline has appeared in TWICE, Sound & Vision, Consumer Reports, and many others. #6292. 2026 Full Moon calendar: When to see the Full Moon and phases

The phenomenon of a Full Moon arises when our planet, Earth, is precisely sandwiched between the Sun and the Moon. This alignment ensures the entire side of the Moon that faces us gleams under sunlight. Thanks to the Moon’s orbit around Earth, the angle of sunlight hitting the lunar surface and being reflected back to our planet changes. That creates different lunar phases.

The next Full Moon will be the November Beaver Moon, which occurs at 9:54 a.m. EST on Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026. It will also be a Super Moon.

We’ll update this article multiple times each week with the latest moonrise, moonset, Full Moon schedule, and some of what you can see in the sky each week.

Here’s the complete list of Full Moons this year and their traditional names.

(All times Eastern; * denotes a Super Moon.)

The images below show the day-by-day phases of the Moon in November. The Full Moon this month will be on Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026.

The times below for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location. All other times are Eastern unless otherwise specified. For more details on upcoming sky events, check out our full Sky This Week column

Sunrise: 6:49 A.M.Sunset: 4:41 P.M.Moonrise: 1:19 P.M.Moonset: 12:03 A.M.Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (67%)

Thursday, November 19Sunrise: 6:50 A.M.Sunset: 4:40 P.M.Moonrise: 1:41 P.M.Moonset: 1:07 A.M.Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (76%)

Friday, November 20The Moon passes 5° north of Neptune at 8 A.M. EST; 12 hours later, our satellite passes 7° north of Saturn at 8 P.M. EST. The trio is visible in the southeastern sky two hours after sunset, forming a triangle with the Moon to the upper left of Saturn, and Neptune to Saturn’s right. Only the Moon and Saturn are visible to the naked eye, while Neptune will require optical aid.

Sunrise: 6:51 A.M.Sunset: 4:40 P.M.Moonrise: 2:04 P.M.Moonset: 2:12 A.M.Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (84%)

The phases of the Moon are: New Moon, waxing crescent, First Quarter, waxing gibbous, Full Moon, waning gibbous, Last Quarter, and waning crescent. A cycle starting from one Full Moon to its next counterpart, termed the synodic month or lunar month, lasts about 29.5 days.

Though a Full Moon only occurs during the exact moment when Earth, Moon, and Sun form a perfect alignment, to our eyes, the Moon seems Full for around three days.

There are a wide variety of specialized names used to identify distinct types or timings of Full Moons. These names primarily trace back to a blend of cultural, agricultural, and natural observations about the Moon, aimed at allowing humans to not only predict seasonal changes, but also track the passage of time.

For instance, almost every month’s Full Moon boasts a name sourced from Native American, Colonial American, or other North American traditions, with their titles mirroring seasonal shifts and nature’s events.

Wolf Moon (January): Inspired by the cries of hungry wolves.

Snow Moon (February): A nod to the month’s often heavy snowfall.

Worm Moon (March): Named after the earthworms that signal thawing grounds.

Pink Moon (April): In honor of the blossoming pink wildflowers.

Flower Moon (May): Celebrating the bloom of flowers.

Strawberry Moon (June): Marks the prime strawberry harvest season.

Buck Moon (July): Recognizing the new antlers on bucks.

Sturgeon Moon (August): Named after the abundant sturgeon fish.

Corn Moon (September): Signifying the corn harvesting period.

Hunter’s Moon (October): Commemorating the hunting season preceding winter.

Beaver Moon (November): Reflects the time when beavers are busy building their winter dams.

Cold Moon (December): Evocative of winter’s chill.

In addition, there are a few additional names for Full Moons that commonly make their way into public conversations and news.

Super Moon: This term is reserved for a Full Moon that aligns with the lunar perigee, which is the Moon’s nearest point to Earth in its orbit. This proximity renders the Full Moon unusually large and luminous. For a Full Moon to earn the Super Moon tag, it should be within approximately 90 percent of its closest distance to Earth.

Blue Moon: A Blue Moon is the second Full Moon in a month that experiences two Full Moons. This phenomenon graces our skies roughly every 2.7 years. Though the term suggests a color, Blue Moons aren’t truly blue. Very occasionally, atmospheric conditions such as recent volcanic eruptions might lend the Moon a slightly blueish tint, but this hue isn’t tied to the term.

Black Moon: A Black Moon is a recent, unofficial term that can describe one of two situations. Either the third of four New Moons in a single astronomical season or the second of two New Moons in a month is a Black Moon. As its name suggests, the Black Moon is completely dark, as it is a New Moon that occurs when the Moon is between the Sun and Earth. The New Moon cannot be observed except during a total solar eclipse.

Harvest Moon: Occurring closest to the autumnal equinox, typically in September, the Harvest Moon is often renowned for a distinct orange tint it might display. This Full Moon rises close to sunset and sets near sunrise, providing extended hours of bright moonlight. Historically, this was invaluable to farmers gathering their produce.

What is the difference between a Full Moon and a New Moon? A Full Moon is witnessed when Earth is between the Sun and the Moon, making the entire Moon’s face visible. Conversely, during a New Moon, the Moon lies between Earth and the Sun, shrouding its Earth-facing side in darkness.

How does the Full Moon influence tides? The Moon’s gravitational tug causes Earth’s waters to bulge, birthing tides. During both Full and New Moons, the Sun, Earth, and Moon are in alignment, generating “spring tides.” These tides can swing exceptionally high or low due to the combined gravitational influences of the Sun and Moon.

#6291. The U.S. just lost its measles elimination status. What now?

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The virus, eliminated in 2000, has now been circulating for more than a year

Flyers provide information about a Pennsylvania Department of Health measles vaccination clinic in Lancaster County aiming to curb an ongoing outbreak.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

After two years with nearly 100 measles outbreaks, thousands sickened and nearly a dozen deaths, the United States has officially lost its measles elimination status.

The highly contagious disease is now endemic in the United States, the Pan American Health Organization declared November 17. Analyses of cases dated from when the first outbreak began in 2025 in West Texas through part of 2026 revealed the virus has been spreading uninterrupted for more than a year. That benchmark signals measles is no longer under control.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The United States is not alone. Mexico and Bolivia also lost their measles elimination status, PAHO announced; Canada had lost it in 2025. “Measles is resurging globally amid persistent gaps in vaccination coverage,” PAHO director Jarbas Barbosa said in a Nov. 17 news conference. “And this global trend is also affecting the Americas.” Countries will need to not only stop ongoing outbreaks, but also prove that no one caught measles within their borders for a full year to regain measles-free status.

That won’t happen overnight. But there is a way, experts say. Vaccinating people across the country, particularly in areas with low vaccination rates, will stifle the virus’s spread. But so far, the U.S. federal public health response has taken a back seat to efforts from state and local health departments to curb ongoing outbreaks.

Measles’s return “is an enormous black eye on the reputation of the United States,” said epidemiologist Jennifer Nuzzo of the Brown University School of Public Health in Providence, R.I., in a Nov. 9 webinar hosted by the university. The Americas led the global campaign to control the virus, and in 2016 the region became the first to eliminate measles transmission from all its countries.

“To lose [elimination status] means we’re going backwards… meaning decades of progress lost,” Nuzzo said. “It’s an indicator of our lack of protection. It is an indicator of our lack of preparedness for disease threats in general.”

PAHO’s verdict comes amid a surge of measles not seen in the United States since 1991. Health officials have recorded more than 7,000 cases since the beginning of the West Texas outbreak. That tally includes nearly 2,300 measles cases in 2025 and 5,412 in 2026 as of November 12, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Over 90 percent of cases have been in people who are unvaccinated or whose status is unknown. States report that 13 people have died, although the CDC so far recognizes only nine of those deaths.

While mild measles symptoms include high fever, cough and a rash, roughly 1 in 5 people will be hospitalized with complications such as pneumonia or brain swelling. Children younger than 5 years and adults over 20 are more likely to get sick, as are pregnant women and their infants. At least 13 babies were born infected, called congenital measles, since the beginning of 2025, researchers report November 16 in NEJM Evidence. Those babies are at risk for developing dangerous brain swelling that is almost always fatal later on in life.

The measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccine helped eliminate measles from the United States in 2000. After that, cases still sometimes popped up. Those cases were mostly in unvaccinated people traveling from parts of the world where the virus still widely circulates. At least 95 percent of people in a community need to be vaccinated to prevent outbreaks.

But widespread misinformation, including a disproven claim that the vaccine causes autism, means fewer children are receiving the MMR shot and more people are questioning its safety. According to the CDC, roughly 92 percent of kindergarteners across the United States had gotten the vaccine in 2025, down from 95 percent in 2019. And in 2025, 83 percent of U.S. adults viewed the MMR vaccine as safe, down from 86 percent in 2024, according to a survey from the University of Pennsylvania’s Annenberg Public Policy Center. Yet decades of evidence show the vaccine is safe and highly effective.

That measles made a comeback is not a surprise, says Nathan Lo, an infectious diseases physician and epidemiologist at Stanford University School of Medicine. Until recently, outbreaks were largely isolated to communities with low vaccination rates and quickly contained. But now, outbreaks seem to be more likely to spill over into neighboring communities, Lo says. “There’s a lot of potential connectedness between the outbreaks.”

What’s more, some infected people aren’t getting tested, making them invisible to officials who are now struggling to trace chains of transmission. An outbreak that hit Arizona and Utah, for instance, was far larger than official numbers suggest, researchers reported July 15 in a preprint at medRxiv.org. The roughly 1,000 confirmed cases may represent just 20 to 30 percent of the outbreak’s true size.

A functional surveillance system is crucial to keeping outbreaks under control, Jonathan Temte, a family medicine physician at the University of Wisconsin School of Medicine and Public Health in Madison, said in the Brown University webinar. Without good surveillance across the entire country, “we can miss pockets out there if people aren’t reporting, if people are hiding cases.”

But surveillance alone won’t stop the virus from “popcorning across the country,” Nuzzo said. “Measles has returned, and it’s going to take vaccination to stop it.”

Over the last two years, measles outbreaks have popped up across the United States, sickening thousands of people since mid-January 2025. Most of those cases, shown by county where they were reported, are in people who are unvaccinated. Colors on the map indicate the relative number of cases reported. Green represents the lowest and red the highest number of cases. Notable outbreaks have appeared in Utah, Arizona, Texas, South Carolina, Wisconsin and Pennsylvania.

Michael Mitchell and Andrea Uhlig/Brown University School of Public Health

Efforts to boost vaccine uptake could be targeted toward areas with low vaccination rates. Most places across the United States still have vaccination rates high enough to fend off measles, but not all. “Figuring out which ones are [high risk] can be a little tricky,” Lo says. “But if you do, then intervening in those places can be quite helpful to mitigate spread.”

Homing in on school districts or individual schools could also help. State health departments typically report vaccination rates among school-age children by county. But that broad metric can hide high risk schools with low vaccination rates, epidemiologists Siyu Chen and Ana Bento reported in August in Nature Medicine. Computer simulations relying on data that included 50,000 schools across the United States showed that school-level estimates best revealed where the virus could gain a foothold. That was true even if county-level vaccination rates were close to 95 percent.

Another element that influenced where measles took off was whether communities with cases were near other areas with low vaccination rates, the team found. The outbreak in Texas, for instance, may have ended faster because communities with low vaccination rates were farther away from one another compared with outbreaks in South Carolina and Pennsylvania, says Bento, of Cornell University. Neighboring areas where many are unvaccinated may face longer-burning outbreaks. “Which is what we are now seeing,” Bento says.

Measles elimination status can be regained. The declaration that the virus is endemic is “not a punishment,” Bento says. It’s a sign that something needs to change. That might include vaccine catch-up campaigns, community outreach or getting rid of nonmedical vaccine exemptions.

Local public health officials are “doing every last thing that you can imagine with limited resources,” health psychologist Noel T. Brewer said in a Nov. 12 webinar hosted by the Association of Health Care Journalists. But a cohesive plan at the federal level could bolster defenses before the virus arrives in new states, noted Brewer, of the University of North Carolina Gillings School of Global Public Health in Chapel Hill.

Such efforts could be targeted toward areas with low vaccination rates. Most places across the United States still have vaccination rates high enough to fend off measles. “A subset [with low vaccination rates] are high risk,” Lo says. “Figuring out which ones are which can be a little tricky. But if you do, then intervening in those places can be quite helpful to mitigate spread.”

There’s also wiggle room in the childhood vaccine schedule to provide kids extra protection. Normally children don’t get their first MMR dose until their first birthday. But doctors can give infants an extra MMR dose at 6 months if there is an active outbreak in their area. Pediatricians can also offer the second dose a month after the first one, rather than waiting until around the time children start kindergarten. Adults, particularly those who received only one dose, can also get a booster. It’s unclear whether health officials will officially recommend such actions.

“The problem is that there’s no trusted source for this vaccine decision anymore,” Lo says. Previous vaccine recommendations were up to the CDC’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices, which was disbanded in March after lawsuits blocked appointments made by Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. “Now, there’s a lot of different medical societies and initiatives to try and fill that void,” Lo says. But it’s unclear which would be best positioned to lead.

CDC director Erica Schwartz has said the health agency will not be changing its response to ongoing outbreaks. “We’re going to be doing the same exact thing that we’ve been doing today, which is working with the states,” she told Reuters. The CDC did not respond to Science News requests for an interview, but shared in a Nov. 17 statement that the agency will “encourage MMR vaccination, expand access to vaccines, and help communities close gaps in protection.”

Eliminating measles again will take dedicated resources and more funding funneled to public health departments across the country, Lo says. “You see increasing measles outbreaks and a lot of time and resources to contain these outbreaks at a time where you’re slashing budgets,” Lo says, “that’s a really bad mismatch.”

Public health responses to measles are expensive. Officials in New Mexico spent an estimated $5.4 million — over $53,000 per case — responding to a 2025 outbreak that was linked to West Texas. The CDC has provided an additional $100 million to states to help fight measles.

Other countries have beaten back measles after an unwelcome return. Extensive vaccination campaigns helped Venezuela and Brazil regain measles elimination status after briefly losing it in 2017 and 2019. The Public Health Agency of Canada also announced that its nearly two-year-long outbreak officially ended in October, though it’s unclear when the country might earn its status back.

“It is not hopeless,” Nuzzo said. “It can be done, and I hope it will be done [in the United States].”

#6290. As Democrats look to next era, the veto and the filibuster await

Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer greets House Minority Whip Katherine Clark at the Center for American Progress Action Fund’s “Results to Roadmap” event on Thursday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

As Democrats continue their victory lap after their big wins on election night, outside groups and incoming freshmen are already turning up the pressure — and laying out competing visions of what the next two years should look like.

For Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer, it bears repeating that “the Democrats aren’t all exactly the same.”

“The most important lesson of this whole election, and one we all need to internalize if we’re going to truly build a durable majority, is populism and moderation are not mutually exclusive,” he said at a Center for American Progress Action Fund event on Thursday.

Voters are expecting results as Democrats claim a mandate to address costs and corruption. “Our majority will be measured against one test and one test only: Have we made your life better?” Schumer said.

He acknowledged, however, that their plans could run into a President Donald Trump-sized wall: the presidential veto.

“Will everything pass? Will Trump sign all of it into law? Knowing Trump’s and Republicans’  intransigence, of course not. But I will promise the American people: The Democratic Party will fight to make your life more affordable, your government more competent, your capital less corrupt, bill by bill, brick by brick, for as long as it takes for you to feel the difference,” Schumer said, hinting the road could be a long one.

But several progressive lawmakers and groups say the next Congress cannot be business as usual.

Indivisible, a progressive political organization that has described the Trump administration as a “fascistic clown show,” sent a memo to Senate Democratic offices Thursday morning urging them not to “squander” their momentum and to “fight at a level that matches the public’s demand for action.”

“Who leads the party in this era must be an open question, not a coronation. It’s time to define what the next era of the Democratic Party will be,” the memo reads.

The group has been encouraging voters to speak up and demand their senators hold “a contested leadership election, not a cleared field for Schumer.”

Meanwhile, Schumer has projected confidence he will keep his spot atop the caucus, especially after he helped pave the way for Tuesday’s blue wave. “I’ll be reelected as majority leader,” he said Wednesday. But the pressure campaign points to some tough math and harsh realities for the top Democrat — including some that mirror the woes of the outgoing Republican Majority Leader John Thune.

Among the demands outlined by Indivisible is one with a troubled recent history: “Breaking the filibuster on the first day of the new session.”

Democrats need to leverage “every procedural tool” if they “want the public to believe their campaign promises weren’t just more talk from politicians who are just like the old politicians they hated,” the memo reads.

The group isn’t alone in floating a new approach to the chamber’s 60-vote threshold for invoking cloture and ending debate. Some current and incoming lawmakers have signaled they would be open to going “nuclear” and abolishing the legislative filibuster, following in the footsteps of past majorities in both parties who have similarly changed how other Senate business is handled, like judicial nominees.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., argued in an op-ed in Time this week that Democrats could in some cases use existing tools, like a party-line process known as budget reconciliation, to pass their priorities. For non-budget items, like “bills to ban stock trading by federal officials or crack down on Trump’s corruption in plain sight,” Democrats should start by putting them up for a vote on the floor and letting “Republicans decide if they want to stay tied to such corruption.”

“And, if they do, then let’s clear away Senate filibuster rules and pass the laws anyway,” she wrote.

Sen.-elect James Talarico of Texas told NBC News on Monday ahead of his victory, “I believe the majority has the right to govern in this country, and the filibuster, which is not in the Constitution and is a Jim Crow relic, is leading to gridlock in our nation’s capital.”

Schumer ignored a question about nuking the filibuster at Wednesday’s event, saying instead, “The first thing we’ll do is reduce costs and work the legislative process.”

It would take 51 votes in the Senate for Democrats to go “nuclear” and establish a new precedent, a math problem that Thune knows all too well. The Republican from South Dakota faced loud criticism from conservatives online and hard-liners in his own party who said he wasn’t doing enough to try to pass a sprawling voter ID bill known as the SAVE America Act. But Thune repeatedly insisted he didn’t have the votes to change the chamber’s filibuster rules.

Many senators fear that blowing up the 60-vote threshold would fundamentally change the role of the Senate and its ability to tap the brakes on legislation that doesn’t have durable bipartisan support. Democrats went through a similar debate over the filibuster in 2022, during Schumer's first stint as majority leader. Even as others in their party pushed to pass sweeping voting rights legislation by any means necessary, Kyrsten Sinema and Joe Manchin, then moderate Democratic senators, held firm against filibuster changes.

And Schumer will have at least one Democrat on his hands who has already spoken up in defense of the filibuster, reversing his previous position. “I now recognize how important the filibuster is and the state our country would be in without it,” Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania wrote in a Washington Post op-ed earlier this summer, praising Sinema and Manchin as “courageous” holdouts who were wrongly “vilified” for holding the line.

None of that points to an easy ride for the incoming Democratic majority leader. And if fights over the filibuster weren’t enough, the caucus is also bracing for a different kind of intraparty angst, this time over impeachment.

The next likely House Judiciary Committee chairman, Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., told reporters on Thursday: “I have not had a single member of Congress or even a candidate say we’ve got to start out by impeaching Donald Trump.”

“For us, impeachment is not a fetish. It’s certainly not a taboo. We’ve impeached the guy twice,” he said, referring to Democrats’ efforts during the first Trump administration. “The problem has been over on the Senate side, and for us, it is a tool in the constitutional toolkit.”

Even if the House were to impeach Trump, a conviction would require a two-thirds supermajority vote in the Senate. And some Democrats are eager not to waste their hard-earned political capital on an impeachment quest that could alienate moderate voters and do nothing to bring down costs for everyday Americans.

Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, who boosted candidates in battleground races and recently released a roadmap for the new Congress, said at the CAP event on Thursday that lawmakers should “hold oversight hearings and expose the corruption of this administration. I’m not suggesting that that necessarily leads to impeachment. Maybe it does.”

Sounding more certain for Democrats in both chambers is their desire to impeach Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth over the war in Iran.

But that could be dealt with in the lame duck if Rep. Thomas Massie’s, R-Ky., resolution prevails next week. His proposal includes eight articles of impeachment, including allegations that Hegseth violated the 1973 War Powers Resolution in his prosecution of the Iran war and acted illegally in military campaigns in Venezuela, Yemen, the Caribbean Sea and the eastern Pacific Ocean.

Hegseth said in a video on Thursday of impeaching: “Didn’t work against President Trump. Won’t work with me. You can rest assured of that.”

Indivisible’s memo names impeaching Hegseth as a priority, as well as blocking a “business-as-usual” National Defense Authorization Act in the lame duck and refusing to fund the Department of Defense if “it doesn’t cut off money for the war.”

But it’s not clear that Democrats in Congress are ready to play that kind of hard ball. As they weigh their approach to the next era, they’re still half-stunned themselves by their larger than expected wins — and trying to put themselves in the best position ahead of the next elections in 2028.

GOP Rep. Christopher H. Smith of New Jersey told reporters on Thursday at the Capitol he hopes Democrats don’t hold up the NDAA “for the good of the country.”

“The NDAA is such an important bill for our national security, and it’s usually very bipartisan. I hope it is,” he said.

John Donnelly and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.
