#6276. How 4 states voted on election-related ballot measures

Maryland voters fill out ballots at a polling site in Bowie on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

More than 100 statewide ballot measures went before voters this week, including a handful that could shape future elections in their states.

Here’s a look at how those measures fared, including one in Alaska that hasn’t been called as yet:

Voters in Maryland on Tuesday approved an amendment to the state’s constitution that will make it easier for the state’s Democrat-controlled legislature to redraw the congressional map for the 2028 elections.

The outcome was a victory for Democrats, who could potentially eliminate the state’s lone Republican-held seat – the 1st District on Maryland’s Eastern Shore, represented by Rep. Andy Harris, the chair of the hard-line conservative House Freedom Caucus.

The Old Line State emerged as a bright spot in Democrats’ plan to counter the redistricting wars initiated by President Donald Trump and turbocharged by the spring Supreme Court ruling that diluted Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act and set off a slew of Republican-led map-remaking across the South.

But those GOP-led efforts appeared to backfire this week, with Democrats holding many of the redrawn seats in states such as Texas, Florida, Alabama and North Carolina.

Still, Maryland Gov. Wes Moore told reporters Wednesday that he was “ready to engage” with the legislature on a new map, citing the threat of further redistricting in Republican states.

“Donald Trump is not done. He has already been very clear about his intention to go after additional states, to go after places like Mississippi and South Carolina and Indiana,” Moore said, according to video posted by WBAL-TV 11 News.

Following an unsuccessful attempt to redraw the Maryland map in February, Moore called a special August legislative session during which state lawmakers voted to put the redistricting amendment, known as Question 3, on the November ballot.

The move faced immediate legal challenges from Republicans. Two Maryland courts ruled to block the measure from appearing on the ballot, finding that lawmakers had missed the legally imposed deadline to refer the ballot measure. The state’s Supreme Court, though, allowed the redistricting amendment to go before the voters, with changes to the ballot text.

State and national Democrats campaigned heavily for Question 3 as some public polling pointed to skepticism among voters. Former President Barack Obama even appeared in an ad urging voters to approve it.

Voters in the Show-Me State overwhelmingly rejected a Republican-drawn congressional map that sought to dismantle a safely Democratic seat in the Kansas City area.

Missouri Republicans enacted the new lines in 2025, aiming to give them an advantage in seven of the state’s eight House districts, including the 5th District held by Democrat Emanuel Cleaver II.

A protracted legal and political tussle over the map ensued.

The group People Not Politicians Missouri started a citizen petition to put the adoption of the map to a statewide vote. While the petition effort was pending, the state held its August primaries under the new lines. But in September, the state Supreme Court ruled that the 2025 map could not be used in the general election because of the pending ballot measure and ordered state officials to hold November’s election under the previous boundaries, first enacted in 2022.

Attempts to challenge the ruling in federal court ultimately proved unsuccessful, with the U.S. Supreme Court issuing an order that reinstated the 2022 map.

Groups on both sides of the ballot measure, known as Proposition A, reportedly spent millions to persuade voters. But St. Louis Public Radio reported last week that while opponents of the 2025 map were actively campaigning against it, organized efforts in favor of Proposition A appeared “nearly nonexistent.”

Republican efforts to try again and enact a new congressional map for 2028 could be complicated by a constitutional amendment, approved by voters Tuesday, that curtails the power of state legislators to override the result of a voter-approved initiative.

Voters in Massachusetts opted this week not to join states such as California and Washington and adopt a nonpartisan primary system.

The ballot initiative, known as Question 3, would have replaced the state’s partisan primaries with an open primary under which all candidates would appear on the same ballot, with the top two vote-getters, regardless of party, advancing to the general election.

The outcome was a victory for the chorus of labor unions and progressive groups, including the Working Families Party, that opposed the measure. Holding so-called jungle primaries, the groups argued, could make it harder for candidates without financial resources or high name recognition to run for office.

A bipartisan coalition that included the NAACP of New England and Republican former Gov. Charlie Baker supported the measure, arguing that open primaries would give voters more choice and create more competitive elections in a state dominated by Democrats.

Alaskans weighed in this year for the second time as many cycles on a ballot measure to revert to partisan primaries and repeal the state's top-four ranked choice voting system.

With over 70 percent of the vote in, The Associated Press had yet to call the ballot initiative, known as Measure 2, which would also roll back certain campaign finance disclosure requirements. As of Thursday evening, the “no” side, which supports keeping the current election system, was narrowly ahead. The state has until Nov. 18 to finish counting outstanding ballots.

Under Alaska’s voting system, all candidates run on the same ballot during the primary. Then the top four candidates, regardless of party, advance to the general election, which is decided by ranked choice voting if no one takes a majority of the vote.

In 2024, Alaska voters narrowly voted to keep the current system in place.

National Republicans, though, have largely opposed ranked choice voting, including Trump, who has characterized Alaska’s voting system as a “scam.”

The state’s use of open primaries and the top-four ranked choice system has drawn fresh scrutiny this year.  Outside groups spent big sums trying to boost underdog candidates during the Senate primary in an effort to hurt the front-runners. And several candidates in the Senate, House and governor’s races dropped out before the deadline to finalize the general election ballot, again trying to prevent splitting votes with their party front-runners.

Then last week, the Senate race was upended by a New York Times investigation that revealed operatives aligned with the Senate campaign of Democratic former Rep. Mary Peltola helped recruit a candidate with a similar name to GOP incumbent Dan Sullivan in an attempt to stack the ballot with two Republicans with the same first and last names. The revelations have fueled an ongoing debate in the state about whether ranked choice voting encourages this kind of alleged campaign chicanery.

“We would not be having this conversation at all if we didn’t have a thing in place called ranked choice voting,” Mike Dunleavy, Alaska's outgoing Republican governor, told Fox News last week.

Dunleavy has ordered an investigation into the revelations, as has the Justice Department. The DOJ also sought to block the certification of the Senate result if the incumbent Sullivan loses. Last weekend, a federal court dismissed the lawsuit.

Alaska and Maine are the only two states that currently use ranked choice voting in regular federal elections, along with the District of Columbia.

Michael Macagnone contributed to this report.

#6275. The Best Airbnbs in Amsterdam, From Canal Houses to a Boat on the Amstel River

Amsterdam today looks remarkably similar to how it did on my first visit as a high schooler over a decade ago, with its maze of canals, steady flow of bikes, and gabled façades—many of which have stood there since the 17th century. To a history-loving teenager visiting Europe for the first time, the Dutch capital was a wonderland of Van Goghs. It felt so different from my hometown, yet still approachable, and sparked my lifelong love of travel.

What has changed since then is the crowds. Amsterdam is now one of Europe's most visited cities, so you'll need to book tickets to the major sites well in advance, especially during summer. The same goes for accommodations. On more than a dozen return trips (many by train from Belgium, where I used to live), I have stayed everywhere from youth hostels to boutique hotels to Airbnbs. And over the years, I've learned that renting an Airbnb offers a completely different way to experience the city.

Whether you're looking for a classic canal house in the Jordaan, a design-forward houseboat along the Amstel, or a multi-level family home near Vondelpark, the rentals on this list can help you settle into the city in your own way. Read on for a few of my favorite Airbnbs in Amsterdam, whether you're here for the art, the nightlife, or to explore by bike.

We've vetted these listings based on Superhost and Guest Favorite status, ratings, amenities, location, previous guest reviews, and decor.

Number of guests: 3Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Canalside location, separate kitchen, quiet street

Couples or small families who want to stay in the heart of old Amsterdam will adore this renovated one-bedroom inside a historic canal house on one of the city's widest canals. The roughly 650-square-foot space sleeps up to three, and the separate kitchen has a large dining table. Step outside and you're around the corner from lively Nieuwmarkt, where cafés line the market square. Or, check out the dim sum spots in nearby Chinatown. Despite the proximity to so much activity, previous guests say the street itself stays peaceful at night. Just be prepared to haul your luggage up a steep staircase, as is expected for most Amsterdam buildings.

Neighborhood: Centrum (Nieuwmarkt)Things to do nearby: Rembrandt House Museum, De Oude Kerk

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 2.5 bathsWhy we love it: Private garden, dedicated playroom, fireplace

As in most big European cities, space is at a premium in Amsterdam, which makes this industrial-style town house a real find for families. It even has a dedicated playroom packed with toys and books. It sits in Oud-West, a grid-like neighborhood just outside the central canal ring, steps from the daily Ten Kate Market. When the weather cooperates, fire up the Weber grill in the private garden out back. Inside, a gas fireplace warms the light-filled living room and kitchen. But you may not find yourself cooking much, since the home's location puts you right near the Foodhallen. Three bedrooms sleep up to four, with a king bed, a double bed, and a toddler bed.

Neighborhood: Oud-WestThings to do nearby: Foodhallen, Ten Kate Market, Vondelpark

Number of guests: 8Bed and bath: 4 bedrooms, 3 bathsWhy we love it: Heated pool, private garden, Nintendo Wii

Groups who want to dip in and out of city life should take a look at this detached four-bedroom house in a tranquil, residential corner of Amsterdam Noord. The nearby metro reaches Central Station in about five minutes (or you can bike there in 15), and the countryside is close by too. The highlight, however, is the large private garden, where you'll find a heated pool (open roughly April through October) and a sauna. There's also a grill and space to dine outdoors. During the colder months, your crew will probably prefer curling up on the cozy couch for a movie or a round of games on the Nintendo Wii. Practical perks include a washer and dryer, a dedicated workspace, and four bedrooms.

Neighborhood: Amsterdam NoordThings to do nearby: Eye Filmmuseum, A'DAM Lookout, NDSM Wharf

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1.5 bathsWhy we love it: King-size bed, canal views, amenities for kids

If your image of the perfect trip to Amsterdam includes staying in an authentic canal house, then consider this character-filled apartment in the leafy Jordaan neighborhood. Guests enter through the roomy breakfast area on the ground floor, and upstairs, you'll find a living area filled with plush furniture, jewel-toned accents, and views of the canal, Anne Frank House, and Westerkerk (Western Church). There's one true bedroom with a king bed and a pull-out couch in the living room. The hosts, who warmly welcome families with little ones, provide lots of kid-friendly necessities, like a high chair.

Neighborhood: JordaanThings to do nearby: The 9 Streets, Anne Frank House, Dam Square

Number of guests: 7Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 1.5 bathsWhy we love it: Piano, record player with vinyl collection, fireplace

If you're looking to house a group, this rental might be the perfect fit. The three bedrooms (a king, a double, and a single) and one-and-a-half bathrooms are scattered across multiple floors. Gather in the dining area (there's also a full kitchen) or around the fireplace in the cozy living room stocked with board games, a vinyl collection, and even a piano. Stained-glass windows and art-covered walls are fitting for the prime location near the Rijksmuseum and Van Gogh Museum. However, be prepared to carry your luggage up some steep and narrow steps.

Neighborhood: VondelparkThings to do nearby: Stedelijk Museum, Van Gogh Museum, Rijksmuseum

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1.5 bathsWhy we love it: Air-conditioning, sparkling water on tap, large garden patio

This spacious luxury apartment in a historic building offers some perks that can be hard to come by in Amsterdam: air-conditioning (in the living room and one bedroom), no stairs to climb, sparkling water on tap, and a living room that opens onto a garden patio with a lovely view of the Rijksmuseum. Families with small kids can also request a travel crib, high chair, and other gear. Plus, there isn't much for little hands to grab onto thanks to the minimalist decor. The two bedrooms each feature plush king beds.

Neighborhood: MuseumpleinThings to do nearby: Stedelijk Museum, Van Gogh Museum, Rijksmuseum

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Fitness equipment, chef's kitchen, dedicated workspace with printer

Want to feel really at home for an extended stay? Save this open-plan loft housed inside a converted 19th-century police station, which stands out with a dedicated workspace (desk, monitor, printer) and fitness equipment (kettlebells, dumbbells, rowing machine). There's also a chef's kitchen and an Art Deco–style bathroom. French doors open up onto a back terrace, and huge bay windows offer a view of a 17th-century church and the Noordermarkt, where an open-air market sets up shop twice a week.

Neighborhood: JordaanThings to do nearby: Noordermarkt, Anne Frank House, The 9 Streets

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Sage espresso machine, speakers and sound system, easy tram access

This bright one-bedroom in Oud-West sits just outside the central canal ring and combines high ceilings and ornate moldings with a modern, open kitchen and sunlit living space. Double doors lead to a quiet queen bedroom with a larger balcony in the back. A smaller front balcony overlooks the street, where a tram stops just outside and connects guests with the rest of the city. Guests will also find a supermarket right across the street and restaurants and cafés around the corner.

Neighborhood: Oud-WestThings to do nearby: Vondelpark, Foodhallen, De Filmhallen

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1.5 bathsWhy we love it: Waterfront views, indoor fireplace, washer and dryer

Think you have to choose between space and character in an Airbnb? Think again. This sleek, 2,600-square-foot houseboat on the Amstel River—yes, the river that gave Amsterdam its name—offers one bedroom, one-and-a-half baths, a full kitchen, and three terraces. In summer, watch boats drift by or take out the provided paddleboards—then cool off inside in the air-conditioning. After winter rolls in, curl up by the suspended fireplace as you gaze out of the floor-to-ceiling windows.

Neighborhood: De PijpThings to do nearby: Heineken Experience, Albert Cuyp Market, Sarphatipark

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Room-darkening shades, television with Chromecast and Netflix, access to outdoor patio

It may be on a quiet street, but this compact studio puts you close to the action, with Central Station just a couple of minutes' walk away. Light floods in through the three large windows with canal views, and the orange and copper-colored accents create a warm and inviting vibe. There's also access to a private rooftop terrace if you need a bit of fresh air. Be prepared to carry your luggage up a tricky flight of steep and narrow stairs in this fairly typical Amsterdam building that dates back to 1790.

Neighborhood: CentrumThings to do nearby: Dam Square, De Oude Kerk

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Canalside location, television with Netflix, washer and dryer

Stay right on the famous Keizersgracht (Emperor's Canal) in this first-floor apartment equipped with a washer and dryer and a full kitchen with a stove, fridge, and sink. Large, front-facing windows flood the crisp white apartment with natural light and offer a front-row seat to the city life buzzing by outside. It's also just around the corner from the Anne Frank House. The bedroom features a king-size bed, ideal for relaxing after a long day of exploring.

Neighborhood: Grachtengordel (Canal ring)Things to do nearby: Anne Frank House, The 9 Streets, Dam Square

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Canal view, garden access, host's personal art collection

Laid-back solo travelers or couples will appreciate this homey rental located on a quiet street near a few museums within walking distance of the lively Leidseplein Square. It’s wonderful for those looking to take a step back from the hustle and bustle—not the best pick for all-night partiers. The living space blends modern and vintage flourishes, featuring French paintings that are part of the owner's personal art collection and front windows overlooking a canal. A floor-to-ceiling window in the back opens to a lovely shared garden with outdoor seating where you can have coffee or tea on warm mornings.

Neighborhood: JordaanThings to do nearby: Leidseplein, Rijksmuseum, Van Gogh Museum

What are the best neighborhoods to stay in Amsterdam?

Book a stay in the Grachtengordel (canal ring) for the quintessential Amsterdam experience. The Jordaan has a similarly atmospheric feel with slightly quieter surroundings, while the Museum District puts the city's famous art museums right at your doorstep.

When is the best season to visit Amsterdam?

Spring is one of the best times to visit. It's when the city wakes up from the long winter and the Netherlands's colorful tulips burst into bloom (plan a day trip to the famous Keukenhof Gardens, about 40 minutes away). Come for King's Day on April 27, when the entire city turns bright orange with street parties and canal boat parades, or visit on the brink of summertime, in late May or June, and you'll enjoy much longer days, with daylight sometimes lasting past 9 p.m.

#6273. The Sanctuary of a Healing God Was Lost for 1,800 Years. Archaeologists May Have Finally Found It.

A century of digs in Epidaurus reveals a sacred site where pilgrims flocked to honor the son of Apollo.

In the second century C.E., a traveler named Pausanias wrote about an open-air sacred precinct featuring statues of Asclepius—the Greek god of healing and the son of Apollo—and his wife, Epione, near the city center of Epidaurus. The only issue: Nobody knew the location. But now, a scholar at the University of Athens thinks there’s enough evidence to claim we’ve solved the 1,800-year-old mystery.

Vassilis Lambrinoudakis of the Department of History and Archaeology of the National and Kapodistrian University of Athens pored over hundreds of years of research and concluded that a site in Epidaurus is the statue-filled spot Pausanias described.

Excavations started in Epidaurus in the early 1900s, and since 1974, hundreds of student archaeologists have painstakingly excavated in and around the city. Lambrinoudakis collated the research, noting that not only has he likely found the mystery location, but that cult worship of Asclepius took place at the site for longer than we knew about.

The oldest religious building in Epidaurus—dated to around 600 B.C.E.—features a structure with an underground chamber cut directly into the bedrock, likely part of early healing traditions. In Greek mythology, Asclepius took over his father Apollo’s role as a healer, and Epione was worshiped for her ability to help soothe pain. The ancient structure has a pebble-lined floor, walls coated in dark red plaster, and a circular basin built into the floor accessible by staircase. The bottoms of four amphorae are embedded in the bedrock floor. In the fourth century B.C.E., crews built a new circular building directly to the west, likely a “deliberate continuity of the same chthonic cult of Asclepius,” the university wrote in a translated statement.

Nearby, the teams found a ground-level altar made of limestone blocks that they believe is older than both buildings. Lambrinoudakis said the combination of the finds shows the cult likely dates to the seventh century B.C.E.

The structure served as a key gathering point in Epidaurus. Excavations revealed walls that created a processional route to and from the building, essentially an uncovered passageway for visitors. A large square in the center of the sanctuary features open space in front of the temple, a key functional element of the site.

“It could accommodate the throngs of pilgrims who arrived at the site to take part in the sacrificial offering to Asclepius, which was accompanied by a festive procession,” the university wrote. To the east, an altar and platforms included seating for prominent families who watched the sacrificial rituals.

Beneath Building K, excavators found an earlier structure from the early third century B.C.E. that sat on an unusually sturdy limestone foundation. The Roman building on top of it, which was rebuilt several times between the second and late fourth centuries C.E., has a central courtyard that probably had colonnades on at least three sides. The courtyard also has a gravel floor and a small basin made from reused marble pieces. In the building’s southwest corner, a large hall with a small basin or bath and a round room resembles spaces in other Epidaurus buildings that have been linked to the worship of Egyptian gods.

In the northwest corner of Building K, on a lower level, sits an unusual, nearly intact crypt that opens to the north. Along its west side, reused column pieces from an unknown earlier building form a three-part niche, and gaps in the wall behind it let sunlight stream in at midday. “The overall character of ‘K’ suggests that it may have been the site of a mystical cult, particularly during the late Roman period,” the university said, adding they were unable to define who—or what—the cult worshipped.

In the agora of ancient Epidaurus, just northwest of the city’s small theater, excavators had already uncovered a monumental fourth-century B.C.E. fountain complex. More recently, they found a large walled enclosure right next to it. Inside were small clay offerings that may once have hung from trees, a piece of a clay heating vessel, and a pottery fragment scratched with part of Asclepius’s name.

At the center of the enclosure, a well fed an underground pointed-arch tunnel that carried water to the fountain. Because water was central to the worship of Asclepius, the university says the offerings, the well, and the fountain together identify the site as the long-lost town sanctuary Pausanias described. Excavators also found a larger-than-life marble statue of a woman in the enclosure. Lambrinoudakis thinks it may be the statue of Epione that Pausanias saw, but without an inscription, he can’t be sure.

A 2,000-year-old tomb was discovered in an elite burial ground of the Xiongnu, some of whom were the ancestors of the Huns.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists have unearthed a massive 2,000-year-old tomb of an elite nomad from the Xiongnu Empire in Central Asia. The nine-level tomb contained more than 400 grave goods and is the largest Xiongnu tomb ever found in Mongolia.

Archaeologists identified the enormous tomb full of riches during a four-year excavation at the site of Duurlig Nars in northern Mongolia, according to a translated statement from the National Museum of Korea, whose researchers have been excavating the site in cooperation with the Institute of Archaeology of the Mongolian Academy of Sciences and the National Museum of Mongolia.

Duurlig Nars is the largest noble burial complex of the Xiongnu Empire, with nearly 300 ancient burial mounds called kurgans. The Xiongnu, also known as the Hunnu, were a collection of nomadic tribes who coalesced into a mobile empire on the Mongolian steppe in 209 B.C. The Xiongnu were connected to a broad trading network that stretched from the Roman Empire in the West to China and the Korean Peninsula in the East.

When the Xiongnu Empire fractured in the late first century B.C., one band moved west, picking up new tribes and eventually becoming the horde known as the Huns. Both the Xiongnu and the Huns were well known for their fighting and horseback riding skills.

The newly announced tomb is roughly square, with a long passageway extending from it, according to the statement. Including the passageway, the tomb is about 240 feet (73 meters) long, roughly the size of the Great Sphinx of Giza. Archaeologists discovered nine concentric layers of stone, each smaller than the last, going down around 48 feet (14.5 m) deep, making the tomb a kind of inverted pyramid.

Jade "bi" discs unearthed on the floor of the coffin.

A glass cup with a handle, possibly made in the Roman Empire.

Archaeologists unearthed a wooden carriage from one of the tomb layers.

In the tomb's central chamber, archaeologists found a wooden burial chamber with a coffin. The burial chamber is smaller than other elite Xiongnu burials, according to the statement, which may suggest that the society was changing and Xiongnu power was declining when the tomb was created in the late first to second century A.D.

Artifacts found in the tomb show the extent of the Xiongnu's connections across Eurasia 2,000 years ago, according to the statement. Among the grave goods recovered from the tomb were silver-and-quartz accessories crafted to decorate horses, as well as a wheel from a lacquered horse-drawn carriage, suggesting the tomb's occupant was a person of high social status.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Additionally, archaeologists found evidence of connections with the Han dynasty, which arose around 200 B.C. and was the second imperial dynasty of ancient China. On the bottom of the wooden coffin, archaeologists recovered 15 flat, overlapping pieces of jade.

Han dynasty burials of important people often included at least one "bi," the term for a jade disk. But unlike the typically circular "bi," the jade pieces in the Xiongnu tomb are irregular and have elaborate designs engraved on them, according to the statement. This may suggest that the Xiongnu adopted a Han burial practice but put their own spin on it.

Archaeologists also found a broken cup in the tomb. The transparent glass cup with a handle may have been manufactured in the Roman Empire, the archaeologists believe. Additional tests will be carried out to try to determine where the glass cup was made.

So far, archaeologists are unsure who was buried in the tomb. But they plan to use DNA analysis techniques on the teeth and hair they recovered from the coffin to figure out the person's chromosomal sex and whether the individual was related to other people interred in the Duurlig Nars burial complex. According to the statement, future analyses of this important tomb will help archaeologists paint a more detailed picture of ancient Xiongnu society two millennia ago.

Kristina Killgrove is a staff writer at Live Science with a focus on archaeology and paleoanthropology news. Her articles have also appeared in venues such as Forbes, Smithsonian, and Mental Floss. Kristina holds a Ph.D. in biological anthropology and an M.A. in classical archaeology from the University of North Carolina, as well as a B.A. in Latin from the University of Virginia, and she was formerly a university professor and researcher. She has received awards from the Society for American Archaeology and the American Anthropological Association for her science writing.

#6271. Foster bill would bolster tech use to monitor AI financial risks

"We cannot afford to rely on outdated systems to oversee an increasingly complex financial sector," said Rep. Bill Foster, D-Ill., (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call file photo)

A leading Democrat on the House Financial Services Committee introduced legislation Thursday aimed at helping regulators use technology to better spot financial stress turbocharged by artificial intelligence and around-the-clock payment systems.

The draft bill, from Rep. Bill Foster, D-Ill., would require the Federal Reserve to work with other regulators to develop, test and publicly release model software that would improve the ability to assess market conditions in real time and respond quickly to cybersecurity and other threats.

The bill is designed to help regulators keep pace with new risks "driven largely by the development of state-of-the-art AI models," according to a summary.

The legislation is intended to help regulators provide financing to banks during crises and wind down failing banks. The model software would reduce the amount of manual compliance work that smaller financial institutions would have to do by providing standard data formats for regulatory reporting and tools to manage and transmit the information to regulators, according to a Foster spokesperson.

“With advances in AI creating new cybersecurity threats and financial risks, it's more important than ever that we modernize the way we monitor the health of our financial institutions,” Foster said in a statement. “We cannot afford to rely on outdated systems to oversee an increasingly complex financial sector.”

Foster, who has a Ph.D. in physics and has been a leader on AI issues on the Financial Services panel, is in line to become chair of the Financial Institutions Subcommittee next year.

He has been mulling a challenge to ranking member Maxine Waters, D-Calif., to chair the full committee in the new Congress. But Foster is now “leaning toward not running,” a person familiar with his thinking said.

Waters already has a confirmed challenger in Rep. Sean Casten, D-Ill., who on Thursday circulated a "Dear Colleague" letter seeking the support of House Democrats for his bid.

Casten touted his “career at the intersection of business, science and public policy." Before entering Congress, he worked in clean energy and co-founded a company that converted industrial waste energy into usable power.

In his letter, Casten cited the need to lower housing and insurance costs, protect consumers from fraud, address risks posed by cryptocurrency and prediction markets and guard against the next financial crisis. He also promised to hold the Trump administration accountable for ethical lapses.

He's got a tough road ahead of him, however. Every Financial Services Democrat except Casten, Foster and Rep. Sam Liccardo of California signed an Oct. 21 letter to House Democrats in support of Waters. That show of support came after Casten made it known he was interested and it was clear that Foster had been considering his own bid.

Although Foster may not compete for the chairmanship, he has recently talked to Waters about changing how the committee operates.

“He wants a variety of members to play a role in legislation brought up in committee,” the source familiar with his thinking said. He’s also seeking more input on witnesses who testify at subcommittee hearings.

The draft bill he released on Thursday covers a topic that Foster is likely to pursue throughout the 120th Congress. He often asks the most questions about the use of AI in financial services at hearings and offers the most amendments related to the issue at markups.

Under the bill, model software would be developed for banking records and operations, regulatory reporting, stress testing, anti-money laundering and fraud screening, AI risk monitoring and other activities.

The software must be open source, publicly available and tested for reliability and accuracy, according to the summary. It would be tested using synthetic or legally permitted historical data rather than actual customer accounts. Regulators would not take financial or supervisory actions during the study.

The software developed during the study would not have to be adopted; rather, it “should be viewed as a starting point for further modernization,” the summary says.

All software models would have to be published within one year of enactment of the bill and a final report assessing feasibility, costs and savings, competition and other criteria, would be due to Congress within two years.

#6270. The Best Aluminum Luggage for Travelers, From Iconic Rimowa Suitcases to Sleek Tumi Trunks

The first time I traveled with an aluminum suitcase, I emerged into the airport with a whole new energy. There’s an undeniable allure to rolling through a terminal with a gleaming statement piece, shimmering as it does against a sea of boring black suitcases. There’s no way to travel more smugly.

Commerce writer Charley Ward testing Rimowa's iconic aluminum carry-on in Mallorca

But while the style is an undeniable draw, beyond the immediate hit of glamour, aluminum luggage offers some practical perks too. It offers greater structural protection than polycarbonate and soft-shell options—you can’t really argue with that, given it’s the type of material they make planes out of. And these durable suitcases are typically fitted with secure latch locking mechanisms over temperamental zippers, with steel corners and frames designed to comfortably absorb bumps, drops, and scrapes on the go.

Investing in high-end aluminum luggage is a serious price commitment—especially when considering that there are plenty of excellent soft-sided and hard-shell suitcases on the market. I packed comfortably for three nights in Milan and Paris: a couple of outfit changes, pajamas, gym clothes, a toiletry bag, and a spare pair of shoes. Ultimately, capacity will depend on how heavy a packer you are, but it’s ideal for a long weekend during the winter at minimum.

What are the benefits of aluminum luggage?

Aluminum luggage offers superior durability and protection compared to fabric or plastic alternatives. Its rigid, crush-proof shell and heavy-duty frame safeguard fragile contents against rough handling and impact during transit. Aluminum is built to last a lifetime, developing a distinctive, travel-worn patina over time rather than tearing or cracking. Then there’s that effortlessly sleek aesthetic at the airport, which is another fun perk.

Our editors have personally tested a wide range of bags from leading luggage brands, carefully selecting their favorites based on function, innovation, and design. #6269. The 8 Best Shop Vacs for Tackling Tough Messes

From sucking up water to blowing sawdust off your tools, these powerful models have what it takes to get the job done. These are the models we’ve used and recommend.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

You can’t make an omelet without breaking a few eggs, and you can’t complete a project at home or in your workshop without making a mess. These are the laws of the universe. I don’t write them; I just obey them.

But because of this, I also know the importance of a reliable shop vac. Unlike the vacuum you use to clean the floors in your home, a shop vac gobbles up large, chunky messes, including sawdust, screws, bits of wood, and other debris (not to mention spills and other wet messes). So if you’re using woodworking tools like sanders, miter saws, and table saws on a regular basis, you need to have one close by.

When it comes to choosing the right shop vac for your home, there’s a lot to consider. Shop vacs come in both cordless and corded electric models and range in size from small, 1.6-gallon portable vacuums for cleaning out cars to large, 12-gallon shop vacs capable of keeping your entire garage sawdust-free.

All of the products written about below were tested by members of the Popular Mechanics team, including myself (Tony Carrick) and Test Editor Brad Ford.

In an effort to evaluate the performance of the shop vacs on this list, we put them through tests that involved collecting both dry materials and liquid. We conducted three timed tests using only each vacuum’s hose, no attachments. The first test involved vacuuming up 12 cups of sawdust to determine how quickly each vac could collect dry material. We then used each vac to drain 2 gallons of water from a bucket. Lastly, we tested suction power by attempting to use each vac to suck up wood screws and metal bolts.

Along with grading each shop vac’s vacuuming capabilities, we also evaluated how easy each model was to use, based on factors like weight, size, capacity, and cord and hose length. Since every person’s shop vac needs may vary, the list below includes a broad range of sizes.

In the latest update of this guide, we tested and added two new shop vacs. The Vacmaster Professional Beast Series FLT+ is a shop vac with next-level features you won’t find on any other shop vacs. Not only does it connect to the exhaust ports of the large sawdust-producing power tools in your workshop, table saws, miter saws, and the like, but it also syncs with them via a wireless remote. With a vacuum cleaner–like dust collection bag and top-mounted HEPA filter, it’s ideally equipped for collecting sawdust.

The Craftsman CMXEVBE17595 Wet-Dry Shop Vac is our largest pick (with its 16-gallon tank) and also one of our most powerful. With a max airflow of 185 cubic feet per minute (cfm), it sucks up material faster than any other shop vac we tested. It’s also powerful enough to pull in heavier objects, including bolts and small chunks of wood.

The Vacmaster’s impressive power and compact design make it the perfect all-around shop vac. One of our editors owns the previous iteration of this model and has found it to be the ideal shop vac for home use. Its 5.5-hp motor is much more powerful than what you’ll find with most other 5-gallon shop vacs. It also has a small, 18.6-by-13.4-inch footprint, so it’s easy to carry and store, though its smaller capacity may not be enough for busier workshops.

With an 18-foot power cord and 7-foot hose, you won’t need an extension cord to clean up a large two-car garage or reach a car in the driveway. Plus, the newest version of the Vacmaster adds wheels that make it even easier to move around. There are also four attachments, which offer enough versatility to handle different jobs, and all of the Vacmaster’s attachments fit neatly into a storage compartment on the vacuum.

Full Vacmaster Beast Series 5-Gallon Shop Vacuum Review

Stanley’s 6-gallon wet-dry vac is a fraction of the cost of other shop vacs, yet it still packs enough power and capacity to handle most cleanups. Though it lagged behind the top performers we tested, it still completed our sawdust test in a respectable 21 seconds, and it swallowed up 2 gallons of water in just 11 seconds. And with its smaller-diameter hose, it produced enough suction to pick up both screws and bolts.

It’s not too bulky, so it won’t crowd your workshop floor, nor is it so compact that it requires emptying too frequently. It sits on swiveling casters and is relatively light, which made it easy to wheel around our tester’s garage. We also liked its accessories, which include two extensions and three nozzles for both floor and spill cleanup. The crevice tool was particularly impressive in that it reached easily into the tight spaces between the seats of one of our cars.

We did find ourselves wishing the power cord was longer than 10 feet so we could reach all corners of the workshop without having to use an extension cord. Still, with its low price and ample capacity, this Stanley vac is a great value option for any home workshop.

Ridgid's shop vac is powerful and affordable enough to fit most budgets, making it an ideal companion for those bigger and messier home improvement projects.

During testing, it collected a pile of sawdust in just over 16 seconds before proceeding to drain a bucket of water in about 6 seconds. While we liked how quickly it picked up light debris, the Ridgid left a little to be desired with lift power. Its large-diameter hose made quick work of lighter material, but it struggled to pick up larger bolts (though we should note that this was an issue with most other vacs with large 2-1/2-inch-diameter hoses).

The Ridgid also has a sturdy feel to it. The hose resisted cracking or denting, even after mistakenly stepping on it, and the tub is made of thick plastic. There’s also a locking system on the hose, which prevents attachments from falling off when the vacuum is in use.

The vacuum’s long, 7-foot hose made it easy to clean a work area without having to repeatedly reposition the base. Attachments include two extension wands, along with a crevice tool and floor tool, all of which fit onto the shop vac for storage. An included wet filter would make this shop vac a real no-brainer purchase, but it’s not far off from that even without one.

Full Ridgid 12-Gallon 5.0 Peak HP NXT Shop Vacuum Review

The speed and capacity the DeWalt Stealthsonic displayed during my tests makes it a great choice for cleaning up wet messes.

It produced some of the most impressive vacuuming results during our tests. Backed by its 5.5-hp motor and 2.5-inch-diameter hose (about the same size as a fire hose), the Stealthsonic gobbled up our pile of sawdust in just 16 seconds and drained our bucket of water in just 5 seconds, which was among the fastest of any shop vac we tested.

It was also one of the largest of the shop vacs we tested, with a 12-gallon capacity. Thanks to its 20-foot-long cord, it covers an entire two-car garage without the need for an extension cord, and it sits on heavy-duty rubber casters that make it easy to wheel around.

While its larger-diameter hose worked well for the quick collection of lighter materials, it’s not ideal for heavier objects. The Stealthsonic struggled to produce enough lift to suck up wood screws and was unable to collect larger bolts like some shop vacs with smaller-diameter hoses could. It also is a bit too bulky to get into tighter spots, such as the small gaps in and around the seats in a car. But if you’re looking for something that quickly cleans up larger spills and messes at the job site or in a workshop, this vacuum is it.

Milwaukee’s M18 Fuel wet-dry vacuum, which runs off an 18-volt lithium-ion battery, is one of the most powerful shop vac options when there’s no electrical outlet in range. The vac impressed during testing, even matching some of the corded shop vacs we tested. It consumed our sawdust pile in 20 seconds flat and a bucket of water in just 11 seconds, which is saying something given that it has a long, 9-foot hose.

We also loved the design of this wet-dry vac. The accessories, which include a floor utility nozzle and crevice tool, fit nicely inside a compartment on the top of the shop vac, and the tray holds both extensions. The extra-long hose and the small profile of the crevice tool were particularly valuable when we used the M18 Fuel wet-dry vacuum to clean out a car.

The M18 6-gallon vacuum is also easy to maneuver. It sits in a sturdy tray with four casters with rubber wheels that rolled easily over our tester’s garage floor and driveway. The M18’s run time was also impressive. When loaded with a 12.0-ampere-hour (Ah) battery, we got 31 minutes of run time when set to high and a whopping 48 minutes on its lower power setting.

This was the priciest wet-dry vacuum we tested, but it’s worth the investment if you want to cut the cord without compromising power.

If the primary demand for your shop vac is to collect the mountains of sawdust left behind following a carpentry project, then look no further than the recently launched Vacmaster Professional Beast Series FLT+. Not only will this shop vac attach to your power tools’ exhaust ports, but it also synchronizes with them. It comes with a Synchro key remote, which you attach to a power tool via a neoprene strap. The key communicates wirelessly with the shop vac. When it senses the vibration of the tool turning on, the key sends a signal that turns on the vacuum, eliminating the need to walk across the room to turn it on manually. I used it with a table saw, and it worked well, reliably turning on as soon as I fired up the table saw and dutifully sucking up dust as I cut, then turning off when I shut down the saw.

The Vacmaster is designed for collecting dust particles, and it did that extremely well. It sucked up 12 cups of sawdust in under 20 seconds, which is impressive given that it comes equipped with a smaller 1-7/8-inch-diameter hose. The Vacmaster Beast FLT+ also comes with a dust bag similar to a vacuum cleaner and a HEPA filter, making it ideal for trapping fine dust particles.

While most shop vacs have a filter located inside the collection tank, the Vacmaster’s is on top. This frees up space inside the tank for more debris collection while also preventing the filter from becoming inundated with dust. Other notable features you won’t find on most shop vacs include an LED display that shows the vacuum's airflow percentage, so you know when it’s time to clean the filter, and a self-cleaning filter. It’s an excellent workshop shop vac for those who don’t mind springing for it.

With its cordless design, light weight, and compact, box-shaped design, Milwaukee’s M12 Fuel shop vac is made for the road. At just 15 inches long, 13 inches wide, and 12 inches high, and with a weight of just under 10 pounds, Milwaukee’s M12 Fuel shop vac was by far the easiest to carry around of the wet-dry vacuums we tested. Its shape also made it ideal for sitting in the trunk of a car or storing on a set of garage shelves.

Per its name, the M12 Fuel shop vac uses a smaller power source—a 12-volt battery—so it doesn’t have the power of the corded and 18-volt cordless models we tested. Still, it took a respectable 35 seconds for it to complete our sawdust test and was capable of sucking down both bolts and wood screws. Its 1.6-gallon capacity and a max runtime of 26 minutes on low and 14 minutes on high limit it to small cleanup jobs, however.

While it lacks the power of larger shop vacs, it’s hard to overstate how convenient it is to use. We appreciated its compact size and cordless design when we toted it into the car for some detailing, then later up to a second-floor bonus room to clean up drywall dust after mounting a TV.

The M12 Fuel is pricey when you factor in the cost of a battery and charger, but its convenience is unmatched, especially if you’ve already bought into Milwaukee’s 12-volt power tool universe and have a 12-volt Fuel battery to load into it.

Full Milwaukee M12 Fuel 1.6-Gallon Shop Vac Review

The Craftsman 16-gallon wet-dry shop vac was built to clean up large masses fast with a max airflow of 185 cfm, well above the 100 cfm I see on most shop vacs. It vacuumed up 12 cups of sawdust faster than any other shop vac I tested and gulped down 2 gallons of water in 5 seconds flat. Most of the shop vacs I tested with a larger 2-1/2-inch-diameter hose struggled to generate enough lift to pick up heavier debris. That wasn’t the case with the Craftsman, which effortlessly vacuumed up a pile of screws, washers, and large bolts.

The Craftsman sits on four sturdy casters that made it easy to maneuver around when I was using it to clean up my large two-car garage, which I was able to do thanks to its 20-foot-long power cord and 7-foot hose.

With its 16-gallon size, the Craftsman was also the largest shop vac I tested, which made it handy for cleaning up big messes and large open areas. It was less effective for cleaning out a car. The crevice tool and its bulkier hose made it difficult to maneuver around a car interior, and there are no crevice tools for cleaning the gaps between seats and other tight spaces.

While its large size makes the Craftsman capable of cleaning up large messes, it also makes it a bit of a space hog in a garage or shed. You also won’t be carrying it inside the house to clean up messes in the home. But if you’re after a shop vac with the muscle and capacity to handle large postproject messes, this is the one.

The drum capacity of a shop vac determines how much material you can vacuum without having to empty it out. While sizes range from 1.6 to 16 gallons, smaller-capacity shop vacs, like the Milwaukee M12 Fuel 1.6-Gallon Wet-Dry Vacuum, provide more versatility to the average user through easier transport and storage. If you’re short on space, a smaller unit that you have to empty more frequently could be more convenient than a larger-capacity machine cluttering up your garage. Keep in mind that the stated gallon capacity doesn't factor in the space taken up by the filter, so don’t expect a 6-gallon model to suck up exactly 6 gallons of material.

While the majority of shop vacs use corded power, cordless models are becoming more common. These battery-powered options offer more mobility—especially useful for car, boat, or RV cleaning—but they lack the runtime for extended projects. If you prefer the mobility of cordless models (especially if you’re interested in a larger-capacity model that requires a lot of power), choose one from the same brand as your existing power tools. This enables you to extend runtime by using additional batteries you already have on hand.

If you decide to go with a corded model, pay attention to the length of the cord. Models with a longer cord, such as the DeWalt Stealthsonic Wet-Dry Shop Vacuum, give you the freedom to cover larger workshops or reach to your driveway without having to get out an extension cord.

A shop vac’s airflow—measured in cubic feet per minute (cfm)—represents the amount of air a vacuum pulls through its nozzle. Roughly speaking, a shop vac with a higher cfm sucks up material faster than one with a lower cfm, though keep in mind this doesn’t include other factors like nozzle design, motor size, and suction power. As we found during testing, shop vacs with smaller-diameter hoses, such as the Milwaukee M18 Fuel 6-Gallon Wet-Dry Vacuum, often produce greater suction power. So while a larger shop vac with a larger-diameter hose will remove lightweight material, such as sawdust, more quickly than a shop vac with a narrower hose, that smaller vac is better able to pick up heavier objects, such as bolts and coins.

While most shop vacs include several nozzle attachments for the hose, some models offer a more useful variety of accessories. Think about the type and scope of your cleaning tasks, and look for a vacuum with applicable accessories. For example, we’ve found a brush-tip nozzle to be essential for automotive interior cleaning, allowing us to quickly clean dust and pet hair from the dashboard and display screen—areas easily scratched by a hard plastic nozzle. Or, if you want to suck up the cobwebs in the corner of your garage or sawdust deep under your workbench, look for vacs with multiple extension wands to extend the nozzle reach.

Biologist Gonzalo Quiroga-Artigas lifts the lid on the secret life of tardigrades in stunning detail for the Nikon Small World photography awards.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It's not often we get to peer into the tiny world of tardigrades (also known as water bears). But through his photography, biologist Gonzalo Quiroga-Artigas is unmasking the secret lives of these creatures in stunning detail.

In one photo, which won Quiroga-Artigas 12th place in Nikon's 2026 Photomicrography Competition, a tardigrade (Hypsibius exemplaris) is seen shedding its tough outer layer, known as a cuticle or an exuvium, while laying an egg in the discarded skin.

"A large part of my research involves imaging, and during the many hours I spend at the confocal microscope, I have come across some incredibly beautiful and unexpected scenes," Quiroga-Artigas, a postdoctoral researcher at the Montpellier Cell Biology Research Center in France, told Live Science in an email.

"An interesting feature of tardigrade reproduction is that some species lay their eggs inside the shed cuticle, or exuvium. The exuvium can therefore provide an additional layer of physical protection for the developing embryos."

In some species, males may place sperm inside the cuticle of a molting female before egg laying, according to National Geographic. In others, the males fertilize the eggs after they have been left inside the cuticle. And some don't even need males to reproduce at all.

"Many species reproduce through parthenogenesis," Quiroga-Artigas said, which is when an embryo develops from an unfertilized egg, also known as a virgin birth. "This means that males are not required for reproduction, and the resulting offspring are genetically very similar to their mothers," he added. The species in the photograph falls into this category.

Molting and egg laying often take place over several hours, but the shedding itself is a relatively fast process. Capturing it on camera is, therefore, no mean feat.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"Once I had collected animals that were laying eggs, I had to fix, stain, and mount the specimens before imaging them," Quiroga-Artigas said. "I then spent a long microscopy session searching for the right specimen and the right orientation to obtain a high-quality image. Finding a specimen at exactly the right stage of molting, and in an orientation that allows the process to be clearly visualized, is largely a matter of patience and luck."

—Tardigrades survive being dried out thanks to proteins found in no other animals on Earth

—Tardigrades may hitchhike on snails ... and then suffocate in their slime

—'Sexy Mantis,' obscene orangutan and prancing sparrowhawk feature in 2026 Nikon Comedy Wildlife Awards

Photographing these animals is also challenging due to their tiny size. "Working with tardigrades in the lab requires a lot of experience with micromanipulation, as they are extremely small," Quiroga-Artigas said. "Hypsibius exemplaris, for example, is only about 250 µm [micrometers] long." That's about twice the width of a human hair.

This particular photo was taken using confocal microscopy, which uses a focused laser beam to light up one section at a time to create a detailed, high-resolution image. Quiroga-Artigas used this technique for a second tardigrade photo that was listed as an Image of Distinction in the same competition.

The second image submitted by Quiroga-Artigas to the Nikon Small World competition of a tardigrade shown from beneath.

He also received an Honorable Mention in the Nikon Small World in Motion Competition for a video of a pregnant tardigrade making contact with another tardigrade, which can then be seen pooping. However, it's not clear whether the contact between the two individuals caused this movement, Quiroga-Artigas said.

Quiroga-Artigas hopes his photography and videos give viewers an idea of just how beautiful and complex the microscopic world really is. "There are tiny animals all around us that we cannot see with the naked eye, yet they live, reproduce, grow, and undergo complex life cycles just like the animals we are more familiar with," he said.

"I will continue capturing images of tardigrades in different contexts related to my future research, without necessarily having a specific photographic goal in mind," he added. "In my experience, some of the best images I have captured were not necessarily the ones I was actively looking for."

Pandora is the trending news editor at Live Science. She is also a science presenter and previously worked as Senior Science and Health Reporter at Newsweek. Pandora holds a Biological Sciences degree from the University of Oxford, where she specialised in biochemistry and molecular biology.

#6267. Inside the 2026 Condé Nast Traveler Points of View Summit

On November 12, our ninth annual Points of View Summit brought together trip designers, luxury planners, and on-the-ground experts in New York City for a day exploring the latest in travel. While unrelenting rain poured outside, the atmosphere inside was anything but dreary and gray.

Global editorial director Divia Thani kicked things off with opening remarks on big-picture trends: how American travelers are driving luxury travel; the transfer of wealth to a younger generation; and a shift from spending on products to lived experiences. These overarching themes gave the audience a preview of what would come later in the day on panels and in breakout sessions. From a talk about Hilton Head’s Gullah culture and a run-through of reasons to visit Morocco—yes, this bit was accompanied by a post-lunch tea ceremony—to an exchange on all-inclusives with Hyatt Inclusive Collection, and a sit-down unpacking food and memory with Antoni Porowski, the day was full of thoughtful exchanges that reminded us why we journey in the first place. After much applause, the summit concluded with a cocktail party featuring wines from San Miguel de Allende and a taste of Lowcountry South Carolina by way of shrimp, grits, and fried green tomatoes—there was lots to celebrate, with a decade of Hilton Head being on our Readers' Choice Awards and its Savannah/Hilton Head International Airport drawing visitors from all over. Below, explore all that went down at our 2026 Points of View Summit.

Our editors discuss next year's editorial coverage themes, including spotlight destinations and how we're tapping into pop culture.

The day kicked off with a roundtable over what’s been on our minds and what'll be on our editorial calendar next year, just in time for our 40th anniversary. Our features director Rebecca Misner led the conversation with Thani, global features director Erin Florio, global executive director of video Dana Kravis, senior features editor Megan Spurrell, and associate editor Charlie Hobbs, who all agreed that a demand for substantive, long-form storytelling is back (though did it ever truly leave?). Spurrell shared an early preview of the now-live Best Places to Go in 2027, including destinations like the Albanian Alps for hiking, Memphis for museum openings, Yunnan for a slew of new restaurants, and more. Kravis spoke about cross-platform stories such as our new video series Made In, exploring craft in a particular destination, and upcoming video iterations of series like On Location, which unpacks beloved film and show locations. On the topic of pop culture, Hobbs highlighted a continued focus on cultural happenings, sporting events, and festivals that we're keeping on our radar as reasons to travel. Ultimately, going into 2027, Florio said, our coverage will explore “what it is that drives us to travel, as opposed to where it is we want to go"—not only the destination for destination's sake, but the experiences and impulses underlying travelers' choices.

Eduardo Schutte and Madison Flager discuss the future of the all-inclusive stay and Hyatt's rapidly growing portfolio.

Next up, commerce director Madison Flager spoke with Eduardo Schutte, Hyatt Inclusive Collection’s commercial SVP, on how all-inclusive stays have evolved and expanded far beyond your typical beachside bubbles to meet globetrotters of all kinds. In an age of optimization, it's only natural that travelers would value the ease and confidence of a bundled vacation, with less time spent planning so that they can enjoy their destination sans stress. Schutte observed that Hyatt Inclusive Collection has grown from two properties in 2013 to over 120 today, with expansion well underway in Europe, the Middle East, Africa, and Asia. “You're going to know exactly how much your vacation is, so it's much more predictable and easier to plan,” Schutte said. Afterwards, one lucky guest won a trip to a Hyatt Inclusive Resort. Perhaps the all-inclusive is a remedy for the times.

Erin Florio helms the conversation on summer travel, from increasing shoulder season trips to less crowded destinations.

We recently unpacked why it seems everyone took a fallcation this year, and spotlighted the year-round appeal of off-season Greece. Though the once-sweltering days of the summer months might be all you’re yearning for as winter fast approaches, increasingly unpredictable weather and overcrowded destinations are shifting and expanding the typical high season. Florio led this panel with Jack Ezon, founder and managing partner of Embark Beyond; Catherine Heald, CEO and founder of Remote Lands; Jade McBride, president of Ted Turner Reserves; Scott Jordan, vice president of sales–East at Delta Air Lines; and Mei Zhang, chairman and founder at WildChina.

To Ezon, it's less about the timing and more about the value of a trip; entry-level Mediterranean rooms can cost $4,000 to $6,000 per night, raising questions about whether the experience delivers value beyond price. Reframing a destination’s appeal beyond one season is key—going to Amalfi in October for wine or December for Christmas markets—as per Jordan, who stressed the value of meeting travelers where they're headed. He noted Delta is extending and adding seasonal service, including earlier flights to Porto and routes to Copenhagen, Sardinia, and Prague. Still, the group wondered whether greater access to Sardinia might relieve pressure on Amalfi and Como or simply congest another destination.

Zhang said her clients aren't choosing between European hotspots at all; they're set on Asia, the choice becoming whether to visit Japan or China. In 2025, China saw sweeping growth in international visitors, which Zhang credited to new visa policies, renewed country perceptions, and a global interest in regional lifestyles. “I just think that's part of wellness. It's drinking hot water, wearing slippers, playing mahjong, being social with family," she said. "A lot of these concepts are promoting China as a way of living, rather than as a destination.”

Katie Mathews and Omolola Campbell on Hilton Head Island's Gullah culture

For a chat presented by Hilton Head Island, senior creative producer Katie Mathews sat down with Omolola Campbell, executive producer of The Spirit We Move With, a short documentary about South Carolina's Gullah community. The Gullah people are the descendants of West Africans who were brought to the Carolinas, Georgia, and Florida, in the 1700s and 1800s for slavery. A sixth-gen Gullah descendant herself, Campbell spoke with Mathews on the importance of leading the narrative and memorializing these stories today. In South Carolina’s case, it’s about hearing from Gullah people themselves. Campbell uses her gift shop on the island, Binya, as a space for educating customers through handwoven sweetgrass baskets, cookbooks, prints, and more. “People say that storytelling is a way of preservation. I like to say conservation, because to preserve something is to put it on a shelf, [but] Gullah culture is still alive and thriving,” Campbell said.

In between panels, Mei Zhang and others tried Moroccan tea.

Hannah Towey and Ms. Siham Fettouhi discuss lesser-known Moroccan cities and itineraries.

After breakout sessions with editors and travel specialists, guests were served Moroccan tea before settling into a chat with news editor Hannah Towey and Ms. Siham Fettouhi, North America executive director of the Moroccan National Tourism Office. Beyond Marrakech and the desert, Fettouhi noted the country's appeal lies in its Atlantic and Mediterranean coastlines and can't-miss surfing spots. "We're talking about a country that offers you the possibility to ski literally in the morning and enjoy sunset in the beach in the afternoon," Fettouhi said. “Morocco has never been this accessible from North America," she continued, mentioning nonstop flights now available from North America through Royal Air Maroc, Air Canada, Air Transat, Delta, and United. And domestic travel is also getting an update, as Morocco's high-speed rail network, Al Boraq, has extensions planned toward Marrakech and Agadir ahead of the 2030 World Cup.

An attendee captures Lale Arikoglu and Antoni Porowski's culinary conversation.

We closed out Points of View with a chat between Lale Arikoglu, director of special projects, and Antoni Porowski, Emmy-winning producer, Queer Eye veteran, and host of National Geographic's Best of the World series, which aired in June. While his other Nat Geo series No Taste Like Home traces family histories through food, this more recent show highlights the people behind well-known destinations' institutions and traditions—think a mustachioed clockmaker at Big Ben's Great Clock or a family-run cheese cave in Paris. “There’s always a beautiful nerd that’s behind this larger-than-life thing that millions of us have had a chance to experience,” Porowski said with a laugh, referencing folks not unlike himself, dedicated to that one experience and sharing it with others.

For Porowski, it's food that has offered a way to connect people with their roots and family histories, inspired in large part by his own journey toward embracing his Polish heritage. While planning a retirement trip for his dad several years ago, Porowski said his dad insisted they visit the Polish mountain village Zakopane. “We tried soups that I hadn't had since I was six or seven years old and got to connect through that,” he recalled. Porowski wrapped up the conversation with a handful of anecdotes from filming No Taste Like Home; a particular favorite was being in Senegal with Issa Rae, where he learned about teraanga, or the concept of generosity and sharing so integral to the West African country. Plus, the conversation would not have been complete without a rapid-fire round—see Porowski's answers below.

Delta does Shake Shack, which I’m not opposed to. I would say nine times out of 10—unless I’m sleeping and it's a red-eye—I’ll always have it, even if the chicken’s rubbery.

When the drinks cart goes by, what’s your go-to?

Chamomile tea, typically. This is so random, but it’s something I had as a child: sparkling water with a splash of apple juice. It feels really chic.

Because my parents taught me to arrive for a flight 10 minutes before it takes off when we lived in West Virginia, Jaeger Airport in Charleston, West Virginia. You can show up like 30 minutes before with checked luggage, and they will let you on.

Aisle, because I get to look at the flight attendants and see if they’re nervous during turbulence. But if they’re not, I know I’m fine.

There’s nothing more powerful than grabbing your carry-on.

Tomato bisque with a patty melt on sourdough focaccia from Il Buco Alimentari with sharp Vermont clothbound cheddar. That would be my appetizer, then puntarelle as my salad dish. For a main course, the shrimp from ABC Cocina—they have a lovely chili oil with lime zest and pink peppercorns—with again more bread to sop up all those oils. Since it’s my last meal, we’re doing surf and turf, scalloped potatoes, and a little broccoli rabe for fiber—no, I don’t care about fiber. For dessert, I was thinking about Campo de’ Fiori’s wild strawberries, with whipped cream and crème brûlée. I would finish it off with that Moroccan tea.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6266. Longtime West Virginia Sen. Rockefeller dies

Sen. John D. Rockefeller IV, D-W.Va., questions witnesses during a Senate Finance hearing on health care on June 23, 2011. (Scott J. Ferrell/CQ Roll Call)

Former Sen. Jay Rockefeller, a five-term West Virginia Democrat and champion for the rural poor, has died at the age of 89.

Rockefeller, who retired after the 2014 elections, played key roles on the tax-writing Senate Finance Committee, where he helped write landmark children’s health insurance legislation, as well as the Commerce, Science and Transportation and Intelligence panels which he chaired.

A staunchly progressive lawmaker, he represented a deeply conservative state that turned further to the right in his later years. Rockefeller, scion of a famous New York family renowned for its wealth, never wavered in his convictions and retired rather than face a potential backlash from voters upset by the then-Obama administration’s attempts to rein in the coal industry.

Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., who challenged Rockefeller for his seat before he decided not to seek reelection, released a statement Friday praising her predecessor’s legacy.

“Jay dedicated his life to serving West Virginia and our nation, leaving a lasting legacy. He was always a true gentleman who treated me with respect, kindness, and encouragement,” Capito said. “Over the years, we developed a wonderful friendship that transcended politics, and I will always be grateful for that.”

West Virginia’s Republican Gov. Patrick Morrisey — himself a transplanted Northerner, with roots in Brooklyn and New Jersey — lauded Rockefeller’s record on health care and aid for coal miners and veterans in their adopted state.

“His work helped shape our state and left a lasting mark on the lives of generations of West Virginians,” Morrisey said.

Rockefeller was born in New York City on June 18, 1937, the great-grandson of Standard Oil Co. founder John D. Rockefeller, who was once considered the world’s richest man. Rockefeller attended Harvard University, graduating with an A.B. in 1961. His passion was for the Far East and he spent three years studying at the International Christian University in Tokyo.

He returned to the states and was appointed by President John F. Kennedy to the National Advisory Council of the Peace Corps in 1961, spearheaded the Peace Corps initial program in the Philippines. He worked for a brief time in what was then known as U.S. Department of Far Eastern Affairs before deciding to embark on a public service role of a more personal nature. He enrolling as a VISTA volunteer, in the program which would later be known as AmeriCorps, and moved to the small mining community of Emmons, W.Va., in 1964 at age 27.

In West Virginia, Rockefeller found his life’s work. He described the experience as being “reborn,” and spoke often the poverty and hardship he encountered living in the small town. “I could not leave,” he said of West Virginia. “I [had] become so devoted to those people and the unfairness."

He had planned to remain only one year, but decided to stay and became active in local politics. He broke from his family's long tradition of Republican loyalty and ran successfully for the House of Delegates as a Democrat in 1966. Two years later, he was elected secretary of state.

Rockefeller lost a bid for governor in 1972, but he became the president of West Virginia Wesleyan College and continued to place roots in the state. He married Sharon Percy Rockefeller in 1967 and they started their family. When he ran for governor again in 1976, he won, and served two terms before winning election to the U.S. Senate in 1984, ultimately serving five terms before retiring in 2014.

Rockefeller was determined to increase economic opportunities for West Virginia, for whom he felt was forgotten and abandoned by the rest of the country. He called the people of his state “the hardest-working people I know,” and believed that bringing more business opportunities would help lift the state out of severe rural poverty and the dependence on the coal industry.

Rockefeller traveled to Japan and worked tirelessly to bring a Toyota manufacturing plant to Buffalo, W.Va, one of over twenty Japanese companies he’d brought to West Virginia. He fought for fair trade policies and targeted tax relief to protect West Virginia industries such as steel and chemicals.

Coal mining had long been the economic backbone of West Virginia, but Rockefeller felt more must be done to protect miners, many of whom worked in unsafe conditions or fell ill with pneumoconiosis, or black lung disease, after years of inhaling coal dust.

But defying the coal industry came with a political cost. When Rockefeller originally ran for governor in 1972, he had opposed mountaintop mining, also called strip mining, or the practice of removing large amounts of earth and rock in order to access underground seams of coal. When he ran again in 1976, he reversed his position and won.

But even as he ascended to the Senate, Rockefeller remained both friend and foe to the coal industry.

Despite growing up on the Upper East Side of Manhattan, figuratively and literally hundreds of miles away from coal mines, Rockefeller understood its deep roots in West Virginia’s economy and culture. He believed it was the miners — rather than industry — for whom he was defending.

He hung a century-old photo of a coal miner in his Senate office in the Hart building, and would point to the photo and remark to visitors that “this is why I’m here and who I work for.”

Rockefeller fought to secure pensions for miners, especially as coal companies would file for bankruptcy and immediately restructure to do away with pension plans.

In 1990, Rockefeller was one of only 11 senators to vote against the bipartisan Clean Air Act, which he felt disadvantaged workers in West Virginia. But those close to him said the decision weighed heavily on him, and Rockefeller privately worried that the lack of such regulations would pollute the air and destroy waterways, the brunt of which would be born by the same disadvantaged people whom he vowed to protect.

He believed strongly in the deliberative aspects of the legislative process, consuming great amounts of reading material to familiarize himself with the issues. During a time of increasing partisan rancor, Rockefeller still reached across the aisle to find a willing partner, even when there was not one to be found.

In 2010, as the Environmental Protection Agency’s greenhouse gas regulations were coming to fruition, Rockefeller came up with a compromise to delay implementation for two years.

He viewed himself as a broker between industry interests and the hard working people from coal-states like West Virginia. He had hoped that his years of standing up for coal miners and West Virginia interests would foster enough goodwill among industries primed to oppose any compromise that was less than an all-out rejection of the existing EPA statutes.

But industry walked away from Rockefeller, preferring a hard-line opposition to EPA regulations, and lobbied other senators to vote against Rockefeller’s measure. Furious, Rockefeller took to the floor of the Senate to denounce the coal industry and its leaders, an unprecedented action for a popular coal-state senator.

“The reality is that many who run the coal industry today would rather attack false enemies and deny real problems then find solutions,” he said on the Senate floor in June 2012. “Scare tactics are a cynical waste of time, money and, worst of all, coal miners’ hopes. But sadly, these coal operators have closed themselves off from any other opposing voices and few dared to speak out for change — even though it’s been staring them in the face for years.”

His fury against the coal industry was heard loudly, many speculating that he would retire rather than face reelection.

He had won reelection to the Senate handily during his five campaigns. In 2008, his final election, he was reelected with nearly 64 percent of the vote. But six months following his fated coal speech, in January 2013, Rockefeller announced he would retire at the end of his fifth term.

Rockefeller’s legacy may best be known for his fight to expand health care for vulnerable populations, including children, the economically disadvantaged and the elderly. Rockefeller served as one of the chief congressional champions for President Bill Clinton’s proposed health care overhaul, and later he played a critical role and was a loud progressive voice in writing and passing the Affordable Care Act in the Senate.

Rockefeller believed strongly in a public health insurance option, offering it as an amendment in the Senate Finance Committee during the ACA markup. A public-run insurance plan, he said, would put patients before profits, and help those people, especially West Virginians, with high health care costs and poor coverage who were left “out in the cold.”

"These are people," Rockefeller said, visibly emotional during his closing arguments to the Senate Finance Committee. "Eleven-year-old kids. These are families, and we have to respect them. And you respect them by giving them a choice."

The amendment was rejected. Rockefeller pivoted to strengthening Medicaid and Children’s Health Insurance Program provisions, believing that poor and disadvantaged families could seek refuge within those programs. CHIP had been one of Rockefeller’s signature legislative victories, helping to write that program initially in 1997 and later working on a major expansion that became law in 2009.

Despite his initial concerns and later disappointments — at one time saying publicly he could not support the measure as it stood — he later added his support to the ACA, citing it as a win for all Americans and actively lobbied his colleagues to support it.

Rockefeller was also known for his role on the Senate Intelligence Committee. A former chairman, he was critical of the nation's mismanagement of the Iraq war and clashed frequently with Republicans over the treatment of detainees. After he retired from Congress, Rockefeller served as a distinguished fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations.

Respect for Rockefeller ran deep on Capitol Hill. He was beloved by staff and known as a thoughtful, deliberative lawmaker. He had a fondness for classical music and served as a board member of the Bach Consort, an organization in Washington devoted to the study and performance of the music of Bach and his contemporaries. He admired art and Asian culture, and served as a board member of the Asia Society.

Rockefeller is survived by his wife, Sharon Percy Rockefeller; four children: John D. Rockefeller V, Valerie Rockefeller, Charles Rockefeller and Justin Rockefeller; and nine grandchildren.

Disclosure: the author served as a staffer in Rockefeller’s Senate office from 2009-11.
