On Wednesday (Nov. 18), NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft became the first human-made object to reach one light-day from Earth. Here, we look back at its most important discoveries, seen through groundbreaking space photos.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Early Wednesday (Nov. 18), NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft hit a new space exploration milestone: The probe, which launched in 1977, became the first spacecraft to reach one light-day from Earth.

The milestone is largely symbolic, but it comes with practical consequences: While Voyager 1 cruises through interstellar space at roughly 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers) from our planet, it now takes a full 24 hours for radio signals moving at the speed of light to get from Voyager 1 to Earth, and vice versa.

The growing space between Voyager and Earth makes it increasingly hard to troubleshoot problems on the nearly 50-year-old probe. But with Voyager 1 still collecting data with two of its science instruments, which are expected to stay powered up into the 2030s, NASA scientists say one thing is certain: The spacecraft isn't done surprising us.

"What Voyager has taught me is to expect the unexpected," Linda Spilker, who joined the Voyager team in 1977 and is the mission's current project scientist, told Live Science in an interview. "So many times the ideas and theories we had, Voyager was able to prove them wrong."

Here, we look back at some of Voyager 1's most groundbreaking discoveries, told through its incredible photos.

NASA's Voyager 1 probe launches atop a Titan/Centaur-6 launch vehicle from the Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

NASA's Voyager 2 probe launched before Voyager 1, on Aug. 20, 1977. Voyager 1 took off a few weeks later, on Sept. 5. (The two spacecraft took slightly different routes through the solar system, allowing Voyager 1 to reach interstellar space first after a gravity boost from Jupiter and Saturn.)

Spilker, who joined NASA right out of college, attended the historic Voyager 2 launch and recalls "that feeling of watching the rocket lift up off the launchpad, feeling the roar of those rocket engines and knowing this was a mission going to visit places I'd always been curious about."

A few weeks after launching, Voyager 1 took this photo of a crescent Earth and moon from 7.25 million miles (11.66 million km) from Earth.

On its way to the outer solar system, Voyager 1 snapped this image of a crescent Earth and its moon, captured in the same frame for the first time ever.

Voyager 1 photographed Jupiter from January to April 1979, reaching a minimum distance of 174,000 miles (280,000 km) in March 1979, according to NASA. As the spacecraft zoomed closer to the giant planet, it snapped an image every 96 seconds, creating this incredible time-lapse animation of the planet's turbulent atmosphere.

A time-lapse animation of Voyager 1 approaching Jupiter over the course of one Earth month

The close-up view showed that Jupiter is a far more dynamic world than previously thought. But Voyager also made key discoveries about the planet's many moons.

While passing by the Jovian moon Io, Voyager 1 witnessed an explosion: the first volcanic eruption ever seen beyond Earth. This proved that there were other geologically active worlds in our solar system, opening up entirely new avenues of inquiry and exploration.

A blue eruption on Jupiter's moon Io, the first volcanic eruption seen on another world

"Going in, we thought that the moons would look a lot like our own moon: ancient dead worlds," Spilker said. "And yet we found out they were very different worlds — like Io with active volcanoes. It was just an incredible change in our thinking."

By viewing these eruptions, scientists saw parts of Io's surface being changed in real time. "As we got closer [to Io], scientists kept saying the surface is getting younger and younger, because they didn't see any big craters, no medium sized craters, no little craters — until finally parts of its surface are just minutes old," Spilker said.

A mosaic view of Callisto taken from Voyager 1 photos at a distance of about 250,000 miles (400,000 km)

Some of Voyager's close-up observations also confirmed old theories. For example, Voyager 1's flyby of the moon Callisto in March 1979 revealed vast fields of well-preserved impact craters, proving that Callisto was geologically dead.

Jupiter and its thin ring of dust backlit by the sun in a Voyager 1 image

A final surprise at Jupiter came when Voyager 1 swooped around the planet's nightside, seeing the gas giant backlit by the sun. This view revealed a thin ring system around the planet, made partly of the dust particles Io spewed into space.

Voyager 1 reached Saturn in November 1980 and made its closest approach to the planet on Nov. 12 of that year. Four days later, the spacecraft took this image of the planet's nightside, showing a broad shadow cast onto the surrounding rings.

"That is one of my favorite pictures: an outbound image, taken by Voyager looking at [Saturn] in a way you could never see from the Earth," Spilker said, noting that we can only ever see Saturn's sunlit side from our planet. "The rings just look so beautiful shining there, and you can actually see the shadow of Saturn on the rings themselves. It's a really, really special picture."

In addition to discovering a previously unknown ring, Voyager 1 spotted five new moons around Saturn and took close-up photos of several other known satellites.

Voyager 1's closeup view of Titan revealed a dense, hazy atmosphere

The mission required Voyager to swing by the moon Titan in order to bend the probe's trajectory, sending it away from the solar system's planetary plane and toward a rendezvous with interstellar space. Before that, Voyager 1 revealed Titan's atmosphere to be so hazy that it completely obscured the moon's surface. This showed that Titan's clogged atmosphere was far denser than those of Earth and Mars.

By 1990, Voyager 1 was so far from the planetary plane that our solar system's planets looked like little more than specks of light. But before turning off its camera for good, Voyager 1 looked back at our cosmic neighborhood and took some of the most iconic space photos of all time.

In a series of 64 images taken from roughly 40 times Earth's distance from the sun, Voyager snapped its solar system "family portrait," a mosaic of images capturing six planets together for the first time. The portrait included views of Venus, Earth, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.

Frames from Voyager 1's family portrait showing Venus, Earth, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune.

The image of Earth from this collection is famously known as the "Pale Blue Dot."

"We took the pictures of the planets in color, and that one is especially one of my favorites," Spilker said. "There's Earth captured in a sunbeam. A tiny world less than a pixel in size representing all the life that we know in our solar system — just a very special image reminding us just how special and precious our planet is."

Earth appears as a pale blue dot in this iconic Voyager 1 image

Voyager 1 turned off its camera immediately after taking these images, concluding its role as the greatest tourist in the history of our solar system. In 2012, Voyager 1 passed beyond the heliopause — the boundary where the sun's radiation gives way to the interstellar medium — becoming the first interstellar spacecraft in history.

Voyager 2 crossed the same boundary in 2018 and is expected to reach its own light-day in 2035. In the meantime, several science instruments remain active on both probes, allowing them to measure the strange and mysterious environment between stars.

Even way out there, the probes are still detecting whispers of the sun's power.

"We are still seeing effects from the sun that come out, hit the heliopause, and send shocks and pressure fronts out into the interstellar medium," Spilker said. "I wonder where we will finally reach the point where the sun doesn't influence what we're seeing, and we're in the pristine interstellar medium — and I hope that happens while Voyager 1 is still operating."

Brandon is the space / physics editor at Live Science. With more than 20 years of editorial experience, his writing has appeared in The Washington Post, Reader's Digest, CBS.com, the Richard Dawkins Foundation website and other outlets. He holds a bachelor's degree in creative writing from the University of Arizona, with minors in journalism and media arts. His interests include black holes, asteroids and comets, and the search for extraterrestrial life.

#6254. Roku Pro Series LX OLED TV Review: One Small Step for OLED, One Big Step for Roku TVs

Roku’s first OLED TV lowers the bar for bringing a new, high-performance OLED screen home.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

It seems that the rumors of the end of OLED supremacy in the TV marketplace were greatly exaggerated. At the start of 2026, flashy new display technologies like RGB LED emerged to challenge that status quo, theoretically offering a brighter alternative to OLED panels, with greater color coverage. But at the end of the year, OLED TVs, with their ability to control each of a TV’s millions of tiny pixels point-by-point, remain the best option for overall picture performance. In fact, despite the fact that only two companies, LG and Samsung, currently make OLED panels, the number of TV brands that actually use those panels is expanding: Roku, the latest brand to jump into the space, released its first two OLED TVs this fall.

As you’d expect from Roku, both the baseline Roku Pro Series and the brighter and slightly fancier Roku Pro Series LX are value-oriented models, with list prices that undercut brands like Samsung and LG. But like many of our favorite picks at Popular Mechanics, they are designed to balance premium performance and great usability, with a simple setup and handy quality-of-life features that competitors lack, like a built-in remote finder.

After spending several days with the flagship Pro LX, I’m happy to report that Roku’s first foray into OLED TVs is already a strong contender for anyone curious about the benefits of upgrading to an OLED screen. The Pro LX’s picture quality doesn’t quite reach the heights of legacy OLED sets like LG’s C6 let alone flagships like the Samsung’s S95H. But it holds its own, and arguably outdoes them both when it comes to actually living with your TV. If you’re after a best-of-both-worlds OLED approach, the Roku Pro LX is an enticing new option at a very nice price.

Everything about setting up the Pro LX is built around simplicity. Like last year’s LED-powered Roku Pro, the LX eschews multi-piece pedestal stands and tiny bags of screws for feet that attach with screw-on knobs—no tools required. Dual stand positions include higher clearance for a soundbar, though the feet’s width of just over 42 inches on the 65-inch model I tested doesn’t leave much space up front on most consoles. The design doesn’t look quite as stylish as its LG and Samsung rivals, but the build feels stout, and the ultra-thin panel of just over an eighth of an inch up top adds a premium vibe.

The TV turns on automatically when plugged in, and immediately walks you through pairing the voice remote, which charges via USB-C so you never have to worry about batteries. It’s not quite as handy as Samsung’s solar-powered remotes, but its design is intuitive, including options like backlit keys and hands-free “Hey, Roku” voice control. If you’re not into an always-ready mic, you can mute it with a hard switch on the remote’s left edge.

Even the LX’s packaging is designed with forethought, including a plastic screen cover that peels off with a feather-light tug. But before you remove it, you’ll see a yellow arrow that points to my favorite feature by far: A remote finder button. A quick press emits a pleasant chirp from the remote buried in your couch cushions or, if you’ve got a toddler like me, hidden in any number of places out of reach from grabby little hands. I have no idea why this isn’t a standard option across brands, but kudos to Roku. It’s the simple things.

At the TV’s left flank, you’ll find a reasonably well-stocked input hub, including dual HDMI 2.1 inputs for gaming in VRR (Variable Refresh Rate) at up to 144 Hz, an HDMI 2.0 port, and a separate HDMI eARC port for connecting a soundbar or audio system. That’s important because the Pro LX’s sound is particularly thin and weak, all but requiring an audio upgrade. Other inputs in the stack include Ethernet to back up WiFi 6 support, USB-C and USB-A inputs, optical input, and a cable/antenna tuner. It would have been nice to get a full set of four HDMI 2.1 inputs, which you’ll find in similar LG and Samsung TVs, but I appreciate that Roku offers two ways for serious gamers to connect apart from the HDMI eARC port.

Notable features include ALLM (Auto Low Latency Mode) for fast-paced gaming and support for all major HDR formats, including the top two advanced options, Dolby Vision and HDR10+. In contrast, LG TVs stop at Dolby Vision, while Samsung only offers HDR10+. It’s always nice to have options, and the addition of Dolby Vision, the most common format for streaming, gives Roku a leg-up over Samsung OLEDs.

As you’d expect from an OLED, the Pro LX delivers fantastic contrast between the lightest and darkest images from the moment you turn it on, starting with perfect black levels from its obsidian screen. A polarizing layer does a fine job diffusing reflections for moderately bright rooms, about on par with LG’s C6. It doesn’t offer the powerful ambient light control of matte screens like Samsung’s S90H, but I generally prefer the richer perceived black levels of glossy screens, and the Pro LX is happy to indulge with impressive depth in darker moments.

Roku claims that the Pro LX is around twice as bright as the standard Roku Pro OLED, and after tinkering with the settings a bit, you’ll get plenty of pep to contrast those rich black levels. Using the TV’s most accurate HDR Dark picture mode, I measured around 1200 nits of peak brightness in a 10 percent window with a Portrait Displays C6 HDR5000 colorimeter, a G1 pattern generator, and Calman software.

That’s around 150 nits less than I got with the C6, but the difference is negligible in real-world watching: both TVs look similarly bright in moments like the sun glancing off a windshield or a glowing candle in a dark room. Roku’s model provides more than enough power for impactful HDR punch and vibrant colors, especially since most streaming content tops out at 1,000 nits. Interestingly, you’ll need to change the TV’s separate Picture Brightness setting to the highest “Brighter” mode to unlock that peak brightness. Unfortunately, the picture doesn’t do as good a job following the intent of directors and mastering engineers here as in the dimmer “normal” mode. That said, while slightly overbright, the TV still looks quite good overall in “brighter” mode. It’s just more of a tradeoff than you’ll see with the C6 at peak brightness.

Likewise, the colors aren’t quite as accurate as the C6. You can see the difference in certain specific shades, like the deep oranges in Mad Max: Fury Road, which sometimes looked a little too, well, orangey. I also noticed some color banding, or image artifacts, in especially challenging test scenes, but it rarely showed up in regular films and TV shows.

For most of my viewing, colors looked rich and natural. The vivid coral adventures in Netflix’s Our Planet provide a dazzling rainbow of shades that gave me chills, and watching Spider-Man: Brand New Day was a cinematic experience, with an almost marbled touch to details. There’s enough vibrancy to get you lost in little moments like the flashing gold of Ego’s palace in Guardians of the Galaxy Volume II, or the glowing beads of light reflecting off the Mandalorian’s helmet in his spaceship.

Speaking of space, the TV’s pinpoint light control makes deep-space scenes look incredibly realistic and engaging, especially compared with backlit models like last year’s mini-LED Roku Pro. Shadow details are also impressive, even in challenging scenes from murky shows like The Chilling Adventures of Sabrina, pairing with the TV’s flashy highlights for a lush experience. And while viewing the screen off-angle adds a slight green tinge, as it does with a lot of LG OLEDs, it’s worlds better than the pale colors and accentuated blooming you’ll see in the vast majority of LED TVs. Such is the advantage of OLED.

Of course, the biggest advantage of a Roku-branded OLED is marrying OLED’s technical prowess with a more accessible smart TV operating system. While Sony’s Google TV OLEDs are a solid alternative, Roku OS is notably simpler, more reliable, and in some ways more joyful to use than Samsung’s Tizen, LG’s webOS, and (especially) Panasonic’s Fire TV.

The fact that Roku OS just works exactly the way it’s supposed to is frankly half the battle. I’ve had fewer glitches with Roku OS in several years of TV reviewing than any other system, going back to TCL’s early Roku TVs. On top of that, I like the little extras Roku still offers like space themes, Star Trek-branded wallpaper, and silly movie references in the ever-expanding Roku City screen saver, like Cameron’s dad’s ill-fated Ferrari from Ferris Bueller’s Day Off.

Like all smart TVs I test, Roku OS has gotten less intuitive and more insidious in recent years, from plays to sell your data like ACR (Automatic Content Recognition) to pushier ads, such as a Home Depot-sponsored holiday wallpaper that suddenly appeared as I was writing this review. Luckily, you can turn that and most other annoying features off (though Roku immediately put the ad elsewhere). I’m also not as pleased with the latest Home screen layout, which pushes features like Continue Watching and the full list of apps below (you guessed it) more ads.

The upshot is that it takes more work to reorganize the layout for the best experience, but the good news is you can customize most options, and Roku OS is still the best built-in streaming system I’ve tested.

Roku’s Pro Series LX isn’t the best-performing OLED in its class, with both the Samsung S90H and LG C6 providing a cleaner, more accurate picture, but it is comparable and cheaper than either one at full price. (And will likely remain so for the rest of the year as holiday sales kick in.) Moreover, its slick blend of usability and performance could make it the top choice for OLED-curious folks who value a TV’s livability as highly as its picture quality. If you want to make the jump to OLED, and your budget is already stretched, Roku’s your new go-to.

Ryan Waniata is a professional writer, editor, video host, and product reviewer. A musician since childhood, his audio hardware roots go back to his days as a studio engineer in Nashville, TN in 2009. In 2011 he left the studio world to became a full-time journalist, with an emphasis on A/V, including TVs, speakers, headphones, and audio gear of all kinds. The author of hundreds of articles, Ryan has a passion for finding readers the best value on the best gear out there.

#6253. Don’t Visit Ko Lipe

After 19 years, I finally went back to Ko Lipe, the Thai island I spent close to a month on in 2006. Back then, it was one of those super off-the-beaten-path destinations that few but the most intrepid travelers visited, where electricity only ran a few hours a day, basic bungalows right on the beach cost something like $2 USD, and there really was a last boat for the season.

There was much to do here but that was the point. You hung out on the beach, read a book, went snorkeling, went back to the beach, drank beers at the one beach bar on the island, rotated meals between the five restaurants there, and went to bed early.

It was paradise – and a place a lot of people got stuck. Days easily turned into weeks here.

If you asked me what the highlight of all my travels was, I would be the time I spent on Ko Lipe. I made incredible friends, lounged around, got to know the locals, learned a bit of Thai, and, overall, lived that idyllic backpacker life we all dream about.

Over the years, I’ve avoided going back to Ko Lipe because the memory of my time there is so strong that I didn’t want to ruin it. Any re-visit would simply be trying to recreated a magic that couldn’t be recreated because the people that it special wouldn’t be there. I’d be chasing travel ghosts. And, since I know my sleepy paradise has been developed greatly over the years, I was also too afraid seeing that would make me sad.

Tourism in Thailand tends toward the unsustainable. No island really develops in a good way. It’s all build, build, build.

And I didn’t want to see my Ko Lipe like that.

But as I was planning my recent trip through Southeast Asia, returning to Ko Lipe made sense. I was heading down the Indian Ocean side of Thailand on my way into Malaysia and I’d pass by it.

And, since I was looking for a lively place for New Year’s Eve, it seemed liked the best choice. I knew there would be travelers there and there were no other nearby islands that would work, especially since Ko Lipe has a boat to Langkawi, which was my next stop.

And I’m sad to report that Ko Lipe took the Ko Phi Phi model of tourism and is now extremely overdeveloped.

Most of the island is now paved over, the old dirt footpaths having become concrete for the cars and construction trucks. Swaths of palm trees are now the sites of high-end resorts with pools (on an island with no natural water supply). Construction of more resorts continues at a fast pace. The coral around the island is dying, a victim of all the boats, anchors, pollution, and overfishing. Beaches are now lined with boats, their exhaust spilling into the ocean, leaving a shiny film you can see as you swim. And the restaurants cater to tourists looking for bad Western food, not great Thai cuisine.

The island’s boom has displaced many locals, who were forced to sell to mainland developers, and much of the island’s workforce is now from the mainland. They see little of the benefits this tourism boom.

So lies Ko Lipe, another victim of Thailand’s all too common overdevelopment and exploitation of limited resources.

I met lots of people there who loved the island. If it’s your first time, I can see why you would love it. After all, the area is postcard perfect, the water is perfectly an azure blue, the sand is a beautiful white, and since you’re surrounded by a national park, a lot of tours take you to some secluded islands.

And, in comparison to Ko Phi Phi, Krabi, or Phuket, it is less developed so I can’t fault someone stepping here for the first time going “wow!”

But, as I reflect on the island and its overdevelopment, I have come to the same conclusion I have about Ko Phi Phi: people shouldn’t visit.

I’m not against growth, but I’m against this kind of growth. It’s not sustainably managed and going there will only tax the island’s limited resources even further. You can’t put the genie back in the bottle and no local is going to say “sure, I’ll stay broke so you can an idealized vision of the world.”

And, with so many other islands to visit that are well managed (Ko Lanta, Ko Jum, and Ko Mook, to name three nearby), I think you should skip Ko Lipe.

A visit there will only make things worse.

It pains me to say that, because it was such a beautiful place, and my original visit had a huge impact on my life. But if we’re going to be good stewards and travelers, sometimes you just have to say enough is enough.

And Ko Lipe is a place where enough is enough.

Go somewhere else that is better managed.

Riding elephants in Thailand went away when consumers became more conscious of it. Eco lodges got big because of consumers. Overtourism is talked about by consumers as much as it is by locals.

Maybe if enough people start to do something, Ko Lipe will change.

But, at the very least, by not going you are at least no contributing to the problem.

#6252. How to Decide Which Ski Pass Is Best For Your Winter Travel Plans

With snow already falling in the Rockies and a strong El Niño weather pattern expected to benefit certain US mountain regions, skiers and riders are already dusting off their gear and booking their winter trips.

Of course, skiing and snowboarding aren’t typically budget-friendly sports. Once you factor in meals, lodging, and transportation in addition to a lift ticket (which costs well over $300 per day at several US resorts), it’s almost worth taking out a loan to pay for a one-week family ski trip.

But in recent years, the industry has moved away from one-day lift tickets in favor of multi-mountain ski passes with heavily discounted rates and additional perks, like Epic’s “Pay Over Time” or Ikon’s deals on friends and family tickets.

The dreamy Big Bear Resort is included on Ikon Pass.

"For those who ski or ride more than six to eight days a season, multi-mountain passes have reshaped the [ski] resort industry,” says Olivia Rowan, publisher of trade magazine Ski Area Management. “The multi-mountain pass opened up new possibilities for snow sports travel and tourism beyond your home hill. They're a great deal for an in-the-know skier or rider.”

Before choosing a pass, determine your skiing goals for the season. If you’re looking to check out a handful of new resorts for a day or two each, the Indy Pass might be your best option. But if you’re hoping to spend a week at a more popular resort like Park City, the Epic or Ikon passes are the way to go. To figure out which pass is best for you and your travel plans, here's a breakdown of the major players.

Best for: Individuals and families who want unlimited access to some of the world's largest and most popular ski areas

When the Vail-owned Epic Pass debuted in 2008, it was the first of its kind and set the stage for the multi-mountain passes that followed in the coming years. Today, it remains one of the biggest players in the industry, offering access to over 90 resorts in North America, Europe, Japan, and Australia.

Pricing: The standard Epic Pass, which offers unlimited access to all its resorts, costs $1,169. But if you don’t plan to ski during holiday weeks and weekends, consider the Epic Local Pass, which excludes peak dates at certain resorts. Epic also offers a customizable pass that lets skiers choose up to 7 days across different resort tiers. The cheapest option, at $337, gives skiers 7 days at 22 resorts in the Midwest, Northeast, and Mid-Atlantic.

Epic Pass offers access to over 90 resorts in North America, Europe, Japan, and Australia.

Vail, Colorado, one of the most popular mountains included with Epic Pass.

Traveler-approved ski resorts near Epic Pass mountains:

Best for: Skiers and riders who want to check out several uncrowded, under-the-radar ski resorts

The Indy Pass, which is the antithesis of larger passes like Epic and Ikon, offers two days of skiing at each of its over 300 partner resorts across four continents. The pass partners with smaller, independently owned resorts that are typically uncrowded and have deeply rooted local vibes. This season, Indy is rolling out an upgrade that lets passholders ski up to five days at 13 resorts, starting at $199. The pass sells out quickly and is already off sale for the 2026-27 ski season, but now is the time to get on the waiting list for next season (sales sometimes reopen mid-season, too).

Pricing: The Indy+ Pass, which doesn’t have blackout dates, costs $469 for adults and $299 for kids 12 and under.

Jay Peak mountain resort in Vermont, which saw record snowfall last winter.

Traveler-approved ski resorts near Indy Pass mountains:

Best for: Skiers who live near one of Ikon’s premier destinations, or families with children who want to take advantage of Ikon’s discounted kids passes

Like the Epic Pass, the Ikon Pass offers unlimited access to some of the world’s most popular ski resorts. The pass includes access to over 70 resorts across 13 countries, including some bigger US destinations like Jackson Hole, Deer Valley, and Aspen Snowmass.

Pricing: Like Epic, Ikon offers tiered passes, with its unlimited pass starting at $1,529 (or $1,129 for young adults ages 13-22 and $499 for children ages 5-12). The base pass, which has some blackout dates, starts at $1,099 for adults over 23. Skiers and riders who want to dip their toes into the sport or who may not have time to get out much during the season should consider a personalized pass that allows two, three, or four days at partner resorts.

Fresh powder at Big Bear Mountain Resort, a gem of a mountain on the Ikon Pass.

Traveler-approved ski resorts near Ikon Pass mountains:

Best for: East Coast skiers and riders who mostly plan on skiing in the Mid-Atlantic, Northeast, or eastern Canada, or individuals looking to supplement another multi-mountain pass; It includes two mountains in Colorado and Wyoming, but they are on the smaller side.

New for the 2026-27 ski season, the Snow Pass is the newest player in the game. Like Indy, the Snow Pass offers two days at each partner resort, but so far it has only 14 resorts to choose from, most of which are in the Northeast. You can buy additional days for 30% off the retail price. Snow Pass offers an alternate three-day pass—Snow Triple Play—that includes three days total at 23 partner resorts.

Pricing: The Snow Pass costs $379.99, and the Snow Triple Play costs $189.99.

Whiteface Mountain Ski Resort is a haven of varied terrain for skiers and snowboarders alike.

Traveler-approved ski resorts near Snow Pass mountains:

Best for: Skiers and riders who want to check some big-name resorts off their list but aren’t looking to ski for an extended period at one ski area, or those looking to supplement another multi-mountain or season pass.

The Mountain Collective Pass offers passholders two days each at its 27 resorts in the US, Canada, Japan, Europe, South America, Australia, and New Zealand. It’s a slightly more affordable alternative to the Epic and Ikon, yet it still gives skiers access to big-name resorts like Jackson Hole and Big Sky.

Pricing: The Mountain Collective Pass goes for $729 for adults, $594 for teens, and $304 for kids 6-12. Skiers and riders who want to ski more than their allotted 2 days at a specific resort can purchase day tickets at half off.

A sprawling mountain view at Jackson Hole, included on the Mountain Collective pass.

#6251. This week: Lame duck kicks off with Hegseth impeachment effort

Departing GOP Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky told CQ Roll Call in late October that the Hegseth impeachment resolution would come up in the first week of the post-election lame duck session. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call file photo) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

The lame-duck session of Congress kicks off this week as the House is expected to consider a resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth while the Senate seeks to advance a bipartisan deal on permitting reform.

Last week’s midterm elections saw Democrats claim sizable majorities in both the House and Senate in the new Congress, and among the immediate questions is whether the demoralized GOP will face attendance woes.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., the expected next speaker of the House, said Sunday that he would support the Hegseth impeachment.

“I'm a hard 'yes' on the Hegseth resolution,” Jeffries said on ABC’s “This Week.” “The so-called secretary of Defense has abused his power, undermined our national security and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran, which has skyrocketed prices on the American people and made the country less safe. Pete Hegseth has got to go.”

Departing Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., told CQ Roll Call in late October that the Hegseth impeachment resolution would come up in the first week of the post-election lame duck session.

It’s also orientation week on Capitol Hill for new members of Congress. House orientation got underway Sunday.

The Senate, meanwhile, looks to take up a bipartisan permitting bill that has the backing of President Donald Trump.

“This Landmark Permitting Reform Legislation will codify our America First Energy Agenda, and ensure that we can build Pipelines, Mines, and Power Plants faster than ever before, lowering Energy Costs for American Families, and creating High Paying American Jobs,” Trump posted on Truth Social.

Senate negotiators over the weekend released text of an amendment seeking to address remaining concerns.

“I’m grateful for the input throughout this process from Senate and House colleagues, environmental and labor organizations, and Tribal leaders. Our manager’s amendment improves [the bill] and addresses the thoughtful feedback we have received,” Senate Environment and Public Works ranking Democrat Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island said in a statement. “Now it’s time to pass this bill so we can lower costs, juice the clean energy economy, build big things again in America, reduce pollution, and create tons of new well-paying union jobs.”

Beyond the permitting bill, the Senate Republican majority may seek to use its remaining time trying to confirm more of Trump’s nominations before the control of the floor agenda passes to the Democrats.

"We've got the farm bill, the NDAA, and we have that third reconciliation bill that we need to get across the finish line, and there are so many things that we need to get done and buttoned up," including nominations, departing Sen. Marsha Blackburn, R-Tenn., said in a weekend Fox News interview. Blackburn, one of the Republicans who had success at the ballot box, is now governor-elect of Tennessee. But it's an open question how long lawmakers will want to stick around.

There’s also the matter of an imminent fight over funding the government and laying the groundwork for the new Congress. Republican leadership elections are scheduled for Tuesday, while Democratic leadership elections are expected in December. Democratic senators-elect are due on Capitol Hill Monday and Tuesday, according to the office of Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y. Schumer is widely expected to be the majority leader in 2027.

There have been some calls for Senate Republicans to delay their elections, though current Majority Leader John Thune of South Dakota has been widely expected to remain as the Republican leader.

“One of the things I learned in business and the Army is that after a failure, you have to start with honesty, transparency, and accountability,” Sen. Dave McCormick, R-Pa., said in a Sunday night statement. “As I’ve shared with Leader Thune, I don’t believe we should move to leadership elections until we have digested and debated the lessons of the midterms and how to move forward.”

Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., has also been circulating a letter calling for a delay, and he has argued the election should not be held, in part, because the makeup of the Senate Republican Conference is not yet final. Senate races are still not called in Alaska and Mississippi.

Absent this week will be Sen. Christopher S. Murphy, D-Conn., who recently had a stroke.

“The doctors are very encouraged by the progress I’ve made so far. In order to take my recovery seriously and get back to work on the quickest timeline possible, I will be spending several weeks at a rehabilitation center after being discharged from the hospital today,” Murphy said in a Friday statement.

#6249. ‘Political malpractice’: Calls grow to delay Senate GOP leadership elections

Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., walks through the Ohio Clock Corridor this summer. Now he’s pushing to delay leadership elections for his conference, urging a discussion of last week’s larger than expected losses. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

After last week’s midterm elections saw them lose at least seven Senate seats and the majority, some Republicans are pushing for a reckoning, saying the conference should stop and think about its future.

“After the stunning defeat [we] just can’t continue on business as usual. That kind of defeat demands change,” Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., said on Monday evening.

Asked if he himself would want to run for Senate minority leader, the Wisconsin Republican responded with a question of his own: “That’s part of our problem. Who’d want the job? Would you want it?”

Though no hopeful had emerged as of Monday afternoon — at least publicly — to challenge current Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., for the top GOP post, the frustration was palpable as Republican senators returned to D.C. and grappled with the election results. Calls grew throughout the day to delay the conference’s leadership elections planned for Tuesday morning.

“Well, I mean, I’m open to hearing what the arguments are for that,” Thune told reporters Monday when asked about the possibility of postponing the leadership votes. “I don’t know if that solves anything, but like I said, it’s going to be a decision that’s ultimately made by Republican senators. We’ll hear them out.”

Johnson told reporters on Monday that if the election is held, he would “leave the room” and walk out. Either way, he seemed certain to at least get a “fulsome” discussion of the topic, as he requested in a letter he sent to Republican Conference Chair Tom Cotton, R-Ark. Four other Republican senators signed on to the letter, hitting the threshold to call a conference meeting under internal GOP rules.

Also signed by Sens. Mike Lee of Utah, Ted Budd of North Carolina, Rick Scott of Florida, and John Kennedy of Louisiana, the letter obtained by CQ Roll Call cites last week’s “stunning defeat” and reads in part: “Holding leadership elections without engaging in a robust discussion and evaluation of how those running for leadership intend to lead would be political malpractice.”

Kennedy said Monday evening that he was asking to postpone the leadership elections because “we need time to talk to each other.”

“We’re like a shop owner who’s losing his customers. It’s not the customer’s job to fix that. It’s the shop owner’s job, and I’m not looking for blame-shifting. I’m looking for self-examination,” he said, adding that he wouldn’t consider running for minority leader himself.

In the letter, the group asked that at the time the leadership elections were set to begin, 9 a.m. on Tuesday, they instead “have a fulsome conference discussion and delay holding leadership elections until we all have a chance to hear from leadership candidates as to what type of collaborative conference governing model we should adopt and what our strategy will be to counter the emboldened Democrats.”

Thune echoed that wording Monday as he spoke to reporters, saying, “I do think that we need to have a very fulsome, robust conversation about where we go from here, and then we’ll see what the consensus of the conference is.”

But Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., who serves as chair of the Senate Republican Policy Committee, said she has seen such requests launched in the past and didn’t think it would do much to affect the ultimate outcome. “I think Sen. Thune will be reelected,” she said.

And several Senate GOP aides said that they suspected a “robust” conversation wouldn’t do much to delay the plans and that leadership elections were still expected to take place Tuesday. They noted similar efforts from some of those same senators in previous years to sow discord in the ranks.

That includes Scott, who unsuccessfully challenged Thune in 2024 and then-GOP leader Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., in 2022. But Scott told Fox News over the weekend, “I don’t want to run again. I’ve run twice.”

Republicans “failed. We had a horrible night,” Scott said. “Instead of having an [leadership] election, the first thing you do is you say, ‘OK, what are we going to change? We have to change something.’”

Lee floated the idea of waiting until after the uncalled Senate races in Mississippi and Alaska are officially resolved.

An online pressure campaign was building in some of the same MAGA corners of the internet that have pushed to pass a sweeping voter ID bill, known as the SAVE America Act, that has stalled in the Senate. On Monday morning, influencer Scott Presler in an X post urged constituents to call their senators while praising the lawmakers who have already pushed for the leadership elections to be postponed. “Where is everyone else?” he wrote.

Sens. Jim Banks of Indiana and Dave McCormick of Pennsylvania also called for a delay, though they did not appear on Johnson’s letter.

“A week ago, we had the worst election results in decades,” McCormick said in a post on X, calling Tuesday “too soon” to vote for leaders. “I know it’s been practice to go straight to leadership elections in recent years, but we should not rush it.”

Banks similarly said Tuesday was “too soon,” posting on social media, “Our conference needs to sit down and have a frank conversation about where we fell short, what we stand for, and what we’re going to do for the working families who sent us here.”

One senator speaking out in Thune’s defense was Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, who competed with Thune for the top spot in 2024 but on Monday said the leader isn’t to blame for the midterm results.

“I think the president needs to look in the mirror and look at the flawed candidates that he endorsed, and the kind of environment that we’re in,” said Cornyn, who is still smarting from losing his primary to a challenger backed by President Donald Trump.

Cornyn’s loss means he has no say in the coming conference leadership elections. But he said, “I think Thune’s a good man, and did as well as he could against a president and an environment that was pretty hostile.”

#6248. The Best Places to Go in Africa in 2027

While editing this year’s list, one thing quickly became very clear: 2027 is poised to be a banner one for cultural experiences across Africa. While chatting with our writers, I kept finding compelling reasons to go back to my favorite corners—the Kigali Triennale’s return to Rwanda in September, Jazzablanca’s 20th anniversary in Casablanca, and an even more vibrant creative landscape in Tunis than the one I reported on six years ago. But now I’m adding Benin to my list, thanks to four—yes, four—eagerly anticipated new museums debuting in the year ahead that will showcase everything from modern art to critical artifacts recently repatriated from Europe. Elsewhere on the continent there are fresh ways to experience some of its familiar pleasures, owing to a high-end resort boom on the beaches of Zanzibar, a host of safari lodge openings in Zambia, eight new marine reserves in São Tomé and Principe, and a groundbreaking five-country trans-frontier conservation area. Be sure to make some time for rarer incentives to travel too, like a once-in-a-generation “superbloom” in South Africa and the “eclipse of the century” over Luxor, Egypt (it also helps that there are some swish new places to stay at these places).But one of the most endearing stories of an African destination of the past year may be Cape Verde: Is the “World Cup effect” going to bring a wave of curious travelers to the archipelago? Read on to decide for yourself. —Sarah Khan

This is part of our global guide to the Best Places to Go in 2027—find more travel inspiration here.

Go for: a museum boom and a vibrant cultural milieu

Home to ancient Kingdom of Dahomey, Benin has transformed into a destination for heritage tourism.

Benin is a place where history runs deep: It’s home to the ancient Kingdom of Dahomey, the spiritual traditions of Vodun, and Ouidah—one of West Africa’s significant ports in the transatlantic slave trade. Now the country is turning that history into a new era of cultural tourism, while creating ways for travelers, particularly people of African descent, to reconnect with their heritage.

Ouidah, an especially important destination for those tracing their ancestry, is central to that effort. In 2025 the government announced plans to invest $1.4 billion in tourism and cultural development, including for infrastructure, heritage restitution, and indigenous traditions. In 2027 that transformation is expected to become more visible with a host of new museum openings, like the Museum of Modern Art in Cotonou; the International Museum of Memory and Slavery in Ouidah; and the Museum of the Epic of the Amazons and Kings of Dahomey in Abomey. The latter of which is expected to house 26 royal artifacts repatriated by France in 2021.

Vodun Days, an eight-day celebration of Benin’s indigenous spiritual traditions taking place January 2–9, 2027, will showcase ceremonies, music, and dance. Meanwhile, Villa Karo in Grand-Popo—a bridge between artists and researchers from Finland, Sweden, and West Africa—will continue its residency program, which brings artists to its seaside research center to connect with the local community through workshops, concerts, and exhibitions. The famous stilt village of Ganvié, meanwhile, remains open to visitors as its Reinventing the Lakeside City of Ganvié project upgrades tourism infrastructure. Benin is also beginning to make appearances on cruise itineraries. Two new Swan Hellenic sailings in 2027 sailings feature the country, including an April voyage from Luanda to Accra and an October sailing from Ghana to Angola. —Harriet Akinyi

Go for: beaches, festivals, and new-found buzz

New Cabo Verde Airlines flight routes launched in May 2026, and coupled with the “World Cup effect,” will make travel to Cape Verde more appealing than ever.

During FIFA World Cup 2026, one of the most impressive performances came from Cape Verde, an archipelago of 10 islands off Africa’s Atlantic Ocean coast. Now the “World Cup effect” has gotten travelers curious about what the destination has to offer. It helps that getting there is easier than ever, thanks to new direct flights launched in May 2026 from Rhode Island’s T.F. Green International Airport on Cabo Verde Airlines. On the island of Sal, which boasts white-sand beaches and over 350 days of sunshine a year, adrenaline-driving activities range from swimming with lemon sharks to kite- and windsurfing, while those seeking a more relaxed experience can float in the saline pools of Pedra de Lume. The island’s luxury accommodation options are also getting an upgrade with Hyatt Regency Cape Verde Sal as well as a family-friendly all-inclusive Bahia Principe set to open in 2027. In March the 322-room Robinson Boa Vista will welcome its first guests to the easternmost island of Boa Vista, known as the Sahara in the Atlantic due to its desert-like flat plains. São Vicente and Praia are the islands to hit for local music—the samba-inspired São Vicente Carnival features dance performances, fireworks, and floats, while Praia hosts the annual Kriol Jazz Festival and the Atlantic Music Expo. Africa’s first Four Points by Sheraton resort opened in the port city of São Vicente last March, with 105 rooms and 22 suites overlooking either Laginha Beach, known for its turquoise waters, or the Monte Verde mountains. —Mazuba Kapambwe

Go for: a vibrant cultural and design scene

Casablanca's 2027 roster of cultural events include the 20th anniversary of Jazzablanca in July and the newly launched Morocco Design fair.

Casablanca stealthily enters 2027 as Africa’s most creative urban reinvention. It’s an apt year to visit, given the pioneering Royal Air Maroc flights, launched in June 2026, linking Casablanca with Los Angeles—the first African connection to America's Pacific Coast. It is a poetic bridge, connecting the dream factory that conjured Casablanca’s mythic character with the modern metropolis redefining itself as a vanguard of contemporary Maghrebi culture. A cornerstone of this cultural renaissance is the 20th anniversary of Jazzablanca in July: Once an intimate gathering, it has evolved into North Africa's best boutique music festival, hosting emerging Afrobeat, jazz, and urban artists beneath the modernist skyscrapers in Anfa Park and on stages in the palm-lined Arab League Park beside the Nevada skate park. Design lovers, meanwhile, can admire the Museum of Photography and Visual Arts, which was inaugurated in June in the medina and is Tadao Ando’s sole architectural project on the continent. The museum and the recently launched annual Morocco Design fair, which spotlights high-end design studios, establish Casablanca as an emerging destination for cutting-edge design, music, and art. The city's heritage sites are getting a revamp too. The iconic 1916 Neo-Moorish Lincoln Hotel by Radisson Collection is being masterfully revived by French Moroccan architects OUALALOU + CHOI, who are pairing its historic façade with an über-minimalist interior. From the hotel’s doorstep, a new tramline whisks you to the Casablanca Finance City (CFC), a glittering new commercial district composed of futuristic, climate-resilient buildings that pay homage to Casablanca’s legacy of concrete experimentation. Nearby, bougie restaurants like Le 7ème Ciel draw crowds and a new Radisson Red will open in 2027 to join an existing Radisson Blu. CFC is built on the old Anfa Airport, from which The Little Prince author and architecture school dropout Antoine de Saint-Exupéry flew a perilous mail route to Dakar in an open-cockpit Bréguet 14 biplane, returned for drinks at Le Petit Poucet, and lived with his fiery Salvadorean muse, Consuelo Suncín. Then, as now, the city was a nexus connecting continents and a frontier to the future. —Paula Hardy

Go for: a ground-breaking cross-border safari project and birding adventure

The Kavango-Zambezi Transfrontier Conservation Area, or KAZA TFCA, is the world's largest terrestrial transboundary conservation area.

Zambia, which has forgone visa requirements of 53 countries and has increased international flights, will be the center of attention.

In a world where ecological degradation and global discord are reasons to despair, Kavango-Zambezi Transfrontier Conservation Area, or KAZA TFCA, is more rising sun than ray of hope. Supported by five countries—Angola, Botswana, Namibia, Zambia, and Zimbabwe, the world’s largest terrestrial transboundary conservation area encompasses a region roughly the size of France and is watered by the Kavango, Zambezi, Chobe, Kwando, and Kafue river systems. Officially launched in 2012, it languished as a plan on paper for years, but recent initiatives have seen it shake off bureaucratic paralysis: Green Growth for KAZA, the umbrella initiative, directly links community benefits to conservation. Several depleted parks have been rewilded; Africa’s first cross-border avitourism project, the Great Kavango Zambezi Birding Route, was recently launched; and connectivity improved—Shearzone Safari launched a charter service in Zambia in early 2026. Notably, Angola has entered the guided-safari arena with Luiana Plains Expedition Camp, the first to open in the 10.3-million-acre Luengue-Luiana National Park in July 2026. It will soon be followed by Natural Selection, which is developing a new 500,000-acre game reserve around Angola’s existing Cuatir Reserve. In Namibia’s unsung Zambezi Region, Thitake River Lodge opens on the banks of the Kwando in Bwabwara National Park late in 2026, while Nkasa Linyanti is the fabulous new linchpin in Nkasa Rupara National Park. But the KAZA TFCA region that’s experiencing the biggest proliferation is Zambia, buoyed by the scrapping of visa requirements of 53 countries and increased international flights. Ker & Downey launched its Zambia division with King Lewanika Lodge in remote Liuwa Plains National Park, the first luxury base from which to witness Africa’s second-largest wildebeest migration; its second location, Musesenji River Camp, opens in April 2027. And luring the well-heeled to 5.5-million-acre Kafue National Park are Anantara with Tented Camp Kafue River, and Classic Zambia with new Lwenge River Camp; both opened this summer. —Pippa de Bruyn

Go for: a wave of gallery and festival openings turning a gorilla trek stopover into an art capital

Kigali's art scene is ramping up as institutions like Kigali Triennial and Gihanga Institute of Contemporary Art platform Rwandan and East African artists.

New Kigali properties are showcases for art, such as the nine-room Pinnacle hotel and members' club.

For years Kigali has been seen as little more than a pit stop before going gorilla trekking. Now the city is making a compelling case for staying awhile. The city’s vibrant food and fashion have already been putting it on the map, and now the art scene is getting noticed as several institutions build platforms for championing Rwandan and East African artists. September 2027 marks the second edition of the Kigali Triennial, which is primed to rival some of the continent’s more established art festivals, like ART X Lagos and Dak'Art Biennale. The Gihanga Institute of Contemporary Art, which opened at the end of 2025, highlights artists from across Africa and its diasporas, with a focus on East Africa with two exhibitions: “Space Encounters,” exploring human connection and memory, which is currently on through December 2026; and a collection of contemporary work by Sudanese artists opening in January 2027. This follows the debut of the Inyuguti Art Hub this year, which brought together 19 artists from across Africa and the UK, including Rwandan Elisa Niyogisubizo (also the gallery’s founder), Burundi-based Peter Kamale, and Nigerian Pascal Ejiofor. The lines between the art and hotel scenes are beginning to blur too, with a new generation of properties doubling as cultural showcases. Among them is the nine-room Pinnacle hotel and members club that opened in early 2026 as Rwanda’s first women-led ultraluxury boutique property, showcasing the owner’s private art collection. Creative events are rippling beyond the capital, as Rwandan artists Willy Karekezi and Cedric Mizero are each launching new spaces in Musanze, the gateway town for gorilla trekking, in 2027: Karekezi will open a residency alongside his Indiba Arts Space in Kigali, and Mizero will open Umugenzi, an addition to the multisite Ikinyugunyugu art residency. —Vivienne Dovi

Go for: the eclipse of the century and nostalgia-soaked Nile cruises

Astrotourism is coming for Luxor and the Nile on August 2, 2027, thanks to the six-minute “eclipse of the century" and a wave of new boats promising prime viewing spots along the ancient waterway.

Dubbed the eclipse of the century, 2027’s much-anticipated celestial event will reach its zenith in Luxor, Egypt, on August 2, when the moon will block out the sun for a record-breaking 6 minutes and 23 seconds. Fitting, perhaps, for a place where the mystical has always loomed large, the mountains hold secret treasures, the temples and tombs have been perfectly preserved roughly 3,000 years after they were built, and the Nile exudes a life force of its own. Travelers have come to this transcendent stretch of Upper Egypt, nearly 400 miles south of Cairo, for millennia. Luxor itself served as Egypt’s capital from 1570 BCE to 1069 BCE, but today is better known as the home of the Valley of the Kings, and the start or end point of nostalgia-infused Nile cruises to and from Aswan, a leisurely four- or five-day sail away. Both destinations are primed for a momentous 2027: In Luxor the much-loved Winter Palace—archaeologist Howard Carter’s base during his 1922 Tutankhamen tomb discovery—will reopen in July as a Mandarin Oriental after an extensive renovation exactly 120 years after its official inauguration. Aswan’s own grande dame, the Old Cataract, which famously inspired Agatha Christie’s best-selling novel Death on the Nile, has also been taken over by Mandarin Oriental and will reopen its Nile Wing in 2027 after a thorough upgrade. Mandarin Oriental will launch its first Nile cruise that connects the two, joining a flurry of other new boats taking to the ancient waterway. Among them the Oberoi Melouk and the Oberoi Malekat dahabiyas, with only seven cabins apiece, and homegrown operator Kemetale’s second boat, Deshret, with its Nile-view sauna, plunge pool, and spa treatments. —Selina Denman

Go for: a rare ‘superbloom’ of endemic flora and world-class wines at Africa’s southern tip.

Cape Agulhas, Africa's southernmost tip, offers a new interpretation center focused on the history and geology of Agulhas, as well as a 177-year-old lighthouse.

Chef Michael Broughton, formerly of Terroir in Stellenbosch, now leads the kitchen at historic Fisherman’s Cottage, putting seafood centerstage.

Cape Town. Winelands. Then head off on safari. That’s the typical circuit for travelers jetting into South Africa. But in 2027 look beyond to the Overberg—“over mountain” in Afrikaans—region, where wildfires have triggered a floral extravaganza not seen in decades. Base yourself in Hermanus for memorable whale watching from the seven-and-a-half-mile Cliff Path. The Marine Hotel, a seafront landmark since 1902, has unveiled a fynbos-inspired revamp of its public spaces and seafood-driven Pavilion Restaurant. There’s a new culinary energy in town too: Chef Michael Broughton, previously at Terroir in Stellenbosch, has turned the historic Fisherman’s Cottage into a hotbed of polished Cape coastal cuisine (don’t miss the spaghetti aglio e olio with local rock lobster). Broughton’s wine list leans into estates from the nearby Hemel-en-Aarde (Heaven and Earth) valley, where cellars are known for exceptional Pinot Noir and Chardonnay. Creation Wines offers a new sculpture-led vineyard walk, and opens a private tasting room in May 2027 aimed at wine lovers looking for a deep dive into the cool-climate terroir. Bouchard Finlayson, one of the oldest estates in the valley, reopens in late 2027 after an extensive renovation, with a new tasting space and art collection.

Set in the heart of the Cape Floristic Region, Grootbos Private Nature Reserve is a biodiversity hot spot. Wildfires that swept the area in 2025 sparked a superbloom of new growth, including dormant species that haven’t flowered in decades like wild orchids and the fire-dependent Gladiolus overbergensis. Guided botanical walks and drives get you in the thick of the fynbos, but a new equestrian center also makes this a great choice for horse-riding holidays. Long popular with families, Coot Club, on the nearby Klein River Lagoon, expands in 2027 with a pair of new two-bedroom boathouses and brings a new wellness focus with outdoor yoga sessions and in-room wellness treatments. Toast it all with a sundowner in the refreshed Flamingo Bar upstairs in the original homestead. An hour’s drive east, Cape Agulhas, the southernmost tip of Africa, is a fitting finale. A new interpretation center delves into the history and geology of Agulhas, after which you can climb the 177-year-old lighthouse and stand on the rocky shoreline where the Indian and Atlantic Oceans meet. —Richard Holmes

Go for: new marine reserves and World Heritage Sites

Often known as the African Galapagos for its high concentration of endemic species, the island nation of São Tomé and Principe is surrounded by clear waters full of manta rays, sharks, and migrating humpback whales.

On the islands of São Tomé and Príncipe, more than 155 miles off the coast of Gabon in the Gulf of Guinea, a thick rainforest punctuated by needle-like rock formations meets shores of white and volcanic black sand. One of the world’s least visited countries, and known as the African Galapagos for its high concentration of endemic species, this island nation is surrounded by clear turquoise waters brimming with manta rays and reef and nurse sharks. Humpback whales migrate through seasonally, and turtles begin to nest on the beaches in November before hatching between February and April. In 2025 the first two of eight new dedicated marine reserves, Santana and Ilhéu das Rolas, were approved; in 2026, six roças, or former Portuguese plantations, were designated UNESCO World Heritage Sites, recognized for their role in shaping the social, economic, and cultural history of the nation, which was once the world’s preeminent supplier of cacao. Two of these roças are a part of the Príncipe Collection—the hospitality arm of sustainable development group HBD Príncipe—meaning you can stay at these historically significant sites. One of the properties on offer is Hotel Belo Monte, which opened in June and sits high up on a hillside overlooking the rainforest and sea. A stay in this eco-hideaway, chicly styled with splashes of bold color, comes with cultural insight and an immersion into the wild surroundings. Another outpost, Sundy Praia, is set within what was once part of Príncipe’s second-largest cocoa plantation on the remote northwest tip and hosts guests in tented villas backing the golden shores on the remote northwest tip of the island. —Lauren Burris Hill

Go for: ancient treasures and contemporary culture by the sea

Villa Kahina, an intimate guesthouse that opened in September in Tunis.

In the blue and white village of Sidi Bou Saïd, the six-room Villa Kahina offers views of the Mediterranean.

Designated 2027’s Arab Capital of Tourism, this languid North African city now pulses with the energy of a new generation of Tunisian creatives and entrepreneurs. Events planned in the historic Medina range from TedX Pasha Street talks and musical retreats to artisanal workshops, many organized by the beloved Dar Ben Gacem boutique hotel and cultural hub, which will also host a rooftop event for August’s solar eclipse. Across the Medina, near the Great Mosque of Zitouna, Dar Ben Turkia's early 2026 opening expands the luxury-hotel options that preserve the area’s history. The elegant eight-suite hideaway has an in-house hammam and spa, so it doubles as a wellness retreat in the heart of the Medina. Beyond the medieval city’s labyrinths, the sun-kissed ruins of ancient Carthage spill toward the coast. Anchoring these archaeological riches is the Carthage National Museum, slated to reopen by year-end after an eight-year overhaul. For more contemporary treasures, head downhill to the city’s leading art gallery, Selma Feriani, which in 2027 will exhibit major Tunisian artists Mohamed Amine Hamouda and Rafik El Kamel.

Nearby, sleek seaside city La Marsa gives way to the historically working-class neighborhood of Bhar Lazreg, where artists and makers have been repurposing spaces. Anchors like the B7L9 Art Centre (built by and for the area’s community), and Phosphor Creative District—showcasing local talent who specialize in everything from fine art to design—are transforming the area into a meeting place for artists, demonstrating why the neighborhood has become known as one of Tunis’s coolest. Meanwhile, fashionable La Marsa remains a firm favorite with the stylish set, and mid-2026 restaurant openings like Oto, a Japanese izakaya, and Sujet, a hybrid café and design store, keep things fresh. When you’re ready for a break, make your way up the coast to Birdie at The Clubhouse in Gammarth, which opened in August 2026, or south to Villa Kahina, an intimate guesthouse that began welcoming guests in September. Perched on the forested edge of the iconic blue and white village of Sidi Bou Saïd, this whitewashed six-room sanctuary with sweeping Mediterranean views feels almost untouched by time. —Lee Middleton

Go for: a host of new hotels from which to experience some of Africa’s best beaches

Beyond its beaches, Zanzibar is set to welcome two new luxury properties: Anantara Zanzibar Resort and Residences in 2027, followed by Four Seasons Resort Zanzibar at Pongwe in 2028.

Most visitors arrive in Zanzibar with postcard perfection already in mind—turquoise shallows, swaying palms, and dhows tipping into the sunset—but the island’s enduring drawcard is still Stone Town: a UNESCO-listed tangle of coral-rag limestone alleys, carved Omani doors, and clove-scented air, where Africa, Arabia, and India have intersected for centuries. In 2027 Zanzibar gets its most serious branded hotel wave yet with the 181-key Anantara Zanzibar Resort & Residences on the north coast, and in 2028 it will welcome, the 60-villa Four Seasons Resort Zanzibar at Pongwe, widely regarded as the loveliest beach on the east coast. The latter is a short flight from the brand’s Serengeti lodge and has been built with a bush-and-beach pairing in mind. The freshest energy is homegrown, though, and it has moved away from the overdeveloped north. In Jambiani, on the sunrise-facing southeast coast, the seven-villa Ma’a Salama (“go in peace”) opened in mid-2026 as a nonprofit that doubles as a hospitality school, training island youth in exchange for a year’s free education. Ma’a Salama’s spacious villas are named for spices and are cooled by bioclimatic design rather than air-conditioning, and four are crowned with rooftop teahouses, designed in Stone Town’s famous Emerson’s teahouses. On the quiet southwest coast at Kizimkazi, Kizikula is the antithesis of a resort: no sign, no jetty, just a jungly pathway leading to what feels more like a private home or artist’s enclave than a hotel. At low tide, guests access the beach through a secret gap in the coral cliff. Designed by Mumbai’s Case Design, its coral-limestone rooms sit in wild permaculture gardens. In 2026 the resort added 19 rooms, and in December it will open a new rooftop sunset bar and a three-floor wellness center, where treatments incorporate ingredients like Zanzibari cinnamon, turmeric, and cardamom. As of October 2026 Airlink flies the first-ever nonstop route between Cape Town and Zanzibar, with low-cost FlySafair rumored to be expanding its regular Johannesburg service to include Cape Town too. The UK gets its own first direct link in November 2027, courtesy of TUI Airways’s Gatwick service, along with a direct London flight from Air Tanzania. —Jane Broughton

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6247. Why This Company is One of the Best for Finding Work

Most travel is extractive and passive. You show up somewhere, take photos of the same landmarks everyone else takes photos of, eat at a restaurant the guidebook recommended, and hit up some bars. You take some tours to learn about the place and, if you’re lucky, get to meet some locals on your trip. You don’t really go deep.

Even long-term travelers who talk about how they “aren’t tourists” do the same – just at a slower pace and while trying to spend less money.

And there’s nothing wrong with that. That’s just the nature of travel. While we all imagine dropping into a place, befriending locals, and having this crazy time like we’re in some movies. But that doesn’t happen. Because we’re just passing through and, for the most part, locals don’t want to become friends with tourists. In fact, most locals don’t interact with tourists. (I mean it does happen but it’s not the norm.)

If you really want a deep travel experience, you need to stay. If you want to understand a place, you need to stay. The most transformative travel experiences I’ve ever had involved contributing something and staying somewhere long enough to build real relationships. It was being embedded in a place rather than just passing through.

I think that more travelers should give back when they travel. In the old days, it was hard to find out what organizations and opportunities were legit, vetted, and actually made the lives of locals better.

Now, there’s a ton of companies that can help you not only find meaningful volunteer jobs when you travel but also paid jobs when you travel and one of the best ones is Global Work & Travel. Use code NOMADICMATT to unlock a discount on your next trip.

Global Work & Travel is the world’s largest gap year company and has been placing people on working holidays, volunteer programs, teaching positions, internships, and more for nearly 2 decades. They’ve helped over 116,000 people and they cover destinations across, the UK and Europe, the Americas, Asia, Africa, and the Pacific.

Even for experienced travelers, moving abroad can be difficult. Finding employment as a traveler, securing permanent accommodation or getting stuck in shared rooms for months on end, transport costs in a new city, interview after interview competing against locals… This is just the beginning of what long term travelers need to consider.

Fortunately, companies like Global Work & Travel provide the scaffolding or safety net that makes working abroad possible for people who don’t want to figure everything out themselves. They handle job matching, pre-departure support, visa guidance, placement, and ongoing assistance through their gWorld portal, a personal trip management app that keeps everything organized in one place. For first-timers especially, having that support structure can be the difference between actually going and endlessly deliberating. The programs they offer span a wide range:

For the past decade, “digital nomad” has been the aspirational version of long term travel. Work remotely, earn in a strong currency, live somewhere cheaper, repeat.

But that model only really works for a small subset of people. You need a remote job, a certain income level, and often a level of career stability that most younger travelers simply don’t have yet.

Instead of bringing a job with you, you get one when you arrive. You integrate into the local economy instead of floating above it. You meet people through work, not just coworking spaces or short-term hostels. And you build a life somewhere, not just a temporary routine.

In a lot of ways, working holiday makers are having a more grounded and accessible version of what people think digital nomad life is. You’re not just passing through, you’re actually living there. You have coworkers, a schedule, a reason to stay longer than a week, and a chance to build real lifetime connections.

It’s also far more realistic for most people. You don’t need a remote business or years of experience. You just need the willingness to go and the right setup to make it happen.

That’s why I think we’re seeing a shift. Less “how do I work remotely?” and more “how do I actually live and work abroad for a year?”

And that’s exactly where structured programs like Global Work & Travel come in. They remove the biggest barriers, finding a job, navigating visas, getting set up, so people can actually make that shift from idea to reality.

For a lot of travelers, this isn’t just an alternative to digital nomad life. It’s a more sustainable, accessible, and realistic way to actually live and work abroad.

Volunteering abroad has a complicated reputation, and it’s worth being honest about that. There are lots of bad volunteer programs out there in the world. Programs that don’t really give back and are designed to make travelers “feel” like they did something but really are just profit driven campaigns. Global Work & Travel’s vets programs in the areas such as wildlife conservation, community development, education, and healthcare in the locations and countries it operates so you know the program you sign up for is legit.

The case for ethical, well-structured volunteering is genuinely strong. When you work alongside local Zanzibar communities on problems they’ve defined as priorities, or with wildlife and conservation in South Africa or Elephant rehabilitation in Thailand — something shifts in how you understand the world. Not only are you helping to give back to a place but you also understand the true needs of a the people and ecosystems living there, but also helping overcome the struggles they go through. It opens your mind and shifts your perspective.

Their Global Animal Welfare Fund also channels resources directly into conservation projects at their partner sites, so the impact extends beyond individual placements.

Working holidays let you truly experience a country instead of just visiting it. You immerse yourself in the culture by living like a local every day. You meet more people both locals and fellow travellers while building real friendships. Best of all, you get paid to travel, so you can stay much longer instead of rushing through in a few weeks. This lets you experience local life deeply, discover hidden spots, and understand how people really live in different places. You also build valuable skills, boost your resume with international experience, and make long-term travel more affordable since your income covers the costs. Plus, you gain a real cultural understanding that no short holiday can match. All that while stil getting paid? Not bad right?!

Working holidays turn travel into a true lifestyle, not just another 2 week vacation.

Global Work & Travel are the world leaders in long term travel and offer a ton of options for travelers looking to volunteer, work, or spend extended time in a destination. Some things I like about them.

Do I need prior experience to work abroad with Global Work & Travel? For most trips, generally nothing more than basic work experience is required. Teaching programs include TEFL training, and volunteering can be started from no experience.

What’s the minimum age? Most programs are open from age 18. Working holiday visas typically cap at 35 depending on the destination country but volunteer and teach programs are open to ages 18–80.

How long does the whole process take? It varies by programs and destination. Most people book their trips 6-12 months in advance for proper planning, job matching and visa quotas. You can get started for as little as $1 here.

Is my money safe if things change? Global Work & Travel and their lifetime deposit policy means your initial payment doesn’t expire. They are also members of many consumer protection services to further support travelers.

Can I go as a solo traveler? Yes, and this is actually one of the most common scenarios. The gWorld Community and programs group connections mean you’ll be meeting others in the same position quickly.

Travel has always been best when it’s been more than tourism. The moments that stay with you — that you actually tell people about five years later — are never the ones where you queued to see a famous landmark. They’re the ones where you connect with people. They are the moments where you did something.

Global Work & Travel makes doing something deep accessible in a way that genuinely wasn’t available a decade ago. If you’ve been thinking about doing something like this but the logistics have felt too complicated, check them out and use code NOMADICMATT to unlock a $100 discount on your trip.
